title: Four years ago countries made a historic deal to save nature. Is it dead in the water? | Cop17 biodiversity summit | The Guardian
description: So far not a single target of the plan has been met. As negotiators convene for Cop17, the pressure is on to find a way to honour the commitments made at previous summits
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: So far not a single target of the plan has been met. As negotiators convene for Cop17, the pressure is on to find a way to honour the commitments made at previous summits
Content: Dead fish in the River Wensum in Norwich, Norfolk, believed to be due to pollution levels rising after rain.Photograph: Norwich Green PartyView image in fullscreenDead fish in the River Wensum in Norwich, Norfolk, believed to be due to pollution levels rising after rain.Photograph: Norwich Green PartyThe age of extinctionCop17 biodiversity summitFour years ago countries made a historic deal to save nature. Is it dead in the water?So far not a single target of the plan has been met. As negotiators convene for Cop17, the pressure is on to find a way to honour the commitments made at previous summitsCop17 at a glance: everything you need to know about the UN’s nature summitSupported byAbout this contentPatrick GreenfieldMon 19 Oct 2026 06.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePassersby could smell the dead fish before they saw them. In August, more than 3,000 pike, roach, carp and rudd were found lifeless along the River Wensum in Norwich. Some gasped for air in their final moments, desperate for the oxygen that heatwave conditions had depleted in the water. Investigators believe that the die-off was triggered by heavy rainfall that flushed through high concentrations of pollution at a time when wildlife were already struggling.The 45-mile (70km) chalk river is one of about 250 in the country. They are a geological accident almost unique to Britain – and one of Earth’s rarest habitats. They emerge from chalk aquifers and are home to species such as freshwater shrimp, otters and stoneflies, also providing drinking water for millions of people. But just 11 have formal protection, with many ravaged by sewage pollution and overextraction. TheNorfolkriver is one of the few that does have legal protection, but it is in poor ecological health.“We are a world away from the crystal clear, free flowing and mineral-rich waters they could, and should be,” says Eliot Lyne, head of the NorfolkWildlifeTrust.This decade was meant to signal a change in humanity’s relationship with the natural world. At the end of 2022, nearly every government on Earthcommitted to an ambitious dealto better protect the world’s rapidly disappearing biodiversity at a summit in Montreal, Canada.Negotiators shook hands on targetsthat included protecting 30% of the planet for nature, restoring nearly a third of the planet’s most degraded ecosystems, and reforming at least $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally harmful subsidies.Some scientists say that we are living through the largest loss of life since the time of the dinosaurs, putting a million species at risk of extinction. This time, humanity is the meteor. The Montreal agreement was the response.View image in fullscreenThe leadership of the COP15 biodiversity conference celebrates passing the deal setting this decade’s global targets in Montreal, Canada, December 2022.Photograph: IISDBut four years later, governments look almost certain tomiss nearly all of the deal’s targets– potentially continuing the record of never having met a single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992. The UK, one of the loudest voices demanding ambition in Montreal, is on track to meetjust three ofthe 23 targets by the end of the decade. This week, countries gather at Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, to decide what to do next.On the eve of the summit, at the launch of a report showing just how far off track the world is on meeting those commitments, António Guterres, secretary general of the UN, warned that lack of progress means “the war on nature has not ended” and that “nature will not survive on good intentions”. Following this, in an address to leaders at an event inArmenia, Guterres once again emphasised the importance of action on subsidies in particular. “Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said.“They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”“There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, former UK government minister when the deal was reached. “That’s where we are today.”British conservationists point to a growing gap between government rhetoric and action. “The UK is back on the international stage on nature,” then environment secretary Steve Reed declared while standing under the skeleton of a blue whale at the Natural History Museum in the first few months of the Starmer government. Since then, the government hasweakened ruleson biodiversity net gain in England,slashed tens of millions of pounds of fundingfor rainforest protection schemes as part of aid cuts, andrejected an outright ban on bottom trawlingin marine protected areas. No new sites of special scientific interest have been designated by Natural England to protect rare wildlife and habitats since 2023.View image in fullscreenYereven, Armenia, where countries will gather to review progress on nature goals, at Cop17 this month.Photograph: Cop17 Yereven“For us to go around the world telling other countries that they must achieve these targets without us having a plan how to deliver them at home is a form of neocolonialism,” says Craig Bennett, head of The Wildlife Trusts. “We’ve got to pull our socks up and get serious about delivery at home. We are the nation of Sir David Attenborough. We are animal and nature lovers.”A UK government spokesperson said it has backed a nature recovery and climate resilience with £7bn of funding, and implemented new powers to tackle water pollution, fund species recovery and support international conservation work.The UK has also reinstated its climate aid commitments, apparentlyabandoned earlier this year, pledging around £6bn of international climate finance from the aid budget over the next three financial years, with around a quarter expected to be spent on nature.Jonathan Hall, managing director ofConservationInternational UK, told the Guardian: “Re-instating the ditched goal for international nature funding as part of UK climate aid is smart politics, given UK public support, and a smart investment in our global security and resilience in the face of ecosystem collapse. This very welcome re-commitment now needs to be accompanied with increased transparency so we can ensure this approximately £1.5bn is disbursed as impactfully as possible.”But the urgency of the warnings has not changed. Earlier this year, a report by intelligence chiefswarned that ecological collapse is a national security risk, threatening the country with food shortages, economic strife and global disorder. But nature has been unable to escape the swirling global current ofpopulist culture wars.In the Netherlands, efforts by the EU, in 2019, to crack down on nitrogen pollution to protect vulnerable ecosystems sparkednationwide farmer protests. While the discontent predates this decade’s biodiversity targets, thenature restoration law, the EU’s flagship package of laws resulting from the deal, also became embroiled in a bitter disagreement with the rightwing bloc in the European parliament, who tried to block the regulations due to the impact on agriculture. It was eventually passed, but only after it wassubstantially watered down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFarmers protest against an EU crackdown on nitrogen pollution in The Hague, the Netherlands, October 2019.Photograph: Vincent Jannink/EPA“In the Netherlands, they tried really hard and you saw this huge backlash. It’s an extremely sensitive issue politically,” says Steven Guilbeault, Canada’s former environment minister, who helped guide the 2022 negotiations alongside China’s environment minister, Huang Runqiu. “Governments are not always the best at communicating these complex policy pieces. It is easy for a critic to come up with a totally meaningless slogan that gets picked up on social media,” he says.The second presidency of Donald Trump has also been catastrophic for the conservation sector. Hundreds of projects had previously received support from Washington DC – from stopping illegal fishing in the Galápagos islands to backing the restoration of Gorongosa national park in Mozambique after the civil war – but Trump’s brutal cuts to USAID and other government agencies have meantfunding evaporated overnightfor many schemes.View image in fullscreenUSAID-supported Ugandan wildlife crime investigators at work in 2016.Photograph: Ashley Netherton/USAIDMany European nations have followed suit – despite signing up to a target to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade. The UK has cut backfunding for the Darwin Initiative, removing eligibility for at least 89 countries earlier this year. Efforts to get the private sector to help have struggled; a new fund to get companies that use digital forms of biodiversity for commercial discoveries, which proponents had hoped would raise hundreds of millions each year, has so far raised just $6,000.It is not a universally gloomy picture. A majority of countries have responded to significant parts of the agreement.One estimateshows that countries could come close to meeting the land portion of the 30x30 target, and the deal has seen the formalisation of more Indigenous territories in many countries.Even bigger protected areas could come: places such asFrench Polynesia have established hugenew marine parks. Countries such as Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort,bringing back the Caspian tiger. But the gap between what the science demands to avert ecological crisis and the current pace of change remains huge – and an urgent task for negotiators in Armenia.View image in fullscreenA tiger is released into Kazakhstan’s wilderness as part of a repopulation programme.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“Protection targets are falling short, promised national plans have yet to materialise, and committed finance is not reaching where it is needed. This is increasingly a shared dynamic across environmental processes: making commitments is the easy part; delivering on them is much harder,” said Li Shuo, director of China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.“Sustainable change will only happen when countries internalise the urgency to act and translate commitments into domestic action. More than halfway through this decade, most countries are still moving far too slowly.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldon the app for all the latest news and features.The Guardian’sclimate forum 2026On Tuesday, October 20, join Zoe Williams, and our panel of experts—including Professor Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening.Book ticketshereor atguardian.liveExplore more on these topicsCop17 biodiversity summitThe age of extinctionConservationBiodiversityWildlifeWaterRiversEndangered habitatsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace | The Guardian
description: While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it
Author: John Crace
Headline: While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it
Content: Matt Goodwin wanted Times Radio listeners to believe that Nigel Farage was actually a buffer against racism in Reform.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMatt Goodwin wanted Times Radio listeners to believe that Nigel Farage was actually a buffer against racism in Reform.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianThe politics sketchReform UKITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad applesJohn CraceWhile the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend itMon 19 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTShareIt was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITVexposé of widespread racism and misogynywithin Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing fromNigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’sfailed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelectionwhose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen JonesRead moreOver in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trumpswitching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims thatNato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review – sublime wonders from the Great Wave to that heroic, eternal peak | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduring
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduring
Content: Mount Fuji is the truth … Under the Wave off Kanagawa, 1830-1833, AKA The Great Wave.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection, on deposit at The National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo. Photo by Norihiro UenoView image in fullscreenMount Fuji is the truth … Under the Wave off Kanagawa, 1830-1833, AKA The Great Wave.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection, on deposit at The National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo. Photo by Norihiro UenoArt and designReviewHokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review – sublime wonders from the Great Wave to that heroic, eternal peakDulwich Picture Gallery, LondonWith its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduringJonathan JonesMon 19 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe giant wave’s foaming white summit spreads high over the heads of the helpless souls huddled in their long thin boats, crackling into what look like many sharp claws. It is a monster, hungry to swallow human flesh. But beyond it, over the wild water, soothing the terror of those in peril on the sea, is Mount Fuji – a solid cone of hope and solace. The mountain, not the wave, is the hero of this masterpiece, as it is the hero of all the prints in Dulwich Picture Gallery’s stunning exhibition – the first in Britain – of the complete Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.When you look closely here at three different, superb impressions of Katsushika Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa – widely known today as the Great Wave – your mental picture of this icon is shattered by the violent onrush of water. In reproductions the wave just seems beautiful, an elegant curl of blue and white. But here, to paraphrase Tennyson, it is nature, blue in tooth and claw. The wretched people are the emotional heart of the picture, their imminent risk of drowning its whole point.double quotation markHokusai delights in epic shifts of perspectiveThe wave is out of control, murderous, yet it is also a passing moment, shows Hokusai, a devout Buddhist. He offers this consolation: the wave looks as vast as a mountain but soon it will break and be gone. Meanwhile the sacred peak of Mount Fuji endures eternally. It can’t be hurt by the ephemeral dragon of saltwater. Put your faith in the essential, enduring things beyond the nightmare of mutable appearances and you will find inner peace. The wave is an illusion. Mount Fuji is the truth.View image in fullscreenEjiri in Suruga Province, 1830-1833, Katsushika Hokusai.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection. Photo by Norihiro UenoYet that colossal truth is easy to forget as we move around it, pass it by, catch sight of it in the everyday rush – a distant peak on the horizon. On a city bridge people swarm without looking up from under their round hats at the mountain in the distance. A man working bare-chested, wiry and worn, has no time to study the far-off peak as he concentrates on making a barrel.Hokusai delights in epic shifts of perspective, seeing Mount Fuji as an apparently small insignificant object while filling the foreground with distracting action. You do a double take at Fuji from Kanaya on the Tōkaidō Highway. Dressed people sit on the shoulders of nude men who are almost completely submerged in turbulent blue and white water, while others are sealed inside boxlike palanquins to be carried too over the water by crushed bearers gasping for air. It is no illusion. This crossing point over the Ōi River was a key military point for the city of Edo, so no bridges were allowed to be built there. Travellers had to be borne across.No one in this strange scene looks at Mount Fuji. And yet not to notice the mountain is to miss out on something very big indeed. In another image a ferryman does pay attention to it, set against a golden evening sky under a layer of deep blue, as he rows people across another river: some passengers also look, while others do not. Other people – tourists as well as pilgrims – seek out the views, like Hokusai himself, delighting in nature and its mystery, even in extreme conditions: one group has trekked to a country teahouse in winter to view Mount Fuji in the snow. They’re rewarded with an icy scene of devastating beauty, picked out in golden white and intense deep blue.View image in fullscreenSekiya Village on the Sumida River, 1830-1833, by Katsushika Hokusai.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection. Photo by Norihiro UenoHokusai’s miracle colour, Prussian blue, came from Europe, where it was first used in the early 18th century. His knowledge of perspective is also coloured by European art. But the traffic of influence went both ways. It is impossible to overstate the centrality of Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji to the birth of modernism. It is the first global masterpiece. When Hokusai created this series of closely linked prints in the early 1830s he reinvented landscape art as a conceptual and symbolic meditation that would thrill and inspire artists across the world.It’s no secret that Van Gogh, Whistler and other members of the European avant garde collected and emulated Japanese woodblock prints. But I hadn’t realised how deeply Cézanne was in his debt: the French painter’s repeated efforts to paintMont Sainte-Victoirein Provence, fragmenting its rocky mass into shards of perception to see its true nature and discover its secret, echo Hokusai’s journey around Mount Fuji. So do Monet’s obsessive paintings of Rouen Cathedral, a haystack and his (very Zen) waterlily garden. Hokusai taught these Frenchmen to see landscape as metaphysical.That we make icons of separate images from this series – and not just the wave – is understandable. Here is Ejiri Station, Province of Suruga, Hokusai’s depiction of people holding on to their hats as the sky fills with blown paper in an unexpected turn in the weather. Jeff Wall famously restaged it in his photographA Sudden Gust of Wind (After Hokusai).What a timeless artist Hokusai is, influencing Monet and Cézanne and still inspiring remakes today. But it distorts his meaning if we focus on his separate images without seeing them as part of one long meditation on Mount Fuji. By itself, Hokusai’s gust of wind may seem an image of crisis and impermanence. But Mount Fuji is in the background: the godlike summit that shows us there’s a serenity beyond the chaos.Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, is atDulwich Picture Gallery, London, from 20 October to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtHokusaiDulwich Picture GalleryExhibitionsModernismreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Maternity care in England is in a doom loop – how has it come to this?  | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Twenty years ago, if a pregnant woman had asked for a C-section because of her fears over poor staffing levels, midwives would have thought she was over-anxious. Now, it seems like a depressingly realist position, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Twenty years ago, if a pregnant woman had asked for a C-section because of her fears over poor staffing levels, midwives would have thought she was over-anxious. Now, it seems like a depressingly realist position, writes Zoe Williams
Content: Childbirth has changed hugely over the last few decades.Photograph: Posed by model; shurkin_son/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChildbirth has changed hugely over the last few decades.Photograph: Posed by model; shurkin_son/Getty ImagesOpinionPregnancyMaternity care in England is in a doom loop – how has it come to this?Zoe WilliamsTwenty years ago, if a pregnant woman had asked for a C-section because of her fears over poor staffing levels, midwives would have thought she was over-anxious. Now, it seems like a depressingly realist positionMon 19 Oct 2026 10.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.29 EDTShareThe classic way to outrage someone who’s pregnant is to touch their stomach without asking. I would never do that and it never, back in the day, happened to me – but I always thought, as outrageous as it might hypothetically be, that it also stood as a vivid analogy for the generalised social intrusiveness you get while you’re visibly pregnant. Endless questions about how you’re feeling, when you’re due, what hospital you’re going to, whether it’s a boy or a girl, how much time you have off. I hated this interrogation 20 years ago, but now I do it on a reflex; some driving force of human fellowship makes me want to know. I realised mid-sentence, asking a stranger about hospitals – and replying “That’s a great hospital, my sister had her kids in there” – that it must be even more grating than it was in the 00s. My nieces are 19 and 21 now, and that great hospital, unless it’s magically unconnected to the rest of the NHS, has probably changed quite a lot.The NHS Alliance has announced that up to 20 of the country’s 155 smaller, consultant-led maternity units, mostly in rural or coastal areas, might have to close, since their safety is in question. The problem – which will seem very pressing and obvious to anyone about to give birth, yet quite abstract and manageable to anyone who isn’t – is that those areas aren’t teeming with alternatives. There are women in Devon whose maternity hospital has been temporarily closed, whose next nearest hospital is53 miles away. Do they even encourage people to write a birthing plan any more? Because nobody’s, surely, would start: “First, I’d like to spend 90 minutes in a car, yelling at my birthing partner.”The headline reason is that caesarean sections have risen dramatically, which makes staffing needs more intense.Last year, 45% of births in England were by C-section, 44% were natural vaginal births and 11% were by ventouse or forceps, which marked the first time C-sections have been the most common method of delivery. Both elective and emergency C-sections hit their highest levels ever. This is often broadly ascribed to more complex pregnancies – older mothers, more existing health conditions – but one midwifery professor, Soo Downe, said that women “don’t really believe they’re going to have the kind of support they need to have a safe, straightforward, positive labour and birth in hospital”.Where on earth they could have got that idea is anyone’s guess: maybe word of mouth, or maybe from the scandals that came out ofthe government’s 2025 national maternity investigation, in which 14 trusts provided rolling horror stories of toxic workplace cultures, avoidable deaths and so-called systemic failures – investigation-speak for “nothing seems to be working”. Emergency C-sections, meanwhile, can also be chalked up to more complex births overall; yet, at the same time, there is no way of knowing how many labours would have proceeded differently had the midwives been less stretched. It’s a doom loop: the more pressure these services are under, the less people trust themselves to fate, the more demand there is for surgical intervention, the greater the pressure.Twenty years ago, if you’d said you wanted a C-section because you didn’t trust the staffing levels to cope with the unpredictability and longueurs of a natural birth, midwives would have looked at you like you were crackers, perhaps mentally chalking you up as an overanxious mother. Now, many of them would surely think you were a realist. If you were lucky enough to be pregnant between 2009 and 2011, they then would have handed you £190, to spend on fruit and vegetables (or whatever you liked) – so you’d just walk out of there thinking, “That midwife is incredibly nice”.Even though childbirth, in its essentials, doesn’t change a lot from one decade to the next, from the perspective of a person in society having to actually do it, it’s changed hugely. Which won’t stop me being curious about the particulars of every fresh miracle – but from now on, I’m working on some tone that isn’t “been there, done that”.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistThe Guardian’s year in review 2026: on Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. With Zoe Williams, John Crace, Pippa Crerar, Jonathan Liew and Lucy Mangan.
