title: Blue for poor, yellow for posh: the London maps exposing centuries of terrible housing | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: From rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persist
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: From rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persist
Content: Poverty and wealth side by side … a section from Charles Booth’s maps showing Clare Market slum (1898-99) in A Place to Call Home at Senate House, London.Photograph: Charles Booth Archive, courtesy of London School of EconomicsView image in fullscreenPoverty and wealth side by side … a section from Charles Booth’s maps showing Clare Market slum (1898-99) in A Place to Call Home at Senate House, London.Photograph: Charles Booth Archive, courtesy of London School of EconomicsExhibitionsBlue for poor, yellow for posh: the London maps exposing centuries of terrible housingFrom rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persistJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharles Booth’spioneering poverty mapsof Victorian London show a vivid colour-coded warren of streets, alleyways and slums tightly packed together. Those marked black and dark blue were classed as being “very poor”, defined by “chronic want”. The light blue ones were poor – “18s to 21s a week for a moderate family”. Pink streets housed those who were “fairly comfortable”, and those where the wealthy lived were marked in yellow.The maps by the British social reformer are the 19th-century equivalent of themodern-day indices of deprivation, which rank every geographic area of the UK by its level of social and economic disadvantage. Comparing the two shows how much has changed in the past 150 years – but also what hasn’t. Historical slums have been cleared away and housing conditions have generally improved, but extreme poverty and extreme wealth continue to live side by side in the capital.Booth’s maps form the backbone of a new exhibition at Senate House library titledA Place to Call Home, which charts the history of housing and poverty in London over the past 200 years. “We may not have the same sort of slums that we used to in Victorian times but there are still issues with living conditions for many people living in rented accommodation,” says academic librarian and curator Mura Ghosh. “These issues are on a continuum – continuity and change underline the whole thinking behind this exhibition.”‘There will still be things people find relatable’ … the ‘crawlers’ of St Giles workhouse, from Street Life in London by John Thomson and Adolphe Smith, 1877.Photograph: Courtesy of Senate House Library, University of LondonA collaboration between the University ofLondonand the London School of Economics (LSE), the exhibition looks at the turbulent timeline of housing over the past two centuries, including wartime and postwar redevelopment, the building of estates and changing housing policy, as well as eviction and squatting. People will be able to view Booth’s maps alongside a laptop displaying the current indices of deprivation, so they can see how conditions in their own postcode have changed over time.The curators have also picked out individual stories from Booth’s notebooks detailing interviews he conducted with ordinary working Londoners, such as a chorus girl working at Drury Lane theatre who talked about how much her tights cost. “We wanted tobring out these stories of individual lives in London because that’s what people can empathise with and feel connected to. They’re talking about a city 140 years ago, but there will still be things people find relatable,” says LSE curator Indy Bhullar.View image in fullscreenSome of the earliest examples of collective tenant resistance … a 1936 handmade issue of the Hampstead Tenant.Photograph: Courtesy of Senate House library, University of LondonOne of the exhibition’s rarest objects is a set of pamphlets from the Hampstead Tenants’ Defence League from 1936-39. Some of the earliest examples of collective tenant resistance, they document protests, rent strikes, opposition to slum clearances and challenges to the local council. “It’s quite a unique piece of history, and also utterly unexpected to find in an academic library,” says Ghosh. “They’re beautifully illustrated, and constructed from homemade paper and staples.”The exhibition shows how the burgeoning collective resistance movement solidified over the subsequent decades. There’s a 1974 squatters’ handbook with practical and legal advice on how to squat, including how to change the locks, do your own plumbing and resist bailiffs.“Collective action, rent strikes and protests, and encouraging people not to feel hopeless about the future – that’s an important message because people often feel like they’re alone in their housing situation,” says Emily Chu, a fellow curator and academic librarian at Senate House library. “The exhibition shows that working together sometimes creates a much bigger impact and a louder voice the government can hear.”Moving towards the present day, there will be audio recordings of interviews with people from St Mungo’s who have experienced homelessness, and discussion of how high rents and poor housing conditions persist into the present day. About 27% of Londonerslive in relative poverty after housing costs are factored in, the highest rate in England, with high rent and housing expenses the primary driver of poverty in the region. London has disproportionately high rates of damp and mould in social housing compared with other English regions – eight of the 10 local authorities in England receiving the highest volume of complaints are in the capital.The curators hope visitors will share their own experiences of this on the comment wall. They also call for groups who are campaigning on housing issues today to keep and donate their materials so the history of housing action can be continued.A Place to Call Home: Poverty and Housing in London is atSenate House library, London, 23 October to 5 March 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsMuseumsSocial historySocial housingLondonHousingSquattingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning
Content: Life through a lens … Georgina McNamara in her Instagram days in Cambridge, 2023.Photograph: Georgina McNamaraView image in fullscreenLife through a lens … Georgina McNamara in her Instagram days in Cambridge, 2023.Photograph: Georgina McNamaraThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private lifeI’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaningGeorgina McNamaraMon 19 Oct 2026 01.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfirst downloadedInstagramwhen I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed.As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all.View image in fullscreenMcNamara pre-epiphany at Sigiriya, Sri Lanka.Photograph: Georgina McNamaraIt wasn’t until a trip to Sri Lanka last year that I realised how far my obsession had gone. My partner and I spent two weeks travelling through Negombo and Kandy, having dinner in front of the Indian Ocean and visiting ancient heritage sites that I will probably never see again.This would have been memorable even without a third guest: my inner Instagram monologue. It commented on everything I saw in those two weeks, debating the merits of each photo I took and the possible captions (or music, or filters) that could accompany it. On one of our last days, we hiked up Sigiriya, an incredible rock fortress that has been inhabited since prehistoric times and is one of the most remarkable places I have ever seen.My first thought upon reaching the top? Thishasto go on my story. Already, I was imagining how it would look on Instagram. I dutifully made several posts upon my return to London, which were accompanied by hours of anxious scrolling and reloading, wondering why more people weren’t liking or commenting on my feed. Did they think I was annoying? Boring? Ugly? Had I been ungenerous with my own likes and comments, causing my followers (a grand total of 400) to band together to punish me? Should I delete the post? Redo it?Within two days, I couldn’t take my own thoughts any more. I decided to delete Instagram from my phone for a month, reset my habits, and then return with a hopefully healthier mindset.Yet in its absence, certain realisations became unavoidable. I came to see how much of my photo-taking was driven by wanting to appeal to an invisible audience, most of whom I hadn’t spoken to in years. In that first month, I started to take photos for myself and my own memories instead. It made me feel like my experiences could belong to me again.double quotation markWithin two days, I couldn’t take my own thoughts any more. I decided to delete Instagram from my phone for a monthOne month turned into three, then six – next month, it will have been a year since I took that first step. In my Instagram days, I expended a great deal of energy comparing the most normal parts of my life to the seemingly wonderful lives of others. Without the app, I was able to direct this energy into other parts of my life. That’s not to say I became productive every minute of every day. I didn’t. But the background noise decreased substantially. I read more, finished writing my first novel and started another.It has been liberating to live my life privately again. You may laugh, because I’m hardly a public figure, but I discovered how joyful it can be to reconnect with your anonymity and do activities knowing that it’s no one’s business whether you liked them or not.Now, moments matter because I’m enjoying them, or sharing them with someone I care about – not because they have been liked and validated by a hundred other people. I remain fully present for each of them, without disappearing halfway through into an Instagram rabbit hole. My life feels smaller in some ways, but also much more like my own. Whether the Insta-verse has noticed my absence, I couldn’t say. Do I care? Thankfully, not any more.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe one change that workedInstagramSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security
Author: Anna Isaac
Headline: Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security
Content: 1:40Dan Jukes reveals Nigel Farage did not take press office line on £5m gift - videoNigel FarageFarage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide saysExclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for securityAnna IsaacFinancial investigations editorMon 19 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne,first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.Faragetold the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other thansecret polling– foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing.Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.The timeline for the gift is disputed.Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.According to financial industry sources,some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discreditReform UK.”They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKParty fundingChristopher HarbornenewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control
Content: One option being considered is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines Thames Water owes into a government stake in the company.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOne option being considered is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines Thames Water owes into a government stake in the company.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Sopa Images/ShutterstockAndy BurnhamBurnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames WaterExclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public controlKiran Stacey,Pippa CrerarandJessica ElgotMon 19 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fixThames Waterand present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life”under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.Burnhampreviously saidhe would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies andcould rewritehow the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary,made clear her oppositionto such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for ThamesWaterbefore it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEnvironment policyThames WaterWaterWater industryUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris | France | The Guardian
description: Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public order
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public order
Content: 1:29'It's hell': residents reel after violent weekend riots across France – videoFranceFrance imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of ParisInterior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public orderJon Henleyin ParisMon 19 Oct 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePartial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts ofParis, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said.His office later announced partial curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille.Police also imposed a curfew from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday in two areas in Paris: Place de la République, where rioting took place on Saturday; and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.A statement from police said the orders banned gatherings and demonstrations and prohibited anyone from entering or remaining in the two designated areas.10:46France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests - The LatestFrance’s second city, Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday. French unions, meanwhile, called for a new ⁠round of strikes and rallies on 5 November.Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.Lecornu’s comments came after France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president,Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.View image in fullscreenLaurent Nuñez, the interior minister, offered his resignation to Emmanuel Macron, which was declined.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/Pool AFP/APThe protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said.France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence,” he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.Darmanin said 2,513 people had been arrested and 67 imprisoned since the violence broke out over the weekend, Libération reported.Some 70% of those arrested were adults and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes have been injured.View image in fullscreenAn estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted across France during the rioting.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesMacron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.View image in fullscreenThe Louvre was unable to open as scheduled on Monday because of protesters blocking its entrance.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersOn Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestEmmanuel MacronParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking fines | Motoring | The Guardian
description: Drivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Drivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends
Content: A new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday.Photograph: Ian Lamond/AlamyView image in fullscreenA new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday.Photograph: Ian Lamond/AlamyMotoringAndy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking finesDrivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session endsRupert JonesMon 19 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers will get a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their parking session ends before they face a fine under new rules for private car parks thatAndy Burnhamsaid were designed to outlaw “rip-off” charges.In the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and give consumers a “fairer” deal, the prime minister said a new official code of practice for the industry meant motorists in England,Scotlandand Wales would enjoy a range of new rights.The consumer body Which? said the “long overdue” rules appeared to fall well short of what was needed to help drivers fight back against private parking “cowboys”, however.Each year in the UK, private firms dish out millions of parking tickets, and the number has been climbing. In August,the RAC saidthe number issued rose 17% in a year to reach a record 16.9m in 2025-26.Complaints about poor behaviour by some operators are rife, and campaigners say reform is years overdue. Legislation waspassed in early 2019, and an official code of practice was unveiled by the then governmentin early 2022– but lasted less than six months after legal challenges by several parking firms forced it to be withdrawn.In a fresh push, a new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though it is unclear when this will take effect. Ministers said they would look to bring the code into force “as soon as possible”.New rights for drivers include “a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park, and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends”.The government is sticking with the existing industry maximum parking charge of £100 despite calls to halve it. Which? said: “It is particularly concerning that the government has shied away from a £50 price cap.” The consumer body had called for a maximum £50 fine, and this was also the amount at which some charges were capped under the withdrawn code.View image in fullscreenThe consumer body Which? had called for a maximum £50 fine.Photograph: jax10289/AlamyMeanwhile, fines will be scrapped on appeal for “honest mistakes”, such as stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations such as a medical emergency, vehicle breakdown or broken ticket machine.For “smaller slip-ups”, such as forgetting to display a parking permit or entering the wrong vehicle’s registration, the government said drivers would face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal. This appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules: the code that was withdrawn required the cancellation of a parking charge “in all mitigating circumstances”.Which? said the government had also shied away from an independent appeals body “that could rein in the industry’s worst practices” and had failed to take action on private parking debt recovery fees, which it said were regularly added without motorists’ knowledge and pushed unfair charges even higher.On the latter point, the government has promised to consult on these fees – which are added when a fine becomes overdue – “as soon as possible next year”. These fees are currently capped at £70, and the consultation will look at whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether.Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes.”Explore more on these topicsMotoringRoad transportConsumer affairsEnglandScotlandWalesUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks
Content: Photojournalist Heidi Levine speaks to journalists from a hospital bed in the West Bank’s Ramallah government hospital.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPhotojournalist Heidi Levine speaks to journalists from a hospital bed in the West Bank’s Ramallah government hospital.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockWest BankIsraeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlersMove comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacksEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemMon 19 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalistHeidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.The Israeli prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across theWest Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.Haaretzreportedon Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.It cited the response to anattack on a CNN crewin March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuJournalist safetyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph
Content: The study is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations yet of how AI analysis of a selfie could help to assess a patient’s health and guide their medical care.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe study is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations yet of how AI analysis of a selfie could help to assess a patient’s health and guide their medical care.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggestsSystem can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photographAndrew GregoryHealth editorMon 19 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.Details of the breakthrough werepublished in the Lancet Digital Health journal.The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face,according to the resultsof a study that examined the model.Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”The results of the studysuggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”Researchers foundlifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HealthCancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Journalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Far-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reporters
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Far-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reporters
Content: Tommy Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court for the start of his trial.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTommy Robinson, real name Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, arrives at Southwark crown court for the start of his trial.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesUK newsJournalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court toldFar-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reportersBen QuinnMon 19 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJournalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson, a court has been told as his harassment trial got under way.Robinson, 42, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was alleged to have targeted journalists from the Daily Mail and Mail Online by circulating images of their homes to millions of online followers and in effect encouraging them to join in making threats.He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber in 2024, which Robinson denies.Dirnhuber, a senior editor at the Mail, and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after the alleged campaign of intimidation by Robinson.Robinson, a former member of the British National Party (BNP) and co-founder of the English Defence League (EDL), is accused of harassment causing fear of violence through X posts and direct messages. He is also alleged to have made a telephone call on 5 August 2024 in which he is accused of telling Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”Opening the case for the prosecution on Monday at Southwark crown court, barrister Ben Holt told the jury Robinson could have chosen to complain to a press regulator after the Mail reported on his alleged role as an “influencer” encouraging the violence that broke out after the Southport murders in July 2024.The paper’s coverage included photos of Robinson reclining on a sunlounger, a phone in hand, while on holiday in Cyprus, where a team from the Daily Mail had located him. Members of the jury were shown an image of a front page which included a photo of Robinson and the headline: “Stoking Race Riots from his Sunbed.”“This trial is about the defendant’s reaction to this, what he perceived to be, unnecessary intrusion into his holiday,” said Holt.“On social media, to millions of followers, he circulated images of their homes. His supporters, followers, got involved, threatening the journalists. Understandably, you might agree, they were scared, in some circumstances being forced to leave their homes.“That is what this trial is actually about. The prosecution say this defendant, using bullyboy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. He sent photographers to their home addresses. He put pictures, albeit redacted, of them out on his timeline on X for the enjoyment and appreciation of his followers.Holt took the jury through Robinson’s reaction on X to the Mail’s coverage, which was said to have changed in tone from being “reasonable” and “concerned” to “retaliatory”.Holt said that it was was inevitable “and would have been known” by Robinson that his online followers and supporters “would pick up the baton and attack” those he was talking about.Examples given included tweets from an X account using the name The Secret SpAd, which posted the home address of Young while the journalist was still in Cyprus. It was posted with the comment: ”Please be sure to congratulate him.”When Young returned home from Cyprus on 6 August, his wife and daughters told him that a man in a grey Audi had parked outside their home. The man was confronted by the journalist’s daughter but ignored her, and a report was made to police. A further report was made of a man sitting under a tree, pointing his camera at the house.Holt told the court: “Mr Young was concerned. His main concern was that while (Robinson) himself might not harm him, one of his many supporters online may seek revenge on him or his family.”The court heard that a third journalist who was involved the mail’s coverage, George Odling, also felt the need to leave his family home after becoming concerned with the publicity surrounding his colleagues.Ted Verity, the editor-in-chief of the newspaper, provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual who identified himself as Tommy Robinson, who allegedly told him: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you.”A video posted by Robinson’s X account was also played to the court, in which he accused the Mail of having “doxxed” his family and children.In the video, he sad: “You broke up my family holiday. Is it fair that I do that to you? You know I know the locations to where you are. To any other journalist, I will find you. So please, think: is it right?”The trial was adjourned until Tuesday morning.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion | The Thames | The Guardian
description: American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard
Content: The final mast of the SS Richard Montgomery is removed from the Thames estuary.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe final mast of the SS Richard Montgomery is removed from the Thames estuary.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesThe ThamesMasts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosionAmerican warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboardGwyn TophamTransport correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate aKentcoastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced.Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery –a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades.The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship.The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”.Map of Kent and the Thames estuaryThe exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs.Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”.Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”View image in fullscreenThe masts have been taken to a maritime museum in Kent.Photograph: Fraser Gray/ShutterstockHe said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”.The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said.A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward hadBoris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airportgone ahead.Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts.Explore more on these topicsThe ThamesKentEnglandSecond world warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Helen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her life | Helen Haines | The Guardian
description: Australia’s politicians have been facing increasing threats and abuse. It can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless comment
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Australia’s politicians have been facing increasing threats and abuse. It can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless comment
Content: Independent MP Helen Haines was taken to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital after being struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIndependent MP Helen Haines was taken to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital after being struck by a car outside her office in Wangaratta.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesHelen HainesAnalysisHelen Haines was chatting with locals at a dog park on Monday morning. By the afternoon, she was fighting for her lifeTom McIlroyAustralia’s politicians have been facing increasing threats and abuse. It can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless commentFollow our live blog for latest updatesPoliticians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injuredWho is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?Mon 19 Oct 2026 17.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 20.07 EDTShareVictorian independent MPHelen Haineswas at the opening of a dog park in Mansfield on Monday, out and about in the sprawling northern Victorian electorate, talking to locals and moving freely.Later in the afternoon, at 3.35pm, she was unpacking a car outside her electorate office when a man understood to be known to authoritiesstruck her with his car. He allegedly completed a U-turn when he saw Haines.What happened will urgently change how MPs assess their personal safety, not least because local settings are no longer free from danger.The prime minister,Anthony Albanese, says the government will act on the advice of security officials but an increase in protection feels inevitable.Helen Haines: independent MP in critical condition in Melbourne’s Alfred hospital after being struck by car in Wangaratta  – follow updatesRead moreThere is much we don’t know about what has happened, including the motivation of the alleged attacker.But a dark tide of threats and abuse has been rising.For years, federal politicians have had an ominous sense that something was shifting in Australia’s national life.Monday’s alleged attack on Haines saw that tide turn into reality, witha much-loved local membercritically injured in the street outside her electorate office.Long having warned against the growing intensity of political debate, Albanese reflected the grave shock of the country in the hours after the incident.Along with the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, Albanese revealed that recorded threats against politicians numbered more than 1,067 last financial year, as the cohort of office holders requiring around-the-clock close personal protection grew.Those responsible for protecting federal politicians in Australia often take their cues from overseas. When a gunman opened fire at the Canadian parliament in 2014, the Abbott government built a fence around Parliament House. Amid threats stemming from Covid-19 lockdowns, and the souring of social media discourse, the Asio director general, Mike Burgess, cautioned in 2025 that the warning light for political violence was “already flashing red”.Albanese was evacuated from The Lodge in February and a blast-resistant facility was added to his Sydney residence. December’s antisemitic massacre at Bondi was only the latest wake-up call, along with incidents overseas such asthe alleged murder of British politician Ann Widdecombe.Here, local MPs have been changing their behaviour. Many no longer publicise where they will be for community events ahead of time, and some MPs’ local electorate offices have been closed for months at a time.‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injuredRead moreBut the alleged attack on Haines shows something rapidly being lost in our politics. The shift in sentiment can no longer be dismissed as social media noise or harmless comment.A review of politicians’ offices last year found a sharp rise in politically motivated hostility, with 85% reporting high levels of abusive or violent behaviour from constituents. This behaviour included verbal threats, intimidation, spitting and throwing of objects.The risk to individuals – especially women in politics – has not been taken seriously enough. Whether security services could have done more will be considered in the weeks and months to come.But dismissing overheated political rhetoric and petty attacks as woke or overly sensitive will not cut it now, as Haines remains in a critical condition after undergoing surgery.More needs to be done to stop a normalisation of violence and gratuitous insults. That includes the importation of rhetoric from the US and Europe, like calls for politicians to be locked up or harmed for their decisions. The politicians dishing out verbal attacks themselves, or inciting individuals to hate online, must be held accountable.The alleged attack on Haines could prove a turning point forAustralian politics, but hard questions about safety and the culture of debate must be answered.Tom McIlroy is Guardian Australia’s political editorExplore more on these topicsHelen HainesAnthony AlbaneseAustralian politicsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Foamy war? St Andrews students play out modern take on ancient ritual | University of St Andrews | The Guardian
description: Scottish university’s annual tradition once involved giving out raisins but fancy dress and shaving cream now in vogue
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Scottish university’s annual tradition once involved giving out raisins but fancy dress and shaving cream now in vogue
Content: Students taking part in the annual Raisin Monday foam fight.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStudents taking part in the annual Raisin Monday foam fight.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianUniversity of St AndrewsFoamy war? St Andrews students play out modern take on ancient ritualScottish university’s annual tradition once involved giving out raisins but fancy dress and shaving cream now in voguePatrick GreenfieldMon 19 Oct 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody at theUniversity of St Andrewsin Scotland seems to remember how Raisin Monday became a giant foam fight. For 600 years, first-year students have taken part in the ritual of thanking older students for mentoring them through their first few weeks of university life.Traditionally, freshers would give their elders a pound of raisins – hence the name. This Monday however, hundreds wore fancy dress as they streamed on to St Salvator’s lower college lawn at 11am armed with cans of shaving foam, covering one another in soapy clouds as they have for the past few decades. Groups of students dress as Smurfs, mice, bananas, grandmas, sunflowers and chefs to participate in the annual rite of passage.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe theme for each group is chosen by second- and third-year students, known as “mums” and “dads”, who have been matched with the first years. The proud “parents” stand on the edge of lawn screaming and waving to their “children”. Within minutes, the smell of shaving foam fills the square as cans are emptied over other students. It quickly becomes impossible to distinguish between costumes.“Traditions like this are much more important because people are less connected face to face than they were before. Getting to do something like this brings everyone together,” says Freya, a first year whose group has been dressed as periodic table elements by their chemistry student parents.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianSimon, who is part of the same family, says: “When you are covering each other in shaving foam, how much more bonded can you get?”Everyone involved recognises that this activity is particularly strange in a crowded field of unusual university rituals. At Merton College, Oxford, students walk backwards around Fellows’ Quadrangle when the clocks go back in October. In Aberdeen, each new rector is carried around campus on the back of a stuffed bull by students.There is a serious point to the St Andrews ritual at this isolated university on the east coast of Fife, the third oldest in the English-speaking world. More than half of the small town is made up of students – who come from all over the world – and the tradition helps break down barriers between students.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDeborah, an American medical student, is looking out at her academic children in the crowd. Her group has dressed as the blue-skinned supervillain, Megamind, from the animated DreamWorks film. “Because it’s such a small university, we get to have these sort of events. It wouldn’t be feasible at a bigger place. It brings people together. We do not have as many things going on because we are so small, so it helps create community and people you wouldn’t usually meet,” she says.Sunday has always been a crucial part of the weekend tradition, when first years are woken early, “kidnapped”, and made to take a dip in the North Sea. But in 2026, that is optional. For the Monday foam fight, students are encouraged to donate to a local food bank before they start spraying from their canisters – and appears to be far less alcohol-fuelled than it has in previous years.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAfter about half an hour, the excited students running around the green begin to slow. The cans of shaving foam are empty and the first years head to the exit to be hosed down despite the single digit temperature. Away from the green, foam-covered students greet their parents with bear hugs, covering them with foam, before heading home for a shower.“It’s amazing,” says Henry, an American student whose camouflage face paint has been completely covered in foam. “I only really know Americans, so getting to meet people from Singapore, England, South America, Africa and the Middle East through this is great. It’s rare to find a place where you can meet such a diverse group of people.”Explore more on these topicsUniversity of St AndrewsHigher educationUniversitiesScotlandStudentsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake | Television | The Guardian
description: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel
Content: ‘It’s a controlled fear’… Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake.Photograph: PeacockView image in fullscreen‘It’s a controlled fear’… Linda Cardellini as Pamela Voorhees in Crystal Lake.Photograph: PeacockTelevisionInterview‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal LakeRebecca NicholsonShe got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequelMon 19 Oct 2026 11.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘The first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God,thisis what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me,Mad Menand DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.Casual filmgoers may associate Friday the 13th with Jason, the hockey-mask-wearing serial killer. But aficionados will know that Pam, Jason’s mother, is the villain of the first movie. “He didn’t even have the mask until the third movie,” says Cardellini, who has clearly done her homework. “Pam is the original killer, in vengeance of his death.” (There is some massaging of previous storylines in Crystal Lake, such as moving Jason’s drowning from the 1950s to the early 70s, but since the franchise is flexible enough to have sent Jason into space at one point, a bit of timeline tweaking feels fair game.)View image in fullscreen‘I like to change it up’ …  Linda Cardellini.Photograph: Valérie Macon/AFP/Getty ImagesThe Friday the 13th franchise has a devoted audience – and Crystal Lake’s showrunner, Brad Caleb Kane, is among them. “He’s such a fan,” says Cardellini. “I felt he would have an idea of what fans were wanting.” Kane wrote the part specifically for her, after seeing her in Netflix thriller Dead to Me, which came as a surprise. “My biggest question was, ‘How did I become the person at the front of your mind for this?’” she laughs. Did they feel any pressure in taking Friday the 13th on? “It’s daunting, but hopefully it’s an opportunity to see more of something that didn’t really get its own avenue.”Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and 90s, as Cardellini did (she is 51), will remember sleepovers with rented VHS tapes and a lot of screaming whenever Freddy Krueger, Michael Myers or Jason Voorhees appeared on screen. “It was forbidden fruit, almost,” she says. “You weren’t supposed to be able to watch it, but you would. And not only the gore but the sexuality – all the things you’re not supposed to be watching. I think it is part of the allure when you’re young. It seems off-limits and rebellious.”double quotation mark‘At one screening, there were gasps and yells – then afterwards, a  laugh. It felt good’She liked the jump scares and the gore, which is handy, because Crystal Lake is full of them. One vivid sequence involves an astronomical amount of blood. “We reserved a whole week for that,” she says, which is highly unusual for TV, as it tends to move quickly. It had to be precisely planned and choreographed, not least because Cardellini’s hair in the show is lighter, and they soon found that the fake blood stained it pink.“Even the guy’s face coming off is done on the day with prosthetics, instead of CGI. It’s what you’re actually looking at, which helps with your reaction.” So that wasn’t done in post-production? “No! They pulled it off with fishing wire. So I saw it for the first time as it came off. It stuck with me for a while, because it’sdisgusting.” It proved to be one of her highlights. “That’s actually one of my favourite parts of the show. It’s like a blood opera.”Crystal Lake arrives on a new wave of mainstream horror, from films such as Obsession and Backrooms to Carrie and Widow’s Bay on TV. Why does Cardellini think horror is having a moment? “It’s a great question. I can imagine there’s something about the experience of it that is very present – and it’s a controlled fear, because you know that in a few hours, you will have a resolution. Maybe that is digestible.”View image in fullscreen‘Trust me, it’s going to get great’ … Cardellini and Jon Hamm in Mad Men.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyRecently, Cardellini was backstage at a screening of the show at New York Comic Con. “There was some gasping and yelling and cheers – and afterwards, a laugh. That’s when you’re like, ‘OK, this is great, because that’s what the movies did.’ They made you afraid, then you laughed out loud. That is what we were going for. That felt good.”Cardellini grew up in California and started acting in the mid-1990s. Her breakout wasFreaks and Geeks, the Paul Feig/Judd Apatow teen comedy in which she played good girl gone bad Lindsay Weir. The early 80s-set series, a fond, witty look at teenage rebellion, burned bright and fast and was promptly cancelled by NBC in 2000, before its first season had finished airing. As well as Cardellini, it rocket-launched the careers of Seth Rogen, Jason Segel and Busy Philipps.“If you got cancelled, you were justgone,” she says now. “You didn’t even know where it went. The idea that it would live on, once we weren’t going to make any more, just didn’t seem possible.” Through DVDs and word of mouth, though, Freaks and Geeks slowly became a classic of the high school TV genre. “That it had a life afterwards was a shock – and that it still has a life is amazing.”View image in fullscreenBreakout role … Cardellini with Jason Segel in Freaks and Geeks.Photograph: All4On the subject of all-time-greatest TV series, Cardellini joined Mad Men in its sixth season, playing Sylvia Rosen, who has an affair with Don Draper. There was such secrecy around this that when she auditioned, names and details were changed. “I had no idea what I would be doing and [creator] Matt Weiner said, ‘Just trust me, it’s gonna get great.’ I think it was the first two scripts I got – I had one line. I thought, ‘What am I doing? What is this?’” But Weiner had told her it would be a great part and he was not lying. Not only does her character go on to remind Don of a sex worker from his youth, she also gets to leave him, triggering an obsession. “It unfolded like a surprise for me,” she says.In September, Cardellini won her first Emmy for her role as Carol Love-Smernitch in HBO’s DTF St Louis. “I’ve been nominated before, but winning is a very different feeling,” she says. “It was a wonderful moment.” DTF St Louis is a singular series: Carol is married to American Sign Language interpreter Floyd, but is having an affair with his best friend Clark, a TV weatherman who rides a weird bike and likes to pretend to be a robot during sex. When Cardellini first heard about the show, she thought she knew how the story would go. “A love triangle between a married couple and a best friend, and somebody turns up dead,” she recalls. “But when I read it, I thought, ‘I’ve never read anything like this.’ Every time I thought I knew where it was going, it went somewhere else, in this beautiful, nuanced, very human way.”View image in fullscreenCardellini in her Emmy-winning role in DTF St Louis.Photograph: SkyThe show is a strange, sweet meditation on loneliness, with an offbeat streak. Carol, for instance, is a part-time baseball umpire. “Since I’ve played an umpire, I’ve met so many people who have told me they are also umpires, and it’s people you don’t expect. Also, the parent attacks that they have to weather are pretty funny.” Could she still umpire a game? “Maybe Little League. I don’t know if I can handle the parents!”That Emmy award now lives on the mantel of her fireplace. Her first appearance on TV was in 1994, when she was a contestant on the quizshow The Price Is Right. You can see it on YouTube – she won a fireplace. Hang on, it’s not the same fireplace is it? “I wish! I don’t have that fireplace any more because, oddly enough, I lost it in a fire.” You lost a fireplace in a fire? “I was working and put a lot of stuff in storage. The storage facility caught fire.” But she had kept it for a long time? “Oh, for years and years and years.”Earlier this year, Cardellini filmed They Know, a psychological horror movie written and directed by Bill Hader, who also stars. “It’s definitely his incredibly extraordinary point of view,” she says, reluctant to give too much away beyond the fact she plays his ex-wife. The fact that it’s another horror does not mean, however, that Cardellini is in her scream queen era. “I like to change it up,” she says. “I went from DTF to Crystal Lake with one week in between. That seemed like a big left turn. So we’ll see what comes up.” She pauses and adds: “But you never know.”Crystal Lake is on Sky Atlantic and Now in the UK, plus on Peacock in the US and on Stan in Australia.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionHorror filmsHorror (TV)Mad MeninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickening | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: As we witness the endless indignities these grieving families have endured in the six decades since the mining disaster, it is impossible not to turn red with rage
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: As we witness the endless indignities these grieving families have endured in the six decades since the mining disaster, it is impossible not to turn red with rage
Content: The scene at Aberfan, Glamorgan, after a mountain of pit waste slid down on to Pantglas junior school and a row of housing, killing 116 children and 28 adults.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenThe scene at Aberfan, Glamorgan, after a mountain of pit waste slid down on to Pantglas junior school and a row of housing, killing 116 children and 28 adults.Photograph: PATV reviewTelevision & radioReviewAberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickeningAs we witness the endless indignities these grieving families have endured in the six decades since the mining disaster, it is impossible not to turn red with rageLucy ManganMon 19 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’d like to have known her that bit longer, really. Those eight years went very, very quickly. I loved the child. I lost her. And that seemed to me to be the end of everything really, when she’d gone.”Ray Lee, now 90, lost his daughter Anne on 21 October 1966. It was the day her primary school, along with several surrounding houses, in Aberfan was engulfed by an estimated 100,000 tonnes of slurry from one of the colliery spoil tips that overshadowed the Welsh mining village. Anne was one of 116 children killed, alongside 28 adults.View image in fullscreen‘It seemed to be the end of everything’ … Ray Lee, who lost his daughter Anne in the disaster.Photograph: BBC Studios/Mei WilliamsGaynor Madgwick (nee Minett) was in the same school and was the same age as Anne when the disaster struck, but she was catapulted back to the far wall by the initial impact and, although severely injured, survived. Her grandfather dug her out. When she asked her father that evening, in hospital, where her brother and sister were, he told her they had both gone to heaven.Marlene Gerlach remembers screaming and screaming for her three children across the unrecognisable school site.
