They all survived. The guilt has never left her.Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back devotes the first quarter of its run time to these stories. Even when the focus of a programme is slightly elsewhere – and this hour-long film attends to the underacknowledged aftermath and the sickening behaviour of the National Coal Board and the government of the day – it must be done. It remains unthinkable, inhumane not to. The suffering lives on and so does the duty to bear witness to it.It also throws into even starker relief the astonishing, appalling reactions of the NCB and the ministers, including and especially the secretary of state for Wales, George Thomas, who failed to stand up to the board and its chairman Sir Alf Robens, whose contemptuous attitude towards the village and its unfathomable grief was evident from day one, the Friday, when he went ahead with his installation ceremony as the first chancellor of the new University of Surrey instead of travelling immediately to Wales. He got there on Saturday evening instead. From the foot alone we may infer the anti-Hercules.The waste heap had been built on top of several springs that made it inherently unstable. The coal board denied knowledge of them, saying they had been covered long before they took over responsibility for the tips. The tribunal that was set up to inquire into the causes of the tragedy found evidence that the NCB knew that this and other tips around the village were, in contravention of all guidelines, built over multiple water sources, and in its report detailed many other failings in the “terrifying tale of bungling ineptitude”. It laid the blame firmly with the NCB but no further action against it was taken.View image in fullscreenGaynor Madgwick, who was severely injured but survived, lost her brother and sister in the mining disaster.Photograph: BBC Studios/Mei WilliamsFurther indignities were caused to the stricken villagers, powerfully evoked in this restrained documentary by well-chosen memories from its interviewees. Gaynor remembers her father sitting puce with rage every evening in his chair as the NCB continued to fight liability for the deaths and deny the (expensive) need to remove the tips. “He said it was murder, every day.” Her mother was on Valium and moved through the days “like a zombie”.The Aberfan Disaster Fund had received charitable donations from more than 50,000 members of the public. When the NCB finally agreed to remove the tip, it demanded £250,000 from the fund towards the cost. The fund – left unprotected by the Charity Commission that should have prevented such a payment – handed over £150,000 and work began.When the time came for disbursing funds to the intended recipients, the Commission offered £500 a household – if the parents could prove they had been close to the dead child.The people of Aberfan fought back, and back, and back and back. They formed committees, wrote letters, visited Thomas’s offices in London (and emptied a bag of slurry on to the floor – “He was our minister but he was a coward”) and remained unbowed by the rebuffs and by the condescension and contempt with which they were treated. Release of government material from the time under the “30-year rule” in 1997 shows how deep it ran. The sense of betrayal felt in 1966 – especially from a Labour government and a Labour-nationalised coal board – was confirmed and renewed. The newly elected Blair government returned the money. Ten years later, the new Welsh Assembly adjusted the payment for inflation and added £2m to the pot.Ray went on to have two more children. “It did help a lot that all the love we wanted to give to Anne and we couldn’t, we could give to them.”Nobody was ever held to personal account or punished for the disaster. Sixty years on, with Hillsborough, Grenfell and so many more national disgraces behind us, it is hard to feel that there are not many more catastrophes to come.Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionAberfan disasterreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s the last Halloween of my 30s and I want to show off my bod’: your favourite DIY costumes | Halloween | The Guardian
description: From bin-bag bats to KPop Demon Hunters-inspired looks, here are the homemade outfits you’ll be rocking this year
Author: Lucy Pavia
Headline: From bin-bag bats to KPop Demon Hunters-inspired looks, here are the homemade outfits you’ll be rocking this year
Content: Pawsitively petrifying …Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP via GettyView image in fullscreenPawsitively petrifying …Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP via GettyThe FilterHalloween‘It’s the last Halloween of my 30s and I want to show off my bod’: your favourite DIY costumesFrom bin-bag bats to KPop Demon Hunters-inspired looks, here are the homemade outfits you’ll be rocking this yearDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereLucy PaviaMon 19 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor everyHalloweenparty I went to as a child, my mum made me the same costume: bin-bag bat. Black base layer, fangs drawn on with eyeliner, and wings cut out of bin bags and attached to the sleeves. Surprisingly effective, cheap and with a five-minute assembly time (particularly helpful as I was the youngest of four), the costume became such a habit that I’ve fallen back on it many times in adulthood too; my friends even dressed up as a colony of bin-bag bats for my hen party.Given the Halloween “season” seems to swell every year like an overgrown gourd (a house on my school run is already covered with fake cobwebs), I asked colleagues, friends and readers about their own DIY costume ideas.Mummy’s on a roll …View image in fullscreenHoly sheet! The toilet-roll mummy is a classic for a reason.Photograph: AnnaStills/Getty“When we were kids we sometimes wore our ballet outfits and then drew ‘scary’ makeup to look like broken ballerinas – ‘cracks’ drawn with eyebrow pencil, bright red lipstick,” says the Filter’s audience editor Ella Jinadu. “These days, I think wearing anLED face maskwithout the light turned on would be pretty terrifying.”One anonymous reader says a ninja is a great idea for kids if you’re pressed for time: “You just need a black turtleneck, an oversized black T-shirt cinched with a belt and a sword – my son made one out of cardboard.” Otherwise, a KPop Demon Hunters look can be “quickly achieved with purple hairspray”. Though for reader Harriet, it’s all about the loo-roll mummy – a classic for a reason: “Budget, and lots of fun.”“In my opinion, an adult Halloween costume has to be homemade (no next-day Amazon deliveries) and scary (sexy nurse is not allowed),” says reader Marie. She recommends her “head on a platter” look using a foil plate around the neck and a large cardboard box “table” to pop your head through (alternatively, try this brilliantcostumehack spotted on Instagram using a backpack, stuffed tights and some old cardboard boxes).Costume dramaOthers told me they’re planning a look that taps into the zeitgeist. “It’s the last Halloween of my 30s, and I want to show off my bod,” my friend Nick told me, “so I’m going as Sydney Sweeney in hercontroversial sports gambling advert. I’m going to wear nude underwear, cut a football in half to put across my chest, have a tennis racket on my back and wear a wig, of course.” Meanwhile, for the thinking woman’s Halloween costume, reader Margaret is planning to go as a Freudian slip, wearing a slip dress with ego, id and preconscious written across it.And because a dog Halloween outfit is nearly always a good idea, reader Leslie thinks this could be the year she finally makes a spider costume for her rescue terrier, Queenie. See the viralmutant giant spider dogvideo for more details. Something spooky this way runs.Explore more on these topicsHalloweenThe FilterBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever? | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtime
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtime
Content: Elizabeth Holmes outside court in San Jose, California, in 2022.Photograph: Amy Osborne/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes outside court in San Jose, California, in 2022.Photograph: Amy Osborne/AFP/Getty ImagesPass notesDocumentary filmsThe reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever?Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtimeMon 19 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:The best reviewed film in history.Age:Not even out yet, except in the US and Canada.Appearance:Coming soon to a screen near you.How exciting! What is it?It’s calledYou Can See Everything.Who’s in it?DiCaprio?De Niro? Both?It’s not that kind of film.What’s it about, then?The subject of the documentary isElizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of …Did you say documentary? No thanks.But reviews of this particular documentary have been overwhelmingly favourable!I don’t go to the cinema to learn things.Critics have been unstinting in their praise forNathan Fielderand Lance Oppenheim’s unflinching three-hour examination of the Theranos scandal’s architect and …You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThree hours? Are you kidding?I know that seems long, but the Guardian’s critic called it “a stupefying and gloriously destabilising hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject”. And audiences have so far been undaunted by the long run time – it logged a phenomenal$15m at the box officein its opening weekend in the US and Canada.Meh.And the film has earned an unprecedented Metacritic score of 99/100.Unprecedented?Certainly for a documentary – in fact, you’d have to go back to the2016 drama Moonlightto find a best picture Oscar-winner with the same score.You mean it’s higher thanThe Odyssey?The Odyssey got 88/100.Bigger than Digger?Digger got 46.At the end of the day, Metacritic is just one review aggregator.On Rotten Tomatoes, You Can See Everything has a 99% rating from 117 reviews so far, putting it in contention for the site’s best-rated film of 2026. It’s also effectively the highest rated cinema release ever on Letterboxd.Effectively?With a 4.7/5 score, it’s the fourth-highest reviewed overall, but the three above it are a live Radiohead concert and two TV shows (Band of Brothers and Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood).Where are some of the other highest-rated films in history?Metacritic’s top 10 best-rated films include Citizen Kane (1941), The Leopard (1963), The Conformist (1970) and Tokyo Story (1972).Those movies all have one thing in common: I haven’t seen them.It’s early days, obviously, but You Can See Everything is already 24th on Metacritic’s all-time list.What are some of the worst-rated films?Rotten Tomatoes’ bottom 10 (of films that have received 20 reviews or more) includes: Tom & Jerry: The Forbidden Compass (2025); Left Behind (2014), starring Nicolas Cage; Roberto Benigni’s adaptation of Pinocchio (2002); and Superbabies: Baby Geniuses 2 (2004), which Joanne Kaufman of the Wall Street Journal described as “unspeakably ghastly”.Fortunately, I haven’t seen any of those either.I don’t know where you would even find them.Do say:“The hype is deserved.”Don’t say:“The nachos were excellent.”Explore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsPass notesNathan FielderYou Can See EverythingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year | You Can See Everything | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder’s secretive Elizabeth Holmes documentary has become a sold-out smash hit and might make Oscars history
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Nathan Fielder’s secretive Elizabeth Holmes documentary has become a sold-out smash hit and might make Oscars history
Content: A still from You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24View image in fullscreenA still from You Can See Everything.Photograph: A24You Can See EverythingSecrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the yearNathan Fielder’s secretive Elizabeth Holmes documentary has become a sold-out smash hit and might make Oscars historySpoilers aheadAdrian HortonMon 19 Oct 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf there is one moment that sums upYou Can See Everything, the new A24 documentary on Elizabeth Holmes that until this weekend was shrouded in spoiler-averse secrecy, it is, perhaps surprisingly, the one everyone already knows: co-director Nathan Fielder, the droll comedian known for deadpanning subjects into submission, sitting eye to eye with Holmes, the unblinking fabulist of Theranos infamy. In tight zoom, saturation turned up – Fielder’s arched brows and Holmes’s oceanic blue eyes as stark as two magnetic poles – he asks her: “Are you being real right now?”‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesRead moreThat question hangs over much of the colossal three-hour movie, particularly a claustrophobic first half that has made headlines since the film’s existence was announced in September. That first half – essentially, the only part of the movie anyone respecting spoiler guidelines and/or the theatrical experience could talk about – takes place entirely in 2023, when Fielder and his co-director Lance Oppenheim, along with a small crew, embedded with Holmes, her husband, Billy Evans, and their two small children in the run-up to her prison sentence for fraud. We watch as Fielder, over a few surreal weeks in a beachfront rental, attempts to puncture Holmes’s indomitable facade of faultlessness. It’s not exactly comedic, this chess game between three norms-ignoring people, but it can be quite funny: TV’s grand illusionist, an absurdist auteur who will go as far as actually obtaining a 737 pilot’s license for the bit, stymied by a world-class fabricator, with her poorly dissembling husband on the side. This section resembles, in feel, the pull of an internet wormhole: the closer you zoom in on a subject, without outside context, the more sense devolves. Was Holmes “being real”, for instance, when she told Fielder, with seemingly complete sincerity, that she hasnevertold a liein her life? Or when she continued to insist, despite plain reality, that Theranos devices could perform 1,000 diagnostic tests?It’s at once astounding how many people took her seriously, given how obviously mendacious she and her husband appear, and also understandable: the more time you spend with her – the more time you spend watching Fielder spend time with her – the more magnetic the force of her delusions. Or is it manipulations? Or both? There is no one correct read on what, exactly, she’s thinking. “I know what you’re feeling,” an obviously irritated Evans tells Fielder after he bristles at Holmes’s indistinction between the meanings ofcan performandcould theoretically perform1,000 diagnostic tests. It is a relief, and one of the best lines of an extremely rich text, when the comedian immediately shoots back with his own irritation: “No, you don’t.” The fundamental unknowability of another person, even a known liar, is fascinating, but also its own dead end.If the first half had been released as a standalone film, it would probably have generated some attention and then faded as an artefact of a particular era of Silicon Valley celebrity, a briefly fascinating but inconclusive stunt. But luckily for us – and the theatrical box office, where You Can See Everything had themost successful opening weekend for a documentary in over 20 years– Fielder and Oppenheim kept filming. You Can See Everything is, essentially, two films in one: an elevated true crime documentary, and then an experiment unraveling the preconceptions of a documentary. It’s the back half of this immense movie, which picks up in 2025, after Holmes has spent some time in prison, makes You Can See Everything the film of the year – a formally ambitious feat that not only pushes the boundaries of nonfiction cinema but speaks to our destabilizing present of endless, inescapable manipulation.There’s a reason You Can See Everything currently holds a rare close-to-perfect score onRotten Tomatoes, is among thehighest-rated films all timeon Letterboxd and has solid odds to become the first doc to ever be nominated for a best picture Oscar. In the second half of the movie – stop now if you haven’t seen – Fielder recruits a shockingly game (andpossibly awards-worthy) Amanda Seyfried, star of The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series on the Theranos debacle. At first, it seems as though Seyfried is participating in her own stunt: how funny and improbable, to see the actor who won an Emmy for playing Elizabeth Holmes watch footage of Holmes watching Seyfried play Holmes. Two very famous people, confronted by famous representations of themselves. Whose reaction is genuine?But Seyfried thrillingly becomes part of the very Fielderian pursuit of emotional truth through arcane artifice. Borrowing logic from hisgroundbreaking HBO series The Rehearsal, Fielder inserts Seyfried into an escalating series of re-enactments, trying to wring some clarity out of his real interactions with Holmes, then out of their own reactions to the simulations. Seyfried oscillates between a conviction that The Dropout was a work of fiction grounded in fact, and that its liberties may have violated another person. Never have I seen an actor really dig into what it means to play a real person like Seyfried here, grappling with her various responsibilities – to Holmes the person, to Holmes the character, to story, to facts, to herself – in real time, shifting with each new piece of info or tilt of perspective.View image in fullscreenNathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.Photograph: Todd Williamson/JanuaryImages for A24/ShutterstockThe Dropout, for what it’s worth, was the best of aseries of scam showsfrom 2022 that tried to turn the rise and fall of inflated 2010s tech companies such as Uber or WeWork into entertainment. (One of the film’s best punchlines is simply observing that Evans, with his “LASERS” license plate and obsession with a new Theranos “device”, continues to push Theranos 2.0 … at a WeWork). You Can See Everything coincidentally arrives amid a new wave of Hollywood attempts to make sense of tech world, from Aaron Sorkin’s dreadful The Social Reckoning to Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI film Artificial to Alex Gibney’s colossal doc Musk, that feel insufficient to the magnitude and lunacy of the moment. By being neither bound to representation nor straightforward journalism, You Can See Everything gets to what we might call the “emotional truth” of this era – and not just because Evans, a professed Charlie Kirk fan seemingly radicalized by his Musk-owned X timeline who commissioned an AI hologram of his wife, emerges as a very 2020s villain, a tech bro with a possible drug problem and a god complex. Layer by layer, Fielder and co deconstruct the underpinnings of their storytelling, from Evans’s original deal to profit from the film to his possible loyalty toward a woman he has evident chemistry with. Truth, in fact, is dependent on what you’re shown.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThis is the pinnacle of Fielder’s longstanding effort to invert assumptions of “reality” on screen. A former producer on Canadian Idol, he’s a student of reality television, a misnomer we readily accept: of course, we know, there is no true reality on TV. But documentary tends to court the benefit of the doubt, as if their presentation did not reflect the makers’ own biases and motivations. The joke is in the title;You Can See Everythingis itself a lie – we cannot. Choices are made, things are not shown. Omniscience is impossible.But we are, in this advent of AI, training to scan everything as manipulated. “Are you being real right now?” applies as much to celebrity bodies as to meme-motivated foreign wars as to the Instagram dog videos sent by my mom as to what, exactly, is going on withElizabeth Holmes. We’re in uncharted waters now, the type best navigated collectively – such as with a theater full of other people, attempting briefly to make sense of the nonsensical, working with material delivered by the biases and motivations of other people, all vying for our attention. At what point, in this hall of mirrors, do you trust? I emerged from You Can See Everything unnerved: you maybe never know, but you still have to try.Explore more on these topicsYou Can See EverythingDocumentary filmsNathan FielderElizabeth HolmesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How we made Come Dine With Me: ‘Someone served sushi off a guy’s naked chest!’  | Come Dine With Me | The Guardian
description: ‘We’re not there to humiliate or to sneer. Channel 4 insisted everyone had to be a decent cook – the threshold was that contestants had to know what coriander was’
Author: Michael Hogan
Headline: ‘We’re not there to humiliate or to sneer. Channel 4 insisted everyone had to be a decent cook – the threshold was that contestants had to know what coriander was’
Content: ‘I hope we helped make dinner parties less formal’ … Come Dine With Me’s sushi episode.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreen‘I hope we helped make dinner parties less formal’ … Come Dine With Me’s sushi episode.Photograph: Channel 4How we madeCome Dine With MeHow we made Come Dine With Me: ‘Someone served sushi off a guy’s naked chest!’‘We’re not there to humiliate or to sneer. Channel 4 insisted everyone had to be a decent cook – the threshold was that contestants had to know what coriander was’Interviews byMichael HoganMon 19 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNell Butler, creatorIt all started in the early 00s when I tried to throw a dinner party. I was an executive producer during the early days of reality TV – and a house-proud young mum. My posh cousin and her even posher husband came for a meal. I was rushing to get the kids to bed and tidy up, so the food was an afterthought. I’d never made couscous before but decided to serve it with chicken. It was awful. Dry chicken with congealed couscous. At one point, my cousin’s husband stuck his fork in this rock-solid lump, lifted it up and said: “What actually is this?”When they left, my husband slumped in his chair and said: “I’d give that a three.” I thought there was something funny about scoring somebody’s hosting skills. Everyone leaves those terrible evenings and dissects it with their partner. I came up with the idea of groups of strangers taking it in turns to host, competing for a cash prize.I pitched it as Ladies Who Lunch, with a Real Housewives vibe. ITV rejected it but Channel 4 daytime were interested. They massively improved it by insisting it should be dinner and everyone had to be a decent cook. The threshold was that contestants had to know what coriander was – that was the test we hit upon. The working title was Let Me Entertain You. Later it became Come Dining, but lawyers worried it was too close to Come Dancing. I suggestedCome Dine With Me.double quotation markStudents alighted on it as hangover viewing. On a Sunday, they’d climb into bed together and watch the omnibus editionThe pilot episode had a narrator who is now a famous actor. He sounded too posh. Replacing him with Dave Lamb’s more casual, sarcastic style took it to another level. The idea of the voiceover talking directly to the contestants was groundbreaking. Dave would throw in “Oh really?” or “God, get a room!”. We’re not there to humiliate or sneer, just to gently take the piss and puncture pomposity, which is a very British trait. Dave walks that tightrope perfectly.Ratings were pretty good but Channel 4 wavered about recommissioning it. What saved us was that it started doing well on catch-up because students, bless them, alighted on it as hangover viewing. On a Sunday, they’d climb into bed together and watch the omnibus edition. That rescued us. It also gave us traction when selling the format abroad. There are now 50-odd international versions.It’s a small show that made a big impact. Dinner parties used to be snooty affairs. I hope we helped make them less formal and more fun. I’ve always believed that hosting isn’t to do with wealth, class, the size of your house, or whether you used napkins or paper serviettes. It’s about the warmth of your welcome.I never imagined Come Dine With Me would run for 21 years. Its staying power is testament to the fact that there’s an endless supply of brilliant ordinary people who make for cracking TV. It’s also cheap to make. We even turned it into a stage musical. I’d like to think we influenced shows like Four in a Bed and Don’t Tell the Bride, maybe even Gogglebox and Love Island’s irreverent narration. And I throw a much better dinner party nowadays. I’ve even nailed couscous.View image in fullscreen‘Dinner parties used to be snooty affairs. I hope we helped make them less formal and more fun’ sausage trifle is served in series 26.Photograph: Channel 4Dave Lamb, narratorIt started out as a slightly more serious food competition, then they looked at the pilot episode and decided there was more fun to be had by focusing on the people, not the cooking. A few of us comedy performers auditioned to take over the narration. I just improvised around the script. Before long, I was doing lots of asides and mucking about.“Mango” and “tiramisu” are some of my favourite words to say. I enjoy pronouncing “chorizo” wrongly because it infuriates people. Bruschetta can either be “bru-shetta” or “bru-sketta”, depending on what part of Italy you’re in. Sometimes I’ll do both pronunciations in the same episode, just for mischief. There are filthy bits that don’t make the cut. Occasionally I’ll let go a barrage of truth, shall we say. Obviously that can never see the light of day.View image in fullscreen‘If I wouldn’t say something to their faces, I won’t say it in the voiceover’ … Dave Lamb.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockI’m keen for my voice performance not to be unkind. If I wouldn’t say something to their faces, I won’t say it in the voiceover – that’s my yardstick. If contestants are being rude or making fools of themselves, you can see it on screen. It doesn’t need me adding some snide comment.I realised the show was a hit in 2008 when I was acting in a series called Moving Wallpaper. All these brilliant actors kept saying, “Oh my god, you’re that guy from Come Dine With Me!” I was becoming known as this shouty voiceover bloke. I used to record it sitting down but started losing my voice; a vocal therapist told me I need to stand up because I push it so hard. We do five episodes per session, and by the end I’m spent. My voice only tends to get recognised if I get overexcited. If I get loud and pitch up the register, people go: “You did a bit of it then!”After this long, it all blurs into one, but certain moments stick in the mind, like sushi being served off a guy’s naked chest. Or the guy who stuck an entire whisk in his mouth. Or the time someone got their pet snake out and it pooed all over the dinner table. One of the most notorious clips is the “What a sad little life, Jane” rant. There’s not much you can add to that, but I was quite pleased with my “Doggy bag, anyone?” line. In terms of horrific dishes, there’s been quite a lot of roadkill.‘It brings people together’: Global hit Come Dine With Me celebrates 20 yearsRead moreThe longevity of it is bonkers. I assumed it would be one and done. It would’ve been beyond my comprehension that 21 years later, I’d be doing the same job. I think the appeal is about people and their houses. We all have a fascination for where other people live and how they feed themselves. The magic for me is this enormously diverse range of people sitting around the same table.It’s nicely paid but the beauty of it has been a steady income over a long period. We’re closing in on 2,500 episodes. That’s a lot of shouting! Apparently, humans change all their cells every seven years, so I’ve had three entire bodies while doing this and we’re just about to crack into the next.Come Dine With Me is available for streaming onchannel4.comExplore more on these topicsCome Dine With MeHow we madeTelevisionFood TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kevin Bridges review – steamroller standup is a joy but what’s with the £10 cloakroom charge? | Comedy | The Guardian
description: In his tour Here If You Need Me, the comic makes laugh-out-loud look easy with jokes about conjugal argy-bargy, smutty downloads – and a bit of politics
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: In his tour Here If You Need Me, the comic makes laugh-out-loud look easy with jokes about conjugal argy-bargy, smutty downloads – and a bit of politics
Content: Brilliantly blunt … Kevin Bridges.Photograph: Andy HollingworthView image in fullscreenBrilliantly blunt … Kevin Bridges.Photograph: Andy HollingworthComedyReviewKevin Bridges review – steamroller standup is a joy but what’s with the £10 cloakroom charge?Hammersmith Apollo, LondonIn his tour Here If You Need Me, the comic makes laugh-out-loud look easy with jokes about conjugal argy-bargy, smutty downloads – and a bit of politicsBrian LoganMon 19 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there a better no-frills standup at work today thanKevin Bridges? You’d struggle to find a more unfussily funny demonstration of the art form’s traditional virtues than at the Glaswegian’s new touring set. It’s a consistently laugh-out-loud suite of observational material on subjects comics have addressed since time immemorial: nostalgia, marital dispute, the latest cultural trends – alongside, asBen Eltonused to have it, a little bit of politics, too. Bridges really does have the X factor, and – without him ever seeming to stretch himself – Here If You Need Me is a steamroller 75 minutes of standup.For me, it needed to be, after being hit by a £10 – 10 pounds! – cloakroom charge because my innocuous wee bag (a notebook, a novel, a pair of glasses) was apparently too incendiary to be allowed into the venue. Oh that Bridges would turn his satirical eye on that racket. But the show starts with more obvious targets: Donald Trump, whose “negotiating” techniques our host burlesques in a violent dialogue with his electrician; and Benjamin Netanyahu, pausing before another act of destruction to check out Bridges’ Instagram feed.‘A vigorous apologist for a cruel emperor’: Is Caryl Churchill’s explosive new play about Trump and his press officers?Read moreThat latter bit features in a wider routine on celebs “using their platform” to promote political causes – and the counter-argument that it’s just virtue signalling. In the face of all that – on which he has a witheringly amusing last word – Bridges retreats into less contentious territory. One very droll skit from this father to a young son ribs the newfound milestone of the nursery graduation. Another looks back to his own youth at the dawn of the internet, downloading smutty pictures – and rapidly multiplying viruses – on to “Big Dell”, the family home computer.Maybe this material, which develops into a routine about teaching his ageing mum to use technology, paddles in over-familiar comedic shallows. But Bridges fishes there for a new and pertinent catch, as with the sly reversal that turns a joke about online shopping into a paean for real-world connection (while pretending to do the opposite). Likewise, you could see later material on the Bridges household’s conjugal argy-bargy as old-school ’er-indoors shtick. And so it is. But there’s often more going on, too, some strand of social satire or surprising nuance at play, as per the gag about mansplaining while his wife drives him to the pub.Bridges’ trick is to present, in both form and content, as a traditionally male, no-nonsense standup while delivering punchlines that reveal a cheerfully engaged, open-minded and egalitarian fellow. That’s apparent in his gag about school kids identifying as cats – and all the more so in his belter of a closing set piece, proposing a brilliantly basic solution to the problem of the super-rich (the profiteers from his venue’s cloakroom included, I hope). Authoritative, generous with his amusement at all he surveys and as brilliantly blunt as only the Glasgow-accented can be, Bridges shepherds us through this tour d’horizon of his life and world via laugh after irresistible laugh.Touringuntil 31 MarchExplore more on these topicsComedyKevin BridgesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: We saw last time what reckless reliance on close polling led to. The omertà on rejoining has now been broken, but it would be folly to move too soon, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: We saw last time what reckless reliance on close polling led to. The omertà on rejoining has now been broken, but it would be folly to move too soon, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: An anti-Brexit protest outside the Houses of Parliament, 28 June 2016.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn anti-Brexit protest outside the Houses of Parliament, 28 June 2016.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionBrexitShall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yetPolly ToynbeeWe saw last time what reckless reliance on close polling led to. The omertà on rejoining has now been broken, but it would be folly to move too soonMon 19 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTShareWhen I hear that word again, a shudder runs down my spine. I want to groan, hold my head in my hands and wail. The horror! No, never again, not another referendum. But the idea is back in play asAndy Burnhamlooks for ways to reverse a decade of economic stagnation.As the prime minister dared to unlock the door to a Brussels reunion, you could hear Ode to Joy burst out from all remainers. But the prospect of a re-run of the most self-destructive vote in our history is dismaying.Remember that morning a decade ago. First came Sunderland’s 12.20am result, a 61.3% vote to leave, but there was still hope for remainers … until the BBC’s 4.40am verdict that leave had won. In that second a great rift tore across the country. Remainers, dubbed remoaners, never recovered. UK politics became a circus: we who paraded as the west’s strong and stable “mother of parliaments” ran wildly through seven prime ministers in 10 years. Both Labour and Tory parties were wrecked by the most shattering event of our political lifetime. It is a wound neither has dared to reopen.Only now Burnham has finally broken the spell ofBrexitsilence, aiming to rejoin, while the Tories will stay in the wilderness until they repent the Brexit disaster they inflicted on the country.As Burnham sets out to explore all the options, outriders scout the way back in. Making the strong case for full EU membership, IPPR, the thinktank closest to Labour, haspublished a weighty reportthis week on how it can happen and why it must: we need it for prosperity, security and democracy. It has left us dangerously alone and friendless in a world of great power blocs. Our once reliable ally, the US, is never to be fully trusted again now we know what its people are capable of voting for. And so the warmth of familiar democracies across the Channel looks welcoming (at least for now). Make this bid to rejoin about who we are, bonding with where we belong, emotionally and historically. We have discovered “sovereignty” is a mirage: every treaty and trade deal requires sharing it with allies.Within a year, a majority of people in the UK thoughtBrexit was a mistake(not quite the same as regretting their own vote). Now we know that Brexit has robbed us of a walloping 8% of GDP.IPPR and Persuasion UK polling finds52% want to rejoin, 29% to stay out. Support grows by the year, partly as older people drop off their perches and young pro-Europeans join the electoral roll. As the IPPR tested every option from Keir Starmer’s slight reset to full membership, the least popular was leaving things as they are. The current Boris Johnson/Lord Frost deal is so dysfunctional that Burnham says keeping it would be a“dereliction of duty”. As ever ignoring the public mood, last year Kemi Badenoch wrote to the EU ambassador warning that, if elected, she wouldrepeal any change, an act of near-treason that could sabotage negotiations in Brussels that start next month. Watch Michael Gove, arch-Brexit manipulator, telling the Guardian’sAditya Chakrabortty heregrets nothing, blaming others for failing to capitalise on those illusory Brexit benefits. Would that bleating work? I think not.But is this shift to 52% v 29% strong enough to dare throw the dice and risk everything? No, not quite yet. The IPPR admits it is still “soft”, and there are familiar echoes of what happened last time. After years in which it felt as if we could talk about nothing else, the EU now has reassuringly low salience. But that’s just as it was until Ukip and Tory Brexiters turbocharged what had been a non-issue. As before, polling figures that encouraged David Cameron to breeze arrogantly into a referendum looked sufficient to someone who assumed he would win. This time we know better. Prepare for Dominic Cummings et al rising from their coffins with Brexit defibrillators to shock new life into the issue. Nigel Farage was at it on Sunday, claiming the EU would charge Britain£42bn a year to rejoin.Brexit’s back – but are British voters ready to contemplate a reversal?Read moreTesting arguments for both sides, this report reveals traps to avoid and what people like about rejoining. Red lights flash over joining the euro, scrapping our other trade deals, giving up fishing rights and high contributions to the EU budget. Top of the most effective reasons for rejoining is passport queues. Second comessecurity: Ukraine has exposed this dangerous Trump/Putin world. Third is the need to bring lost foreign investment back to Britain.But reasoned, fact-based focus groups in a calm and rational atmosphere can’t begin to replicate the monstrous lies, fabrications and devilry of a TikTok, Instagram and X referendum campaign. Remember the £350m-a-week bus, the Turks are coming, immigration will end and, best of all, “take back control”. Of what? Everything! That’s what referendums do.So not yet. The case for joining has to be powerfully made, the argument won overwhelmingly for allied EU forces to circle the wagons against what Peter Ricketts, ex-national security adviser, along with the head of MI5, warns are“more reckless, more dangerous”cyber-attacks on vital services, such as energy, water, transport, banking or air traffic control. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, meeting with the EU home affairs commissioner today to restoredata cooperation on crime and migrationis a reminder of how insanely self-destructive Brexit was.In a decade, Britain has changed. Though Brexiters will threaten floods of migrants storming the border on joining the EU, IPPR polling shows freedom of movement no longer alarms voters as it once did. The cost of living is now the top national concern, not immigration. Look how poorer countries have caught up to us: per capita income in Bucharest, Romania’s capital, is far higher than Sunderland’s.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the EU has changed too. The question is what kind ofEuropewe would join if Marine Le Pen and the Alternative für Deutschland became its new axis of power. Here’s the answer: that would make joining even more urgent, to be inside to influence what we can, bolstering the democrats. Staying out leaves us powerless.This report sets to work on the campaign Burnham ignited when he proposed going“all the way”. The goal is clear and the need is growing urgent. As the EU ambassador told the Guardian’s Patrick Wintour, the ball is in our court. Brussels,he said, is “ready to engage”, once Britain decides what it wants.Let’s decide, but proceed with extreme caution. Would you risk the next general election by putting this into Labour’s manifesto, certain to become the right’s battle-flag? Yes, when a strong pro-EU campaign makes it winnable. But there should be no referendum until public opinion is so solid that it would be a mere rubber-stamping of the overwhelming public will.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsBrexitOpinionEuropean UnionEuropeAndy BurnhamForeign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: My critics think speaking fluently is vital for fee-paying pupils, but not for anyone else. Here’s why I reject that | Lucy Powell | The Guardian
description: We are accused of dumbing down, but that’s nonsense: this is levelling up. All the evidence shows helping children articulate improves their life chances, says Labour’s deputy leader Lucy Powell
Author: Lucy Powell
Headline: We are accused of dumbing down, but that’s nonsense: this is levelling up. All the evidence shows helping children articulate improves their life chances, says Labour’s deputy leader Lucy Powell
Content: ‘In a fast-changing world, every young person deserves the confidence to speak up’Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In a fast-changing world, every young person deserves the confidence to speak up’Photograph: sturti/Getty ImagesOpinionEducationMy critics think speaking fluently is vital for fee-paying pupils, but not for anyone else. Here’s why I reject thatLucy PowellWe are accused of dumbing down, but that’s nonsense: this is levelling up. All the evidence shows helping children articulate improves their life chancesLucy Powell is UK education secretary and deputy leader of the Labour partyMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrivate schools don’t leave confident communication to chance. They teach it. Debating, public speaking, presentations, interview preparation. It’s all part of the deal. And parents paying the fees would soon have something to say if it wasn’t. They know that being able to speak up, make your case and hold your own can open doors. I want that for every young person, wherever they grow up and whichever school they go to.This matters now more than ever.Young peopleare more connected than they’ve ever been, yet too many feel isolated and unheard. Social media is transforming their friendships and relationships. Artificial intelligence is changing the world they will work in. And in an age dominated by screens and algorithms, the human ability to connect, communicate and make yourself heard has never been more important. But the ability to find your voice should never depend on your parents’ income or the school you attend.Spoken communication is not a soft skill or a bolt on. That is why we are strengthening oracy across the curriculum, from primary to post-16, in all types of lessons and subjects. Being good or not good at these skills affects whether a young person can get ahead. Yet critics have called our proposals a sign of “dumbing down” and a departure from high standards. This is hypocrisy. Support for developing these skills has stretched across political divides for years. It’s what we want, but also the wish of Conservatives, such as ex schools ministerNick Gibband former culture ministerLucy Frazer.I do not accept a two-tier system where confident communication is seen as essential for children whose parents can afford school fees, but optional for everyone else.Raising standards means giving children knowledge, and the confidence to use it, hold their own, make their case, seize opportunities and succeed in work and life. And the evidence supports this. The Education Endowment Foundation identifies oral language approaches asamong the most effective interventions available, with particularly strong benefits for disadvantaged pupils, delivering six months’ worth of additional progress in primary school and five months in secondary school.Earlier this week, author Michael Rosenwelcomed a rebalancingtowards speaking as a key component of how we use language, calling it “a great bridge between the mind and the page”, and the basis of our thinking.And former general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Geoff Barton,now chair of the Oracy Education Commission, pointed to high-performing systems in Japan, Singapore and the Netherlands, where pupils in maths, for example, are expected to explain their reasoning, listen to others and defend their approach. Far from lowering standards, he said it makes them better mathematicians.Employers understand this too. When they talk about work readiness, they mean being able to articulate yourself, work with others, respond to feedback and deal confidently with customers and clients. A recent Chartered Management Institutesurveyfound managers concerned about gaps in workplace readiness, specifically highlighting gaps in communication skills.The evidence has not changed, the politics has. Because this was never really about standards. It was about who gets the chance to succeed. And if we’re serious about social mobility, raising standards and tackling the fact that one in eight young people are not in education, employment or training, we cannot pretend that the ability to communicate, persuade, present ideas and work with others does not matter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a fast-changing world, every young person deserves the confidence to speak up, the skills to be heard and the power to shape their own future.Lucy Powell is education secretary and deputy leader of theLabourpartyExplore more on these topicsEducationOpinionYoung peopleSchoolsPrivate schoolsLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: After the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: Far-right extremism and rhetoric is coming from activists and unvetted councillors, but party leaders who peddle fear and rage can’t escape blame, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: Far-right extremism and rhetoric is coming from activists and unvetted councillors, but party leaders who peddle fear and rage can’t escape blame, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Nigel Farage at a Reform rally in Doncaster, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage at a Reform rally in Doncaster, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionHate crimeAfter the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really isOwen JonesFar-right extremism and rhetoric is coming from activists and unvetted councillors, but party leaders who peddle fear and rage can’t escape blameMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.31 EDTShareWho are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists? As thehead of MI5 warnsthat anti-migrant haters are increasingly considering terrorist attacks, it is surely a question we must ask. After all, the role of hate preachers in Islamist terrorism has long been debated.After the London Bridge Islamist terrorist attack in 2017, Nigel Faragedemandedthat Sadiq Khan – “as the first Muslim mayor of London” – declare that he would do all he could “to work with the Muslim community to drive out the extremist preachers from our mosques” and to fight radicalisation in schools and prisons. More recently, he suggested that Muslim parents in the United Arab Emiratesfearedsending their children to study in British universities “given the risk of radicalisation here”. His colleague Suella Braverman agrees. “There should be zero tolerance for hate preachers in mosques or radicalising imams in prisons,”she says.And what of Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s self-styled shadow chancellor, whowarnsof “terrorist influencers and radicalising inmates” in prisons anddemands“complete zero tolerance on hate preachers”?Yeton the very dayof MI5’s warning, Jenrick declared that Royal Marines would be deployed to turn back migrants in the Channel – and that “if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so”. Here was one of Britain’s most prominent politicians injecting violence into our already deeply toxic debate about immigration.Farage sought to backtrack on Jenrick’s behalf, claiming force “would be used only if soldiers were fired at” and insisting that Jenrick had been “utterly misconstrued”. This made little sense: theHome Officesaid last year that it had no record of firearms being brought in via small boats over the previous seven years.Not that long ago, there was supposed to be a strict demarcation between the mainstream right and extremists. No longer. Consider theITV investigation, screened last night, that exposed Reform councillors describing Asian families as “parasites” and Black children as “animals”. Another spoke of training young men to round up migrants “street by street, house by house”. One spoke of holding asylum seekersin “concentration camps”. Another Reform figure spoke of criminals facing“Sunday morning rose garden executions”. Some of these individuals have since stood down. But while the leaders of Reform have not yet plunged to such extreme depths, what effect might their own words have on impressionable people?Consider that last week, Jenrick appeared on the YouTube channel of former GB News presenter Dan Wootton, a supporter of bothTommy Robinsonand the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, the latter of whom hecalls“a British hero”.Take the anti-migrant protests outside hotels housing asylum seekers. Last August, Jenrick turned up tosuch a demonstrationin Epping, Essex, where far-right activists were also present, praising the “peaceful, patriotic protesters”. A month earlier, following clashes which left eight police officers injured,Bravermaninsisted the protests had been “largely … peaceful”.Farage, meanwhile, warnedthat Britain was close to “civil disobedience on a vast scale” and said he understood the anger in Epping: “You bet your life I do.”Asked about Thomas’s group, Patriot Platform, Jenricksympathisedwith masked protesters, arguing that, without a face covering, “you can lose your job, you can be cancelled”. When he was pushed on whether he would accept Robinson supporters into Reform, Jenrick’s response was telling. “Ultimately [it’s] not my call who comes into the party, that’s for Nigel and others in the party to determine,”he said. “But look, I want to build as broad a coalition as possible of people who share my values, who want us to fix this country.” How to square this with Jenrick’s denunciation of Islamist hate preachers?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis civil war on the British right is a charade – its politics are more united than ever | Jonathan LiewRead moreIn the recent past, Reform politicians –Farage,JenrickandBravermanamong them – have described migrants arriving in small boats as an “invasion”. It is the language of war: a nation under siege, an enemy to be repelled. It is hardly a leap for fearful people to conclude that those who resort to violence are not really dangerous extremists, but patriots defending their country.We can hardly forget that Farage called for “pure, cold rage” in response to alleged police failings over the murder of Henry Nowak. Hours later, violence erupted on the streets of Southampton. He increasinglyembracesthe language of white resentment, claiming that “anti-whiteness is institutionalised into every aspect of public life”, calling diversity policies a form of “social cleansing” and warning of white Britons becoming a minority by the end of the century. Such rhetoric echoes the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which argues that white people are being deliberately displaced by mass immigration.Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, meanwhile, describes Conservative and Labour politicians as “traitors to their country”,warning– without elaboration – that a “reckoning is coming”.None of these statements constitute a direct incitement to violence. But taken together, they can conjure up a terrifying picture in impressionable minds: a nation and a people under attack, its own political leaders conspiring in its destruction and time running out to save it.This can’t be divorced from rightwing media outlets echoing and amplifying such rhetoric. We’ve already had thefar-right uprisingof August 2024, when racist mobs assaulted people of colour in the streets, attacked mosques and migrant-owned businesses, and tried to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers. We’ve had far-right terrorist attacks, such as the neo-Naziattempted murderof an Eritrean man in 2024, thefirebombingof an immigration centre in Dover in 2022, the attack on the Finsbury Park mosque in 2017 and the murder of Jo Cox a year earlier.None made a dent on the national discourse. It has only become cruder, more toxic and more inflammatory. So, with all we know, time to ask again. Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists?Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West, is out now. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsHate crimeOpinionThe far rightImmigration and asylumReform UKCrimecommentShareReuse this content

title: The housing crisis is now global. It shows just how undemocratic our nations have become  | Leilani Farha | The Guardian
description: When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power?, asks the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, Leilani Farha
Author: Leilani Farha
Headline: When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power?, asks the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, Leilani Farha
Content: Illustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nathalie Lees/The GuardianOpinionHousingThe housing crisis is now global. It shows just how undemocratic our nations have becomeLeilani FarhaWhen we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power?Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housingMon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTShareIn the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada, and spoke to one of the residents. He was living in a tent in the shadow of brand new skyscrapers, and had been homeless for about five years. At one point he swivelled around, pointed up at a crane on the skyline, and said: “Who are they building those for? Definitely not for me.”He was right. And he captured something experienced by ordinary people around the world: the growing conviction that the housing system is no longer tethered to their needs. What he was pointing at is not just a housing crisis. It is a crisis of democracy.Democracy promises that our living conditions are shaped by all of us, regardless of our station in life. Yet decisions about housing have been systematically removed from democratic control and handed to financial actors such as private equity firms, pension funds and real-estate investment trusts. Working hand in hand with governments and banks, these actors have decoupled the price of housing from what ordinary people earn. They’ve transformed our homes into a toy for wealthy investors. I call this allianceHousingInc.The tools available to the large financial actors driving and profiting from the housing crisis are not available to the rest of us. They hire armies of lobbyists to squash rent-control laws. They fund political campaigns. They rotate in and out of government positions. They are in the rooms and hallways where decisions are made.Even governments trying to fight the growing influence of the financial sector in housing face intense pressure. In Copenhagen, after the private equity giant Blackstone bought up apartment blocks across the city, renovated them and, in some cases, doubled the rent for new tenants, the Danish parliament passed legislation barring new owners from raising rents on renovated apartments for five years. While this “Blackstone law”, as it was commonly called, was a brave measure, it was weaker than the government had wanted. Kaare Dybvad, then Denmark’s housing minister, had proposed a 10-year freeze. Faced with fury from landlords and pension funds, and needing rightwing party votes to pass it, he cut it to five.The average tenant, the person experiencing homelessness, the young person locked out of the housing market – what do they have? They have a vote. That is all.And the vote changes less than we are promised. As the economist Yanis Varoufakis hasargued, elections no longer determine economic policy. Governments of the left and the right come and go, and regardless of who is in power, rents keep rising, because the economic model always stays the same: money flows to wherever the returns are highest, which means into unproductive assets such as real estate, and away from the public investment that would actually house people. We can change our governments. We cannot, it seems, change the economic policies they all adhere to.Who decided that financial firms could use our homes as investments? Not the public. Consider the bundling of mortgages into securities, which laid the groundwork for the 2008 financial crisis, or the decision in more than 40 jurisdictions to exempt real-estate investment trusts from corporate income tax. Both happened out of public view, shaped by governments and financial actors, with no public debate.The same thing happens with other kinds of housing investment. Take short-term rentals in Athens. While democracy may have been born there, it hasn’t always thrived. After the global financial crisis, Greeks were held to brutal austerity measures against their will. Property values collapsed, wages fell and ordinary families struggled to make ends meet. For many property owners, renting to tourists through short-let platforms such as Airbnb became a lifeline – a way to generate income from an asset that had lost most of its value.But what began as a survival strategy for families became an investment strategy for foreign buyers. The governmentintroduceda “golden visa” programme in 2013, offering residency to any foreigner who bought Greek property. Thousands did – not to live there, but to convert apartments into short-term rentals, banking on Greece’s tourism industry as a good investment. As foreign capital flooded in, long-term housing became scarcer, rents spiked and neighbourhoods such as Exarchia and Koukaki began to change beyond recognition.Athenians protested and their government responded by sending in the riot police and steamrollering dissent to defend its decisions.What’s on offer in terms of genuine civic engagement for the people most affected by the housing crisis tends to be defanged, inadequate or inaccessible. Tenants who speak out about poor conditions risk eviction, and they need landlord references for their next place. People holding down multiple jobs just to pay their rent don’t have time for city council meetings, or surveys and questionnaires that lead nowhere. When people have no means to participate in decisions about their own housing, they feel abandoned by government. This creates a vacuum thatrightwing populismis perfectly designed to fill.Which brings us back to democracy’s promise. Can it be a democracy when a place to live is governed not by human beings and their needs but by financial firms and profit, pricing people out of their homes and onto the streets? Around the world, people are forcing that question into the open.In Madrid, 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal (better known asMaricarmen) had lived in the same flat for 71 years when the investment firm that owns itdemanded she pay€2,650 (£2,280) a month instead of €500. On 23 September, after earlier attempts had been blocked, police cleared hundreds of her neighbours from the doorway and she was evicted. That evening, thousands took to the streets of Madrid. Within days there were tens of thousands, a protest camp had filled the Puerta del Sol square, and demonstrations had spread to cities across the country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSix days after the eviction, the Spanish government passed emergency decrees extending rental contracts and shielding vulnerable tenants from eviction. People called it the “Maricarmen decree”. Three days later,parliament struck it down. The parties of the right had voted against it, one of them calling automatic lease renewal an “expropriation of property rights”. Maricarmen passed away not long after.In Berlin in 2021, more than one million people – 59.1% of valid votes –backed a referendumto take the homes owned by the city’s largest corporate landlords into public ownership. The result was non-binding, and successive governments have ignored it. So Berliners used the one tool they had, blunt as it was. On 20 September this year, Die Linke, which had campaigned on the promise to carry out the referendum,won the state electionsand became the largest party in the city’s parliament for the first time. One day later, before a government had even been formed, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced that he would fast-track a national lawbanningthe “expropriation” of housing. Berliners had voted for a change in economic policy on housing, and the chancellor then made it clear that this was not theirs to decide.But the movement had known better than to rely on the broken promise of democracy. Last year, it wrote an expropriation law itself, so that it could be passed by a willing government – or, failing that, put to a second, binding vote. In its own words: “Alles muss man selber machen” – we have to do everything ourselves.That is what it takes to reclaim democracy.Leilani Farha is the 2026 CBC Massey lecturer. This piece is based on her new book:Housing Inc.: A Global Takeover and Our Fight for Home. She is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing and the global director of the international human rights organisation,The ShiftExplore more on these topicsHousingOpinionCommunitiesVenture capitalSpainGreeceEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: This carnival of protest on the streets of Delhi has shaken Narendra Modi like nothing before | Meena Kandasamy | The Guardian
description: The singing, dancing and sheer joy in the face of police brutality at the protests led by the Cockroach Janta party show people no longer fear India’s regime, says poet and writer Meena Kandasamy
Author: Meena Kandasamy
Headline: The singing, dancing and sheer joy in the face of police brutality at the protests led by the Cockroach Janta party show people no longer fear India’s regime, says poet and writer Meena Kandasamy
Content: Demonstrators and police at a protest march organised by India’s Cockroach Janta party, Delhi, 12 October 2026.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDemonstrators and police at a protest march organised by India’s Cockroach Janta party, Delhi, 12 October 2026.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty ImagesOpinionIndiaThis carnival of protest on the streets of Delhi has shaken Narendra Modi like nothing beforeMeena KandasamyThe singing, dancing and sheer joy in the face of police brutality at the protests led by the Cockroach Janta party show people no longer fear India’s regimeMon 19 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTShareIn July, as supporters of the Cockroach movementtook to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.People inIndiahave been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) has shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.This time the Cockroaches aredemanding the resignationof India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through apurge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions andarrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, aninternet blackoutin the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.So atprotests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora,Aishe Ghosh,Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, thestreets of Delhiwere filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forcesnumbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka,were detainedand subsequently sent to jail for five days.Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is MikhailBakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.One of the most popular slogans has beenJab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai(“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Bora was released from detention the following morning, and Dipke could walk free on conditional bail.For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.The powerlessness of the state could alsobe seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summonedMeta officials over the summerand imposed aninternet shutdownearlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIndia’s cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown – The LatestRead moreFor the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying:“This istandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and“This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in ChennaiExplore more on these topicsIndiaOpinionNarendra ModiProtestYoung peopleSouth and central AsiacommentShareReuse this content

title: Saudi Arabia is learning the hard way: they can’t count on Trump for protection | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: After Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for help
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: After Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for help
Content: ‘But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreen‘But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APOpinionMohammed bin SalmanSaudi Arabia is learning the hard way: they can’t count on Trump for protectionMohamad BazziAfter Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for helpMon 19 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTShareFor years, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince,Mohammed bin Salman, cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump and his son-in-law and former top adviser, Jared Kushner. The prince understood the president’s transactional approach to power: he signed deals to buy billions of dollars’ worth of US weapons and invested billions more in American companies.Days after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, Prince Mohammed pledged to expand investment and trade with the USby $600bnover four years. He later promised to increase that investment to nearly $1tn, although it wasn’t entirely clear how Saudi Arabia would manage to plough a sum close to the kingdom’sentire annual GDPinto a foreign economy over a few years.On a visit to Washington last November, Prince Mohammed sealed a defense cooperation agreement with the US and signed a deal for the monarchy to buy dozens of F-35 stealth fighter jets, America’s most advanced warplane.Behind this flurry of deal-making, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler expected the US to defend the kingdom if it was attacked, as Washington has done in the past. But Prince Mohammed, like the leaders of other Arab petrostates who have investedbillions of dollarsto appease Trump, is learning a hard lesson: never count on Trump to protect you.Over the summer, Trump’s war against Iran rekindled a years-long conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen. Last month, as the Houthis intensified their attacks on Saudi territory and the kingdom’s Yemeni allies, the prince called Trumpmultiple timesin September, urging him to launch US airstrikes against the Houthis, who are allied with Iran.For now, Trump has resisted appeals from Prince Mohammed to drag American forces into the Houthi-Saudi battle – one of the best foreign policy decisions of an otherwise disastrous second term.But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways. On 10 October, the Houthisfired a cruise missileat the international airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300.After that attack, when reporters in Washington asked Trump whether he would be more willing to order US strikes against Yemeni rebels, he was non-committal. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision.”The Houthi-Saudi conflagration is the latest illustration of Trump’s decision to attack Iran spiraling into an unpredictable regional conflict, as Middle East experts and someUS intelligence officialswarned would happen. It also reveals that Saudi Arabia and other Arab Gulf countries can’t rely on the Trump administration to protect them, even after they have spent tens of billions of dollars to buy American weapons and build US bases – some of which were decimated byIranian attacksover the past seven months.Trump’s resistance to ordering US attacks on the Houthis has been particularly embarrassing for Prince Mohammed.Billions of dollarsin Saudi investments have been directed into Kushner’s private equity firm and the president’s family business, the Trump Organization. Now Saudi Arabia is being rewarded with lukewarm US support against Yemeni rebels.For now, Trump seems worried about expanding the US role in a regional war that is deeply unpopular among Americans, including segments of Trump’s own Maga base that believed his repeated promises not to start new wars. The Iran conflict has increased gasoline and other energy prices, driving up the US inflation rate to3.7% in September, weeks before midterm elections where Republicans are facing widespread anger over the cost of living.It’s unclear if Trump will continue to resist launching airstrikes against theHouthisafter next month’s elections, when Democrats could win control of both houses of Congress. If the Houthis keep up their attacks on Saudi infrastructure and capture more territory held by Yemen’s Saudi-aligned government, Trump could face more pressure to intervene from the Saudis and hawkish Republicans. And he would be less constrained by worries about expanding the Iran war shortly before the midterms.Prince Mohammed, who is reeling from the war’s impact on Saudi oil exports, could also ratchet up pressure on Trump by threatening to withhold Saudi investments in the US economy and the president’s family business. That’s another danger underlying Trump’s corrupt and transactional style of governing: US interests can be subsumed by wealthy autocrats who try to exploit Trump through his extensive business ventures. In this case, rather than bombing one side to help another, there’s a clear US interest in promoting diplomacy and de-escalating the Houthi-Saudi conflict.Early in Trump’s first term, the Saudi leader developed a relationship with the president and his key advisers, especially Kushner. In May 2017, Trump upended tradition and choseSaudi Arabiaas the first stop of his maiden overseas trip as president. The Saudis realized that Trump craved flattery: they feted him with banquets in gilded palaces and awarded him the kingdom’s highest civilian honor.At the time, Prince Mohammed was consolidating power as the monarchy’s de facto ruler under his ailing father, King Salman. The prince had also presided over a series of destructive regional policies, including a Saudi-led invasion of Yemen in 2015, and a subsequent campaign to blockade the kingdom’s tiny neighbor, Qatar.Trump and Kushner proved to be invaluable allies to the young, ambitious royal. In October 2018, Jamal Khashoggi, a dissident Saudi journalist, was assassinated inside the Saudi consulate in Istanbul by a 15-member hit team, who dismembered his body with a bone saw.US intelligence agenciesquickly concludedthat Prince Mohammed had ordered the killing, but Trump protected the royal from US sanctions and pressure from outraged members of Congress.A few years later, the prince found a way to return Trump’s favor.
