In January 2021, after a mob of Trump supporters stormed the US Capitol in an attempt to overturn the presidential election results, US banks and several large companies distanced themselves from the Trump Organization. But Saudi Arabia stood by Trump while he was out of power, generating real estate deals andnew golf partnershipsthat helped Trump’s family business at one of its weakest points.After the uproar over Khashoggi’s assassination, the prince stayed away from the US for seven years – until Trump returned to office and invited him for a victory tour last November. Trump rolled out the red carpet, hosting Prince Mohammed for lunch with top administration officials at the White House. Trump also held a black-tie dinner with business executives who were eager to solicit new investments from the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund, which is controlled by the crown prince.Beyond the extravagant welcome, Trump also defended Prince Mohammed when a reporter asked about Khashoggi’s killing. “A lot of people didn’t like that gentleman that you’re talking about,”Trump said, referring to the murdered journalist, who was a US permanent resident and contributor to the Washington Post.“Things happen,” Trump added, as he sat next to the Saudi leader in the Oval Office. He insisted that the prince “knew nothing about” Khashoggi’s assassination – despite the CIA reaching the opposite conclusion during Trump’s first term.Trump spent years defending and protecting his Saudi ally and benefactor. In the coming weeks, Trump risks expanding US involvement in a disastrous regional war to help the prince.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Hagop Kevorkian Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsMohammed bin SalmanOpinionDonald TrumpSaudi ArabiaTrump administrationMiddle East and north AfricaUS politicsHouthiscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The scenes of social unrest and violence at the weekend are an ominous portent, ahead of elections which may deliver a far-right presidency
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The scenes of social unrest and violence at the weekend are an ominous portent, ahead of elections which may deliver a far-right presidency
Content: A car burns at Place de la République during a protest on 17 October 2026.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APView image in fullscreenA car burns at Place de la République during a protest on 17 October 2026.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APOpinionFranceThe Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political momentEditorialThe scenes of social unrest and violence at the weekend are an ominous portent, ahead of elections which may deliver a far-right presidencyMon 19 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTShareIn Emmanuel Macron’s bookRevolution, published ahead of the 2017 presidential election that he went on to win, he promised to restore hope to a country that was losing faith in its future. As Mr Macron’s lame-duck second term enters its last phase against a quasi-insurrectionary backdrop of torched public buildings and looted shops, the failure of that political project appears total.The worstscenesof urban violence for years overshadowed a weekend ofprotestthat gravely undermined what is left of the French president’s authority. As police lost control of the streets, more than 2,000 shops were ransacked. Far-left groups targeted town halls and local buildings, and engaged in pitched battles with the police, whose disastrously heavy-handed response to last week’s high school protests has succeeded only in escalating tensions.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/AFP/GettyIn a statement on Sunday evening, Mr Macron rightly condemned what he described as episodes of “unbridled violence”. On the far right, Marine Le Pen is already exploiting a national sense of dismay to present herself as the law-and-order solution to the crisis. But the shocking actions of a minority should not obscure the significance of the vast, peaceful demonstrations that took place throughout France on Saturday. Calls to unite the student protests and the yellow vest movement, which disrupted Mr Macron’s first term over cost of living issues,mobilisedup to 800,000 people.The root cause of the unrest is a widespread perception that France’s social contract is broken. The young feel let down by anunderfundedand unequal education system, and are fearful of the future impact of AI and the climate emergency. As is increasingly the caseacrossEurope, they no longer trust mainstream politicians to find answers. The scale of the weekend protests showed that gen Z’s discontent has merged with that felt in the country’s neglected towns andbanlieues, which have suffered repeated economic shocks since the Covid pandemic.The obtuse and stubborn response from Mr Macron has been to double down on a cost‑cutting agenda to reduce France’s public debt, in order to appease the financial markets. But in an era where the asset-rich have continued to flourish, and the wealthiest have done best of all, to argue that that there is no alternative to spending less on schools andhealthcarewon’t wash. The economist Thomas Pikettypointedout during last week’s student protests that the boom in private wealth means that, despite the size of its public debt, “France has never been richer”.Mr Macron’s recklessdecisionto call a snap election in 2024, which cost him his majority, left him a diminished political figure. His biggest subsequent error has been to haughtily persist with the economics of austerity, despite clear evidence of deepening political polarisation and rising popular anger. With each week that passes, the social consequences appear more ominous, ahead of presidential elections in six months’ time.The latestpollssuggest that the far right’s huge lead is widening ahead of that contest. Meanwhile, the hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to outscore progressive rivals, though the numbers suggest that he would heavily lose a runoff against Ms Le Pen. In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong
Content: ‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreen‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APOpinionTrump administrationThe Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain awayEditorialRussia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strongMon 19 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTShareDoes Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history ofchummyphone calls, high-profilemeetingsand attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees tonegotiateUkraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales arefallingfrom European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be abetrayal. European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.Photograph: China Pool/GettyTheWall Street Journallaid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite mostanalystssaying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. MoreRepublicansshould find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from theWhite House. Heated denials from the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, are no substitute for answers.A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “strategically and culturally vital”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments mustprepareto meet that challenge.History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo theThree Emperors’ Leaguethat brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in1881, the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Funding social care is a collective responsibility | Social care | The Guardian
description: Letters: Roger Steer says the solution is to adopt the NHS model, Janet Dubé suggests an audit, while Sally Byers says language that respects people living with dementia is crucial
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Roger Steer says the solution is to adopt the NHS model, Janet Dubé suggests an audit, while Sally Byers says language that respects people living with dementia is crucial
Content: ‘The fact that the state’s bill for residential care increased more than twentyfold within seven years is scandalous.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘The fact that the state’s bill for residential care increased more than twentyfold within seven years is scandalous.’Photograph: Getty/iStockphotoSocial careLettersFunding social care is a collective responsibilityRoger Steersays the solution is to adopt the NHS model,Janet Dubésuggests an audit, whileSally Byerssayslanguage that respects people living with dementia is crucialMon 19 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTSharePolly Toynbee asks a seemingly difficult question and discusses a knotty issue (In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?, 13 October). Her question is framed as an issue of individual choice inviting the response: “Not me if I can avoid it.”The responsible answer is, of course, all of us – collectively. It is an uninsurable risk that can only be solved equitably and efficiently as a collective solution. By entangling the issue of funding with provision of services, moral clarity is lost. Issues of matching funding distort and influence the level of care provided and ensure that progress toward resolving the question of who determines the need for care is delayed.The solution is to fund social care in the same way as theNHSwas envisaged: as a right, free at the point of need, and funded out of general taxation as part of annually managed expenditure, like pensions and social security, as needs are presented and professionally agreed.The Treasury has the ways and means, and nothing more needs to be discussed. The additional costs as a percentage of GDP are small and affordable by reference to other countries.The issue of affordability is exaggerated out of all proportion by politicians who are afraid of being accused of raising taxes. In fact, because of the very high economic multiplier effect of boosting spending on low-paid workers, it is certain that it will pay for itself without impacting government deficits (unlike defence spending).Andy Burnham knows this, and needs to overrule his cautious advisers. This is his big chance to demonstrate leadership. People don’t vote for ditherers.Roger SteerSheffieldThank you, Polly Toynbee, for your article about your visit to Liverpool withLouise Casey. Ms Casey is clearly right when she says: “If it’s public money, it should mainly be publicly run.”I am old enough to recall the 1970s Tory privatisation of social care, and I remember sales of council facilities being forced through by rate-capping. Blatantly paying staff in the private sector less and lowering their standards and conditions of service was supposed to save money. I wasn’t aware at the time of the massive shift of public money into private establishments. The fact that the state’s bill for residential care increased more than twentyfold within seven years is scandalous, and should have been at the time.Was the Tory government from 1979 the most ideologically driven UK government ever? Surely it is not too late to carry out an “audit” of the transfer of public assets to private individuals and companies? Until Ms Toynbee’s article, I would have suggested starting with council housing or water boards. Now I think social care is the place to start, soon.Janet DubéPeebles, Scottish BordersPolly Toynbee’s description of people with advanced dementia as having “glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape” and “that terrible human vacancy” is deeply troubling. Such language dehumanises people and reinforces the stigma surrounding dementia.People living with dementia deserve, like everyone else, to be treated and spoken about with respect and dignity. I suggest she consult theguide to language for journalistsproduced by the Dementia Engagement and Empowerment Project, published in 2014 and written by people with lived experience of the impact of careless descriptors.Sally ByersSheffieldHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Pleaseemailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in ourletterssection.Explore more on these topicsSocial careLouise CaseyAgeingLabourAndy BurnhamNHSHealthlettersShareReuse this content

title: We need to stop disinformation in UK political adverts. Here’s a chance to do so | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Letters: Alex Tait on a proposed amendment to the representation of the people bill, and Dr Joseph Mullen on Russian interference in the Brexit referendum
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Alex Tait on a proposed amendment to the representation of the people bill, and Dr Joseph Mullen on Russian interference in the Brexit referendum
Content: Andy Burnham has said that it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum.Photograph: Tuomas A Lehtinen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has said that it is clear Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum.Photograph: Tuomas A Lehtinen/Getty ImagesBrexitLettersWe need to stop disinformation in UK political adverts. Here’s a chance to do soAlex Taiton a proposed amendment to the representation of the people bill, andDr Joseph Mullenon Russian interference in the Brexit referendumMon 19 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.19 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s comments about Russian interference in Brexit (Report, 11 October) and the warning by the MI5 chief, Ken McCallum, against exaggerating its impact (Report, 13 October) risk overlooking another serious threat to electoral integrity: disinformation from our own political parties and campaigners.Foreign interference deserves scrutiny, but misleading factual claims in electoral advertising are unregulated, unlike in commercial advertising. We have four sets of rules to ensure an advert for a packet of sausages is accurate, but none for the most important advertising of all – ads that influence how we vote.With our fragmented five-party politics producing increasingly close elections, misleading advertising can be decisive. Brexit was decided by a 51.9%-48.1% vote split. Ourresearchinto May’s local elections found that 41.4% of wards in England were won by margins of less than 5%, with nine decided by a single vote. We also identified misleading electoral advertising in some of the closest contests.Regulating factual claims in electoral advertising was akey recommendationof the House of Lords select committee on democracy and digital technologies in 2020. Therepresentation of the people bill, currently going through parliament, offers an opportunity to act. An amendment covering the same scope attracted 37 MPs as sponsors in the Commons, and we are working with peers in the Lords to take it forward. Burnhamsigned upto our voluntary code for honest electoral advertising in 2024, which forms part of the proposed amendments.We should tackle foreign interference, but we can’t continue to ignore the disinformation put out by our own political parties.Alex TaitReform Political AdvertisingThe head of MI5 confirming thatRussiadid try to interfere in the Brexit referendum is highly significant to the result. The vote share achieved by the leave campaign was 51.9%, as against 48.1% for the remainers. This was a majority of just 3.8%. If Russian interference swayed just 2% of voting intentions, this would erode the much-vaunted majority of the leave group, and remainers would emerge as victors. MI5 should carry out an impact assessment of Russian interference using the most up-to-date AI, and attempt to quantify shifts in voting patterns. This would go a long way towards introducing a new referendum.Dr Joseph MullenFormer senior lecturer, University of ManchesterHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The cinema, punk music and swimming helped me through grief | Bereavement | The Guardian
description: Letter: Rachel Walsh responds to an article by Georgina Elliott in which she describes the comfort she felt sitting alone in the cinema after losing her brother
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Rachel Walsh responds to an article by Georgina Elliott in which she describes the comfort she felt sitting alone in the cinema after losing her brother
Content: ‘Being enveloped in water took me out of my physical numbness and grief and buoyed me up.’Photograph: SolStock/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Being enveloped in water took me out of my physical numbness and grief and buoyed me up.’Photograph: SolStock/GettyBereavementLettersThe cinema, punk music and swimming helped me through griefRachel Walshresponds to an article by Georgina Elliott in which she describes the comfort she felt sitting alone in the cinema after losing her brotherMon 19 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.19 EDTShareI could relate to Georgina Elliott’s finding comfort and relief in the dark at the cinema (The one change that worked: numb with grief, I sat in the dark, surrounded by strangers – and began to heal, 12 October). After my mum died, I felt like a balloon floating further and further from my life, incorporeal and ghostly.The cinema was a world within the world to live someone else’s life, experience their triumphs and adventures, and escape the sharpness of my own painful reality.Punk gigs also offered me relief from grief, their raw honesty stripping away at this distance, bringing me back to an immediacy that I could cope with, and giving me a feeling of solidarity and acceptance. I could go alone, not talk to anyone if I didn’t feel like it, yet still be accepted as a member. It was OK to be broken there – no one was trying to pretend anything was fixed, and that gave me relief.Later, swimming helped me recover. Being enveloped in water took me out of my physical numbness and buoyed me up, escaping the weight of grief pressing me down.To be weightless was freedom. To swim out into the sea and look at the vastness of the sky, and be alone with my thoughts, infused me with a peace. And a power. I felt strong swimming and moving through water. I recovered something frozen in me, a connection with the world, with my own power in it. I felt held and comforted there, as if by a parent’s love.Rachel WalshDublin, IrelandHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Birmingham was a BBC radio powerhouse. Now even The Archers is leaving | The Archers | The Guardian
description: Letters: Former BBC employee Owen Bentley laments the final nail in the coffin for what once was a hub of quality programming
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Former BBC employee Owen Bentley laments the final nail in the coffin for what once was a hub of quality programming
Content: An episode recording on the set of The Archers in 2008.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn episode recording on the set of The Archers in 2008.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianThe ArchersLettersBirmingham was a BBC radio powerhouse. Now even The Archers is leavingFormer BBC employeeOwen Bentleylaments the final nail in the coffin for what once was a hub of quality programmingMon 19 Oct 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTShareI can understand why the BBC is reluctant to build a new drama studio for The Archers when it moves to Digbeth, seeing that there is no other radio drama being made in Birmingham that would plump out its use (BBC to stop recording The Archers in Birmingham for first time in its 75-year history, 12 October).Is this to be the final nail in the coffin of programme-making for the national networks in the Midlands? At its peak in the 90s the Birmingham Network Radio department was the major provider of programmes to Radio 2 and 5 outside London, and for Radio 4 and 3 it had award-winning specialisms in features, environment, farming, drama and music programming plus, of course,The Archers.The radio studios were busy then contributing more than 3,000 hours per year to the networks before, in a fit of reorganisation, all programmes other than The Archers were scattered to Manchester, Bristol and London, a route that the everyday story of countryfolk may now follow.Owen BentleyFormerBBChead of network and local radio in the MidlandsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Davies ensures Spurs off the bottom after first win of season against Coventry | Premier League | The Guardian
description: James Maddison scored an excellent first goal, before Omar Marmoush and Ben Davies wrapped up the scoring as Spurs beat a stubborn Coventry 3-1
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: James Maddison scored an excellent first goal, before Omar Marmoush and Ben Davies wrapped up the scoring as Spurs beat a stubborn Coventry 3-1
Content: Ben Davies scored from just outside the area in stoppage time, which made it 3-1 to Spurs.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBen Davies scored from just outside the area in stoppage time, which made it 3-1 to Spurs.Photograph: Kieran McManus/ShutterstockPremier LeagueDavies ensures Spurs off the bottom after first win of season against CoventryJacob Steinbergat the Tottenham Hotspur StadiumMon 19 Oct 2026 17.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTottenham are level with Beyoncé at last. Progress is represented in Roberto De Zerbi’s side earning only their sixth home win in thePremier Leaguesince November 2024. Cynics will point out that this spectacular stadium has hosted as many Beyoncé gigs during that time, but Spurs are finally singing a happier tune after dragging themselves out of the bottom three thanks to a messy but gritty 3-1 win over Coventry.It was not especially convincing. Coventry raged at the second Spurs goal, delivered when Omar Marmoush responded to Jack Rudoni’s equaliser for the visitors with a vicious effort in the 59th minute. Relief poured out of Marmoush after his first goal since joining on loan from Manchester City, but should it have stood? The Egyptian forward, who otherwise had a quiet game, was fortunate not to be penalised for an elbow on Milan van Ewijk.‘Like a family’: De Zerbi credits players’ talk and bonding trip for improving TottenhamRead moreFrank Lampard looked bewildered. The night belonged to Spurs, who have their first win of the season. James Maddison marked his first start in 536 days by opening the scoring with a brilliant goal. Ben Davies, on as a substitute, calmed the nerves by drilling in the third goal in added time and the home fans were also cheered by Dejan Kulusevski coming on to make his first appearance after more than a season out.The hope for Spurs was that the sight of Kulusevski on the bench would give the crowd an emotional lift. The Swede was back in the squad for the first time since sustaining a knee injury in May 2025 and has been missed. Spurs, who have struggled without Kuluseveki’s creativity, needed to cling to the positivity after their resolute draw at Manchester United.The encouraging thing is that they have been starting games well. This time, though, there were some early jitters after De Zerbi’s switch to a back three. Mohammed Kudus was a surprise choice as an attacking right wing-back, Archie Gray partnered Sandro Tonali in midfield and Coventry had the first chance, a fast break ending with Tatsuhiro Sakamoto watching his deflected shot spin over.View image in fullscreenJack Rudoni beats Antonin Kinsky to give the visitors hope.Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianThere were a few groans, but Spurs showed rare mental fortitude and struck through another creator rebuilding his career after serious injury. Kudus, lively and direct, provided the spark with a dart past Jay Dasilva. The Ghanaian laid a pass off to Maddison and the No 10, whose every touch had been booed by Coventry supporters apparently still seething with the England international leaving his boyhood club 10 years ago, used his right instep to beat Carl Rushworth with a crisp bending shot from 25 yards.It was a lovely movement for Maddison, who beamed at his first goal since scoring in aEuropa League semi-finalagainst Bodø/Glimt on 1 May 2025. He slogged through his rehab, never giving in, and his enthusiasm was infectious. Even Lampard had to smile when Maddison tracked back to stop a counterattack and apologised after smashing the ball into the Coventry bench.Coventry were slow to respond. Not that Spurs were flowing before half-time. Maddison was involved in some bright moves and Dominic Solanke jabbed a shot over but De Zerbi must have wanted the passing to be sharper. A slick exchange between Sidiki Cherif and Brandon Thomas-Asante was a reminder that this was not over. Thomas-Asante surged past Jan Paul van Hecke and towards Antonin Kinsky, only for Micky van de Ven to intervene with a crucial challenge.Spurs did not heed the warning. A lethargic start to the second half featured Van Hecke ambling out of defence and losing the ball. Coventry countered, Rudoni pushing down the left. The midfielder exchanged passes with Caleb Yirenkyi and Spurs froze. Rudoni shot against Thomas-Asante, retrieved possession, chested the ball down and jabbed it past Kinsky to draw Coventry level.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJames Maddison curls his shot home for Tottenham’s first goal.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersStung into action, Spurs raised the intensity and Tonali sent two shots over. Coventry looked uncertain but they raged when the home side regained their lead. Marmoush took a pass, turned and caught Van Ewijk in the face with an elbow. Yet Andrew Madley permitted play to continue with the Coventry right-back on the floor, allowing Marmoush to spin into space and blast an exquisite shot past Rushworth from 20 yards.It was a stunning way for the Egyptian to score for the first time since May. There was no intervention from Paul Tierney, the video assistant referee, and the away end reacted with astonishment when the goal was replayed on the big screens.Coventry were fired by a sense of injustice. They pushed for another equaliser and produced a spell of concerted pressure, only for Spurs to defend their box with determination.De Zerbi sought more energy by bringing on Mateus Fernandes and Conor Gallagher. The Italian took his squad to Marbella for some warm weather training last week. Spurs, who pushed Coventry into 17th place, will hope sunnier times are on the way.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTottenham HotspurCoventry Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Money and medals over safety’: Nassar judge warns gymnasts are still being failed | Gymnastics | The Guardian
description: A decade after Larry Nassar’s crimes were first exposed, survivors and advocates have gathered at the World Gymnastics Championships to call for reform to be a priority
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: A decade after Larry Nassar’s crimes were first exposed, survivors and advocates have gathered at the World Gymnastics Championships to call for reform to be a priority
Content: Larry Nassar in court in Michigan in January 2018.Photograph: Rebecca Cook/ReutersView image in fullscreenLarry Nassar in court in Michigan in January 2018.Photograph: Rebecca Cook/ReutersGymnastics‘Money and medals over safety’: Nassar judge warns gymnasts are still being failedLarry Nassar’s sexual abuse crimes came to light 10 years agoSurvivors gather at world championships to call for reformSuzanne Wrackin RotterdamMon 19 Oct 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe judge who sentenced the former USA Gymnastics team doctorLarry Nassar to up to 175 years in jailin 2018 for the sexual abuse of more than 250 women and girls has condemned the lack of meaningful change in the decade since Nassar’s crimes were exposed.With the WorldGymnasticsChampionships taking place here this week, Judge Rosemarie Aquilina said human rights must be prioritised over the desire for sporting success.“Nassar was 10 years ago and there have been very few changes that are meaningful,” said Aquilina, who insisted on all 169 impact statements being heard in her courtroom after Nasser’s guilty plea.“I’m not looking for little changes that a lot of people get credit for, I want meaningful change, a lot of meaningful changes, and we’re just not there yet, not in sports, not in life, not in the courtroom, not in the classroom or in the legislature.“I have to ask why? It’s the same answer: it’s money, medals and notoriety over the safety of children and safety is a human right.”Aquilina joined activists, survivors and advocates from Gymnasts for Change International (G4CI) in Rotterdam, who gathered to question why the level of change has been inadequate and what can be done.View image in fullscreen(Left to right): gymnasts Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney, Aly Raisman and Maggie Nichols at a senate hearing about the Larry Nassar case in 2021.Photograph: Saul Loeb/APClaire Heafford, a survivor of abuse within the sport and the chief executive of G4CI, said: “We’re still in a place where survivors aren’t being listened to and where the scale of the reform hasn’t met the scale of the revelations.”Heafford puts the unwillingness to engage with systemic change post-Nassar as “institutional fear, blinkeredness, and the fact that people who work in sport are not very creative”.She said: “It’s incredibly difficult for anybody in the system who wants to create change to do so if there’s resistance above them. It’s incredibly difficult for people in the system to feel empowered as change makers when you’re in such fixed hierarchies.”Gymnastics’ ongoing reckoning: inside fight for survivor-led reform 10 years on from Nasser caseThe event was timed to reflect an opportunity for genuine change as World Gymnastics appoints a new secretary general with Nicolas Buompane stepping down at the end of the year.Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, said the reckoning sport faced since Nassar took the wrong form. “On the one hand, you can measure progress in athlete voice and advocacy, in some whistleblower protections, in safeguarding rules across sport – though the rules are there, but the implementation is not,” she said.“Then, on the other hand, you can measure it in the impact gymnastics had in all other sports. I’ve interviewed hundreds of survivors in about 50 sports, winter and summer. Ten years on, just the scale and the severity and the duration of the abuses by the so-called Olympic doctor Larry Nassar caused a reckoning across sport. But the reckoning often took the wrong shape, it took the shape of defence.View image in fullscreenJudge Rosemarie Aquilina addresses Larry Nassar in January 2018.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters“Except, this is not a small problem, it is a severe problem and any fair assessment would have to say that sport, broadly speaking, including gymnastics, retains the exceptionalism the Catholic church and schools once had.“There was a time when it was really hard to get rid of the abusive priest or teacher because they were moved around to different jurisdictions and continued abusing. That is why the scale and the duration of those abuse catastrophes was so great. Sports still has the same problem.”The former elite acrobatic gymnast Eloise Jotischky, who became the first person towin a civil case against British Gymnasticsfor the abuse she experienced between 2016 and 2018, which included inappropriate weight management techniques and verbal abuse, said there have been some changes, but the issue is with implementation.“There’s still a lot to be done. For example, British Gymnastics have come out with a number of policies, they’ve got their hydration policies, they’ve got their weight management policies. That’s brilliant, but let’s implement them. It’s the implementation that matters because if you don’t implement them and if you’re not monitoring them then what’s the point?”Kim Shore, of Gymnasts for Change Canada, who is a survivor of abuse within the sport and an independent safe sport advocate, wants World Gymnastics to adopt and implement huge cultural reforms if things are to improve. “There’s a crisis of abuse across sport in Canada and yet we’ve seen really no reform and I would say that same lack of action, that same apathy is happening at World Gymnastics,” she said.“Sure, they’ve taken some steps, but they could post new rules anywhere that say: ‘No more weighing of gymnasts. No more gymnasts returning to competition without a doctor’s note. No more coaches moving from one country to another country, if you’re banned in the US, you can’t just take a gymnast from Mexico to the Olympics.’“They could have a whole list of rules and regulations, even if they don’t have any sort of legislative jurisdiction in an area, that’s still going to influence the culture because as soon as the leading body says we’re not weighing gymnasts any more, then when the weighing gets done those coaches know they’re breaking the rules.“If World Gymnastics would come out with a whole list of cultural reforms and started to normalise those within the national federations and then give them backing so that the national federations can go to the clubs all the way down to grassroots, I think we would see faster reform and less resistance.”World Gymnastics, USA Gymnastics, Gymnastics Canada and British Gymnastics have been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsGymnasticsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Uefa demands Fifa releases documents relating to World Cup sell-off scheme | Fifa | The Guardian
description: The European governing body has given Fifa a two-week deadline to release key material in a letter which also addresses other controversies including the Folarian Balogun affair, peace prize and relations with Donald Trump
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The European governing body has given Fifa a two-week deadline to release key material in a letter which also addresses other controversies including the Folarian Balogun affair, peace prize and relations with Donald Trump
Content: The letter sent by Uefa claims Gianni Infantino’s responses at last week’s meeting of the Fifa council ‘have not begun satisfactorily to address a number of fundamental questions’.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe letter sent by Uefa claims Gianni Infantino’s responses at last week’s meeting of the Fifa council ‘have not begun satisfactorily to address a number of fundamental questions’.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersFifaUefa demands Fifa releases documents relating to World Cup sell-off schemeEuropean governing body gives two-week deadlineLetter addresses other issues including Balogun affairMatt HughesMon 19 Oct 2026 14.52 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUefa has given Fifa a two-week deadline to release key documents relating to Gianni Infantino’sWorld Cup sell-off planand other governance issues inits latest critique of football’s world governing body.A letter sent to Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, by his counterpart at Uefa, Theodore Theodoridis, is accompanied by an eight-page document that has more than 50 questions about Fifa’s handling of dozens of issues over the past 12 months. These include the proposed sale of 20% of its commercial rights,the Folarin Balogun affair,the peace prize and relations with Donald Trumpand the arrangements for next year’s Fifa presidential election. Uefa’s document also makes a number of allegations about potential conflicts of interests at Fifa, as well as repeating calls for a “genuinely independent” governance review.Apologetic Infantino ‘not fit’ to lead Fifa, claim European FA heads after meetingRead moreUefa’s latest intervention follows last week’s meeting of the Fifa council in Zurich, the first time it had gathered since the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) controversy in July. Infantino listened to questions on FFE and other matters, but declined to provide substantive answers, instead asking council members to submit them in writing before their next meeting in Doha on 16 December.In a letter sent on Monday, Theodoridis wrote: “These explanations have not begun satisfactorily to address a number of fundamental questions raised by Council members.“Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided.“Following the invitation made during the meeting to submit our questions in writing, we therefore enclose a consolidated set of questions and requests for information.“We formally request a substantive written response to each question, together with all supporting documentation by Monday 2nd November. Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon.“These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of theFifaCouncil – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.”View image in fullscreenAleksander Ceferin (centre), the Uefa president, and Theodore Theodoridis, the organisation’s general secretary, pictured in 2023.Photograph: Massimo Pinca/ReutersThe accompanying document and list of supplementary questions constitutes a damning takedown of Fifa’s leadership under Infantino, who, as it stands, is on course to be re-elected unopposed as president next year, although Uefa is increasingly hopeful of identifying a candidate to take him on before nominations close on 18 November.Uefa also wants answers on the processes behind other major decisions taken by Fifa over the past 12 months including moving the men’s World Cup draw to Washington DC from Las Vegas, the introduction of hydration breaks and the 27-minute half-time at the World Cup final.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“A series of decisions, transactions and interventions involving the Fifa President, the President of the United States and individuals associated with him raise serious questions concerning potential conflicts of interest, transparency and institutional accountability,” Uefa states.The amount Fifa is paying to rent office space in Trump Tower is also queried, as is a report in the Times last week that Infantino in 2024 “received substantial additional remuneration which was not disclosed in Fifa’s annual report”. Fifa has said it “does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation”.Uefa also raises concerns about March’s presidential election, specifically regarding the involvement of Bruno Chiomento, the chair of Fifa’s electoral committee. “We understand that Mr Chiomento has known the Fifa President for approximately 20 years and is regularly invited to Fifa events and competitions at Fifa’s expense,” Uefa’s document states. “We further understand that he attended the entire 2026 World Cup as an accredited individual, with his expenses covered by Fifa for more than five weeks.”Uefa has also requested a complete list of Fifa guests in VIP and VVIP areas at the World Cup final, on the grounds that “numerous guests were apparently given priority over Presidents of Member Associations and Secretaries General of Confederations”.Fifa has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsFifaUefaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo receives 30-day suspension and £215 fine over Portugal walkout | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: The Portuguese FA’s disciplinary council has upheld the charge against the 41-year-old, though the federation’s president has left the door open for a return
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Portuguese FA’s disciplinary council has upheld the charge against the 41-year-old, though the federation’s president has left the door open for a return
Content: It is unclear whether time already served under a provisional suspension will count towards Cristiano Ronaldo’s 30-day sanction.Photograph: Zed Jameson/PAView image in fullscreenIt is unclear whether time already served under a provisional suspension will count towards Cristiano Ronaldo’s 30-day sanction.Photograph: Zed Jameson/PACristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo receives 30-day suspension and £215 fine over Portugal walkoutDisciplinary council upholds charge against 41-year-oldFifa suspends Egypt’s Hossam Hassan and Mostafa ZikoReutersMon 19 Oct 2026 16.34 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo has been suspended for 30 days by the Portuguese ⁠FA after leaving the national team camp following a rift with the coach, ⁠Jorge Jesus, over ⁠his role in the side. The federation’s disciplinary council saidit had upheld the chargeagainst ⁠the 41-year-old forward in full and imposed a fine of €255 (£215).Ronaldoleft Portugal’s base in ⁠Copenhagenbefore their Nations League match against Denmark this month,having accused ‌Jesus of twice ‌breaking his wordabout his role after he was an ‌unused substitute against Norway. Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return after Portugal’s 2-1 win.Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue | Jonathan WilsonRead moreThe disciplinary council’s non-professional section found Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) ‌of the federation’s disciplinary regulations. Proceedings were opened on 9 October over facts reported two days earlier.The statement did not specify which matches or activities the suspension would cover, or whether time already served under a provisional suspension would count towards the 30-day sanction.Ronaldo later ⁠apologised for failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates, saying he remained available for selection after serving any ‌punishment arising from the incident.The Portuguese FA president, Pedro Proença, has said everyone within the federation wanted Ronaldo to return to the national team once the matter was resolved.Meanwhile, Fifa has suspended the Egypt coach, Hossam Hassan, and the forward Mostafa Ziko for ⁠three and five matches respectively, the Egyptian Football Association said on Monday, after they ⁠criticised the referee ⁠following their​3-2 defeat by Argentinain the World Cup.The 60-year-old Hassan was sanctioned after blaming ⁠refereeing errors for his country’s elimination from the tournament in the last 16, while Ziko insulted the ⁠referee in a post-match interview.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIbrahim Hassan, Hossam’s twin and ​Egypt’s national team director, ‌has also been suspended ‌for three matches.“The decisions include the suspension of Hossam Hassan ‌and Ibrahim Hassan for three matches each, while Ziko has been suspended for five matches,” the EFA said in a statement.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Eagles QB Hurts reportedly played after not sleeping for 36 hours amid blood clot diagnosis | Philadelphia Eagles | The Guardian
description: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will remain sidelined indefinitely with blood clots that have traveled to his lungs
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts will remain sidelined indefinitely with blood clots that have traveled to his lungs
Content: Jalen Hurts won Super Bowl LIX with the Eagles.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenJalen Hurts won Super Bowl LIX with the Eagles.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APPhiladelphia EaglesEagles QB Hurts reportedly played after not sleeping for 36 hours amid blood clot diagnosis28-year-old set to miss season after diagnosisTanner McKee has taken over as Eagles starterAgenciesMon 19 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhiladelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is set to miss the rest of the season after further testing ⁠revealedblood clotshad traveled from his leg to his lungs, the team announced on Monday.Hurts’s condition is considered stable and ⁠he “has no significant ⁠functional limitations,” ​the team said. His treatment for a new diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary ⁠emboli will involve blood thinners, during which time he is unable to participate in contact activities.The Rams have managed to transform themselves from a superteam to a midteamRead moreThe 28-year-old’s prognosis is good and the Eagles said they expect ​a full recovery with no long-term ‌effects.Specialists in England ‌initially diagnosed superficial clots in Hurts’s left calf before Philadelphia’s loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on 11 October.According to NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport, he was at the hospital until 4am and was advised by doctors not to sleep as a precautionary measure. That would mean he had not slept for 36 hours when the Eagles kicked off against the Jaguars.Further testing has discovered multiple blood clots in his lungs.“We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners,” the team’s statement concluded. “In the meantime, he ‌will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will ​have no long-term effects.”Hurts hadn’t missed more than two games in a season since becoming the Eagles’ full-time starter in 2021. He has led the Eagles to five straight playoff appearances, three NFC East titles and two Super Bowl appearances, beating the Chiefs 40-22 two years ago.Tanner McKee started for Hurts against the Panthers. McKee finished 26 of 45 for 215 yards and a touchdown in the Eagles’ 25-14 loss to Carolina. The Eagles (2-4) have lost four consecutive games for the first time since 2020.Hurts has eight touchdown passes and three interceptions with 933 yards passing this season. He is in the middle ofa five-year, $255m extension, including $179.3m guaranteed, that takes him through the 2028 season.The Eagles stunned fans when they drafted Hurts out of Oklahoma in the second round in 2020. They seemingly had Carson Wentz entrenched at QB and had more pressing needs. But Hurts supplanted Wentz and became one of the top quarterbacks in theNFL.Explore more on these topicsPhiladelphia EaglesNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cheltenham jumps into action after fixing its troublesome hole  | Cheltenham | The Guardian
description: Cheltenham has undergone extensive work on its drainage system in preparation for new season
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Cheltenham has undergone extensive work on its drainage system in preparation for new season
Content: The hot, dry summer took its toll on Cheltenham racecourse.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenThe hot, dry summer took its toll on Cheltenham racecourse.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PATalking HorsesCheltenhamCheltenham jumps into action after fixing its troublesome holeHome of National Hunt racing has undergone extensive work on its drainage system in preparation for new seasonGreg WoodMon 19 Oct 2026 12.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 17.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is little chance to catch your breath as the racing seasons turn and six days on fromAscot’s exhilarating Champions DayCheltenham will open its gates on Friday for the first card of the 2026-27 campaign.Racing will return to the spiritual home of National Hunt after an abrupt curtailment to Cheltenham’s latest season. That was to allow for extensive work on the track’s drainage system afterthe discovery of a significant holein the racing surface on Trials day in late January.‘I’m bored when I’m not riding’: Billy Loughnane on drive that made him champion jockey at 20Read moreThe festival meeting in March went ahead as planned, but the Jockey Club, which owns the course,announced soon afterwardsthat the popular mid-April meeting and the hunter-chase card in May had been sacrificed to allow sufficient time for remedial work to take place.More than a kilometre of drainage has been replaced or upgraded and the Old and New courses received a thorough examination with ground-penetrating radar, which showed no additional causes for concern.“We’re really pleased with how the track has responded to the significant drainage works,” Jon Pullin, Cheltenham’s clerk of the course, said on Monday. “Our decision to cancel the last three racedays of last season in order to maximise the time to carry out the work and for the ground to recover was certainly the right one.“Everyone knows how long, hot and dry our summer was and the team here have been working tirelessly, just like grounds teams all over the UK, to irrigate and prepare the track ahead of our season opener.”The Showcase meeting was once little more than a loosener after the summer break to ease Cheltenham back into the swing. As a two-day midweek meeting at the turn of the century, it attracted 16,000 racegoers. Like most of the non-festival days at Cheltenham its popularity has increased steadily over the past 20 years, to the point where the 21,113 for the Saturday card last year was more than three times the attendance for the Flat card at Doncaster the same afternoon featuring the Futurity Trophy, the final Group One of the year.Cheltenham races so sparingly over the winter that there is no longer any such thing as a minor day at the track, in the main part of the season at least. The loss of three cards in April and May was a small price to pay to ensure that the ground was right for the return of racing in October. As one problem with the going is apparently solved, another, less tractable issue remains, for Cheltenham and for National Hunt racing more generally.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Tuesday tipsShowYarmouth1.20Gorgeous Mr George1.50Avebury Ring2.20Oliaku2.53Lady Magu3.28Potters Prince4.03Court Drive4.38Rambuso Creek5.08Call TimeHexham2.01Biglesisback2.32Littletown Lad3.07Conquer The Breeze3.42Coded Welder4.17Royal Infantry4.50LuminariesNewcastle4.22Empress Jingu4.57Circus Of Rome (nap)5.30Bobby Joe Leg6.00Alkumatic Jo Jo6.30Bajan Bandit7.00Northern Viola7.30Brazen Idol8.00Wee Mary8.30Speeding Bullet (nb)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Cheltenham has already been forced to abandon the cross-country race at the November meeting because of firm ground and that is just the latest in a series of cancellations over jumps in recent weeks. Kempton, Exeter, Ludlow, Fakenham, Warwick and Wincanton have been forced to abandon meetings due to unsuitably fast ground, while Chepstow’s Welsh Racing Festival from 9 to 11 October ended up as an all-hurdles meeting.Cheltenham has a watering system, but even that has its limitations. The going for this week’s meeting is now officially good, having been good, good-to-firm in places on Sunday, but the taps are now off due to an unsettled forecast.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We had 8mm of rain overnight last night [Sunday into Monday] and expect some further rain tonight into tomorrow,” Pullin said. “As a result, and in light of the uncertain forecast for the end of this week, we’ve stopped watering. We’re good ground all over currently, but we’ll have to wait and see how much rainfall we get on Thursday and Friday before I can say with any real confidence what we’ll be when the tapes go up.”Cheltenham’s struggle to maintain attendance at the festival meeting has been well-documented in recent years, thoughlast season’s meeting had a modest, but very welcome increaseafter three years of steady decline. But that has been at least partially balanced by the increasing popularity of the non-festival meetings, including a remarkable turnout of 44,900 on New Year’s Day that was 232 below the total for the second day of the festival.The festival experience has clearly been a tricky sell since the post-Covid high of 2022, but the core Cheltenham experience – the atmosphere, the setting and, above all, the excitement and competitiveness of the racing – has remained in high demand. To maintain that all-important competitiveness the track needs big fields with fit, in-form horses and improving youngsters and novices moving up the pyramid. If this year’s long, dry summer is becoming the rule and not the exception, the base of the pyramid could steadily erode.The next scheduled fixtures at Exeter and Wincanton are the biggest events of the year at both tracks and form a mini-festival – the West Country Weekend – on 6 and 7 November featuring the Haldon Gold Cup and the Badger Beers Chase. Since both tracks have already lost cards this season – Exeter, has cancelled two – there must be serious doubt about both days if the dry weather continues.The long, dry summer was a boon for Champions Day at Ascot, which has often been staged on deep winter ground. For the country’s smaller jumps tracks, however, the climate crisis could increasingly been seen as an existential threat.Explore more on these topicsCheltenhamTalking HorsesHorse racingHorse racing tipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sarina Wiegman signs contract extension to stay as England women head coach until 2029 | England women's football team | The Guardian
description: Sarina Wiegman has the chance to lead the Lionesses to three European championship titles in a row after extending her deal by two years
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Sarina Wiegman has the chance to lead the Lionesses to three European championship titles in a row after extending her deal by two years
Content: Sarina Wiegman celebrates with Leah Williamson after England win the Euro 2025 final.Photograph: Maja Hitij/UEFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSarina Wiegman celebrates with Leah Williamson after England win the Euro 2025 final.Photograph: Maja Hitij/UEFA/Getty ImagesEngland women's football teamSarina Wiegman signs contract extension to stay as England women head coach until 2029Wiegman says she ‘cannot think of a better job in football’She can target three European titles in row with LionessesSuzanne WrackMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSarina Wiegman has extended her contract to continue as the head coach of England women for Euro 2029. Her deal was due to expire after the World Cup next summer and this extension gives her the chance to lead the Lionesses to three European championship titles in a row.Wiegman, whotook on the role in September 2021, also led her native Netherlands side to European Championship glory in 2017 and has reached the final of the past five major tournaments, twice finishing as a World Cup runner-up.“I am so happy to be able to carry on with this squad and cannot think of a better job in football,” Wiegman said. “Working for a world-class organisation like the FA, and alongside so many people dedicated to winning England teams and the growth of our game, excites me every day.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.England will reach the World Cup finals, to be held in Brazil in June and July, if they come through a two-leg playoff against Ukraine for which they are heavy favourites. “My main concern right now is absolutely the World Cup, and helping this squad realise their potential in the years to come,” Wiegman said.This is Wiegman’s second contract extension with England and opens the possibility that she could coach Team GB at the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles should the team qualify. Wiegman, who turns 57 next Monday, will continue to be assisted by Janneke Bijl, Arvid Smit and Darren Ward.“Sarina is an incredible coach with an unparalleled record in major tournaments and I am so happy to continue to work with her for the next Euro cycle,” the Football Association’s chief executive, Mark Bullingham, said.Wiegman had refused to be drawn on questions over her future before England’s two games against Greece during the recent international break, but the Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh last week said “obviously I’d want her to stay” when asked about the head coach’s future.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Sarina’s the boss, I would never ask her those questions, but I think everyone in England would love her to stay,” Walsh said. “I’ve played a lot of games for her and I really appreciate her as a manager.”Explore more on these topicsEngland women's football teamSarina WiegmanThe FAWomen's footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Actions speak louder than words’: England’s white-ball captain Harry Brook relishes responsibility | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Harry Brook is approaching an unwanted Wellington anniversary as England take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Harry Brook is approaching an unwanted Wellington anniversary as England take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI series
Content: Head coach Brendon McCullum chats to Harry Brook at the Rawalpindi cricket stadium before England play in the tri-nations series.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHead coach Brendon McCullum chats to Harry Brook at the Rawalpindi cricket stadium before England play in the tri-nations series.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesEngland cricket team‘Actions speak louder than words’: England’s white-ball captain Harry Brook relishes responsibilityBatter approaching unwanted Wellington anniversaryEngland take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI seriesPress AssociationMon 19 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Brook is embracing leadership and responsibility as he nears the one-year anniversary of his Wellington altercation, insisting he wants to be “the man England fans and the team rely on”.Brook has in the past admitted he could have been sacked as white-ball captain after being punched by a nightclub bouncer, hours before leading England in an ODI against New Zealand on Halloween last year.Brook and Jacks lead resurgent England into tri-series with World Cup in sightRead moreSince then, though, Brook has stabilised an ailing 50-over side, with England winning their last three series having lost seven of eight before then, while the T20 team sit top of the world rankings.With just under a year to go until the 50-over World Cup, Brook’s ODI average as skipper is 51.3 compared to 25.2 in the rank and file and he is adamant he has grown in the last 12 months.He said: “I’ve learnt a lot as a captain, I’ve learnt a lot as a person. I know it wasn’t an ideal situation to put myself in, but as a captain and a leader I’ve learnt a lot. Responsibilities and leadership aren’t just on the field, they’re more so off the field as well and actions speak louder than words.“I enjoy the extra responsibility. I like the extra little bit of added pressure. I’m not going to go out there and score runs every time I bat but I want to be the man that is in that match-winning situation who can get us over the line.“There have been a few innings where I haven’t managed to do that but hopefully I’ve turned that corner and I can really be the man England fans and the team rely on.”Brook’s Test average of 53.08 is the highest among any England batter to have played at least 20 matches in more than 50 years, but former captain Ben Stokes revealed recently he told the Yorkshireman it should be as high as 65 or 70.View image in fullscreenBen Stokes (left) believes Harry Brook should be averaging 65 or 70 in Test cricket.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesAsked what his initial reaction was, Brook replied with a laugh: “I mean 65 or 70 is a massive average, isn’t it, wow! Personally I’m not that bothered about the stats, I’ve always said I think there should be a match-winning column in your stats – that’s not there.“I write stuff down and I try and judge myself on whether I’ve had a match-winning performance or match-winning impact in that specific game and I try and tally it up at the end of the year and see how well I’ve done.”Brook’s immediate focus is on England’s tri-series against hosts Pakistan, whom they open their campaign against on Tuesday in Rawalpindi, and Sri Lanka, with every team playing each other twice and the top-two finishers contesting the final on Halloween.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRehan Ahmed was overlooked in favour of fellow leg-spinner Mason Crane, more than eight years after his last appearance for England.Brook said: “There’s certainly no line through Rehan’s name at all. Mason’s just performed exceptionally well and we think that he deserves an opportunity to be in and around the squads.”The injured Jos Buttler and rested Jofra Archer are also missing from England’s 16-strong contingent ahead of facing a Pakistan side who beat Sri Lanka on Sunday and are a much more of a force in ODIs than they showed in three abject losses to Joe Root’s Test side recently.Brook added: “It’s a great experience for us and with the potential of getting to a final, it gives us even more experience in those games where it’s do-or-die. It’s going to be one hell of a series.“In the last six to eight months and we’re certainly trending in the right direction as a squad. I think we’re really building towards the make-up of the side that we want.“Me and Baz [head coach Brendon McCullum] feel like we’ve got a squad where if someone does go down five minutes before the toss, we’re in a position where someone else can come in and fill that role perfectly well.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamHarry BrookPakistan cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘What the war has done to me inside’: Ukraine’s Svitolina announces separation from Monfils | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The World No 6 Elina Svitolina has opened up about the toll of Russia’s war and the breakup of her marriage with Gaël Monfils
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The World No 6 Elina Svitolina has opened up about the toll of Russia’s war and the breakup of her marriage with Gaël Monfils
Content: ‘This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share,’ Elina Svitolina wrote.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share,’ Elina Svitolina wrote.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesTennis‘What the war has done to me inside’: Ukraine’s Svitolina announces separation from MonfilsWorld No 6 Svitolina opens up about toll of Russia’s warFrench star Monfils has retired after glittering careerPress AssociationMon 19 Oct 2026 06.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world No 6 Elina Svitolina has announced she has separated from her husband Gaël Monfils.In an emotional Instagram post, the 32-year-old Ukrainian opened up about the mental toll of Russia’s war against her country, describing sleepless nights and self-doubt. Svitolina said she had come to realise she needed to rediscover herself and could no longer do so within her marriage.“This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share,” she wrote. “Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me. What I have rarely spoken about is what the war has done to me inside. With time, I came to understand that I need to find my way back to myself and that I cannot do that within our marriage.“It is the hardest truth I have ever had to face and the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love. Gaël listened. He has respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget.”View image in fullscreenFans recently learned that Gaël Monfils would not be playing in what was supposed to be his final professional tournament, the Paris Masters, which begins later this month.Photograph: Anne-Christine Poujoulat/AFP/Getty ImagesSvitolina – a four-time grand slam semi-finalist – and the French former world No 6 Monfils, 40, were married in 2021 and have a four-year-old daughter, Skai.“Skai will always come first,” Svitolina added. “Our marriage is ending, but our family is not. Please know that there is no one to blame here. There are only two people who loved each other deeply and a story that is changing shape.”Monfils has seemingly brought forward his retirement from the sport, which was expected to come following a farewell outing at the Paris Masters which begins on 31 October. It emerged last week that the Frenchman, who won 13 career titles, is now featured on the InternationalTennisIntegrity Agency’s list of retired players.Explore more on these topicsTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Once-in-a-lifetime chance’: Japan launches historic mission to collect rocks from Mars’s moon Phobos | Japan | The Guardian
description: Scientists hope Martian material collected will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Scientists hope Martian material collected will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth
Content: The H3 rocket carrying the unmanned Martian Moons exploration (MMX) probe blasted off from the Tanegashima Space Centre at 4:41 am (1941 GMT Monday).Photograph: KYODO/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe H3 rocket carrying the unmanned Martian Moons exploration (MMX) probe blasted off from the Tanegashima Space Centre at 4:41 am (1941 GMT Monday).Photograph: KYODO/ReutersJapan‘Once-in-a-lifetime chance’: Japan launches historic mission to collect rocks from Mars’s moon PhobosScientists hope Martian material collected will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on EarthJustin McCurryin Tokyo and agenciesMon 19 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJapan has successfully launched a spacecraft on anunprecedented missionto bring back samples from one of Mars’s moons that scientists hope will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.The Martian ⁠Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft, propelled by Japan’s flagship H3 rocket, lifted off before dawn from Tanegashima island in the country’s far south-west, theJapanAerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) said.The spacecraft is expected to reach Mars’s orbit in August next year and collect at least 10g of soil and rock from the surface of Phobos, one of two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting the planet. It is scheduled to return in 2031, Jaxa said.Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggestsRead moreThe pock-marked moon, which has a diameter measuring 14 miles (22.5km), orbits Mars three times a day about 6,000km above its surface.The flagship H3 rocket carrying the unmanned probe blasted off into a pitch black sky from TanegashimaSpaceCentre at 4:41am, witnessed by thousands of people who had woken up early to follow a livestream.An hour later, Jaxa scientists declared the launch a success when the spacecraft separated from the rocket’s upper stage, prompting scenes of celebration in the flight control room.Nasahas landed nine spacecraft onMarsover the past half a century, while China landed on the Martian surface in 2021, but this is the first time anyone has attempted to land on Phobos or the planet’s smaller moon, Deimos.“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said Nasa astrophysicist Tom Statler, who is involved in the Japan-led project to collect samples.Five space agencies are collaborating on thefive-year mission, which will attempt to land a robotic prospector and a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of the two moons.The $578m mission features a five-tonne spacecraft that will sync with Phobos’ tight orbit around Mars when it arrives next summer. It will then eject a small French-German rover, named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.If all goes according to plan, the four-wheeled rover will bounce (due to gravity on Phobos being1/1,000th as strong as Earth) for several minutes on Mars’s surface before coming to a halt. It will spend 100 days surveying the planet’s surface to find safe landing and sampling sites ahead of the arrival of the main craft, a four-legged stationary lander that will gather the samples.The lander will spend only two hours on Phobos drilling and vacuuming up material, before launching back into space. Officials said it would observe Deimos during several flybys before leaving Mars’s orbit in November 2030.“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the Germany Space Agency’s rover chief Markus Grebenstein.View image in fullscreenPhobos, the larger of Mars’ two moons, is seen in this undated image taken by Nasa’s High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter.Photograph: NASA/JPL-Caltech/University of Arizona/ReutersScientists hope the samples will help them establish how Phobos and Deimos were formed and even offer clues about the origins of life. MMX’s findings will also help shape future Mars missions, including crewed expeditions, Nasa said.According to one theory – the “giant impact” hypothesis – the two moons formed after a celestial body collided with Mars. A second proposition, known as the “capture” hypothesis, suggests that the moons are asteroids pulled in by Mars’s gravity.Determining which theory is correct will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, Jaxa said, referring to the four planets closest to the sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.The US and China are in a race to be the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars. Nasa’s Perseverance rover, which has been roaming across Mars since 2021, has already collected samples, but its return to Earth was halted by the Trump administration after a congressional vote in January this year.China’s Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled to launch around 2028 and could bring back Mars samples as early as 2031, potentially before the Japanese moon mission’s return.Explore more on these topicsJapanSpaceMarsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited | Yemen | The Guardian
description: More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
Content: People line up to refill gas bottles at a refilling station in Taiz on Monday. Fighting is under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the city.Photograph: Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople line up to refill gas bottles at a refilling station in Taiz on Monday. Fighting is under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the city.Photograph: Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignitedMore than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forcesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 19 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreThere will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.Map of YemenReliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify theHouthisas a foreign terrorist organisation.The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.A person walks past bodies on the groundBodies lie on the ground after the explosion at al-Alam camp in YemenThe killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions.
