The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.TheSaudi Aramco headquarters was strucklast weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after beingattacked this month.Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops toSaudi Arabiadespite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Over three dozen Congress members’ offices targeted with white powder envelopes | US Congress | The Guardian
description: Envelopes containing powder come weeks before midterms as federal agents try to identify who is behind campaign
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Envelopes containing powder come weeks before midterms as federal agents try to identify who is behind campaign
Content: The US Capitol building in Washington DC.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US Capitol building in Washington DC.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersUS CongressOver three dozen Congress members’ offices targeted with white powder envelopesEnvelopes containing powder come weeks before midterms as federal agents try to identify who is behind campaignJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonMon 19 Oct 2026 15.44 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 15.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than three dozen members ofUS Congresshave had their offices targeted with envelopes containing white powder, less than three weeks before the 3 November midterms, as federal agents try to identify who is behind the campaign.The latest is theVirginia Democrat Suhas Subramanyam, whose Leesburg district office was evacuated on Monday after an envelope containing a suspicious substance arrived. He said the office was cleared quickly, adding that “acts of political intimidation have no place in our country”.Subramanyam’s office said preliminary tests showed the powder was not hazardous.Law enforcement sourcestold ABC Newsthat more than 100 letters thought to contain white powder are circulating in the US mail system. The FBI, Capitol police and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating, according to a notice sent to Senate staff on Thursday.Election offices in at least 15 states had reported receiving or being targeted by suspicious mail by Thursday evening, according to the Tampa Free Press, which cited federal authorities. No suspect has been named, and federal authorities have not released a confirmed figure.The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”Senators have been targeted across the political spectrum, and country. Letters addressed to the Democratic Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and California senator Alex Padilla were intercepted by authorities, while Chris Murphy of Connecticut said the FBI, the Senate sergeant at arms and Capitol police alerted his team of a letter as well. Republicans in South Dakota, Texas and Nebraska were also targeted, with Mike Rounds saying his Sioux Falls office was evacuated, along with Pete Ricketts and Ted Cruz also reporting a suspicious letter.In the House, at least 10 people were exposed after white powder was sent to the offices of the New York Democrats Hakeem Jeffries, Ritchie Torres and Tom Suozzi. In California, Jimmy Panetta said a staffer opened an envelope at his Santa Cruz office, then cleared the room and called 911. He said such attempts to intimidate “will not deter us from doing our job”. In Massachusetts, five staffers left Seth Moulton’s Salem office while police investigated, and testing found no substances of concern.Investigators have described several common features connecting the suspicious letters sent to public officials and election centers.The FBI has stated that the recovered envelopes were processed through a north Texas mail processing center and carry a postmark or stamp reading “Thinking of You”. Senate staff and House offices were warned to watch for plain white envelopes featuring these distinct markings.The vast majority of these envelopes were intercepted by the US Postal Inspection Service and screening facilities before being delivered.In 2024, election officials weretargeted in 17 statesbefore the 2024 presidential election, and no suspect has been named in this case.Explore more on these topicsUS CongressUS midterm elections 2026US politicsVirginianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injured | Helen Haines | The Guardian
description: Anthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta
Author: Nino Bucci
Headline: Anthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta
Content: Helen Haines has been injured in an incident outside her office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHelen Haines has been injured in an incident outside her office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty ImagesHelen Haines‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injuredAnthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in WangarattaWho is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?What we know so farGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastNino BucciandKrishani DhanjiMon 19 Oct 2026 07.10 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 03.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe independent MPHelen Haineshas been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria.The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, confirmed on Monday night that a man was in custody after the alleged attack on Haines that was now being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce.He said the motive for the alleged attack was not known, and would not comment on whether the suspect was known to police.Helen Haines is in a critical condition after an alleged attack. Here’s what we know so farRead more“Helen Haines is incredibly hard-working. She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her, she is a well-loved member of her community, and this will come as an incredible shock to that community,” Albanese said.He said he respected her integrity most of all.“It doesn’t mean we always agree, but I always agree that her motives are good,” Albanese said.“Our thoughts remain with Helen Haines at this very difficult time.”View image in fullscreenABC vision from the scene near where Helen Haines was allegedly struck by a vehicle.Photograph: ABCThe prime minister andVictoriapolice said they were not aware of any recent direct threats to Haines.Haines has represented the electorate of Indi since 2019.Albanese later said on the ABC’s 7.30 program that while he did not want to speculate on the motivation for the alleged attack, he had repeatedly warned “the temperature has increased in recent times” in relation to politics.He had feared that would increase the risk of political violence occurring in Australia that had been seen in other western democracies.Albanese, who became emotional at times during the interview, said he first was told that Haines had been injured in a car accident, before being informed it was allegedly a deliberate act.“This wasn’t an accident,” he said.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also said there had been an increase in threats towards politicians.“The year before last, we had 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against various high officeholders,” he said.“The more recent financial year, that 951 has gone to 1,067.”‘Our beloved Helen’In a statement, Haines’s family confirmed that she had been injured and thanked bystanders for their assistance.“This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” they said in the statement.“We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response.“Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media.“Please keep Helen in your thoughts.”Wangaratta mapHaines was airlifted to hospital in Melbourne.In a statement, Victoria police said a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, about 10km from Wangaratta, was in custody and that a knife had allegedly been found in his car. They alleged he had been detained by a passerby when he exited the car.The statement said the woman that was struck was in a critical condition.“Police have arrested a man after a woman was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta this afternoon.“It is understood a white Toyota LandCruiser struck the 65-year-old woman outside an office on Murphy Street about 3.35pm.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPolice said that they were investigating as to whether it was an intentional act, and it was not known if “the parties are known to each other”.Speaking at the scene, acting Supt Ashley Mason said it was being treated as an isolated incident.He said that the bystanders who assisted in the arrest and with Haines should be commended for acting as they did when confronted with a “horrific tragic incident”.It was a “dynamic incident” with an extensive crime scene, he said.‘Deeply appalled’The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said he knew the alleged attack would be devastating for the Wangaratta community and all those Haines represented.“I am deeply appalled by this [alleged] violent attack on Helen Haines,” he said in a statement.“My thoughts – and the thoughts of all Victorians – are with Helen, her family, her friends, her colleagues and her community.”The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said political attacks cannot be normalised in Australia.Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?Read moreThe Liberal leader said he was “deeply saddened and distressed” and was praying for Haines and her family.“This is a shocking day for our nation … Australians will be angry and appalled by the [alleged] attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta,” he said in a statement on social media.Monique Ryan, the independent MP for Kooyong, said on Instagram that Haines was “the very best of people” and that she was “respected and loved” by everyone in parliament.In a social media post, the Nationals MP Michael McCormack said it was “such awful news”.“Sending my love and best wishes to Helen Haines for a full and speedy recovery,” McCormack said.‘Politically motivated violence’Asio has in recent years repeatedly warned about therising threat of politically motivated violence.“Political differences, political debates and political protests are essential parts of a healthy democracy,” Mike Burgess, the Asio director general, said in 2025.“Unfortunately, here and overseas, levels of personal grievance and frustration are growing.“Rightly or wrongly some Australians feel dispossessed, disaffected, disenfranchised … many of the aggrieved do not necessarily espouse violent views, but may still see violence as a legitimate way to effect political or societal change.”He added last year that although Australia’s terrorism threat level remained at probable, the system was not “designed for a situation like the one we now face”.“We do know the environment is degrading and acts of politically motivated violence are becoming more likely than probable suggests,” he said.“Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack.”Explore more on these topicsHelen HainesAustralian politicsVictoriaIndependentsAustralian security and counter-terrorismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds | Colorado | The Guardian
description: Elk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completion
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Elk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completion
Content: A wildlife overpass for elk, deer, and pronghorn on Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA wildlife overpass for elk, deer, and pronghorn on Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesColoradoColorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report findsElk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completionDara KerrMon 19 Oct 2026 19.17 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger system built by the state to assist wildlife crossing the highway, which also includes miles of 8-ft tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses.“One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when [Colorado department of transportation] sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under [Interstate-25],” Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist for Colorado parks and wildlife,told CBS News. “All came to fruition in that one moment. That elk with her calf was just standing there in safety.”The Colorado department of transportation said before the overpass system wasbuilt, there was an average of one wildlife-vehicle crash a day in this corridor.Such wildlife crossings are popping up across the country as a way to protect wildlife habitat and reduce collisions, which can result in injuries and deaths in humans and animals. Research has shown thatoverpass systems are successfulin “nearly eliminating” these accidents and that such infrastructure buildouts often “pay for themselves” by preventing costly crashes.Tents, night-vision goggles and bear tracking kits: America’s first nature library opensRead moreNearly 20 wildlife crossings are under way in the US, with the structure in Colorado currently the biggest. The overpass, which sits between the state’s two biggest cities, Denver and Colorado Springs,spans six lanes of trafficand connects 39,000 acres of habitat on both sides of the interstate. The bridge is covered in grass and measures 200ft wide and 209ft long with gradually sloped entrances to ease crossings for animals.This region of Colorado is known for high movement of large game. State officials say that wildlife underpasses and tunnels often don’t work for big animals, such as bullelk, because they restrict mobility and don’t accommodate their antlers.“Elk and pronghorn like these big open structures where they can see for miles in each direction,” Chuck Attardo, the environmental manager for Colorado department of transportation, told CBS News. “For decades, pronghorn going from Trinidad to Greenland were looking for a place to cross on I-25. And when we open this up, we have pronghorn on video using the overpass, and for the first time in decades they’re coming over here to the west side.”While large game animals have been taking advantage of the crossing, officials have also tracked smaller wildlife using the corridor, including mule deer, coyotes, rabbits, frogs and the threatened Preble’s meadow jumping mouse.The project received $22m in federal funding and $8m from the state, but officials say they were able to complete it for just $15m. Now, the Colorado department of transportation says it is hoping to build other wildlife crossings across the state.Explore more on these topicsColoradoAnimalsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline | Cop17 biodiversity summit | The Guardian
description: As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps
Content: A bee pollinating a cherry tree in Athy, County Kildare. The study confirms that many pollinator species are losing populations.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenA bee pollinating a cherry tree in Athy, County Kildare. The study confirms that many pollinator species are losing populations.Photograph: Niall Carson/PACop17 biodiversity summit‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in declineAs Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the AlpsAjit NiranjanEurope environment correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, astudyhas found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia.Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts ofEuropeexcept the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive.The data, which covers 88% of bee and hover fly species across the continent, suggests pollinator communities have been reshaped by the “gradual loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few”, according to the scientists. They warned of “deeper functional disruptions” if existing trends were not addressed.Nearly 90% of wild flowering plants, as well as more than three-quarters of major food crop types, depend in part on animal pollination. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization has warned the decline of pollinators sets off a chain reaction that threatens wildlife and weakens the ability of ecosystems to withstand climate change and environmental stress.Carlos Martínez-Núñez, an ecologist at the Spanish National Research Council and lead author of the study, said the findings showed that biodiversity loss could remain hidden behind apparently stable species numbers, “giving us a crucial opportunity to act before further declines occur”.“The fact that some species are increasing today does not mean they will remain winners as climate change and habitat loss intensify,” he added.The findings come as diplomats gather in Yerevan for the 17th UN conference on biodiversity. The summit, known asCop17, will focus on the conservation and sustainable use of the natural world, and the shared benefits of its genetic resources.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCan countries deliver on a deal to save the world’s plants and animals?Read moreThe study found 91% of the species logged over the last century had also been recorded at least once in the modern period, between 2001 and 2020. Although this suggests as many as 9% of species could have been wiped out in Europe, many of the species not spotted recently occur only rarely in the historical record, and the researchers said they “do not expect widespread extinctions to have occurred yet”.However, the species’ occupancy – the probability of being found at a given site – had mostly fallen.Ainhoa ​​Magrach, an environmental researcher at the Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3), who was not involved in the study, said it “confirms what has long been suspected: many pollinator species are losing populations, and the decline is not affecting all of them equally”.“Until now, most of the evidence came from a few north-western European countries, such as the UK, Belgium and the Netherlands,” she said. “This work shows that the pattern extends across the continent, although some regional differences exist.”Cop17 at a glance: everything you need to know about the UN’s nature summitRead moreWildlife is dying out at an unprecedented rate as humans destroy habitats, spray pesticides, and warp the weather with planet-heating pollution. Despite far-reaching consequences for humanity, including threats to food systems and further breakdown of the climate, governmentshave not meta single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created in Rio in 1992.The Cop17 summit is expected to focus on assessing progress toward this decade’s targets, which include protecting 30% of land and sea, reforming $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies and restoring 30% of the planet’s degraded ecosystems.Explore more on these topicsCop17 biodiversity summitBeesEuropeArmeniaWildlifeInsectsAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Melting Ron DeSantis statue unveiled to call out his inaction on climate crisis | Ron DeSantis | The Guardian
description: Florida governor has consistently opposed any legislation to curb planet-heating emissions, calling it a ‘radical climate agenda’
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Florida governor has consistently opposed any legislation to curb planet-heating emissions, calling it a ‘radical climate agenda’
Content: Cast from gallium, which melts at 85.6F, the silvery-statue quickly began meltingPhotograph: 350 ActionView image in fullscreenCast from gallium, which melts at 85.6F, the silvery-statue quickly began meltingPhotograph: 350 ActionRon DeSantisMelting Ron DeSantis statue unveiled to call out his inaction on climate crisisFlorida governor has consistently opposed any legislation to curb planet-heating emissions, calling it a ‘radical climate agenda’Oliver MilmanMon 19 Oct 2026 15.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 15.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA life-sized statue ofRon DeSantis, the Florida governor, was unveiled and promptly began melting in front of an audience in Tallahassee in a symbolic protest at his rejection of action on the climate crisis.The silvery statue, revealed to an audience of onlookers last week, melted away to show a skull under DeSantis’s face. The structure was cast from solid gallium, a metal that melts at 85.6F (29.8C), which is below summertime high temperatures frequently reached in Tallahassee, Florida’s capital.The environmentalists behind the statue-based protest said it was a fitting monument to DeSantis’s eight years as Florida governor, which comes to an end in January.View image in fullscreenThe face of the statue melted away to reveal a skull-like structure under it.Photograph: 350 ActionThe Republican has frequently criticized what he has called a “radical climate agenda”, blocking the ability of Florida municipalities to slash planet-heating pollution andeven erased terms such as “climate change” and “greenhouse gas emissions” from Florida state law.This law has hindered the ability of state agencies to even mention a climate crisis that poses an outsized threat to Florida. In classrooms, meanwhile, state education regulations are also ensuring the steady elimination of any reference to climate change.“I am not a global warming person, I don’t want that label on me,” DeSantis, who unsuccessfully ran to become Republican nominee for US president in 2024, said in 2018.Southern Florida isacutely threatened by sea level rise, while homes and businesses across the entire state have been increasingly lashed by powerful hurricanes, worsened by rising global temperatures. The increasing damage wrought by storms supercharged by ocean and atmospheric heat has proved so costly that several major insurers haveexitedFlorida entirely.The state’s stance towards the climate crisis looks unlikely to change, however. Florida has become a Republican bastion in recent years and Byron Donalds, the GOP candidate, is heavilyfavoredto win the governor’s race in next month’s midterm elections.View image in fullscreenThe installation, called ‘DENIAL,’ was created by Uncommon, an advertising agency, climate advocacy group 350 Action and M ss ng P eces, a production company.Photograph: 350 ActionDonalds hassaidhe wants to maintain Florida’s environment but hassaid he doesn’t acceptthe link between climate change and human actions, despite scientific consensus that the burning of fossil fuels is causing temperatures to rise.“The climate crisis is one of the top issues facing our planet today. And yet, some candidates running for office still deny it’s happening, and deny the bold climate action that the people want.” said Candice Fortin, campaign manager at 350Action, the environmental group behind the DeSantis statue, along with advertising agency Uncommon.“That’s why it’s more important than ever to deny them back at the ballot box,” Fortin added. “If everyone who cares about people and our planet makes their voices heard on election cay, we’ll be too loud to deny.”DeSantis has defended his position on climate. “We’re restoring sanity in our approach to energy and rejecting the agenda of the radical green zealots,” DeSantis said in a post on the X social media platform whenmaking climate a lower state priority in May 2024.Explore more on these topicsRon DeSantisClimate crisisFloridaRepublican convention 2008newsShareReuse this content

title: Ofcom investigates Huw Edwards complaint over Channel 5 drama | Huw Edwards | The Guardian
description: Former BBC presenter says programme starring Martin Clunes gave a misleading and unfair account of his downfall
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Former BBC presenter says programme starring Martin Clunes gave a misleading and unfair account of his downfall
Content: Huw Edwards pleaded guilty in July 2024 to accessing indecent photographs of children and later received a suspended prison sentence.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenHuw Edwards pleaded guilty in July 2024 to accessing indecent photographs of children and later received a suspended prison sentence.Photograph: Thomas Krych/ZUMA Press Wire/REX/ShutterstockHuw EdwardsOfcom investigates Huw Edwards complaint over Channel 5 dramaFormer BBC presenter says programme starring Martin Clunes gave a misleading and unfair account of his downfallMichael SavageMedia editorMon 19 Oct 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritain’s media regulator is investigating a complaint from the former BBC news presenterHuw Edwardsabout a Channel 5 drama depicting his downfall.Ofcom said it was investigatingPower: The Downfall of Huw Edwards, which starred Martin Clunes and was broadcast earlier this year, under its “fairness and privacy” rules.The drama became the channel’shighest-rated show of the yearafter its broadcast in March, attracting 3.8 million viewers in four weeks.Edwards, once one of the BBC’s highest-paid newsreaders, confirmed to the Guardian that he had made the complaint. He said he had a series of concerns about its depiction of the events that led up to his disgrace.The 65-year-oldpleaded guiltyto accessing indecent photographs of children in July 2024 and was sentenced to six months in prison, suspended for two years.TheChannel 5two-part series, produced by Wonderhood Studios and Krempelwood Entertainment, focuses on an earlier allegation made by the Sun in July 2023 that claimed that a “top BBC star” paid a teenager more than £35,000 for sexual pictures.Edwards waslater revealedto be the star in question.He has previously claimed that the producers of the Channel 5 show failed to “check with me the truth of any aspect of their narrative”, saying that it was “hardly likely to convey the reality of what happened”.Channel 5 has defended the programme, saying it was based on “extensive interviews with the victim, his family, the journalists who revealed his story, text exchanges between the victim and Edwards, and court reporting”.View image in fullscreenMartin Clunes as Huw Edwards in the Channel 5 drama about the former BBC presenter’s downfall.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting Limited/PAWhen the broadcaster announced it was making the show, it said it would explore how someone “was groomed by one of the most powerful figures in television”.In a statement to the Guardian, Edwards said: “I am relieved thatOfcomhas seen fit to investigate the ‘factual drama’ made by Channel 5 and Wonderhood Studios.“The drama gave viewers a wholly misleading and unfair version of events. I was not given a fair opportunity to respond to the many inaccuracies and fabrications in the programme.“I can say no more at this stage. I hope Ofcom is allowed to consider my complaint objectively, free from intimidation from hostile parts of the press.”A Channel 5 spokesperson said: “We stand by the programme and will be robustly defending this complaint.”Edwards appears to bedisputing some of the detailsof his interactions with the person he is alleged to have groomed.Ofcom has not given details of the grounds for its investigation. However, under broadcasting rules, it can investigate “unjust or unfair treatment of individuals or organisations in programmes” or “unwarranted infringement of privacy in programmes”.The regulator will examine the material supplied by Edwards and Channel 5 before reaching a ruling.An Ofcom spokesperson said: “We are investigating a fairness and privacy complaint about this programme.”Edwards, who has been taking tentative steps back into public life with a blog, has previously suggested heplanned to produce his own accountof “these terrible events”.“This is a slow process given the fragile state of my health,” he said in March, before the broadcast of Channel 5’s drama. “I have been open about my struggle with persistent mental illness over a period of 25 years. What is less well known is the severity of that condition, which was managed successfully until the downward spiral, which led to an appalling outcome.“Mental illness is misunderstood by many but can never be an excuse for criminality. It can, however, at least help explain why people sometimes behave in shocking and reprehensible ways, and why things fell apart for me in the way they did.”Explore more on these topicsHuw EdwardsChannel 5OfcomTelevisionPrivacy & the mediaPress intrusionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand had ‘maniacal grin’ as he dragged woman into toilet and raped her, court told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Comedian, who is on trial at Southwark crown court, allegedly sexually assaulted woman within minute of meeting her
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Comedian, who is on trial at Southwark crown court, allegedly sexually assaulted woman within minute of meeting her
Content: Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court in London on Monday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court in London on Monday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAUK newsRussell Brand had ‘maniacal grin’ as he dragged woman into toilet and raped her, court toldComedian, who is on trial at Southwark crown court, allegedly sexually assaulted woman within minute of meeting herEmine SinmazMon 19 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand had a “weird maniacal” grin on his face like a clown when he grabbed a woman’s breasts before dragging her into a toilet and raping her, a court has heard.The 51-year-old comedian is accused of orally raping the MTV worker as he told her: “You want to do this,” and: “Come on, don’t be a spoilsport.”The woman said she felt her innocence had been taken and that she was scared, shaking and “numb” after the alleged assault at a birthday party at a bar in Soho, London, in 2004.Brand faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.The TV personality sat still and upright in the dock on Monday as the woman’s pre-recorded police interview was played to jurors at Southwark crown court.She told officers she found Brand funny on Big Brother spin-off shows on Channel 4, but that he sexually assaulted her within a minute of meeting her at the bar.She said: “He literally just grabbed my boobs, out of nowhere, just in the middle of a conversation and I just remember this weird maniacal grin, looming in front of me as he just grabbed my boobs.“I was completely in shock and was like: ‘What the hell are you doing? I’ve literally just met you.’ Then literally he grabbed my arm and dragged me into the toilets.”She broke down in tears as she recounted how, within seconds, Brand allegedly orally raped her in a locked, flooded toilet as she told him: “What are you doing? I don’t want to do this.”She said: “I pushed him away and he said: ‘Come on, come on, don’t be a spoilsport.’ He kept pushing my head down and wouldn’t let me go. I just froze. I didn’t know what to do.”She said she closed her eyes during the alleged attack and remembered a man knocking on the toilet door saying: “Are you OK?” before she walked out in a daze.“I remember this really, really clearly – he [Brand] turned to me and went: ‘Oh, I guess we should swap numbers now’, like it was just all normal, like he hadn’t just forced me to do that,” she recalled.When she was asked to go over the alleged attack in more detail, the woman described how Brand had a “big grin … like a clown” and a “weird look” in his eye after he assaulted her at the bar. “There was no sexual flirting, it was just a normal conversation about him being on Big Brother,” she said.The woman alleged she then recalled being “steered” into Brand’s car before the comedian’s driver ferried them to a different bar in Camden.“I was in disbelief and shock and I felt this nudge and I looked around and he [Brand] had his penis out again in the car and he was going ‘come on, come on, suck it’ and I was just like ‘no’. He took ‘no’ for an answer then.”She did not report the alleged sexual assault and rape to police until 2023, when media reports about Brand’s alleged misconduct were published.“I just felt this shame that I allowed him to do that to me,” she told officers in her interview. “I just didn’t want to admit it to myself, not to anyone.”She did tell a friend and colleague that Brand had “tried to” assault her and that he was a “sexual predator”.Giving evidence from behind a screen on Monday afternoon, the woman said she was “terrified” to report the attack at the time because of the “lad culture” of the 2000s.She said: “He was a celebrity and it would be his words against mine. I would be ostracised in my work environment or friends.“I just thought the odds weren’t in my favour and I didn’t want to have to go through a court where somebody is tearing down my character.”In cross-examination, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why the woman had not reported the alleged attack during the #MeToo movement and suggested she had “willingly” gone into the toilet with Brand for “a kiss and a cuddle”.She denied that was the case, and the barrister’s suggestion that she had been excited and charmed to meet Brand.She said: “I was not charmed in the slightest. I’d met this person for a minute before I was sexually assaulted.”She insisted she “wasn’t a giddy schoolgirl” and denied being “starstruck”.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Youth services in parts of England in state of emergency, children’s commissioner says | Children | The Guardian
description: Rachel de Souza names Middlesbrough and Hounslow among hardest places in which to grow up and says some children are being ‘radically failed’
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Rachel de Souza names Middlesbrough and Hounslow among hardest places in which to grow up and says some children are being ‘radically failed’
Content: The children’s commissioner has spoken to children on recent visits to schools, youth clubs and young offender institutions around the country.Photograph: Luigi Masella/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe children’s commissioner has spoken to children on recent visits to schools, youth clubs and young offender institutions around the country.Photograph: Luigi Masella/Getty ImagesChildrenYouth services in parts of England in state of emergency, children’s commissioner saysRachel de Souza names Middlesbrough and Hounslow among hardest places in which to grow up and says some children are being ‘radically failed’Patrick ButlerSocial policy editorMon 19 Oct 2026 08.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleServices for children in parts ofEnglandare in a “state of emergency”, according to a report that identifies what it claims to be the hardest places in the country for young people to grow up in.The children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, said in some local authorities individual service failures or systemic problems meant “no child could reasonably be expected to thrive and those that do thrive do so against the odds”.She said she had spoken to children on recent visits to schools, youth clubs and young offender institutions around the country and some of the things she had heard and seen had “utterly disgusted” her.On a recent visit to Middlesbrough, a 14-year-old-girl had informed her of the crime statistics in her area. “Children should not have to know those statistics,” De Souza said.She added: “Their parents should not have to talk about them over dinner to explain why children cannot play outside. Schools should not have administrative staff dealing with drug overdoses and racist thugs. Nowhere in England should ‘a chase from the police’ be a primary source of entertainment.”De Souza said she wanted to shine a light on areas where childhood was hardest. “We cannot shy away from the fact that indicators such as poor education outcomes, long health waiting lists or simply feeling unsafe converge in particular places,” she said.“In some communities, these challenges amount to nothing less than a state of emergency. Not for every child. Not everywhere. But what we see here is a litany of failure. In so many areas of the country, children are being radically failed.”View image in fullscreenRachel de Souza is the children’s commissioner for England.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAHer analysis is based on official data covering more than 160 measures, including child poverty, educational outcomes, community safety, NHS waiting times and access to playgrounds.It names a clutch of relatively deprived areas – Middlesbrough, Hounslow, Bradford, Nottingham, Halton, Peterborough, Leicester, Liverpool, Sunderland and Medway as the hardest places in which to grow up in England.By contrast, a series of relatively wealthy areas – Cheshire East, Merton, Surrey, Richmond upon Thames, Hertfordshire, Cheshire West and Chester, Haringey, Leicestershire, Central Bedfordshire and Wokingham – are identified as the least challenging places in which to be a child.“What children across the country feel to be true is in fact true. That it simply is harder to be a child in Middlesbrough than it is in Cheshire … the outcomes are shocking … an unacceptable failure,” the report says.It adds: “When areas are unsafe, that is not a point on a dashboard, it is children being the subject of racist abuse and violence on the way to school. When local services fail, it is not a failure to hit KPIs [key performance indicators], it is a child on the phone to their school with their parents dead in the other room.”The report, calledThe Childhood Lottery, says a north-south divide exists, with authorities in the south more likely to score higher across the metrics, and those in the north more likely to score lower, with the Midlands in between.De Souza said children should be a priority in the government’s devolution agenda and she urged the government to draw up a series of minimum standards for education, policing, health and youth services. A national fund should be created to invest in areas that fail to hit the benchmarks.She recommended that every strategic authority should have a deputy mayor for children, accountable for delivering on a “children’s test” ensuring that local policies bring benefits and improvements to young people’s services.The Department for Education said it was working to improve childcare support and school standards, and it was giving more power to “local leaders” to shape the future of their education.Explore more on these topicsChildrenYoung peopleLocal governmentNorth-south divideEnglandLondonPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Stop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MP  | Environment | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Chris Hinchliff urges environment watchdog to block rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in one of UK’s most protected areas
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: Exclusive: Chris Hinchliff urges environment watchdog to block rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in one of UK’s most protected areas
Content: Coltishall on the Norfolk Broads. Critics say the planning rules are a ‘licence to kill nature’.Photograph: Jim Laws/AlamyView image in fullscreenColtishall on the Norfolk Broads. Critics say the planning rules are a ‘licence to kill nature’.Photograph: Jim Laws/AlamyEnvironmentStop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MPExclusive: Chris Hinchliff urges environment watchdog to block rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in one of UK’s most protected areasSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 08.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe environment watchdog is being urged to intervene in “cash to trash” planning rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in theNorfolkBroads despite the damage to one of the UK’s most environmentally protected areas.Labour’s flagship planning reforms allow damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked if developers pay into a central nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date. These environmental delivery plans (EDPs) have beencalled “cash to trash” by critics, who say they roll back decades of environmental law and are a “licence to kill nature”.The Norfolk Broads, a heavily protected biodiversity hotspot that is home to more than a quarter of the UK’s rarest plants and animals, is the guinea pig for the first EDP. Developers will pay £2,675 per house – £42m in total – and in return get permission to build 15,780 new homes in the Broads.The government’s nature adviser,Natural England, which created the plan, states the development will cause environmental harm in the form of physical, chemical, hydrological and biological damage to the habitats and rare species from increased nitrogen and phosphorus pollution. The Broads are already in ecological decline and require cuts of 91-97% in nutrient pollution to recover.Chris Hinchliff, the Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, is calling on the Office for Environmental Protection (OEP) to intervene and stop theapproval of the plan. He said the first EDP – which will be used as a blueprint for others – is in breach of the requirements of the government’s Planning and Infrastructure Act, is not based on the best available science and does not address pollution. In a letter to Natalie Prosser, the chief executive of the OEP, he said: “Unless the OEP acts now, those failures will be locked into the first plan of its kind and repeated in every future EDP that follows.“On Natural England’s own figures, the conservation measures it funds would leave about 83% of the extra nitrogen and up to 61% of the extra phosphorus going into the water, every year and permanently. These are protected sites that the plan itself says need pollution inputs cut by up to 97% to recover,” he said.Hinchliff said measures that would have reduced nutrient pollution from the new homes, such as upgrading septic tanks, using small-scale underground treatment plants for homes not connected to the mains sewers and planting riverside buffer strips, were not included in Natural England’s EDP.“In their place, the plan relies on indirect measures: fen cutting, deer control, catch-dyke works, removing one weir and restoring one kilometre of river,” he said.“A plan that leaves most of the pollution unaddressed, that ‘locks in’ ecological degraded status, does not ‘address’ the harm in any ordinary sense of the word,” he added.Ministers say the EDPs are needed to unblock growth as they pursue a target to build 1.5m new homes by the end of this parliament and are a “win-win” for nature and economic growth. The nature restoration fund, they say, will deliver coordinated, larger-scale conservation measures rather than piecemeal offsets.BroadcasterChris Packham, who is supporting the campaign against the Norfolk EDP by the charity WildFish, said environmental laws fought for over decades would be cancelled at the stroke of a pen.“The Norfolk Broads are among Europe’s most precious wetlands: swallowtails and fen orchids, bitterns booming in the reeds and lamprey and bullhead in the gravels of the Wensum, one of England’s finest chalk rivers,” said Packham.“But … they are drowning in pollution and the government has devised a cunning scheme to pour in a whole lot more.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWild beaver kits born in Norfolk for first time in more than 500 yearsRead moreThe push for growth comes as the UK is in a nature crisis: wild bird populationshave fallento their lowest level since records began, with nearly half of species in decline,hedgehog numbershave plummeted by 66% and sewage, agricultural runoff and chemicals have left rivers suffering with atoxic cocktail of pollution.The Norfolk Broads EDP is out to consultation, which ends on 27 October. The Wildlife Trusts said the EDP would allow phosphorus from new homes to increase existing pollution levels on the rivers Yare, Bure and Wensum – a delicate chalk stream – without sufficient action from developers to mitigate for the impact.“Even minor increases could be enough to tip the health of these rivers over the edge, with calamitous consequences for the Norfolk Broads,” said Matthew Browne, the head of public affairs at the Wildlife Trusts.Bradley Tooze, the nature restoration fund director at Natural England, said: “The environment delivery plan aims to deliver better outcomes to protect the precious habitats of the Norfolk Broads while enabling sustainable development, including through river restoration measures and wetland habitat creation.“We welcome all views on our proposals and encourage stakeholders to share their expertise to help shape this new approach to nature restoration.”A government spokesperson said: “The aim of this environmental delivery plan is to protect and boost the natural environment. It’s based on the latest evidence and has been scrutinised by a scientific panel including independent experts. We welcome contributions to the ongoing consultation where people or organisations have views about how best to secure the aims we all share – protecting and restoring nature at a scale the status quo isn’t delivering.”Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentNorfolkConstruction industryPollutionConservationRiversChris PackhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult | Kenya | The Guardian
description: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors
Content: Doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie during a court session of his murder trial judgment at the Mombasa law courts, Kenya on Monday.Photograph: EPAView image in fullscreenDoomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie during a court session of his murder trial judgment at the Mombasa law courts, Kenya on Monday.Photograph: EPAKenyaKenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adultPaul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutorsReutersMon 19 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.View image in fullscreenKenyan high court judge Diana Kavedza Mochache on 19 October.Photograph: EPAMackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.View image in fullscreenA Kenyan national youth service officer talks to a woman while on guard at the entrance to the Mombasa law courts on Monday 19 October.Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty ImagesThe case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.View image in fullscreenPaul Mackenzie and his co-accused during their court appearance on 19 October.Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty ImagesThe plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.Mackenzie facesother charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.Explore more on these topicsKenyaReligionAfricaChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Three deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivals | Japan | The Guardian
description: Deputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhere
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Deputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhere
Content: The Saijo festival in Saijo, western Japan. The events are held in thanks to Shinto deities for a plentiful harvest.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Saijo festival in Saijo, western Japan. The events are held in thanks to Shinto deities for a plentiful harvest.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesJapanThree deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivalsDeputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhereJustin McCurryin TokyoMon 19 Oct 2026 05.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.View image in fullscreenParticipants push and pull a float during the Danjiri festival celebrations in Anan, Tokushima.Photograph: Keiichi Miyashita/AFLO/ShutterstockThe accidents occurred when the floats, which can weigh up to 4 tonnes, toppled as they were being pulled at speed around tight corners by hundreds of men, police said. The turns, known asyarimawashi, are a highlight of the festivals, originally held to pray for good autumn harvests.It is not clear if Nabae lost his balance or if the contraption toppled on to him, according to police in Saijo, where the festival has been held annually since the Edo period (1603-1868).Media reports said 11 floats, each weighing as much as 3 tonnes, were lined up side by side at the time of the accident.The annual Saijo festivals, featuring more than 100 floats, are held to thank Shinto deities for plentiful grain crops, the Jiji news agency said.View image in fullscreenThe floats weigh up to 4 tonnes each.Photograph: Keiichi Miyashita/AFLO/ShutterstockSaijo’s mayor, Mitsuyoshi Ochi, voiced shock and sadness at Nabae’s death. “Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still can’t believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” he said in a statement.In February, two people died in a crush at the “naked man festival” in Okayama, where as many as 10,000 men dressed infundoshiloincloths squeeze into the grounds of a temple and compete to seize a pair of sacred wooden sticks thrown into the crowd by the head priest. The two men who succeed are declared “lucky men” for the year.Explore more on these topicsJapanAsia PacificFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Christiane Amanpour announces she’s leaving CNN after 43 years | CNN | The Guardian
description: Anchor’s departure not thought to be linked to company’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance Media
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Anchor’s departure not thought to be linked to company’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance Media
Content: Christiane Amanpour in Bayeux, France, in 2018.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChristiane Amanpour in Bayeux, France, in 2018.Photograph: Charly Triballeau/AFP/Getty ImagesCNNChristiane Amanpour announces she’s leaving CNN after 43 yearsAnchor’s departure not thought to be linked to company’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance MediaJeremy BarrMon 19 Oct 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChristiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She also hosts a show for PBS, Amanpour and Company, that will conclude at the end of this year.In the statement, Amanpour said she came to the decision to “separate” from the network “after many months of thought and a few sleepless nights”.“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf war, to the horrors of the Bosnian war, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor,” she wrote.She ended her statement by encouraging her CNN colleagues: “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”Amanpour, 68, has been open about her ongoing treatment for ovarian cancer, which she was diagnosed with in 2021.Her decision comes at a notable time for the network, which is now part of a larger media conglomerate called Skydance that is run by David Ellison, with heavy backing from Larry Ellison, his Trump-donor father and Oracle co-founder.Her exit is not thought to be specifically tied to the network’s new ownership, which is viewed skeptically by some CNN journalists because of its perceived closeness to the Trump administration. But, in her statement, Amanpour seemed to nod to concerns about the network’s future, saying that she “will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism”.She expanded on that commitment to independence in a taped message to viewers of her CNN International show on Monday afternoon.“You know that I’ve always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you for as long as I am here and beyond,” she said. “That’s especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides – political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field.”In his own memo, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson,who announced earlier this monththat he will be remaining with the merged company, thanked Amanpour “for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship”.“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”Amanpour said she will continue hosting her podcast, The Ex Files and that she “[looks] forward to interesting new projects down the line”.Explore more on these topicsCNNThe news on TVTV newsTelevisionTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan | Sudan | The Guardian
description: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war
Content: A man stands in a hole filled with drone components in El Obeid, Sudan, in March. There has been an escalation in the use of drones in the war.Photograph: Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man stands in a hole filled with drone components in El Obeid, Sudan, in March. There has been an escalation in the use of drones in the war.Photograph: Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesSudanDrone attack near market kills 80 in SudanWitness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of warCarlos Mureithiand agenciesMon 19 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA drone strike near a market in southernSudanon Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led byMohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.The fighting in Sudan has killedhundreds of thousandsof people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN,warnedthe security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”AFP contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsSudanAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns | Industrial action | The Guardian
description: More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies
Content: North Sea oil companies have cut investment in UK assets, blaming government energy policies and the tax regime.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyView image in fullscreenNorth Sea oil companies have cut investment in UK assets, blaming government energy policies and the tax regime.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyIndustrial actionNorth Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warnsMore than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companiesJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorth Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.TheUniteunion said on ⁠Monday that more than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers would take part ⁠in a 24-hour ​strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decisionon the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.Explore more on these topicsIndustrial actionOilUniteTrade unionsEnergy industryOil and gas companiesFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Concerning issues’ found at GB power grid by inquiry into cover-up claims | Energy industry | The Guardian
description: Neso control room staff accused senior executives of covering up extent of blackout risks during June heatwave
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Neso control room staff accused senior executives of covering up extent of blackout risks during June heatwave
Content: Investigators found ‘no evidence’ inappropriate influence over Neso’s operational decisions or that control room engineers were warned against leaving a paper trail of their efforts to stabilise the grid.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInvestigators found ‘no evidence’ inappropriate influence over Neso’s operational decisions or that control room engineers were warned against leaving a paper trail of their efforts to stabilise the grid.Photograph: Darren Staples/AFP/Getty ImagesEnergy industry‘Concerning issues’ found at GB power grid by inquiry into cover-up claimsNeso control room staff accused senior executives of covering up extent of blackout risks during June heatwaveJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndependent investigators have found significant and concerning “cultural issues” at Great Britain’s grid operator after control room staff accused senior executives of covering up the extent of blackout risks in the UK during the June heatwave.An external legal firm tasked with investigating a series of whistleblower allegations against the National Energy System Operator (Neso) raised concerns over how high levels stress among control room engineers was handled by the company.The three-month investigation began after whistleblowers accused Neso ofa cover-up over the growing risk of blackouts. They claimed the grid was becoming increasingly unmanageable, and that control room decisions were subject to “interference” by the company’s corporate affairs team to protect the reputation of the government-owned operator.Theunprecedented control room revoltincluded multiple internal complaints, the leak of internal documents to the press, and accusations of whistleblower intimidation.Neso was forced to abandon plans for an internal investigation into the claims in favour of an independent investigation by the law firm Evershed Sutherlands, whosefindings were published on Monday.The law firm said that while it found “no evidence” of inappropriate influence over operational decisions, or that control room engineers were warned against leaving a paper trail of their efforts to stabilise the grid, the investigation found “cultural, governance and control issues” that were “significant findings in their own right”.The allegations against Neso emerged after the June heatwave caused grid frequency levels to fall below normal operating limits on a number of occasionsand required emergency assistancefrom neighbouring countries to keep the lights on.The grid woes were caused by near-record temperatures that caused demand for electricity to run air-conditioning systems to surge while a high pressure heat dome slowed wind turbines and prompted unplanned outages at gas and nuclear plants across Europe.Tim Jarvis, the chief executive of the regulator Ofgem, said that although the investigation did not uphold the whistleblower’s specific allegations, it raised “important and concerning issues about working culture and practices at Neso”.The investigation found there were “high levels of stress and concern” within the control room over how staff would be able to keep the power system balanced as renewable energy replaces legacy fossil fuel power plants in line with the government’s net zero ambitions.It said there was a view that senior Neso executives did not fully appreciate or understand the pressures faced by the control room engineers who were responsible for keeping the lights on “on the frontline”.In addition, staff felt that their concerns or complaints went “largely unheard” because of the need to keep external stakeholders including the government and the regulators happy, according to the law firm’s report.Fintan Slye, Neso’s chief executive, said the report was “constructive” in identifying areas in which the grid operator could improve how staff could raise concerns and how to respond to them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I want all colleagues at Neso to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make,” he said.A separate Ofgem investigation, which is ongoing, will look into whether the cultural issues identified by Eversheds played a role in the operational decision-making, system security or raising energy costs for consumers.“We will not prejudge that assessment,” Jarvis said, “But nor will we shy away from its conclusions. Our job is to establish the facts, identify the lessons and ensure action is taken.”The Ofgem findings, which will be published no later than 31 March 2027, could lead to an enforcement investigation by the regulator if it believes Neso has not complied with obligations under market rules.Michael Shanks, the minister for energy, said the government expected “significant action without delay” and would “keep progress under close review”.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryEnglandScotlandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bank of England said to be reviewing Barclays’ handling of private credit loans | Barclays | The Guardian
description: Concerns financial contracts known as derivatives were incorrectly logged, potentially boosting Barclays’ profits
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Concerns financial contracts known as derivatives were incorrectly logged, potentially boosting Barclays’ profits
Content: Barclays is said to have built up billions of dollars’ worth of exposure to private credit loans using derivatives, sources cited by the Financial Times said.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersView image in fullscreenBarclays is said to have built up billions of dollars’ worth of exposure to private credit loans using derivatives, sources cited by the Financial Times said.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersBarclaysBank of England said to be reviewing Barclays’ handling of private credit loansConcerns financial contracts known as derivatives were incorrectly logged, potentially boosting Barclays’ profitsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBank of Englandis reportedly looking into Barclays’ handling of loans linked to the embattled private credit sector.The Bank’s regulatory arm, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), started reviewing the matter this year after concerns were raised by a Barclays insider, according to the Financial Times.The concerns related to the wayBarclayslogged the derivatives, known as total return swaps, used to finance the loans it issues to private credit firms.
