Those derivatives – financial contracts that track the performance of an underlying asset – are said to have been logged in the wrong portfolio, indicating they were less risky than they actually were.That could mean the bank was not holding enough capital to cover potential losses, and could have boosted its profitability.Barclays is said to have built up billions of dollars’ worth of exposure to private credit loans using derivatives, according to sources cited by the Financial Times.The bank said: “Barclays’ treatment of total return swaps is consistent with accounting and regulatory capital requirements.”It added that it followed capital rules when deciding where to log certain assets. “Those conditions were met and supported by appropriate governance internally and by external advisers,” Barclays said.The bank said its total exposure to the private credit sector was worth about £15bn, and that the relevant derivatives accounted for £300m of that total.The Bank of England declined to comment.Shares in Barclays fell by 3.5% on Monday, the second-biggest faller on the FTSE 100 index, amid a wider sell-off in the banking sector. The bank is due to report its latest financial results on Thursday.The report could prove awkward for the new PRA boss, Katharine Braddick, who spent six years as Barclays’ head of strategic policy and senior adviser to its chief executive, before becoming head of the bank regulator this spring.The Bank of England said Braddick was recused from all matters relating to Barclays until the end of 2026.Last year, Barclays’ chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan,insisted it had the right controls in placeto manage its exposure to the private credit industry, where critics worry lending standards have slipped.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPrivate credit firms – which form a core part of the shadow banking sector – use investor money to fund their loans to companies, rather than customer loans or deposits, and face less regulation as a result.Traditional banks, worried about missing out on a booming market, started lending directly to private credit firms or their funds, and to companies that simultaneously borrowed from private credit firms. A growing number of banks have also been partnering with asset managers on private credit deals.However, critics worry that private credit players have been too lenient in deciding who to lend to, and regulators have said any fallout could destabilise traditional banks that are now intertwined with the industry.Growing anxieties also triggered a multibillion-poundsurge in withdrawals from some private credit fundsearlier this year, forcing some to cap the amount of money that clients can pull out.The private credit industry has been trying to recover after some high-profile company failures, including two private credit-backed US automotive companies, Tricolor and First Brands, last year, both of which were hit by fraud allegations. That was followed by the mortgage lender Market Financial Solutions (MFS), which collapsed in February amid allegations of fraud.Barclays was among the banks that suffered losses on the back of Tricolor’s collapse,alongside JP Morgan. Barclays also took a £228m hit after the MFS failure.Explore more on these topicsBarclaysPrudential Regulation Authority (PRA)Bank of EnglandBankingFinancial sectorRegulatorsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguards | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: Despite recent progress, almost a fifth of air travellers with disabilities are still dissatisfied with their experience
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Despite recent progress, almost a fifth of air travellers with disabilities are still dissatisfied with their experience
Content: A report from an industry-led accessibility group says there is ‘much more to be done’ a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson.Photograph: Ian Patrick/AlamyView image in fullscreenA report from an industry-led accessibility group says there is ‘much more to be done’ a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson.Photograph: Ian Patrick/AlamyAirline industryUK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguardsDespite recent progress, almost a fifth of air travellers with disabilities are still dissatisfied with their experienceGwyn TophamTransport correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDisabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the government has pledged, including protection from damaged wheelchairs and support from trained staff.A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after areview led by Tanni Grey-Thompsondemanded action to improve air travel in response tonumerous incidentsin which passengers had beenleft strandedwithout assistance.The Department forTransportsaid airports had added more staff training and a new standardised system has been set up to prepare airlines for handling mobility aids, after more than 1,000 wheelchairs were damaged in transit in 2024, equivalent to more than 80 a month.Almost one in five disabled passengers are still dissatisfied with their air travel experience though, according to an industry body, and requests for assistance are continuing to rise.The government is planning to remove the maximum payout in compensation for lost and damaged wheelchairs, and to give the aviation regulator new powers to fine airlines and airports when passengers are not given the assistance they need to travel.The changes are expected to be in the civil aviation bill which is progressing through parliament and which the government said would give air passengers stronger protection and consumer rights.The transport secretary,Heidi Alexander, said: “People must be able to fly with dignity and peace of mind. For disabled passengers this means not worrying about their wheelchair coming back in one piece, or whether staff will be there to support them around the airport.“We’ve backed industry to overhaul staff training, prevent damage to mobility aids and create easy, simple ways for passengers to share key information before they fly.”The co-chairs of the aviation accessibility implementation group, which is assessing progress on the 19 recommendations in Grey-Thompson’s report, said: “There is much more to be done, but we have made a positive start. We will be focusing now on embedding more of the changes that are needed to enable disabled people to fly with confidence and dignity.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe chief executive of lobby group Airlines UK, Tim Alderslade, said the number of passengers requiring assistance was up nearly 10% year on year.“82% report that they are satisfied with their air travel experience which demonstrates the efforts and progress airlines are making for those who require additional support when they fly,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAirline industryDisabilityAir transportTransportTransport policyHeidi AlexandernewsShareReuse this content

title: Pedigree chums: why the movies are killing off fewer dogs | Movies | The Guardian
description: Are film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch? Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch?
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: Are film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch? Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch?
Content: Paw patrol … Brad Pitt and his best friend in Heart of the Beast.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyView image in fullscreenPaw patrol … Brad Pitt and his best friend in Heart of the Beast.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyMoviesPedigree chums: why the movies are killing off fewer dogsAre film-makers wary of alienating increasingly sensitive audiences by offing a pooch? Or is humanity now just too soft to deal with the trauma of a Turner & Hooch?Stuart HeritageMon 19 Oct 2026 07.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 10.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere was a time, not so long ago, when watching a film was a clearcut experience. There would be a good guy and a bad guy, and you would know who the bad guy was because they would shoot a dog in the face.It happened more times than you might expect. Mad Max 2, dog gets shot. Revenge, dog gets shot. Turner & Hooch, dog gets shot. Red, dog gets shot. Man with the Gun, dog gets shot. Badlands, dog gets shot. Dog Soldiers, you’ll never guess.But how things change. These days – thanks to either political correctness gone mad or basic human decency or whatever – dogs are much less likely to be murdered in films.A study by (of course) pet insurance firm Lassie has discovered that the number of dogs that die in movies dropped by a whopping 80% between 2020 and 2025. It reports that six years ago, 10 of the 100 highest-grossing films featured a dog dying either on or off screen. But by 2025, this number fell to just two.Now, this could be down to any number of reasons. The first, and possibly most important, is that cinema finds itself in a perilous position. The future of the entire medium is at stake and every dollar counts, so why risk alienating a swathe of the audience by gratuitously offing a pup? Things are so bad that there is an entire website –Does the Dog Die?– purely to warn viewers of any enjoyment-spoiling canine fatalities.View image in fullscreenNo spoilers … Tom Hanks and Hooch.Photograph: Cinetext Collection/Sportsphoto/AllstarIn fact, we may have become so sensitive to animal-related deaths onscreen that it has been offered as one potential reason for the Digger flop. After all, the film’s trailer heavily focused on Digger’s sick cat as it was given a terminal diagnosis. Now obviously it was a deliberately bad animatronic prop cat, but that didn’t stop large numbers of Does the Dog Die?’s users from warning people of its death.So nervous are we as an audience that film-makers cannot even make dog movies without explicitly reassuring us that the animals are going to make it out OK. As early as June, Richard Raymond – the producer of Brad Pitt’s new canine movie Heart of the Beast – took to social media to literally spoil the ending of his own film, just to set our minds at rest, tweeting:“The dog does not die. You’re welcome.”And then there’s Anne Hathaway, whose film The End of Oak Street concerns a family, a dog, and a very hungry T rex. During promotion for the (12A) film, Hathaway tacitly managed to reassure audiences that the dog wasn’t going to become dino chow, by stating that“I feel like movies that kill dogs should automatically be rated R.”Of course, however, this leads me to suspect that Anne Hathaway hasn’t actually watched all of her films. Her highest-grossing of the year was Christopher Nolan’sThe Odyssey, which features a dog death so absolutely gratuitous that it legitimately borders on slapstick. In short, a dog gets hurled off a cliff. Is it central to the story? No, it isn’t even remotely peripheral to the story. It’s just a thing that happens. The sun rises. The sun sets. John Leguizamo lobs a puppy off the side of a cliff.Obviously Hathaway is wrong here. An automatic R-rating for a dog death would change the texture of films as we know them. In Turner & Hooch, Hooch’s death was the entire point of the movie. Did it permanently traumatise a generation of children who thought they had signed up for a funny dog flick? Yes. But did it also work to brace us better against the cruel realities of the world? Also yes.View image in fullscreenWhen the going gets ruff … Anne Hathaway and canine companion in The End of Oak Street.Photograph: Ent-movie/AlamyAnd perhaps that’s what we all need. We live in deeply uncertain times, and sometimes it feels like we still aren’t fully prepared for the horrors that await us. So ask yourself this: is this the right time to cosset ourselves away from things that upset us, or is it time that film-makers started to act responsibly again by killing as many dogs as they possibly can? It doesn’t matter what sort of film it is, whether it’s a drama or a horror or a Paw Patrol cartoon. Let’s impose a mandatory canine death quota to toughen us up again.Who’s with me? Nobody? What if it was just Paw Patrol, then? What if it was just Chase from Paw Patrol? Still no? Suit yourselves.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimalsDogsAnne HathawayAnimal welfarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunion | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In the dazzling archival documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a 1972 cocktail party brings together various creative luminaries as they discuss and debate
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: In the dazzling archival documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a 1972 cocktail party brings together various creative luminaries as they discuss and debate
Content: Aaron Douglas, Jean Blackwell Hutson, Richard Bruce Nugent, Eubie Blake, and Irvin C Miller in Once Upon a Time in Harlem.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAaron Douglas, Jean Blackwell Hutson, Richard Bruce Nugent, Eubie Blake, and Irvin C Miller in Once Upon a Time in Harlem.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonDocumentary films‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunionIn the dazzling archival documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a 1972 cocktail party brings together various creative luminaries as they discuss and debateAndrew LawrenceMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a flowering of the arts at the dawn of the 20th century, the Harlem Renaissance marked the breakthrough moment when Black Americans asserted their creative control, defining a culture that had been purpose-built to exclude them. The imprints were all over the Jazz Age – on bookshelves and radio, in flapper dresses and cloche hats, in Hubert Julian’s daring flights and the fractious debates between Marcus Garvey and WEB Du Bois.Once Upon a Time in Harlem review – remarkable Harlem Renaissance documentaryRead moreLike theDavid committeeof the Italian Renaissance or the American Revolution’s Continental Congress, the Harlem Renaissance is one of those moments that makes you wonder: what was itreallylike? The Dark Tower salons? Those Cotton Club nights? The rent parties with all those New Negroes – a heady brew of southern émigrés, Caribbean vanguards and New York lifers – holding forth and hootin’ and hollerin’, high on the fact that they had found one another? Could they appreciate the significance of the moment as they were making it? “I remember being in Brooklyn in the 1990s and seeing various artists around,” says film-maker Liani Greaves, reflecting on her early career working with Tupac on Above the Rim and the director Hype Williams on Biggie music videos. “Brooklyn Moon Cafe was the spot. Sometimes we forget that it is The Now. We’re constantly looking to the next thing, looking outside.”Once Upon a Time in Harlem looks back – to the August day in 1972 when Liani’s grandfather, the prolific and pioneering film-maker William Greaves, threw a cocktail party at Duke Ellington House, invited over the surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance and switched on the cameras. (With Ellington himself too ill to attend, it fell to his sister, Ruth, to play host.) For four hours, these extraordinary partygoers – some seeing one another for the first time in 50 years – reminisced, made merry and reckoned with the Harlem Renaissance’s modern-day legacy. The 100-minute film itself is a time capsule, a cinematic Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in which the Harlem Renaissance gazes back at its own legacy, leaving future generations to unearth, interrogate and work from the reflections they find.It’s the kind of artefact today’s Black creatives should have in their library – for inspiration, for accountability, to ground themselves. But until hard copies are available – “That will exist!” says William’s son, director David Greaves, adding that streaming is still a long way off – audiences will have to catch Once Upon a Time in theaters, as the film opens nationwide this month. “We’ve always imagined people coming in groups, going with their family,” says Liani, a producer on the film. “We want people to be in community, visit with the film, and really experience it in that way.”Following in the tradition of A Great Day in Harlem, the documentary about Art Kane’sstunning photograph of jazz greatsgathered on Harlem stoop, Once Upon a Time is a home movie in every sense. William Greaves – an Actors Studio member alongside Marlon Brando before directing the groundbreaking meta-documentary Symbiopsychotaxiplasm – devoted himself to the project until his death in 2014 at age 87. Greaves kept rolling after the party, through the 80s and 90s. Liani remembers William and his wife, Louise Archambault Greaves, turning up with their cameras to a Harlem Aids walk she was working in the 2000s. Among Liani and David’s inheritances was some 60,000 feet of 16mm film held in storage. “I think they were shooting a lot of events, looking for evidence of the Harlem Renaissance,” Liani says. “But it felt to me that they had kind of lost their way. And just like in Symbiopsychotaxiplasm, he had to kind of step away in order for the film to be great.”So Liani and David kept the focus squarely on the party. They enlisted the help of preservation specialist Bill Brand to restore the 1972 footage, an 18-month process, before sending it off to a finishing house. “They did stuff that we could never have done 50 years ago,” David says. “Color correction, cleaning and also – I’ll be honest – taking hair out of the gate.” The results are visible in the richness, warmth and texture of the footage – the kind of craftsmanship movie-making used to be about.View image in fullscreenThomas Harvey, Ernest Crichlow, William Patterson, Romare Bearden, John Henrick Clarke, Ida Mae Cullen and Louise Patterson.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonAnd then the titans of the Harlem Renaissance start filling the frame: the photographer James Van Der Zee, demurring from an invitation to play Duke’s piano before letting his shockingly nimble fingers wander. Ragtime composer Eubie Blake reeling back to the time the papers misquoted him saying he’d never extend his hand to a white man. (He said he’d never extend itfirst, a distinction that mattered under segregation.) Regina Andrews, the essential librarian and curator, considered whether a Black artist could have worked in isolation while the movement was happening around them. “There was no way not to be caught up,” she says. “You were pulled along.”As the 1972 reunion unfolds, the film scrambles to capture every moment, following the connections and conversations across three rooms. David was part of the six-man crew his father assembled for the shoot, each member having to split their attention between the scene unfolding before them and whatever might be bubbling up somewhere else. There’s a lovely moment when one cameraman catches William slating him on from the edge of a scene, the silent soundman confirming with his eyes as another cameraman crosses the shot. (Syncing the picture to the sound was another puzzle that came together in restoration.)As William strains to impose a bit of film-making order on action already beyond his control, it’s clear he wouldn’t have it any other way, that he’s getting exactly what he wants from this crowd – big personalities, lively crosstalk, a tangible sense of those bygone salons. Partygoers in their 70s and 80s, flashing their modern finery, are stirred to youthful passion when the subjects that once animated them resurface – especially in the one-on-one interviews William Greaves shot with some Renaissance contributors after the party. “My father had them wear the same clothes so they would not be clashing,” David remembers fondly.It’s hard not to be awestruck when the Negro Actors Guild president, Leigh Whipper, drops into his Haile Selassie monologue from the Stalinist film Mission to Moscow, or when the civil rights activist Richard B Moore delivers a perfect recitation of the Claude McKay’s poem If We Must Die on cue. “I always say this is what it looks like when your brain is not on electronics,” Liani says. “I have to imagine many of them were writing with one another, to one another – some by hand, which is a different kind of brain skill. They were brilliant people.”View image in fullscreenLiani Greaves and David Greaves speak onstage.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images for FLCThe Harlem romantics also had a knack for expressing their disagreements with one another in erudite style – polite shade, we call it now. In one meaty scene, the multimedia artist Romare Bearden takes exception to the way artists like him were minimized in the seminal book on the Harlem Renaissance by Nathan Huggins; the Harvard professor is standing across the room, holding it. Huggins, though, does offer a credible defense – arguing that art and music are intrinsically more difficult to translate than the written word. “It is kind of poetic, the way they clap back,” Liani says. “It’s all in love and friendship.”Still, there wasn’t genuine affection for everyone in the room. Apparently, the presence of George Schuyler – the commentator who came up during the Renaissance before turning against progressivism and, later, the civil rights movement – was met with twisted faces and cold shoulders. One barb directed at him was cut out entirely. It speaks to the depth of the disagreements among the Renaissance’s vanguards, and the intensity with which they still cared. “It’s like [Garveyite community organizer] Thomas Harvey said at the end of the film: ‘We were on different roads, but all going toward the same goal,’” David says. “It shows that the Renaissance was not a monolith of thinking.”But the issue that really hung over the party was how the Harlem Renaissance would be remembered. Already, William’s guests were lamenting how the younger generation had moved on to zeitgeistier fare: comic books, funk music, blaxploitation films. David Greaves makes a point of tracking the change his father set out to chronicle in the documentary, moving from James Van Der Zee’s gorgeous black-and-white photographs of the neighborhood in full flower to William’s 70s footage of vacant faces and graffiti-strewn walls.Now those kids are the ones clamoring for respect for their artistic contributions. It shows how quickly times change, and how much Black creatives stand to gain by looking to the past as they take the culture forward. “I often think about this film as a recipe for a renaissance,” Liani says. “If you watch, the [Black Renaissance vanguards] tell you what to do. They talk about the importance of being in community, of being audacious. That’s how you create a moment.“Once Upon a Time in Harlem is out in US cinemas now and in the UK and Australia at a later dateExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Night Is Fading Away review – hypnotic homage to cinema as a force for public good | Movies | The Guardian
description: A local cinema becomes a refuge after Javier Milei’s election ushers in an era of far-right conservatism in Argentina
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: A local cinema becomes a refuge after Javier Milei’s election ushers in an era of far-right conservatism in Argentina
Content: Night watchman … Pelu (Octavio Bertone) in The Night Is Fading AwayView image in fullscreenNight watchman … Pelu (Octavio Bertone) in The Night Is Fading AwayMoviesReviewThe Night Is Fading Away review – hypnotic homage to cinema as a force for public goodA local cinema becomes a refuge after Javier Milei’s election ushers in an era of far-right conservatism in ArgentinaPhuong LeMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCinema halls – or dream palaces, as they’re affectionately called – offer a retreat into the realm of make-believe, and everyday drudgery is left at the door. Though set within a single-screen theatre in the Argentinian city of Córdoba, Ramiro Sonzini and Ezequiel Salinas’s hypnotic film invokes a more porous relationship between the screen and its audience. Here, the messiness of life beguilingly sneaks into this domain of fantasies, blurring the borders between public and private spaces.While the luminous black-and-white cinematography lends a dreamy fuzziness to the images, the narrative concerns are grounded in thorny economic realities. A film projectionist at his local cinema called Pelu (Octavio Bertone) is reassigned to the post of a night watchman due to budget cuts at the city hall. The cinema soon becomes his literal refuge: he moves out of his cramped rented flat and secretly takes up occupation at his workplace. He then welcomes a horde of other outsiders, including his unemployed roommate, an ageing drifter and a sex worker who livestreams her erotic shows from the cinema. Every night, they watch classic films from the old masters – Jean Renoir, Yasujiro Ozu and Robert Bresson to name a few – until the early hours.Despite these self-referential touches, the film steers clear of nostalgia; cinephilia is transformed into a force for public good, and a conduit to direct action. In the wake ofJavier Milei’s election win in 2023, which ushered in a new era of far-right conservatism, Pelu and his friends’ radical acts of vandalism transform a commercialised space into a restorative commune. In an echo of classic westerns, there’s a galvanising scene where these wayward outcasts gather around a fire to exchange songs and stories. No longer tethered to flickering images on a silver screen, the flames of camaraderie are also alive beyond the frame.The Night Is Fading Away is at theICA, London, from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsArgentinareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ghost in the Cell review – Indonesian prison-slasher-satire contains the most unhinged punch-up in decades | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Joko Anwar uses horror for social commentary as he skewers corruption and hypocrisy with likable silliness and raucous energy
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Director Joko Anwar uses horror for social commentary as he skewers corruption and hypocrisy with likable silliness and raucous energy
Content: Enjoyable blend of camp and politics … Ghost in the Cell.Photograph: Come and See PicturesView image in fullscreenEnjoyable blend of camp and politics … Ghost in the Cell.Photograph: Come and See PicturesMoviesReviewGhost in the Cell review – Indonesian prison-slasher-satire contains the most unhinged punch-up in decadesDirector Joko Anwar uses horror for social commentary as he skewers corruption and hypocrisy with likable silliness and raucous energyPhil HoadMon 19 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGiven the 2020s horror boom, Indonesia’s prolific Joko Anwar – who has worked more often in that genre than any other – should be better known. Using horror for social commentary, as Anwar has done often in the past, this prison-slasher-satire features the kind of scabrous broadsides against injustice you see in Bong Joon-ho’s films, andPark Chan-wook’s recent No Other Choice. But in skewering the corruption and hypocrisy of the director’s native country, it has its own likable silliness and raucous energy. As the inmates keep saying: this is Indonesia, not Norway!Fitted up for the murder of his boss, who is found gutted and spreadeagled on a ceiling fan, timid investigative journalist Dimas (Endy Arfian) winds up in the slammer. But murder, immediately followed by the flamboyant flaying of the victim, dogs him wherever he goes: the prison hitman assigned to dispose of him is in turn found in the washroom rendered into flesh origami. Charismatic prison refusenik Anggoro (Abimana Aryasatya) takes Dimas under his wing; as the victims stack up, an apparently clairvoyant member of his clique called Six (Yoga Pratama) admits that all of them manifested a red aura, signifying anger, prior to dying.You suspect Anwar himself is no stranger to the old red aura from time to time: from the warden-facilitated drug-dealing network to the separate wing of pampered elitist offenders, his film overspills with droll outrage over Indonesian corruption. Dimas’s exposé of an illegal forestry scheme is what appears to have dislodged the demonic entity that is now attached to him, and feeding off the local abundance of negative energy. But Six figures out that partaking in wholesome activities, like praying and dancing, lowers their chances of being picked off.Little more than a string of showpiece slaughters, Ghost in the Cell’s thin plot is really an excuse for Anwar to reel off his hitlist: he takes aim at cronyism, institutional brutality, private militias, secret mistresses, lapsed political idealism and the general degrading influence of money. But his film kidney-punches even harder when fully disguised and dramatised as comedy. This includes scenes where the aura-obsessed lags take a sudden interest in Qur’anic and twerking classes, and the most unhinged punch-up since John Carpenter’s They Live, during which Anggoro must periodically break into dancing to de-escalate his rage. Dynamically shot by Anwar, this is a very enjoyable blend of grand-guignol camp and political manifesto.Ghost in the Cell is on digital platforms in Australia and the UK from 26 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersHorror filmsCrime filmsIndonesiaWorld cinemareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Vampire Carnival review – it’s Twilight at the fairground as abs run wild in pointy-toothed tug of war | Movies | The Guardian
description: A mortal twentysomething is caught in a love triangle with two hunky vampire carnival workers in a film with good looks but not much to chew on
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: A mortal twentysomething is caught in a love triangle with two hunky vampire carnival workers in a film with good looks but not much to chew on
Content: Fair enough … Paulina Chávez and Corrado Martini in Vampire CarnivalView image in fullscreenFair enough … Paulina Chávez and Corrado Martini in Vampire CarnivalMoviesReviewVampire Carnival review – it’s Twilight at the fairground as abs run wild in pointy-toothed tug of warA mortal twentysomething is caught in a love triangle with two hunky vampire carnival workers in a film with good looks but not much to chew onPhil HoadMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Does this whole Edward Cullen act actually work?” A distinctTwilightfeeling is in the air in this initially enlivening vampire flick, with willowy twentysomething mortal Gemma (Nell Verlaque) caught in the middle of a pointy-toothed tug of war between tender Italian hunk Sebastian (Alvise Rigo) and her bad boy ex Eric (Kieron Moore). When she strolls with her friends into a hot vampire carnival, the ab count nearly outdoes the haemoglobin one. But this good-looking whirligig winds up disappointingly disjointed.Gemma is still regrouping after her father’s suicide, an unspecified amount of time earlier. So her mum is relieved when she takes a night off from grieving by checking out the local fair with pals Ryan (Corrado Martini) and Olivia (Pauline Chávez). Absent for many years, creepy Eric has apparently joined the circus, featuring as the ostentatiously self-harming Man Who Feels No Pain. But when Sebastian invites Gemma into the carnival’s orgiastic inner sanctum, she learns they are a coven of bloodsuckers who, under leader Toussaint (Jason Isaac), have a strict no-killing code of conduct. Or, in the case of potential initiates like Gemma, obtaining consent. “No means no,” says immortal softboi Sebastian.As befits any self-respecting ringmasters, directors David Charbonier and Justin Douglas Powell operate with much visual panache. They announce the trio’s entrance into the carnival with a splendid one-shot, tracking them, the denizens and local cop Dan (Cedrick Cooper). Later, they mount a crystalline confrontation between Ryan and Eric in a hall of mirrors. But, as with such stage endeavours, some of the effects are a bit cheesy: the supposedly Dionysian bolthole comes over more like a gastropub on deep-house DJ night. And Isaacs, playing the head vamp like a Rada fetish Gandalf, is at odds with the tone of what was previously a pleasingly downbeat slice of American alt.culturedom.The emphasis on general flamboyant ambience is more detrimental story-wise. In particular, the film vacillates between positioning the increasingly insubordinate Eric as kooky undead loose cannon and genuine tragic antihero, though the charismatic Moore does a lot to tie him into a satisfying, lethal whole. The schism in vampire philosophies is underexplored, and not enough ground is laid for the final reveal about Gemma and Eric’s troubled backstories. To turn Sebastian’s come-on to Gemma on its head, Vampire Carnival is too taken with the illusion instead of the truth.Vampire Carnival is on digital platforms from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsJason IsaacsTwilightreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movie | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most easily rewatched comfort films is an appreciation of a smart, funny and tender ode to fan culture
Author: Rachael Sigee
Headline: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most easily rewatched comfort films is an appreciation of a smart, funny and tender ode to fan culture
Content: Tim Allen, Alan Rickman, Sigourney Weaver and Patrick Breen in Galaxy Quest.Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarView image in fullscreenTim Allen, Alan Rickman, Sigourney Weaver and Patrick Breen in Galaxy Quest.Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarMy feelgood movieComedy films‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers detailing their most easily rewatched comfort films is an appreciation of a smart, funny and tender ode to fan cultureRachael SigeeMon 19 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“By Grabthar’s hammer, by the sons of Worvan … you shall be avenged.”If you have seen Galaxy Quest, those words may bring you close to tears. They mark the moment when Alan Rickman’s character – a Shakespearean luvvie turned sci-fi sidekick – realises that the ludicrous catchphrase he has reluctantly uttered thousands of times does matter after all.‘A rare indulgence’: why Black Swan is my feelgood movieRead more1999’s Galaxy Quest is such a good sci-fi parody that it was once voted the seventh best Star Trek film of all time … by Star Trek fans. Its genre send-up is effective and affectionate, with gags about underwritten female characters and illogical spaceship design. It is also a genuinely fun space caper: there’s a properly scary baddie, a spaceship chase sequence, a high-jeopardy mission on a foreign planet and not one but two romantic subplots. There are Beryllium spheres and a rock monster and an Omega-13 (whatever that is).Rickman’s character, Alexander Dane, is one of a group of washed-up actors from a cancelled cult 1980s sci-fi show, now reduced to appearing at fan conventions. He’s joined by Sigourney Weaver’s continually objectified Gwen DeMarco (“My TV Guide interview was six paragraphs about my boobs and how they fit into my suit”), Tony Shalhoub’s eternally laid-back (read: stoned) Fred Kwan, Daryl Mitchell as former child star Tommy Webber and the show’s insufferable lead, Tim Allen’s Jason Nesmith, AKA “Commander Peter Quincy Taggart”.When some apparent superfans prove to be actual aliens who have intercepted and misinterpreted the TV episodes as “historical documents”, the show’s cast find themselves beamed up to help defeat a lizard-like warlord named Sarris. It is every sci-fi fan’s dream come true: it was all real, all along.What ensues is a beautiful dismantling of cynicism via a comedy in which everyone is totally committed to the bit. Nowhere is that more true than the aliens in question. The Thermians are squid-like creatures who assume a human form albeit one with some of the most unusual mannerisms ever committed to screen. Their utterly bizarre speech patterns were created by Enrico Colantoni, who plays Thermian leader Mathesar in a performance that should have won him a best supporting actor Oscar: hysterically funny but deeply – ironically for an alien – human.When Mathesar confidently puts his people’s future in the hands of their beloved Galaxy Quest crew, the actors must play their parts for real this time. And of course, in pretending to be something they’re not, they discover who they really are.Author and film-maker David Mamet has called Galaxy Quest a “perfect” movie, and I would agree. It is a film in which every decision – every line delivery, every splatter of space goo – feels like the right one. In particular, there is the most satisfying character arc for a scene-stealing Sam Rockwell as Guy Fleegman, an actor who appeared as “Crewman Number Six” in a single episode of the show and was swiftly killed off. As a result, he spends the entire film terrified he’s about to be offed in reality. Another parody might revel in giving him a stupid death but there is an innate kindness to Galaxy Quest. Instead, Guy is gifted many of the film’s best lines – “Look around you. Can you form some sort of rudimentary lathe?” – and sees himself shift from “glorified extra” to “plucky comic relief”.This is indicative of Galaxy Quest’s determination never to punch down. At its heart, there is a deep respect for fandom in a genre where it is often mocked. It understands the inherently funny visual of punters in homemade alien costumes lined up at the urinals, but it never makes jokes at the expense of those people. Indeed, the film’s climax is a salute to the power of nerdery as Justin Long’s teen superfan Brandon – crushingly dismissed by Jason early on in the film – ultimately saves the day (in between his mum making him take the bins out).You don’t need to be even a casual Trekkie to appreciate Galaxy Quest’s brilliance because, really, it is about the value of storytelling. For the Thermians, Galaxy Quest was literal: they genuinely believed that what they were watching was real. But the lesson is that it doesn’t matter how hammy the acting is, how poundshop the sets look or how ridiculous the lore seems if it means something to you. Galaxy Quest gives you permission to immerse yourself in the culture that you love, even – or especially – if it appears silly and slight to everyone around you. In the words of Commander Taggart, “Never give up! Never surrender!”Galaxy Quest is available on Paramount+ in the US, YouTube in the UK and to rent digitally in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsMy feelgood movieScience fiction and fantasy filmsSigourney WeaverComedyAlan RickmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Michael Kiwanuka: Fudge review – rough and instinctive, but also lush and alive with melody | Music | The Guardian
description: Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album
Content: A change of tempo … Michael Kiwanuka recording Fudge.Photograph: Jodie CanwellView image in fullscreenA change of tempo … Michael Kiwanuka recording Fudge.Photograph: Jodie CanwellMusicReviewMichael Kiwanuka: Fudge review – rough and instinctive, but also lush and alive with melody(Polydor)Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion albumAlexis PetridisMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn November 2024, Michael Kiwanuka released his fourth album,Small Changes, an extremely poised and self-assured piece of work. After three gold albums, a Grammy nomination, a Mercury prize win and the ongoing success ofCold Little Heart, a 2017 single hoisted to virality and million-selling status in the US after its use in TV drama Big Little Lies, Kiwanuka – and his long-term production collaborators Danger Mouse and Inflo – evidently felt confident enough to release a beautiful but wilfully understated album. Recorded in LA, some impressive names lurked in the credits: legendary session musicians including bassist Pino Palladino and the drummer James Gadson, who played on Marvin Gaye’s I Want You and Donald Fagen’s The Nightfly; the similarly legendary R&B producer Jimmy Jam served as organist on three tracks. It attracted the kind of critical praise in which adjectives like “unhurried” and “meditative” figured heavily.But it also wasn’t the whole story. It turned out there was a second album, its songs written – or rather, jammed into existence by Kiwanuka and members of his live band – concurrently with Small Changes. It was made not in LA but in a studio that “looks like a medieval hut” in Southampton. August session musicians and legendary R&B producers were not present during its recording, nor were Danger Mouse and Inflo. Indeed, you could read its opening track,Summer Clothes, as a kind of Dear John letter to both of them (“I’m OK, I found another way … we’ll be back here soon, just not today”).Fudge’s release was announced in 2025, hard on the heels of Small Changes: it was reviewed in a handful of heritage rock magazines. Then it just disappeared from the schedules without explanation, until the end of last month, when Kiwanuka made a statement andgave an interview to the Guardian, explaining that he had a stroke. After months in hospital, he is now in residential care in Hampshire. He is belatedly releasing Fudge, he said, “because I don’t know how long it will be until I can release another record”.It opens with a recording of jazz pianist Chick Corea being interviewed: “You have to be certain what you like, not what you think sounds good to someone else,” he avers. It feels like a bullish, abandon-your-preconceptions-now start, but that perhaps tells you more about the pressures brought to bear on artists in the mid-2020s than the actual contents of Fudge.It’s certainly rougher around the edges than Small Changes – there’s a lot of audible tape hiss, the acoustic Across the Sky starts abruptly in the middle of a chord, as if someone frantically hit the “record” button after Kiwanuka started playing – but it’s by no stretch of the imagination a confounding WTF? gesture destined to baffle Kiwanuka’s audience.View image in fullscreenNever self-indulgent … Michael Kiwanuka and collaborators.Photograph: Jodie CanwellThere’s a pleasingly gritty, live-in-the-studio quality to the performances, but there are also beautiful, impressively luscious string arrangements: there’s a particularly lovely example weaving around the vintage drum machine and Why Can’t We Live Together?-style organ stabs of Love in My Heart. You can probably make out the songs’ origins as jams from the extended codas of Just Another Moment or Stars, where Kiwanuka and his band linger on one endlessly repeated chord sequence, but these moments never smack of noodling self-indulgence. Rather, they feel vivid and alive, the sound changing as they proceed. There’s a lambent melancholy to the organ-driven coda of Steve’s Paradise, a spikiness about Kiwanuka’s guitar soloing at the climax of Stars that chafes against the track’s opulent strings. Indeed, whatever their genesis, the songs here might be melodically stronger than those on Small Changes: whether they’re doleful (as on California) or lovestruck (You Sent Me Flying), the tunes are uniformly memorable.‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating strokeRead moreIndeed, you’re left thinking that Fudge could probably have been released as the new Michael Kiwanuka album, with no explanation of its genesis, without spooking any horses. Certainly, it’s as abundant in the kind of qualities you might have come to expect from its author. Warm and unforced, it occasionally takes on a distinctly lysergic cast – the final minutes of Love in Your Heart are dense with psychedelic guitar effects – and the lyrics are plain-spoken and believable, whether putting a concerned arm around the shoulder of a troubled friend on Drowning in Your Heart or expressing uncertainty about his career, a theme that keeps cropping up, onSing, Stars and Across the Sky.Of course, those songs that ponder Michael Kiwanuka’s future in music take on a slightly different resonance, given what’s happened since he recorded them. But on the evidence of Fudge, you do wonder at the crisis of confidence he describes. It may have had experimental beginnings, but it sounds remarkably like the work of a man who knows exactly what he wants to do. You leave it hoping that he’s able to continue doing it at some point in the not-too-distant future.Fudge is released 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicMichael KiwanukaPop and rockSoulPsychedeliaalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger review – does this sequel measure up to The Time Traveler’s Wife? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-up
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-up
Content: Love and loss on loop … Audrey Niffenegger.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLove and loss on loop … Audrey Niffenegger.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianFictionReviewLife Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger review – does this sequel measure up to The Time Traveler’s Wife?More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-upBeejay SilcoxMon 19 Oct 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIrun a reading workshop which begins with a little shelf assessment. Participants bring a stack of books that have shaped who they are: childhood treasures; new revelations; comfort reads. Books they once cherished but have now outgrown. The usual suspect in that category is Audrey Niffenegger’s 2003 novelThe Time Traveler’s Wife. Once smitten, readers now find that time-warped romance cruel. What felt like destiny now feels like a cage. As they explain, I’m always struck by the same thought: Wasn’t it always cruel? Wasn’t that the point?Henry DeTamble and Clare Abshire are a couple caught in a causal loop. The irresolvable question is where that loop starts: does a bright young art student fall in love with a junior librarian, or does a time-travelling man groom a child to become his future wife? If the answer is both – and it has to be – what are we to make of their marriage? Can you truly choose someone if you believe the choice is already made?In the last two decades, The Time Traveler’s Wife has been adapted for Hollywood and HBO and sold more than 9m copies in 40 languages. Readers are still arguing about free will and fate. We may have grown queasier about the bind Clare and Henry are in, but Niffenegger’s novel was never hiding its dark heart. Just look at the original cover: a little girl guarding a pair of men’s shoes. She’s in knee-high socks and Mary Janes, her hands by her sides like a tiny soldier. What is she waiting for? A future or a trap? Is there a difference?There’s now a sequel: Life Out of Order. Will Niffenegger conjure the same unease? To cut a 560-page story short, no. There’s plenty of unease here – political, ecological, technological – but none of it gets under the skin (the ick-factor of The Time Traveler’s Wife is treated like an in-joke). We’re in dystopia territory. Again. And it’s hard to get excited about more literary ruin.double quotation markLife Out of Order is at the mercy of every small gust of an idea, and there are decades’ worth blowing about in hereFor all its temporal complexity, the emotional logic of The Time Traveler’s Wife was simple: for better and worse, it was a love story. The book was a kite with a strong string. The sequel cuts that string. Life Out of Order is at the mercy of every small gust of an idea, and there are decades’ worth of them blowing about in here.Just setting out the cast feels like pinning a murder board: Henry is now dead, though he still pops in from the past, and Clare has raised their daughter, Alba, alone. Alba has inherited her father’s time-travel gene, but has more control. Unbound by the conventions of clock time, Alba is married to Zach in the present, Oliver in the past, and both of them in the future. Oliver is a fellow time-traveller seeking refuge in the past (the future is sticky); Zach is mostly harmless and thinks Oliver is his drinking buddy. Clare is now married to Beck, who makes herself scarce when Henry visits from beyond the grave. Beck is the mother of Isadora, a “menace” of a child who spends her days locked in a basement, for spoilery reasons. Isadora is catalytic – everyone can feel it. Will she bring havoc or salvation? Probably both. Whatever happens, it will involve Alba’s violin and a mouldering yellow house in the outer suburbs of Chicago.View image in fullscreenRose Leslie and Theo James in the TV adaptation of The Time Traveler’s WifePhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThere are half a dozen ways – at least – to describe Life Out of Order: as ethical non-monogamy meets the space-time continuum; a study of grief and its manifestations; a cautionary tale about teaching machines to dream; a grim vision of a coming America; a hymn to music and all the ways it salves and saves us; and a fatalist eco-dystopia: what it means to fight for a planet that is assuredly doomed.Niffenegger starts some of these stories, and finishes others. Major characters disappear for hundreds of pages; hundreds of years are leapt in a paragraph or two. We seem to be in a counter-historical version of the US, which mightexplain why everyone from the previous book is acting so strangely. Most of the cast have been recruited by Antifa, until that plotline evaporates. What also vanishes is the genetic science of time travel: “Chrono-displacement”. At the end of The Time Traveler’s Wife, that discovery seemed poised to reshape the world (imagine what it would do to financial markets alone). Here, it’s dispatched with a shrug: “I never hear about time travel anymore,” Zach muses. “There was that big announcement, and then it just – died.”In the end, it’s almost impossible to say whose story this is. Alba is the most likely candidate, but also the least interesting. Where her father grappled with the ethics of time travel – those lurking causal cruelties – Alba mostly does what she does because she’s already done it. Why bother to fret or regret when predestination does the moral work for you? She slips in and out of the plot dropping nuggets of portent, juggling husbands, and fiddling (literally) while the world burns. It feels callous rather than cruel: cold-blooded.That’s the big difference here: heat – something a little more carnal than planetary warming. There was ferocity in Henry and Clare’s love, a hunger that twisted their causal loop into a knot. They adored one another, even though their adoration was selfish; each loved the person they helped to make. Because isn’t that what we all do, in our own quiet and needful ways: create the people we love?Life Out of Order is bereft of hunger. What we have in its place is exhaustion. Who has time for the body when the body politic is rotten? When the very notion of embodiment may be obsolete? Alba is not waiting for a pair of shoes to be filled, she’s waiting for the end of the world. “I have loved time travel and have wished to be done with it,” she tells us on the opening page of Life Out of Order. That feels like the prophecy here.Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger is published by Jonathan Cape (£22). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Emperor of Nothing by Blake J Harris review – the definitive portrait of Larry David | Biography books | The Guardian
description: The Seinfeld creator went from luckless standup to multi-millionaire – but what’s his secret?
Author: Dorian Lynskey
Headline: The Seinfeld creator went from luckless standup to multi-millionaire – but what’s his secret?
Content: Larry David in the HBO comedy series Curb Your Enthusiasm.Photograph: John P. Johnson/HBOView image in fullscreenLarry David in the HBO comedy series Curb Your Enthusiasm.Photograph: John P. Johnson/HBOBook of the dayBiography booksReviewEmperor of Nothing by Blake J Harris review – the definitive portrait of Larry DavidThe Seinfeld creator went from luckless standup to multi-millionaire – but what’s his secret?Dorian LynskeyMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLarry David agreed to this authorised biography with a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.” As Blake J Harris tells it, the comedy writer has always been adept at finding reasons not to do something, or to stop doing it, even when there’s nothing to fall back on. As a peppery standup in 1970s New York, David was notorious for storming off stage if the audience displeased him. He walked out of his first TV job, on the Saturday Night Live clone Fridays, because “I stunk.” He twice quit Seinfeld, the sitcom he co-created in 1989, over meddling by NBC executives and fantasised about the network giving him an excuse to leave for good. In 1992, just before it became the biggest show in America, he told friends, “Honestly, I would rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld. It would be peaceful. Nobody would make me write anything.” He was only half joking.David’s career proves that it is in fact possible to be immensely, groundbreakingly successful without ever displaying great ambition. Growing up in Brooklyn amid a boisterous extended family, Lawrence Gene David loved baseball and tall tales but, oddly, not making people laugh. “I can’t recall him ever saying a funny thing,” remembers his older brother Ken. After a spell in the army reserve, he drifted through low-effort jobs – limo driver, bra salesman – and dropped out of acting school, partly because his classmate Jeff Goldblum showed him what a real actor looked like. “Most of the time I was just waiting for other people tostoptalking so that I couldstarttalking,” he admits.Hence standup. In 1977, Variety magazine summed up David’s themes as “sexual fantasies, oriental yodeling, baldness, hypochondria, growing up with Jewish parents, college, porno movies, etc”. Much as they admired his integrity, his peers considered him too self-destructive and uncompromising to make it. One contemporary says that if you had polled New York’s standups, “Larry would have been voted Least Likely to Ever Accomplish Anything. Including by Larry himself!” After a few unhappy forays into television, David was already 41 when he began writing a pilot with the amiable, ultra-professional JerrySeinfeld.double quotation markDavid is as much an observer of his own life as a participant, turning everything into materialAuthorised biographies tend to flatter their subjects, but then there doesn’t seem to be much dirt to dig. Compared with Harris’s last subject, the obnoxious virtual reality entrepreneur Palmer Luckey, David is a pretty solid guy who still has the close friends he made 50 years ago. There is no evidence here of those familiar funnyman archetypes, the sad clown and the secret monster. Harris was therefore able to access every important figure in his life, including fellow comedian Richard Lewis, his best friend, and Rob Reiner, whose company produced Seinfeld, before they died. Augmented by transcripts and memos, the quotes are so plentiful that the book often feels more like an oral history than a conventional biography, especially the Seinfeld section. If you want to read multi-page breakdowns of classic episodes like The Soup Nazi and The Chinese Restaurant (I do), then you’re in luck.In the self-referential fourth season, Jerry pitches a sitcom, starring himself, that is “about nothing”. Seinfeld itself was never that but it was the first show to root itself in everyday conversations, altercations and humiliations, many of which David had been recording in notebooks for years. One of the pleasures of this book is encountering a funny incident in the 70s that resurfaces on screen 20 years later. “There are people in this world that funny things happen to,” says Seinfeld. “And he is one of them.” Jason Alexander once complained to David that his character George Costanza had an implausible storyline: nobody would behave like this in real life. “What are you talking about?” David replied. “This happened to me, and this is exactly what I did.”Making Seinfeld was all-consuming (“I missed the whole 90s,” its star once joked) but a creative dream. David, the stubborn catastrophiser, and Seinfeld, the breezy optimist, would write episodes face-to-face across a double desk and almost never argue. What began as a cult show beneath the dangling sword of cancellation (“too Jewish” was a common critique) suddenly became a cultural juggernaut in season four as David mastered his two great skills: escalating a slim premise into comic delirium and dovetailing multiple storylines with a satisfying click. For a network sitcom, Seinfeld was radically unsentimental – “No hugging, no learning” was the writers’ credo. “I was shocked that they were letting us do this show,” David admits.Another curious feature of David’s career is that he didn’t become recognisable until he was in his 50s. Even when he was the showrunner and chief writer of the biggest show on television, with more than 35 million viewers a week, he was effectively unknown. That phase ended in 1998 when the divisively downbeat Seinfeld finale coincided with the abject failure of his first movie, Sour Grapes. For want of a better idea, he decided to return to standup.Curb Your Enthusiasm began as a one-hour HBO special, framing the routine with a mockumentary, but the frame proved funnier than the picture so Curb turned into a show about “Larry David” at war with the world. Like Seinfeld, it built complex stories out of minute observations and petty grievances but this time there was no script, just an outline to improvise around. “Your job, basically, is to push Larry David into a corner so that he comes bursting out even more Larry,” explains his friend Ted Danson, who played himself. As abrasive as David’s buzzsaw voice, Curb made Seinfeld look like Friends. Its success made David famous as his worst self. “I know people don’t realise it,” says Danson’s wife and Curb co-star Mary Steenburgen, “but Larry really is a sweetheart.”This is the kind of biography you read for the work rather than the life. Fiercely private and averse to analysis, David doesn’t say much about his divorce in 2007 or Lewis’s death in 2024, nor money (he’s worth an estimated $400m), nor politics (he’s a ferocious Trump-basher). Most of the details about his childhood come from his brother Ken. His only hobby is golf. As Harris notes, David is as much an observer of his own life as a participant, turning everything into material.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo what do we learn about Larry David? He’s a loyal friend, a loving father and a generous comedy partner. His comedy idols are Mel Brooks, Woody Allen and Phil Silvers’ character Sgt Bilko. As seen on Curb, he tends to start laughing when people are upset with him and gets absurdly indignant about minor injustices (though less so since becoming a father in 1994). He bypasses niceties – a “social assassin” in Curb-speak. “He’s comfortable being uncomfortable,” summarises Lewis. “He knows exactly what he wants to do. And he doesn’t need praise.”Perhaps the key is David’s paradoxical self-esteem. According to Alexander, “At any given moment, he could say, ‘I’m the most worthless, pathetic no-talent in the world,’ and ‘Why is no one giving me my due? I should be doing much better than I’m doing!’ And it was all in the same breath.” Such a person either sinks without trace or, very occasionally, triumphs despite himself.Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David by Blake J Harris is published by HarperCollins (£22). title: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movement | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin
Author: Tom Sperlinger
Headline: A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin
Content: Writer and philosopher Hannah Arendt, who foresaw ‘a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security’.Photograph: Fred Stein Archive/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWriter and philosopher Hannah Arendt, who foresaw ‘a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security’.Photograph: Fred Stein Archive/Getty ImagesPolitics booksReviewAnti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movementA biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan GoldinTom SperlingerMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Everyone in America – at least as far as I knew – was a Zionist,” recalls Benjamin Moser, “especially but not only if you were Jewish.” A Pulitzer-winning biographer of Susan Sontag, he remembers being brought up short in his 20s, when a friend described Israel as “a bunch of foreigners who had no business in the Middle East” and Zionism as a “terrible mistake”. Moser, who recently turned 50, admits: “I was not even aware that Zionism was controversial.” The shift in perspective culminated in a visit to the occupied territories in 2016, during which he found “the reality of the occupation of Palestine … deranging”.His new book includes 12 portraits of Jewish figures who have opposed Zionism, a movement formed in the late 19th century to advocate for the creation of a homeland for Jewish people in Palestine. It is contentious to oppose Zionism today, but Moser wants contemporary Jewish activists to “feel less alone” by showing that debates about Zionism were once mainstream in Jewish communal life. While around90% of American Jewsnow support Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state (although fewer identify as Zionists),fewer than 1%belonged to the largest American Zionist organisation in 1914. The first character study is of Rabbi Aaron Samuel Tamares, who thought that Judaism offered a vision of a world beyond the devastating nationalism of the first world war. The book closes with a moving account of the photographer Nan Goldin, who spoke out, at considerable cost, as the assault on Gaza began in 2023 following the October 7th attacks.Many of the protagonists, like Moser, were once committed Zionists. When he was 10, Ronnie Kasrils set up a stall in front of his home in South Africa to sell toys and raise funds for Israel. He was later an anti-apartheid leader who became an ardent anti-Zionist during 27 years living abroad in exile: “Ronnie drives them crazy,” a friend of his tells Moser. “And a lot of it is because he’sso Jewish.”Jacob Israël de Haan, an influential Dutch poet, wrote in 1912: “We want our own Land, our own Language, our own Art.” He was horrified after he relocated to Mandatory Palestine: “Zionism is a beautiful ideal,” he lamented, but it had “fallen into the hands of hustlers”. He was murdered in 1924 by Avraham Tehomi, a 21-year-old member of the Haganah paramilitary organisation, after his increasingly outspoken opposition to the Zionist leadership.double quotation markThe sheer scale of the devastation wreaked on the Palestinians disturbs each of Moser’s subjectsHannah Arendt worked for Youth Aliyah in Paris, supporting refugee children to immigrate to Palestine, after fleeing from Germany herself in 1933. Her orientation changed after the Biltmore Conference in 1942, when some 600 delegates from Zionist organisations gathered in New York. Before Biltmore, some in the movement still imagined a single state rooted in the historically strong relations between Jews, Muslims and Christians in Palestine. The Holocaust sharpened the urgency of the argument for a Jewish state instead, but Arendt warned that this would leave the Arabs with “the choice between voluntary emigration or second-class citizenship”. She foresaw, Moser writes, that “a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: artist Molly Crabapple, actor Debra Winger and photographer Nan Goldin take part in a pro-Palestinian demonstration outside the New York Stock Exchange in October 2024.Photograph: Molly Crabapple via InstagramMoser’s study includes many instances of despair. The scale of the devastation wreaked on the Palestinians disturbs each of Moser’s subjects, many of whom are demonised or accused of antisemitism “so promiscuously that the word would eventually become meaningless”. After the Occupation of Gaza and the West Bank began in 1967, the lawyer Felicia Langer dedicated her life to representing Palestinians. Her first clients, Sheikh Musa al-Bukhari and his wife, knew their son was in prison: “Nobody would tell them why, but when he had picked up his son’s clothes to wash them, he had found a shirt covered with blood.” Langer came to see “the State of Israel as a criminal enterprise” and emigrated in 1990 because she no longer believed it could be reformed.The Arab-Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, who was born in Iraq, was at the forefront of revising the established Israeli histories of 1948 and describes being “radicalised in the [Israeli State] archives … I didn’t have any revisionist ideas. It was the material I was reading which completely, flatly contradicted the official line.” Shlaim describes the situation today as “utterly bleak”. In 2023 he argued: “For all its sins, Israel has not engaged in genocide.” In 2025 he published a book called Genocide in Gaza.Moser’s focus on individual lives is affecting. He makes no claims to be writing a definitive history and is aware of the Palestinian lives that shadow those of his protagonists but fall outside the scope of this study. There are nonetheless gaps. For example, there is no mention of the Satmar Hasidic movement, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish group that believes it is forbidden to establish a Jewish state before the Messiah’s arrival, showing that anti-Zionism can also be theological and conservative.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarly in Anti-Zionism, Moser reads his grandfather’s copy of Theodor Herzl’s founding Zionist text, Der Judenstaat, and finds it “disquieting”, at best a fairytale and at worst a profoundly disturbing vision. Moser wonders how his own life might have been different “if I had grown up with the Palestinian story” instead. This beautifully written cri de coeur is inspired by an “exilic vision” of equality, an alternative Jewish tradition, resistant to nationalism and rooted in solidarity with others.Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser is published by 4th Estate. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography review – a rhapsodic show to stop you in your tracks | Photography | The Guardian
description: From a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everyday
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: From a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everyday
Content: Vision of love …  Yip Cheong Fun, Father's Care.Photograph: Yip Cheong Fun, Collection of National Gallery Singapore. © Andrew Yip Weng Kee.View image in fullscreenVision of love …  Yip Cheong Fun, Father's Care.Photograph: Yip Cheong Fun, Collection of National Gallery Singapore. © Andrew Yip Weng Kee.PhotographyReviewLight and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography review – a rhapsodic show to stop you in your tracksTate Modern, LondonFrom a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everydayCharlotte JansenMon 19 Oct 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t remember the last time I saw such a well-researched and truly globally representative exhibition that doesn’t patronise but quietly makes its case unapologetically, fearlessly and through sheer quality. Apart from being the first retelling of the international, pluralistic pictorialism movement, Tate’s new show allows for some refreshing encounters with unknown works for British audiences – around half of the works included here have never been shown in the UK. The effect is to radically deepen and widen our understanding not only of art history but the human impulses that drive us to make images in the first place.We move seamlessly from the sudden shock of colour in three-colour carbon prints of flowers in a London garden in the 1920s to works born of the photographic salons, circles and clubs of Sydney, Hong Kong and Brazil. Historical moments collide; the epic emerges from the everyday. A man rows home across the Norfolk Broads, another works on a construction site in Singapore. None of it feels out of place. It all belongs. It is all extremely, almost ecclesiastically, beautiful.More than a few times, I stopped in my tracks. I could spend hours with Yip Cheong Fun’s 1940 Father’s Care, a cinematic image of a man holding one child with his hand extended to another, helping them down from the rocky crag they are walking over, on a journey across an open rural landscape somewhere. It’s a touching image of parenthood and the passage of time. Like this show overall, it’s about gestures rather than flashy declarations of feeling.View image in fullscreenNoirish … Han Youngsoo, Untitled 1955.Photograph: Collection of Han Youngsoo FoundationFrom this purist vision of love, we find a more ambiguous exploration in Lionel Wendt’s excruciatingly charged study of a young Sri Lankan man’s loincloth-clad body in the private intimacy of his Colombo studio, revealing hidden desires and truths the camera can’t conceal. It’s beauty as a kind of torture: the same medium that can expose the body to anthropological scrutiny transforms looking into something far more complicated.I’m equally intrigued by a 1955 series by Han Youngsoo: small, noirish works of Korean street scenes that beg for narration from the viewer. Two 1925 bromide prints by Kate Smith show a woman in a flowing pre-Raphaelite style, pausing in a field dense with vegetation and foliage. Its title draws me closer: The Listener. What is she listening to, and what does this photograph want us to hear? It leaves me hovering between the visible and the imagined, its silence and stillness charged with the possibility.View image in fullscreenEthereal … Limb Eung-Sik, Feet 2.Photograph: Limb Eung Sik Photo Archive © Estate of Limb Eung Sik.Limb Eung-sik’s Feet 2 has a similarly ethereal atmosphere: flowing, diaphanous material folds around a dancer’s feet so that they dissolve into light and shadows. Nostalgia and sentimentality are dialled up, but it’s irresistible. If you’re attuned to it, these images suggest that anything – shells, shadows, a faucet, a wilting flower, a fishing net – can become magic, and these pictorialists teach us how to see the world that way.This is not by any means a critical look at pictorialism. Mysteries are left intact, politics are largely left at the door. There’s no attempt to unravel the reductionist pitfalls of pursuing the fantasy of beauty. Some of the educational intrusions feel unnecessary – a timeline of photographic techniques is helpful and interesting but risks putting “art photography” back in the realm of craft, as does a full-scale recreation of a darkroom that you cannot enter. The magic of the darkroom is not that it is a dark room with a bunch of dirty aprons hanging outside. It is the transformation that happens within it: the strange alchemy of chemistry and light, which is already accounted for in abundance in the photographs.But I can forgive these things. There’s genuine care and awe here. It’s a reminder that seeking moments of magic and breathtaking beauty is a human instinct, and we have a right to it. This is an exhibition about things that are universally shared and eternally human, that cannot be destroyed by the politics of a time or place, that survive and thrive. Light and Magic is as intelligent as it is beautiful, as whimsical as it is informative, as rhapsodic as it is real.AtTate Modern, London, until 21 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsPhotographyTate ModernArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: LSO/Pappano review – bold, dramatic and cohesive reading of Mahler 2 | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The London Symphony Orchestra opened their Barbican season with Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony, preceded by the UK premiere of Dai Fujikura’s engaging and intricate Amber Alchemy
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The London Symphony Orchestra opened their Barbican season with Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony, preceded by the UK premiere of Dai Fujikura’s engaging and intricate Amber Alchemy
Content: Sound and fury.,… Antonio Pappano conducting the London Symphony Orchestra and Chorus at Barbican Hall, London, on Sunday.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenSound and fury.,… Antonio Pappano conducting the London Symphony Orchestra and Chorus at Barbican Hall, London, on Sunday.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewLSO/Pappano review – bold, dramatic and cohesive reading of Mahler 2Barbican Hall, LondonThe London Symphony Orchestra opened their Barbican season with Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony, preceded by the UK premiere of Dai Fujikura’s engaging and intricate Amber AlchemyClive PagetMon 19 Oct 2026 08.12 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have beena fair few Resurrection Symphoniesthis year, anda positive glut on disc, but Antonio Pappano has form with Mahler and the London Symphony Orchestra can be relied upon to follow where he leads. First, though, the UK premiere of a new work byDai Fujikurathat had precisely nothing to do with the main event but was no less interesting for that.Amber Alchemy, commissioned to celebrate the centenary of Nomura Holdings, was inspired by the beehives atop the Japanese financial company’s London offices. In his programme note, the composer expressed his intention to evoke rather than illustrate, yet it was hard to ignore the orchestral buzz that underpinned much of this engaging 10-minute work. Quivering strings and a shimmer of vibraphones opened proceedings with striking instrumental gestures trailing off in flickering diminuendos. Pappano and the LSO brought a commendable clarity to Fujikura’s intricately interwoven lines, contrasting the music’s romantic outward sweep with its apian inner restlessness.View image in fullscreenIntention to evoke rather than illustrate… Dai Fujikura with Antonio Pappano at the UK premiere of his Amber Alchemy.Photograph: Mark AllanAs for the Mahler, conductor and orchestra hit the ground running with a resolute and dramatically turbocharged account of the opening movement. Pappano unearthed much that felt fresh in a ferociously instinctual reading where clipped marches resolved in walloping payoffs and a massive rallentando two-thirds of the way through caused hearts to leap into mouths. Despite the sound and fury, balance and discipline were outstanding, spotlighting limber woodwind solos and clattering col legno strings that bristled with theatricality.Choices throughout were bold, and yet pretty much everything came out right as Pappano bound potentially disparate episodes into a cohesive whole. The central scherzo was a sinuous delight, an aqueous perpetuum mobile that saw the orchestra transmogrified into a pool of wriggling fishes.ContraltoNoa Beinartdelivered an unaffected Urlicht, before the orchestra launched into a formidable finale: at one point the terrifying army of the dead sounded as if it was battering on the very doors of the concert hall. Only the divine apotheosis, where at first the otherwise excellent London Symphony Chorus felt overly urgent, faltered, hampered by the boxy acoustic of an auditorium unable to contain such a heavenly climax.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicLondon Symphony OrchestraAntonio PappanoreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after all | Movies | The Guardian
description: After Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEU
Author: Ben Child
Headline: After Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEU
Content: Taking flight … Ben Affleck as Batman in Justice League.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenTaking flight … Ben Affleck as Batman in Justice League.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarWeek in geekMoviesA Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after allBen ChildAfter Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEUMon 19 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTShareNine years after superhero epic Justice League arrived in cinemas, there ought to be very little left to say about how it all went wrong.
