Zack Snyder shot the film,Joss Whedonsubstantially rewrote and reshot it, and audiences eventually got to see both men’s versions. Any debate over their relative merits long ago disappeared. Whedon is pretty much cancelled; Snyder has reinvented himself as the writer-director of extremely average ersatz Star Wars movies for Netflix, and an entirely new DC universe is under way that has very little to do with either of them.To a greater or lesser extent, the world has moved on. But Ben Affleck’s latest comments raise an uncomfortable question about whether Snyder’s departure was ever presented honestly.Speaking to Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Affleck, who played Batman, described the Justice League reshoots as the lowest point of his career, but reserved his strongest criticism for the circumstances of Snyder’s departure. The directorstepped away in May 2017, two months after his daughter Autumn killed herself, aged 20, with the public explanation that he needed to be with his family. Affleck, however, alleged that studio Warner Bros had used the tragedy to justify replacing him. “The way in which that was, I thought, used as an excuse was one of the shittiest things I’ve ever seen,” Affleck said. “It was so gross.”In July 2020 another Justice League actor, Ray Fisher (who played Cyborg),accused Whedon of abusive and unprofessional behaviour, prompting WarnerMedia to launch an investigation into the film’s production. In December 2020, the company announcedthe probe had concluded and said that unspecified “remedial action” had been taken. In May 2021, Gal Gadot (who played Wonder Woman) saidWhedon had “threatened her career”during production of the film. Whedondenied both allegations in January 2022, but has been largely absent from Hollywood since.Affleck stressed that much of what he knew about his co-stars’ experiences came secondhand. His reaction was blunt: “Wow. This is about as gross as it gets.” On Snyder eventually releasing his own version (a four-hour-plus extended takethat became a draw for Warner’s fledgling HBO Max streaming platform after a fierce social media campaign by Snyder fans), he added: “That was fucking great. I was really happy for him.”View image in fullscreenFurrow-browed … Zack Snyder.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APThis is a story that seems to shift and morph the more time passes. Initially, the baton being passed from Snyder to Whedon was framed as a mercy, though there wererumours as early as February 2018 that Snyder might have been forced out for creative reasons. Now, almost a decade on, the film’s biggest star feels comfortable alleging that Warners used a family death to justify bringing in Whedon, who at the time was one of the biggest names in superhero movies (having overseen Marvel’s early Avengers films), but whose breezy, wisecracking writing style couldn’t have been further from Snyder’s furrow-browed, heavy-metal film-making. Warners had spent years allowing Snyder to turn its superheroes into tormented deities, then developed an urgent concern that none of them knew how to do banter.If what actually happened matters, in 2026, it’s because this was the moment that the DC extended universe (DCEU) really began to enter its death spiral. Snyder had probably already lost the confidence of studio executives after 2016’s Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice tanked with critics, but audiences had still flocked to see that movie to the tune of$874m at the global box office. If a Snyder-led Justice League had reached cinemas in 2017 and proved a hit, it’s not impossible to imagine Warners allowing him to continue his vision for the future of the comic book studio. While the director of Watchmen wasn’t exactly the Kevin Feige of DC, he controlled the general direction of travel as the guy who oversaw its highest-profile ensemble efforts. After Justice League, the DCEU’s films crossed $500m at the worldwide box office only once, with 2018’s Aquaman. Somewhere along the way, the promise that everything was connected had become a warning that you might need to slog through another one.The decline, to be fair, cannot all be blamed on one disastrous handover: the pandemic alone was probably responsible for at least some of the dramatic downturn in the DCEU’s fortunes after 2018. Nor does it follow that Snyder would have necessarily delivered a triumphant decade of superbly interconnected superhero cinema if everyone had simply left him to get on with it. His films could be ponderous, self-important and oddly embarrassed by the possibility that being Superman might occasionally be enjoyable. I’m not sure I even want to visit the alternative universe in which this grand plan actually came to fruition but it seems like a lot of DC fans at the time did.Instead, Batman and Superman discovered themselves trapped in a universe whose supreme beings could create entire galaxies but found it impossible to agree on the appropriate number of jokes. Affleck’s comments bring us back to the human cost of all that studio indecision. Nine years on, DC has built a new universe, but still struggles to explain what happened to the old one.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekZack SnyderDC ComicsSuperhero moviesBatman v Superman: Dawn of JusticeBen AffleckJoss WhedoncommentShareReuse this content

title: With nine new recordings of Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony this year alone, which rises above the rest? | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?
Content: Apocalyptic visions: The London Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Sir Antonio Pappano with Maria Bengtsson soprano and Noa Beinart contralto perform Mahler’s Symphony No 2, ‘Resurrection’ in the Barbican Hall, London on 18 October 2026.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenApocalyptic visions: The London Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Sir Antonio Pappano with Maria Bengtsson soprano and Noa Beinart contralto perform Mahler’s Symphony No 2, ‘Resurrection’ in the Barbican Hall, London on 18 October 2026.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewWith nine new recordings of Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony this year alone, which rises above the rest?The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?Clive PagetMon 19 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs it something in the water? Or is it simply that triumph over adversity sells in today’s uncertain world? Whatever the reason, Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony has already received four major UK performances this year: aseason finale for the BBC Philharmonicin Manchester, a season opener for both theCity of Birmingham Symphony Orchestraandthe London Symphony Orchestra, and an 80th season celebratory concert for thePhilharmonia Orchestra in London. Next month the London City Orchestra perform it in Croydon’s Fairfield Halls.On disc, the field of Mahler 2s is even more crowded. Apple Music Classical currently throws up 222 listings;Presto Music’s search engine returns 260 results, many of them complete recordings to download or buy on CD or vinyl (some of these, of course, are reissues of recognised classic accounts).View image in fullscreenSecond opinions … Gustav Mahler in 1892.Photograph: AlamyThree new recordings of the symphony are out this month alone, which will bring the total released into the UK market to an astonishing nine over just 12 months. The lineup of conductors is certainly impressive – including Kahchun Wong,Simon Rattle, Andris Nelsons, Esa-Pekka Salonen, Donald Runnicles and Paavo Järvi – but is it possible the market has reached saturation point? Or is it that we just can’t get enough of Mahler’s apocalyptic vision and the dopamine fix that accompanies the symphony’s choral finale?The statistics clearly speak for themselves: this year there have been nine Mahler 2s released. By way of comparison, the 5th and the 8th symphonies received just four releases each in 2026; Mahler’s other symphonies even fewer.Mahler wasn’t always popular, of course. For all sorts of reasons, not least the Nazis’ aversion to the composer in general, his works were slow to enter the catalogue. The Second was in fact the first Mahler symphony to be recorded in its entirety when Oskar Fried and a pared-back Berlin State Opera Orchestra committed it to wax cylinders during sessions in 1923 and 1924. Perhaps as few as 40 players were huddled around the acoustic horn, but Fried had been coached by the composer himself for a performance of the work in 1905, and, so, tinny as it sounds today, it carries the imprimatur of authenticity.It was over a decade later thatEugene Ormandyand the Minneapolis Symphony Orchestra made the work’s second recording, captured live in 1935, this time using electrical microphones. Acoustically it was a major leap forward, and thanks to the conductor’s urgency – he’s 12 minutes faster than Fried – it still lands blows today.Sixteen years would pass before Otto Klemperer, who as a young man had known and worked with the composer, stepped into a studio with the Vienna Symphony Orchestra in 1951. His visceral, though boxy sounding, account was followed in 1958 by Mahler’s protege Bruno Walter who recorded the work with the New York Philharmonic. At this point we are talking one or two recordings every decade, a far cry from the current rate of almost one per month.Klemperer’s 1962 HMV stereo version with the Philharmonia Orchestra, capturing the conductor at his most monumental, rightly remains a benchmark recording, one of several made in the 60s that would still sit on most recommended listening lists. Bernstein’s first studio recording with the New York Phil, more urgent and certainly more wilful than his 1983 Deutsche Grammophon effort, appeared in 1963 and has now been lovingly remastered. Fine accounts by Solti and the LSO and Haitink with the Concertgebouw were among half a dozen to appear across the decade, while the 70s saw the likes of Mehta, Abbado and Tennstedt enter the lists.The digital revolution of the 80s produced a slew of new Mahler 2s (including Simon Rattle’s first attempt, which won him and the CBSOa Gramophone award), as well as first appearances on disc for some of the great performances of the past (anyone looking for the frisson of a live event should try Tennstedt’s account captured in 1989 with the London Philharmonic at the Royal Festival Hall).The subsequent transition from expensive studio recordings to the easier option of releasing a live performance, often with patching taken from rehearsals, has become prevalent in recent decades and is partly behind this year’s boom. Indeed, none of these nine new recordings was made in a studio.View image in fullscreenGoosebump raiser … Simon Rattle.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianSo which to listen to? Streamers today of course can take their pick, dipping into each in turn. But for collectors on a budget, the question of where best to spend your hard-earned cash is a thorny one.Among the frontrunners,Paavo Järvi’s accountwith the Tonhalle-Orchester Zürich (released 30 October on Alpha Classics) packs a considerable creative punch. The production values are hugely impressive: just listen to the orchestra’s pristine articulation of the declamatory opening demisemiquavers on cellos and basses. Järvi’s tempi are sound, and Anna Lucia Richter is a glorious mezzo-soprano soloist. It beats Cristian Măcelaru’s muddy, monochrome version with the Orchestre National de France into a cocked hat (released last month on Naïve). Esa-Pekka Salonen’s San Francisco reading is, as would be expected,supple and clean(on SFS Media) but occasionally breathless speeds temper the drama despite a well-thought-through finale.In the end, experience tells. That’s what makesSimon Rattle’s interpretationwith the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra (released on 2 October on BR Klassik) so rewarding. Forty years on from his CBSO recording for EMI, Rattle is now a more spontaneous and organic beast. Changes of tempo and dynamics feel entirely instinctual without any loss of expressive weight and power. The dramatic arc is secure, but the complex journey from a hero’s graveside to the heavens provides ample opportunities for Rattle to raise goosebumps. Like Järvi, he’s blessed with state-of-the-art engineering.The opening and closing movements are emotional rollercoasters daring the listener to come along for the ride. The inner movements are full of telling detail, such as the unselfconscious Viennese portamenti in the elegant Andante moderato and the reedy pungency conductor and orchestra bring to bear on the slippery scherzo. Scottish mezzo-soprano Beth Taylor is an arresting soloist, and the Bavarian Radio Chorus lift the roof as well as our collective spirits in the finale. One hundred and two years on from Oskar Fried’s pioneering account, Rattle delivers another Mahler 2 for the ages.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicSimon Rattlealbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture | Music | The Guardian
description: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview
Author: Garth Cartwright
Headline: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview
Content: ‘I’ve always been a peacenik’ … Ed Sanders, right, with his Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg, pictured in 2003.Photograph: Stephen Chernin/APView image in fullscreen‘I’ve always been a peacenik’ … Ed Sanders, right, with his Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg, pictured in 2003.Photograph: Stephen Chernin/APMusicInterview‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US countercultureGarth CartwrightHe gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interviewMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Charles Manson once wrote me a letter saying, ‘If I was as powerful as you claim then you wouldn’t be here,’” Ed Sanders tells me over a video call, savouring the menace in that sentence.Sanders is an American maverick; a musician, poet, activist, journalist and author whose greatest hit remains his bestselling 1971 book The Family, in which he chronicled the lives, crimes and trials of Manson and his followers. Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview.“I’ve always been a peacenik,” says Sanders. “I got locked in a cell in 1961 for protesting against nuclear armed submarines, and today I’m protesting against the Trumpster. I don’t subscribe to apathy and nihilism.”Aged 87, Sanders is speaking with me as Fugs Film!, a feature-length documentary about the Fugs, the offbeat folk-garage-psych band Sanders initially led from 1964-69, and re-formed in the 1980s, gets its UK premiere this week. “I don’t do many interviews,” he notes. “I’m constantly approached by people requesting them. And often they are wanting access only because I knew Jimi Hendrix and Allen Ginsberg and Andy Warhol and Janis Joplin and …” He shakes his head. “Everybody now wants to make a documentary about someone I once knew.”View image in fullscreen‘We thought we could change the world’ … the Fugs in 1968. Ed Sanders top left, with – left to right – Ken Pine, Tuli Kupferberg, Ken Weaver, Bob Mason, Charles Larkey.Photograph: Courtesy of Ed Sanders ArchiveIndeed, Sanders was a Zelig of the Lower East Side, friendly with Ginsberg (“A great man”), William Burroughs (“Unnerving, brilliant”), a then unknown Jimi Hendrix (“He was trading as Jimmy James. We gave him his first wah-wah pedal. Nice, talented guy”), to name just a few of his associates. In concert, the Fugs shared bills with the Velvet Underground, the Stooges and the Grateful Dead, but the biggest impression was made by a then unknown band who opened for the Fugs in Detroit’s Grande Ballroom in March 1968. “I’d never heard of Sly and the Family Stone,” Sanders recalls. “They came on and aroused the audience to ecstasy. When we came on, everyone was limp, worn out by how high Sly had taken them.”Sanders and his bandmates Tuli Kupferberg and Ken Weaver were rudimentary musicians who fused street theatre and dadaist spectacle with poetry and ramshackle songs. Long-haired, anti-war, pro-drugs and articulate, the Fugs attracted plenty of media attention but never troubled the Top 40 and are relatively little known today, so Fugs Film! allows a fresh look at a band at the heart of a nascent counterculture. Blending archive footage with contemporary interviews, director Chuck Smith’s film focuses on New York when it was a cheap city to live in, and many artists shared the absurdist mentality of the west coast’s “merry prankster” dropout hippie-artists.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to meet the best minds of my generation – and I did’ … Sanders on the cover of Life magazine in 1967.Photograph: Life MagazineInspired by Ginsberg’s epic poem Howl, Sanders had hitchhiked from Kansas to New York City as a teenager. “I wanted to meet ‘the best minds of my generation’, as Allen put it – and I did,” he says. “Both Tuli and I came from the beat poetry scene. We formed the Fugs to blend poetry with rock’n’roll after seeing beat poets dancing to a jukebox playing Martha Reeves and the Vandellas and the Beatles. It seemed an obvious thing to do.”Sanders’ literary leanings meant he also ran the city’s Peace Eye Bookstore and published the cheaply mimeographed zine Fuck You/A Magazine of the Arts, which featured writing by Burroughs, Norman Mailer, Ginsberg and other beat poets such as Gregory Corso.“Fuck You’s motto was ‘total assault on the culture,’” recalls Sanders. “We thought we could change the world with words. I sent copies to Picasso, Beckett, Sartre, Castro and Khrushchev inviting contributions, but none of them replied.” He laughs at his youthful audacity, adding that he did get attention from the NYPD, who attempted to prosecute Sanders for obscenity: Fuck You was frequently, cartoonishly sexual. Sanders was “fighting for free speech alongside the beats and Lenny Bruce,” he says.The musicologist Harry Smith produced the Fugs’ eponymous 1965 debut album for the Folkways label. The band shifted to ESP-Disk, home to free jazz pioneers Albert Ayler and Sun Ra, but neither label had any commercial heft, so Sanders was overjoyed when Jerry Wexler of Atlantic Records – who had helped make Ray Charles a star and was about to do the same with Aretha Franklin and Led Zeppelin – signed the band.Yet on hearing the finished masters, Atlantic dropped them. “Wexler told me the Ertegun brothers [co-founders of Atlantic] found a song called Coca Cola Douche offensive,” Sanders says. “I should have said ‘OK, we’ll leave it off’ but I got all pious about it. A mistake, as it meant we didn’t release an album in 1967, so we missed out on all the attention those Summer of Love albums got.”Given Sanders continually faced censorship, I ask him aboutMacklemore: shortly before we speak, the rapper was booted from Ed Sheeran’s US tour due to his onstage calls for a free Palestine. “There are always people wanting to censor you,” Sanders replies, “and when its a very rich guy who owns the stadiums and doesn’t want people to hear your opinion then, yeah, he can order such. For me, being older, it’s inspiring to see young musicians putting their shoulder to the wheel.”The Fugs survived their spat with Atlantic, joining the roster of Frank Sinatra’s Reprise Records in 1968. Label head Mo Ostin had to play Fugs demos to Sinatra before he could sign them. “Apparently Frank said: ‘I guess you know what you’re doing.’” The label released the terrific Fugs album Tenderness Junction, which includes Exorcising the Evil Spirits from the Pentagon Oct 21, 1967, a recording made at the Fugs-led mass protest at which thousands formed a human chain around the Pentagon and chanted “Out, demons, out!”“The Fugs existed to protest against the American war machine, as much as we did to make music,” says Sanders, “and we understood that spectacle draws attention. So to suggest we were going to try and levitate the Pentagon, well, it might sound ridiculous but it gave a focus to our protest and attracted a lot of attention.”Mailer, who attended the protest, wrote about it in his Pulitzer prize-winning book The Armies of the Night, and the Pentagon protests are now regarded as high points in the anti-Vietnam war movement. “We celebrated the 50th anniversary of the protest in 2017 by forming a human chain around the White House and attempting to levitate it,” says Sanders. “Again, we shouted ‘out, demons, out!’ and, again, nothing happened. Just as the Vietnam war continued for another nine years, Trump is back in the White House.”Did that make Sanders feel defeated? “No,” he replies firmly. “I’m an optimist. We must keep pushing, we can’t give in to despair. While things are terrible in the US right now, I do believe the American people will come to their senses and vote out the Republicans.”Alongside public exorcisms and psychedelic hymns, Fugs albums featured a mishmash of satirical skits, choral music, protest folk, mock country, Hare Krishna chants, Yiddish songs from Kupferberg’s heritage and poems by William Blake, Matthew Arnold and Ginsberg read to music. Their eclecticism can be maddening, though the band’s first two albums are very elemental, more akin to US punk bands such as the Dead Kennedys and the Dead Milkmen in their broad humour and anti-establishment fervour than to their 60s contemporaries. Songs such as Kill for Peace remain relevant today, though I’m Gonna Kill Myself Over Your Dead Body (“if you fuck anybody but me”) leaves a nasty taste.View image in fullscreen‘We existed to protest the American war machine as much as we did to make music’ … Sanders (above ‘for’) and bandmate Ken Weaver on an anti-Vietnam war march in 1967.Photograph: Courtesy of Ed Sanders Archive“Some of the songs we wrote then we probably wouldn’t write now,” says Sanders, today more professorial than hippie in appearance and speech. Other songs celebrated marijuana, amphetamine and LSD: “We advocated for mellow drugs, never hard drugs. We had a guitarist who was a junkie and it messed him up. And we avoided cocaine. Today pot is legal in New York, so that’s one of the battles we fought that we actually won.”In 1968, the Fugs visited Britain for the first time, where they were championed by John Peel, played the Roundhouse in London and visited Stonehenge, not returning until 2011 when Ray Davies invited them to play the Meltdown festival he curated. In between those visits, Sanders, tiring of the workload that leading a band involves, disbanded the Fugs in 1969, released two underwhelming mock-country solo albums, then focused on writing.“I couldn’t believe it when I first heard of these hippies driving stolen dune buggies murdering this famous actress,” says Sanders as to why he determined to investigate Manson’s cult. “So I went to LA and attended the trials and looked at how this guy, fresh out of prison, had managed to have these teenage runaways believe he was some kind of messiah.”‘His ache is real’: Bob Dylan and more on the wild genius of honky-tonk hellraiser Gary StewartRead moreHe reformed the band in 1984 with Kupferberg (who died in 2010 aged 86), occasionally performing and recording. Today, Sanders, long resident in leafy Woodstock, keeps the Fugs going with younger musicians. “I still like to jump about on stage,” he says, “and working with young musicians means they all have other bands, so its not like I have to keep them busy”.Sanders hopes Fugs Film! can inspire others to continue the noble tradition of kicking against the pricks. Fighting that American war machine, he says, “is a constant struggle. A holy struggle. A brilliant struggle. To let the human spirit struggle against the warrior caste.”Fugs Film! is showing at the Barbican, London, on 23 October, as part of theDoc’n Roll film festivalExplore more on these topicsMusicExperimental musicPop and rockMusic documentaryPoetryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A vigorous apologist for a cruel emperor’: Is Caryl Churchill’s explosive new play about Trump and his press officers? | Caryl Churchill | The Guardian
description: From Thatcherism to global crisis to an ever-online world, Caryl Churchill has chronicled our race to the abyss. Now she’s written a play about a blond-wigged apologist for an un-named, strongman ruler
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: From Thatcherism to global crisis to an ever-online world, Caryl Churchill has chronicled our race to the abyss. Now she’s written a play about a blond-wigged apologist for an un-named, strongman ruler
Content: Reveals the truth on camera … Kate O’Flynn as press officer Iris in Triumph at the Almeida theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenReveals the truth on camera … Kate O’Flynn as press officer Iris in Triumph at the Almeida theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerCaryl Churchill‘A vigorous apologist for a cruel emperor’: Is Caryl Churchill’s explosive new play about Trump and his press officers?From Thatcherism to global crisis to an ever-online world, she has chronicled our race to the abyss. Now she’s written a play about a blond-wigged voicepiece for an un-named, strongman ruler. Who can she mean?Michael BillingtonMon 19 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 02.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTriumph, which has just opened at London’sAlmeida theatre, is Caryl Churchill’s latest piece of explosive minimalism. Running at just 20 minutes, it skewers contemporary barbarism without mentioning the names of Trump, Putin or any of the other supposedly strong national leaders. It works through historical analogy and is a reminder that Churchill – while “always ahead of the game” in the words of the play’s director, James Macdonald – has in recent years developed a form of elliptical drama for which the apt word might be compressionism.At the heart of Churchill’s new play is an edgy romance between a male journalist and a female press officer who dons a blond wig for her screen appearances and who is a vigorous apologist for a cruel, vindictive, narcissistic emperor.double quotation markInstead of retribution, she is showered with praise as ratings rocket. ‘The people like a strong emperor,’ she is toldAt first she merrily trumpets his more acceptable achievements: pearls imported from Britain, gold from the temples of Gaul, statues erected to his own glory. But through her lover she learns of the monstrosities of the regime she represents – such as prisoners trapped in claustrophobic cages and sawn in half – and reveals the truth on camera.Expecting retribution, she is instead showered with praise as the ratings rocket and she is told: “The people like a strong emperor.” Standing at a lectern backed by imperial purple and speaking in an overtly American accent, Kate O’Flynn shows perfectly the way the authentic human being emerges from the glamorised robot who speaks for power: in James Macdonald’s production she even looks uncannily like the most recent and short-lived White House incumbent, Katie Zacharia.View image in fullscreen‘Brilliantly nailed the Thatcherite ethos’ … Top Girls at the Minerva theatre, Chichester, in 2011.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianSo what is Churchill up to? Since all the crimes perpetrated by the emperor are drawn from Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars, it is clear that a parallel is being drawn between then and now.Two examples prove the point. When Triumph’s emperor reminds his wife that he has the power of life and death over her, it is a direct echo of Caligula’s threat to a spouse, in Suetonius, that “This beautiful throat will be cut whenever I please”. At another point a fisherman, who has terrified the emperor by presenting him with a giant mullet, finds his face rubbed in it. Having foolishly thanked heaven that it wasn’t a crab, he then finds the emperor ensuring that his features are badly scarred by a giant crustacean: a slice of whimsical sadism from the reign of Tiberius.Lest anyone think that Churchill is overstating the case by linking Roman and contemporary decadence, one has only to look at recent events. We live in a world where the idea oflivestreaming a military execution, although now abandoned, was originally endorsed by President Trump and his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth. We have also seen ICE agents shooting nonviolent protesters, whilefishermen in the Caribbean have been killed by American troopson the totally unproved grounds that they were drug smugglers. Churchill’s point in Triumph is that today governments in the western world not only commit acts of extreme brutality: they also attempt to massage them through skilled media presentation.View image in fullscreenVibrant satire … Gary Oldman and Alfred Molina in Serious Money at the Royal Court, London, in 1987.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyAll this is conveyed in a short, sharp shock of a play that is proof of Churchill’s restless experimentalism. But while she never writes the same play twice, I see a clear division between her earlier and later work. In the 1970s and 80s she wrote a series of momentous plays that used a range of expansive devices to expose the defects of our society. Latterly she has created a number of works in which formal brevity is accompanied by a bleak worldview. That may be an oversimplified view of a complex artist but what I see in the later Churchill is a form of cosmic minimalism.In the earlier period she was clearly animated by the absurdities, inequities and injustices she found in British life. That was evident in Cloud 9,about to be revived by the National Theatreand which I signally failed to understand on its first appearance in 1979. The first half is a very funny exposé of Victorian Anglo-Saxon attitudes in which imperialist supremacy is linked to sexual dominance. “There is something dark about women that threatens what is best in us,” one male colonialist tells another. The second half transports us to the more libertarian sexual relationships of the 1970s but, while Churchill palpably applauds progress, she implies that the old class barriers have by no means disappeared.The play that changed my life: ‘Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9 had us dancing in the aisles’Read moreThat was even more obvious inTop Girls. Appearing in 1982, it brilliantly nailed the Thatcherite ethos by suggesting that the replication by women of the male success ethic was pointless. It began with the famous dinner-party scene in which five notable women from history were seen as both radical pioneers and social victims. It went on to explore the contradictions of the modern working woman. But the visceral showdown came in the final scene where the striving Maggie Thatcher-worshipping Marlene confronted her working-class sister, Joyce.View image in fullscreenThe nature of identity … Daniel Craig and Michael Gambon in A Number, at the Royal Court in 2002.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWhat was great was Churchill’s understanding of both points of view. Joyce’s sense of deprivation led to a rancorous bitterness while the outwardly successful Marlene was conscious of the dubious bargain she had made in sacrificing her child to her career. As Lesley Manville pointed out when introducing a reshowing of the play on BBC Four, this was one of the great plays of the century. I suspect it will last longer than Churchill’s vibrant satire on the greed-is-good philosophy of the City of London inSerious Money. I loved the play in 1987 but seeing it revived recently by a young company called Mad Spirit I felt that it belonged to its moment. Today, I felt, Churchill would be writing about City jitters, cyber-plots and fears of financial collapse.One of Churchill’s qualities, in fact, is her nimbleness of spirit and ability to respond to the times – even to be way ahead of them.Far Away, which premiered in 2000, was a startling evocation of the threat both of localised fascism and of global crisis. The first scene, in which a niece tells her aunt that she has seen her uncle beating people and bundling them into lorries, has acquired an ugly resonance in an age when the far-right sanctions violence towards immigrants. But the final scene offered a terrifying image of a world at war and of nature absorbed into a cycle of unending destruction. I wondered at the time if there was something determinist about Churchill’s vision of catastrophe. A quarter of a century later I find myself admiring her foresight.The same is true ofA Number, first seen at the Royal Court in 2002 with Michael Gambon and Daniel Craig and revived many times since. In the play a father confronts three of his adult sons: from the cells of one taken into care at the age of four a doctor has created a series of clones. But this was less a play about the ethics of cloning than about the nature of identity. If the first son was disturbed, was it the result of a depressive mother or paternal neglect? If the second cloned son was his physical match but psychological opposite, was that because of scientific skill or a stable environment? In a 60-minute play Churchill was posing fundamental questions that have grown ever more urgent in an age when AI poses a threat to human survival.View image in fullscreenDark visions … Linda Bassett, Deborah Findlay, Kika Markham and June Watson in Churchill’s Escaped Alone at the Royal Court, London, in 2016.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianChurchill’s compressionism was equally apparent inEscaped Alone, from 2016, which showed a group of women amiably chatting in a sunlit garden. While talking of times past, they also relished the benefits of living today: “whole worlds in your pocket,” said one of mobile phones. But in their midst was a septuagenarian Cassandra who offered a vision of global catastrophe: a world of flood, fire, thirst and starvation where 80% of food was diverted to TV studios and “commuters watched breakfast on iPlayer on their way to work”.This strikes me as quintessential Churchill. She is a writer with a strong sense of life’s quotidian pleasures and its unexpected delights. But she is also more alert than most to the possibility, whether from geopolitics, climate crisis or technological advance, that we are speeding towards the abyss. To express this, as she does, in works that get briefer and more concentrated with each year makes her the most pungent theatrical prophet alive today.Triumph is at the Almeida, London, until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsCaryl ChurchillTheatreAlmeida theatreClassics and ancient historyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshoots | Social media | The Guardian
description: Backlash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bans
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Backlash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bans
Content: Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc, in Antibes on the Côte d'Azur, no longer allows photoshoots without prior permission.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/PRView image in fullscreenHotel du Cap-Eden-Roc, in Antibes on the Côte d'Azur, no longer allows photoshoots without prior permission.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/PRSocial media‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshootsBacklash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bansLauren CochraneMon 19 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStand in any vaguely photogenic spot these days on holiday and the chances are you will come across people posing with raised phones and even ring lights. Some may be influencers with huge audiences on social media, others just overkeenInstagramusers. With hotels and beauty spots now so overrun, however, bans on photography are coming into place.The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, known for its glamorous clientele, views of the Côte d’Azur and a stunning infinity pool, has brought in rules against photoshoots: no longer allowed without prior permission.According toreports, this has been prompted by people booking lunch reservations and bringing bags of clothing and jewellery. Instead of sitting down to eat, they have used their time at the hotel for photoshoots of themselves in different outfits, creating images to post to their social media accounts.View image in fullscreenThe Hollies farm shop in Cheshire has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.Photograph: chasephoto/AlamyLess glamorous spots are also clamping down. The Hollies, a Cheshire farm shop which has become a popular content stop thanks to the Love Island star Molly-Mae Hague posting images from there, has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.Meanwhile Jeremy King, the London restaurateur behind places such asSimpson’s in the Strandandthe Park, wrotean articlein the Evening Standard earlier this year titled: “I’m fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant – enough is enough.”In the US, a shop on Nantucket, an island off Cape Cod, Massachusetts, went viral earlier this year for a sign reading “no influencers”, while the town of Pomfret in Vermont has banned influencers taking pictures in front of foliage in autumn. In Fujikawaguchiko inJapan, a screen has been put up near a convenience store to stop people taking pictures there in front of Mount Fuji.Part of the argument from venues is that these photoshoots jeopardise privacy and discretion, especially as expected at expensive hotels. Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc’s manager, Sophie Volant, toldTravel Weekly: “As much as [guests] appreciate having people in the restaurants and in the bars, they also want their summer home to remain private. We had to think about a solution.”View image in fullscreenSimpson’s in the Strand: Jeremy King, whoreopened this London institution earlier this year, said he was ‘fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant’.Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianAnna Fedou, the chief marketing officer at the Beaumier hotel group, says it sometimes works with influencers to capture content to promote its luxury hotels, which include Les Roches Rouges near Marseille, loved for its photogenic pool. The group does not have specific rules around photography, Fedou says, but stays mindful of its primary purpose.“We’re in the business of hospitality, not running photo studios,” she says. “People travel from all over the world to experience the atmosphere, sense of space and feeling that make a hotel unique. It’s our responsibility to protect that.”Rules around photography at hotels and restaurants mirror a trend away from capturing the moment and towards being in it. Alex Goat, the founder of the youth culture agency Livity, compares these rules to clubs asking visitors to put stickers over their phones’ cameras. “They want to signify that they’re here for people who love music. There’s something potentially similar [here],” she says. “It’s ‘I’m here because I want to enjoy the space’ rather than ‘I’m here to document something to other people’.”View image in fullscreenSleepy Hollow Farm in Pomfret, Vermont. The town of Pomfret has banned influencers taking pictures in front of autumn foliage.Photograph: Michael McCormack/AlamyPart of the disapproval towards influencers is a common misconception is that they are paid well for such content. Sometimes, as with Beaumier hotels, influencers will produce posts in exchange for a free room, but the idea is that brands will want to make deals with influencers due to their association with glamorous locations. “The majority are creating most of their content for their audiences for free,” explains Nicole Ocran, an influencer who set upthe Creator Unionto represent those in the industry. “They create content in the hope of courting brands and seeing who will bite.”There has been previous outrage around influencers’ behaviour, asin 2021when Love Island stars travelled to Dubai during lockdown, for example. And if there is an underlying snobbery to a luxury hotel instigating anti-photoshoot policies, there may be sexism, too. “Influencer culture has always been vilified in popular culture,” says Sophie Bishop, the author ofInfluencer Creep. “It’s a very feminised form of media, that’s bound up in promotional culture.”Ocran agrees. “Most people have a particular stereotype in mind,” she says. “That isn’t to say that influencers and content creators can’t overstep or be insufferable when getting their shots and filming in public.”View image in fullscreenA screen was erected to block the view of Mount Fuji from outside the Fujikawaguchiko Lawsons convenience store after tourists crowded the area to take photographs.Photograph: Franck Robichon/EPAFedou believes that the key is to walk a balance that engages with social media content while keeping a restful experience at hotels. “Influencers will generally choose quieter moments for shooting content, to capture the space without disturbing others,” she says. “Les Roches Rouges has a relaxed atmosphere, but guest experience always comes first.”While the backlash might be aimed at influencers with lots of followers,over 5.4 billion people use social media every day.Ocran hopes that rules around photography might promote a more balanced attitude to social media in general. “[It’s] pushing back against the idea that not every space is meant for public consumption, and not every experience should be turned into content,” she says. “And as a creator, that’s quite a healthy message to send to us all.”Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaHospitality industryOvertourismInstagramFranceLondonJapannewsShareReuse this content

title: Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol | Indian food and drink | The Guardian
description: These snacks are easy to turn into a more substantial supper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: These snacks are easy to turn into a more substantial supper
Content: Gurdeep Loyal’s masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenGurdeep Loyal’s masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.Quick and easyIndian food and drinkGurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambolTasty, spicy fritters to dip into coconut sambol as a snack or treat, or serve with avocado or egg for a more substantial supperGurdeep LoyalMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese warmly spiced fritters are inspired by the tikki-chaat carts found all over India, which sizzle fresh chickpea, potato or lentil patties on hot-plates until crisp, then slather them with chutneys. The coconut sambol ushers forth the flavours of south India – coconut, mustard seeds and lime; add a teaspoon of tamarind paste to increase the tartness, if you like. A good dollop of yoghurt is a must, and a fried egg or avocado on the side turns these fritters into a satisfying supper.Masala chickpea and parsnip fritters with coconut sambolPrep10 minCook30 minServes2-360g red chillies(about 4 large ones)5tbsp vegetable oil,plus extra for frying4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed65g desiccated coconut2tsp black mustard seeds1½tsp fine sea salt2tbsp brown sugar2tbsp tomato pureeJuice and grated zest of 1 largelime, plus 1 lime extra, cut into wedges, to serve400g tinchickpeas, drained2 largeparsnips, peeled and grated2tspgarammasala2tsp coriander seeds, crushed100g ricotta3tbsp plain flour1tbsp baking powder15g fresh coriander, finely chopped, plus extra to serveYoghurt, to serveFried egg or avocado, to serve (optional)In a small blender, blitz the chillies, four tablespoons of vegetable oil and two crushed garlic cloves to make a smooth paste.Toast the coconut and mustard seeds in a small frying pan over a medium heat for one to two minutes, until they take on a little colour. Pour in the chilli paste with 100ml water, then cook for four to five minutes, until much of the water has evaporated and the paste begins to darken. Add a teaspoon of fine salt, the brown sugar, tomato puree, lime juice and zest, then cook for another two minutes, until you have a thick sambol. Empty into a bowl and leave to cool.Blitz the chickpeas and the remaining tablespoon of vegetable oil to a coarse paste in a blender or food processor. Put this in a large bowl with the grated parsnips, the remaining two crushed garlic cloves, the garam masala, crushed coriander seeds, ricotta, plain flour, baking powder, fresh coriander and a half-teaspoon of salt. Mix together using your hands until fully combined, then shape into six large patties, about 4-5cm wide and 1½cm thick.Heat a little vegetable oil in a nonstick frying pan, then cook the fritters in batches over medium heat for seven to eight minutes, flipping occasionally, until golden brown on both sides. Serve warm with a dollop of yoghurt, a generous spoon of coconut sambol and a fried egg or avocado, if you like. Garnish with fresh coriander and a wedge of lime.Explore more on these topicsIndian food and drinkQuick and easyFoodCurryMain courseSnacksVegetablesBeans, pulses and legumesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Core values: the Austrian scheme bringing forgotten apple varieties back to life | Fruit | The Guardian
description: Spar pilot scheme will test whether heirloom fruit can thrive in today’s commercial and environmental conditions
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Spar pilot scheme will test whether heirloom fruit can thrive in today’s commercial and environmental conditions
Content: An apple pilot scheme will test whether long-lost varieties can thrive under today’s conditions.Photograph: Marek Slusarczyk/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn apple pilot scheme will test whether long-lost varieties can thrive under today’s conditions.Photograph: Marek Slusarczyk/AlamyFruitCore values: the Austrian scheme bringing forgotten apple varieties back to lifeSpar pilot scheme will test whether heirloom fruit can thrive in today’s commercial and environmental conditionsDeborah ColeMon 19 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnly about 10 of the 2,000 types of apples growing inAustriacan be found in supermarkets among the polished, pristine fruit usually on display – a sad ratio according to fans of historic varieties being primed for a comeback.One of the country’s biggest retail chains has embarked on a pilot rollout of unusual and long-forgotten apples enjoyed in previous centuries, riding an international trend of reviving heirloom fruit and vegetables.The Spar group is working with produce distributor Frutura to return two rare varieties to shops:Ilzer Rosenapfel(Ilzer Rose apple), dating from about 1840 from the southern state of Styria, andFalchs Gulderling, identified in the 1870s in South Tirol.“Farming never stands still,” said Frutura co-managing director Katrin Hohensinner-Häupl, calling it a dance between knowledge passed down through generations and innovation.Rediscovering antique apples using modern cultivation methods are “bringing their history and flavour back to life,” she said.Beyond opening up lost worlds of flavour, colour and consistency for today’s foodies, the efforts to bring back native fruit varieties are rooted in increased consciousness around biodiversity and the preservation of ancient crops.Experts fromenvironmentalist NGO, Arche Noah (Noah’s Ark), were enlisted to identify kinds of heritage apples that best lend themselves to modern large-scale cultivation methods.“Many consumers today are once again taking a greater interest in where food comes from, the varieties involved and how it tastes,” said Markus Kaser, Spar Austria’s deputy chair.The pilot scheme will test whether the long-lost varieties “can thrive in commercial fruit growing under today’s conditions”. “If we succeed, we would like to offer these special varieties throughout the region,” Kaser said.The team will be putting the new-old apples to the test in terms of taste, growth performance, susceptibility to disease and shelf life.An experimental orchard in Styria now has 2,150 trees growing. The first fruits were picked this week for sampling and will head to a trial supermarket in Vienna as well as regional daycare centres and schools next month.Hohensinner-Häupl said her first impressions were positive, with the ripe Gulderling particularly oversized and deep red, and theIlzer Rosenapfelmore diminutive and paler in complexion. As far as taste, “they recall apples from childhood,” she said.The Austrian project has taken a page from smaller-scale artisanal orchards and farm stands acrossEuropeand the US experimenting with unique apple varieties.The German-speaking world boasts a richness of apple names harkening back to bygone eras:Steirische Schafnase(Styrian sheep nose), Crown Prince Rudolf, Kaiser Wilhelm and the juicy, robustNapoleonsapfel,rediscovered in 2018.The oldest still available may be theGoldparmäne(King of the Pippins), stemming from early 16th-century Normandy.“The names show just how much work and love the growers put into their fruit trees,” Daniela Dirr, an expert at the historic orchards of Schleißheim Palace in the German state of Bavaria, told regional newspaper Merkur.Connoisseurs also rave about a broader spectrum of flavours from varieties nearly wiped out by war, industrialised agriculture and a marketplace favouring the sugary over the distinctive. Notes of raspberry, clove, nut and lemon are back.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPomologists, experts in the field of the rosy orbs, say old apple varieties such as theBerner Rosenapfelalso contain significantly more polyphenols in their skin, acting as antioxidants and anti-inflammatory agents, which have been bred out of modern varieties.Researchers at Charité, Berlin’s university hospital, found that a high concentration of polyphenols in heirloom varieties canallow many people with a lifelong allergy to enjoy the fruit.The study also showed that people with allergies who regularly consume the varieties they can tolerate experience fewer hay fever symptoms. In adults, hay fever is often associated with an apple allergy.The south-western German city of Reutlingen has a public “Pomologie” park, stemming from a gardening school founded in 1860 and home to 50 types of apple trees.A boutique in the Schöneberg district of Berlin, Apfelgalerie, curates a selection from 200 varieties grown at a dedicated orchard near the Polish border. Staff offer taste tests of apples with intriguing names such as Apollo and Count Etzo, and sell sampler gift boxes.In the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein, gardener Jochen Bock has been cultivating his own private Eden for more than three decades.It now boasts a single tree growing more than 100 apple varieties thanks to a sophisticated homespun grafting technique.“I had a problem: we didn’t have enough space left in the garden, and I was determined to collect lots of apples, particularly historic ones,” Bock told local media this month. “So I started with regional varieties, and one thing led to another.”Explore more on these topicsFruitAustriaFoodBiodiversityFarmingConservationEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Spaghetti with lentils, and aubergine veggie-balls: Jacob Kenedy’s autumn pasta recipes | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: They’re vegetarian and full of complex, savoury flavours
Author: Jacob Kenedy
Headline: They’re vegetarian and full of complex, savoury flavours
Content: Jacob Kenedy’s lentils and spaghetti.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenJacob Kenedy’s lentils and spaghetti.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.Italian food and drinkSpaghetti with lentils, and aubergine veggie-balls: Jacob Kenedy’s autumn pasta recipesA deliciously humble lentil and spaghetti dish, and a meat-free riff on meatball pasta made with aubergine veggie-ballsJacob KenedyMon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome plant-based pasta dishes are light, bright and summery –pesto genovese, tomato sauce,aglio e olio– but some have an umami and complexity that is normally associated with more carnal pleasures. Here are two.Pastawith lentils is a firm personal and family favourite – my mum and I make this dish whenever we fancy something really comforting, and the earthiness of the lentils plays against grassy olive oil and parsley, and the texture of the pasta. Truecucina povera– a humble meal, and deliciously so. Veggie-balls are also great things.Polpette(normally translated as meatballs) is just balls (of anything pulped), after all. They can be made of white fish, oily fish or vegetables. I particularly love courgette for its bright, green, fresh flavour, and, above all, rich, velvety, chocolatey aubergine. Of course, you can eat them on their own, but I also love them through pasta, as a vegetarian riff on spaghetti and meatballs.Lentils and spaghetti (pictured top)As I write this, my mum is just as alive and at least as vital as she was when she used to make this dish for me, but, for some reason, this is now a dish I make more often, and for her. I adore it, but every time I have offered it to an Italian they look at me as though I have just insulted their mother. Don’t ask me why; people can be as inexplicable as this dish is delicious. You can add some chilli (dried or fresh) when you fry the garlic, if you like, but I prefer this comfortingly bland and without pep.Prep5 minCook55 minServes4For the lentils (can be made ahead)180g small brown lentils, such as castelluccio or puy2 bay leavesWhen ready to eat400g dried spaghetti– this is also good withbigoli, ditali/ditalini, farfalle, garganelli, linguine, mafaldine, orecchiette, pappardelle or tagliatelleSea salt4 garlic cloves, peeled and chopped5 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil4 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley leaves50g butter, or 3 tbsp more extra-virgin olive oil60gparmesan, suitable for vegetarians, grated (optional)Put the lentils into a small saucepan with the bay leaves and about 500ml water. Bring them to a simmer and cook until completely tender and mushy – about 45 minutes; noal dentehere – adding water so the lentils and water are level at the end of cooking.Cook the pasta according to packet instructions in abundant, well-salted water (10g per litre).Meanwhile, fry the garlic in a saucepan in half the oil over a medium heat until golden, no darker. Add the lentils and a splash of pasta water, then bring to the boil.Drain the pasta a minute or so moreal dentethan you like to eat it, reserving some of the cooking water. Put the drained pasta in the lentil pan, add the parsley, the remaining two and a half tablespoons of oil and the butter (or three more tablespoons of oil), then stir or toss over a high heat until the pasta is asal denteas you like, and the sauce is thickened by pasta starch and mostly emulsified; you may need to add more pasta cooking water as you go. Serve immediately, with or without cheese.Aubergine veggie-balls and pastaView image in fullscreenJacob Kenedy’s aubergine veggie-balls and pasta.The Italian wordpolpette(usually translated as “meatballs”) in fact encompasses any balls of minced or pulped vegetables, fish or meat. They could be made from beef or pork or chicken or veal, or aubergines or courgettes or pulses, or bread or greens, or white fish or salted fish or oily fish or prawns: if you can pulp it, you canpolpetteit.Prep15 minDrain1 hrCook2 hrServes4For the sauce (can be made ahead)2 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil1 small pinch chilli flakes(optional)800g chopped tomatoes(if fresh, keep their skins and seeds and chop finely; if canned, this is 2 cans)Sea salt and black pepperFor the veggie balls (can be made ahead)2 large aubergines(total weight 1kg)1 egg, lightly beaten100g parmesan, suitable for vegetarians, grated, or pecorino romano,100g dried breadcrumbs2 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley leaves1 tbsp chopped mint leaves1 tbsp chopped basil leaves1 garlic clove, peeled and crushedSea salt and black pepperAbout 40g plain flourOlive oil, for fryingWhen ready to eat400g dried spaghetti– this is also good withbucatini, cavatelli, fusilli, linguine, mafaldine, penne or spaghettini1 quantity simple tomato sauce(see below and method)3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil12 basil leaves80g pecorino romano, suitable for vegetarians, gratedFor the sauce, heat a saucepan over a medium heat, not until smoking, but until you think something might sizzle. Add the garlic and oil and fry until the garlic slices just barely start to colour at the edges. Add the chilli flakes if using, then straight after, the tomatoes.Season with salt and pepper and simmer, stirring often, over a low heat, until slightly thickened and with oil rising to the top – 20–30 minutes. Taste carefully for seasoning.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Prick the aubergines and roast them for one hour until completely tender. Cool until safe to handle, then peel them. Drain the peeled flesh in a colander under a weight for an hour or so (or, if you’re in a rush, lay it in a long sausage shape in a clean tea towel, then wring it dry). You should end up with roughly 230g drained aubergine.Chop it finely, put in a bowl and mix in the egg, cheese, crumbs, herbs and garlic, and season to taste. Form into walnut-sized balls and coat in the flour.Fry the veggie balls in the oil until cooked through and nicely golden brown. You can choose either to deep-fry them, in oil not more than one-third of your chosen pan’s depth, for safety reasons, at 180C for four minutes; or shallow-fry them in oil 1cm deep, turning every couple of minutes to cook on all sides. Drain and leave to cool on kitchen paper.Cook the pasta according to the packet instructions in abundant, well-salted water (10g per litre).Meanwhile, reheat the tomato sauce in a wide pan over a medium heat. Add the veggie balls and simmer, stirring occasionally, for five to 10 minutes. Drain the pasta and set it in a large wide bowl.At the last moment, stir the oil and basil into the sauce and pour the sauce and aubergine balls over the pasta. At the table, toss the sauce gently into the pasta and serve on warmed plates with a little pecorino atop.This is an edited extract from Pasta Tricolore: Recipes in Green, White and Red by Jacob Kenedy, published by Bloomsbury at £18.99. To order a copy for £17.09, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkPastaFoodMain courseCheeseVegetablesBeans, pulses and legumesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Wrong’ type of credit card wrecked my Enterprise car hire pickup | Money | The Guardian
description: Not having the right kind when picking up a vehicle can leave travellers scrambling to find alternative transport
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: Not having the right kind when picking up a vehicle can leave travellers scrambling to find alternative transport
Content: An Enterprise desk at an airport refused to hand over the keys to a car hire when a First Direct credit card was used.Photograph: Alex Ramsay/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn Enterprise desk at an airport refused to hand over the keys to a car hire when a First Direct credit card was used.Photograph: Alex Ramsay/AlamyConsumer championsMoney‘Wrong’ type of credit card wrecked my Enterprise car hire pickupNot having the right kind when picking up a vehicle can leave travellers scrambling to find alternative transportAnna TimsMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf your children are on half-term holiday soon and you are planning to collect a hire car, make sure you have the right kind of credit card. These cautionary tales show the costly consequences if yours does not pass muster.I hired a car for a family holiday from Enterprise Rent-A-Car in France. Thecollectiondesk at Carcassonne airport refused to hand over the keys when I presented the Visa credit card used for the booking because it was issued by First Direct. It told me it did not accept cards from online banks.The rental branch subsequently confirmed this in writing. Enterprise’s terms and conditions state that Visa, Mastercard and American Express are accepted, while virtual, single-use and prepaid cards are not. We were forced to arrange alternative rail and taxi transport for our group of10, costing us €440 [£370] and causing considerable stress.The booking agent has refunded the £388.44 rental cost, but Enterprise first ignored, then refused, my requests for my expenses to be refunded.JM,OxfordThis is an extraordinary stance on the part of Enterprise, given that First Direct is part of HSBC and that terms and conditions not explicitly stated in a contract are unenforceable.You have been battling vainly for redress since May, so it’s provoking that Enterprise instantly rolled over when I waded in. It admitted that First Direct Visa cards were accepted and that branch staff blundered.Apparently, it says, staff are now “very apologetic” three months after the event despite the company having doubled down in writing when you complained.It has now refunded your expenses, though not a penny more to reflect the impact of its error.It says: “On this occasion, the customer did not receive the high level of service and support that we aim to provide. We sincerely regret the inconvenience caused in this situation.”VDof London was also caught out by unexpected credit card rules when she tried to collect a prepaid car from Warsaw airport that had been booked through Holiday Autos. The provider, Flex To Go, refused to release it because her credit card bore her initials instead of her forename.“The Holiday Autos confirmation did say ‘no abbreviations’, but I took that to mean shortened names rather than initials, and I have had no problems with my card over many years of hiring cars,” she says. “In the end, we had to get a Polish friend to call the car hire desk and pay over £145 for their comprehensive insurance – when we already had our own – so we could have the car.”Although it is common for UK credit cards to replace a customer’s forename with initials, it is not unusual for car rental companies to refuse them as security guarantees. Instead, they insist the name on the card matches the name on the lead driver’s licence.However, I agree that Holiday Autos’ warning about this was open to misinterpretation. Flex To Go’s Ts & Cs did specify it, but these were not given to you until you had completed the transaction at the collection desk. Those Ts & Cs conceal other nasty surprises.Buried in the small print are clauses stating that the company charges customers for “minor expenses for ordinary use of the vehicle, ie refilling screen washer liquid and washing the vehicle”.Customers are also required to carry out “daily inspections” of brake fluid, oil and liquid coolant control, regardless of any dashboard warnings.These terms strike me as onerous and unusual, and were neither highlighted by Flex To Go as “onerous and unusual” terms must be, nor were they mentioned by Holiday Autos.Flex To Go did not respond to any of these points. Holiday Autos ignored the point about the ambiguity of “abbreviations” and its supplier’s maintenance demands.It told me that names on cards and driver licences must match for identity verification and fraud prevention, and that customers should review terms and conditions before travel. “We appreciate how frustrating this situation must have been,” it says.Always read reviews of car rental firms before booking to discover which ones to avoid. Looking at the Ts & Cs of Flex To Go, which operates on three continents, I will not be using them. And don’t be caught out by hire firms’ rules on credit cards that are designed not only for identity verification, but to ensure deductions from a customer’s bank account are possible if a vehicle is damaged.Hire companies tend to accept physical credit cards only, not Apple Pay, as one reader found to his cost. If the firms can’t reliably match the card to the licence and booking name, they are likely to insist that you pay for their comprehensive insurance, which can be expensive.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer rightsConsumer affairsMotoringfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … you need to take 10,000 steps a day to be healthy? | Walking | The Guardian
description: The fitness benchmark has surprisingly unscientific origins – yet it does contain more than a kernel of truth
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: The fitness benchmark has surprisingly unscientific origins – yet it does contain more than a kernel of truth
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …WalkingIs it true that … you need to take 10,000 steps a day to be healthy?The fitness benchmark has surprisingly unscientific origins – yet it does contain more than a kernel of truthKate LloydMon 19 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe idea that we need to walk 10,000 steps a day originated not in medical research but in a 1960s marketing campaign for a pedometer, says Jack McNamara, senior lecturer in clinical exercise physiology at the University of East London. The round number was easy to remember and the idea caught on, despite there being no scientific evidence for 10,000 steps as a specific threshold for health.“When the research community looked into it, they found that there were health benefits, so it didn’t necessarily get thrown out as pseudoscience,” says McNamara.Walking has been shown to benefit cardiovascular and cardiorespiratory health, as well as reducing the likelihood of some cancers. It also breaks up sedentary time, which is hugely harmful to health. “But when we look into it with systematic reviews andlarge-scale studies, there start to be diminishing returns the more steps you do.”double quotation markThe problem comes when you start chasing step counts for their own sake, then punish yourself for missing themIs it true that … cycling affects fertility?Read moreMcNamara says the health improvement is huge when someone goes from a sedentary lifestyle, or 2,000 steps a day to 4,000. But going from 8,000 to 10,000 or 10,000 to 12,000 brings a much smaller benefit. “It still has some benefits, just not as many as people might expect.”That’s not to say we should spend more time sitting down. If you enjoy walking, McNamara says, walk for as long as you like. The problem comes when you start chasing step counts for their own sake, particularly if you punish yourself for missing them.If you’re already clocking up plenty of daily steps, he suggests switching some walking for higher-intensity exercise, if you can, to get greater health benefits. “Going for a run, or swimming at pace, or walking uphill, or power walking – something that gets your breathing up. You’d be so much better doing something that’s a little bit more vigorous.”Explore more on these topicsWalkingIs it true that …FitnessHealth & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A perfect weekend in the Lincolnshire Wolds: wide skies and gentle walks | Lincolnshire holidays | The Guardian
description: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to miss
Author: Phoebe Taplin
Headline: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to miss
Content: A footpath through the Lincolnshire Wolds near Somersby.Photograph: Keith Skingle/AlamyView image in fullscreenA footpath through the Lincolnshire Wolds near Somersby.Photograph: Keith Skingle/AlamyA perfect weekend in …Lincolnshire holidaysA perfect weekend in the Lincolnshire Wolds: wide skies and gentle walksThe landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to missPhoebe TaplinMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWide skies, gentle footpaths through gold and copper wooded hills, thatched cottages, cosy pubs and quirky shops: the Lincolnshire Wolds have all the ingredients for the perfect autumnal mini break. Victorian poet Alfred Tennyson lived in the village of Somersby for most of his first three decades and the local landscapes echo through his verses. In The Lady of Shalott: “Long fields of barley and of rye / That clothe the wold and meet the sky …”TheLincolnshire Wolds National Landscapecovers an area of 216 sq miles. On its southern boundary, halfway between Lincoln and the coast, the friendly market town ofHorncastlebills itself as the “gateway to the Wolds”. With handsome brick houses, great cafes, a market on Thursdays and Saturdays and decent public transport links, it’s a perfect base for exploring the area.View image in fullscreenThe market town of Horncastle is a good base for exploring the area.Photograph: Jasmine Bryan/AlamyHorncastle overflows with antique shops.Laurence Shaw, with half a century’s knowledge of the trade, runs an elegant wholesaler on the corner of East Street. In an old chapel across the road, theTrinity Centrehas all kinds of ancient treasures piled in fantastical heaps under lancets of Victorian glass: porcelain milkmaids, jelly moulds, cotton reels, teetering piles of teacups and thick vines of jewellery. Round the corner inStanhope Antique Centreyou may find anything from a wooden decoy duck to a roulette wheel between chandeliers and grandfather clocks.By the “Ducks Crossing!” sign opposite Tesco, mallards gather on the reedy River Bain. And in the 13th-centurySt Mary’schurch there are gold angels in the rafters and lines from Tennyson’s poemRing out, wild bellsin stained glass. The newRiverscape Walk, launched last year, will take you past the canal basin, watermill and former leather tanning warehouses.Take a hikeThere are plenty of rewarding walks nearby and you don’t always need a car to reach them. The hourly56 busfrom Lincoln to Skegness stops in Horncastle and, 10 minutes later, in Hagworthingham, a peaceful Wold-edge village. From here, asix-mile loopof undulating lanes and footpaths takes in tiny Somersby, Tennyson’s birthplace, andBag Enderby(which sounds straight out of Tolkien), where St Margaret’s church has an intricate 15th-century font, carved with religious symbols and medieval scenes. Bag Enderby’s -by suffix comes from an Old Norse word for village.From Hagworthingham, you can also stroll throughSnipe Dalesnature reserve, where a 3-metre (10ft) wooden snipe, carved by local sculptor Nigel Sardeson,has just been installed on a wooded bank. The valleys here are fragrant with late meadowsweet and water mint and the trees are full of birdsong, from tiny goldcrests in the conifers to huge buzzards over the oaks. If you have time and energy to spare, theViking Waylong-distance walk – waymarked with horned Viking helmets – runs through Horncastle and the Wolds on its 149-mile journey from Rutland Water to the Humber.View image in fullscreenA steel sculpture along the Viking Way near Woodhall Spa.Photograph: Nick Hatton/AlamyDon’t missIn Horncastle, theJoseph Banks Centremultitasks as a tourist info point, local museum and natural history hub.Banks, a botanist and Horncastle’s most famous inhabitant, sailed with Captain Cook and oversaw the creation of Kew Gardens. The museum courtyard is bright with hydrangeas, which Banks helped introduce into Britain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Bath, Harrogate … Woodhall?’ A short break in one of the UK’s most forgotten spa townsRead moreThe Edwardian village ofWoodhall Spa, six miles from Horncastle, has wide leafy avenues and smart black-and-white buildings; even the public loos next to the Tory club are half timbered. Nineteenth-century entrepreneurs, digging for coal, found instead a source of mineral-rich water, a magnet for the era’s wellness-seekers. I meander past theDambusters memorialand mural, the thrivingKinema in the Woods, opened in 1922, the nearbyTea HouseandCottage Museum, then back to Horncastle along the sculpture-dotted Viking Way.Where to eatHorncastle’s top lunch spots include the cafe atMyers Bakery, fragrant with spice and yeast, where you can buy Lincolnshire plum loaf. Round the corner, the spacious and welcoming bike-themedPedal and Pawsserves pizzas, salads and cakes.No 8 Coffee Shop, which opened in March 2026, is already popular for inventive hot drinks such as cinnamon-bun matcha and pistachio hot chocolate.Montebello, in the former Angel Inn, serves home-cooked Italian food, whileMagpiesoffers refined white linen and candlelight dining, with dishes such as Grimsby crab linguine or loin of Lincolnshire lamb. Magpies also has rooms, in cottages next to a Tardis-likeguitar shop.View image in fullscreenCoffee and cake at Pedal and Paws.Illustration: Phoebe TaplinWhere to stayThe cheerful, timewornAdmiral Rodney Hotelis right in the middle of Horncastle, with affordable rooms and details you might see in pricier places: speedy wifi, retro radio, Twinings teabags. It offers great veggie breakfast options, fresh fruit and pastries, served in a big glass-walled conservatory with peacock fanlights. Dinner dishes such as pan-fried sea bass with pickled fennel, or sticky date pudding with butterscotch sauce, chicly garnished with edible flowers and micro-herbs, make a celebratory end to days spent hiking through the Wolds.Getting there and aroundThe56 busheads to Horncastle from Lincoln bus station hourly and takes 50 minutes. The less frequent30 bustakes 10 minutes longer and winds through warm-stoned villages. Local buses include thenew B617from Horncastle to Woodhall Spa. The coast is 20 miles away, on a bus with top-deck views across the Wolds.Accommodation was provided by theAdmiral Rodney,doubles from around £100, room only. Train travel was provided byLNERExplore more on these topicsLincolnshire holidaysA perfect weekend in …England holidaysUnited Kingdom holidaysPublic transport tripsShort breaksfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: On midnight shifts as a Subway ‘sandwich artist’, I served clubbers, cops and sailors | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: In Perth’s nightlife precinct in the 1990s, I made a lot of sandwiches – but the sandwiches also made me
Author: Max Veenhuyzen
Headline: In Perth’s nightlife precinct in the 1990s, I made a lot of sandwiches – but the sandwiches also made me
Content: ‘Did Subway set me on my current path as a food writer?’Composite: Amy Batey-McManus/Guardian design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Did Subway set me on my current path as a food writer?’Composite: Amy Batey-McManus/Guardian design/Getty ImagesA job that changed meAustralian lifestyleA job that changed me: On midnight shifts as a Subway ‘sandwich artist’, I served clubbers, cops and sailorsIn Perth’s nightlife precinct in the 1990s, I made a lot of sandwiches – but the sandwiches also made meRead more in thea job that changed me seriesMax VeenhuyzenMon 19 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDelivering pizzas, with all due respect, was a cruisy gig that fit in with my uni commitments. It was 1998, for Pizza Hut at Como, a well-established suburb 15 minutes fromPerth’s city centre. I blasted hip-hop through my car stereo and brought home cash tips and – if I was rostered until close – any pizzas that were unclaimed or undelivered that night. Between deliveries, drivers sat in the alley behind the shop and shot the breeze while folding pizza boxes.The job’s biggest downside was that it didn’t pay much, especially once you factored in the costs of fuel and vehicle maintenance. So I applied for a job as a “sandwich artist” at Subway in Northbridge, Perth’s nightlife district. I figured that switching to a job where I was on my feet instead of on the road would significantly extend the life expectancy of my hand-me-down Mitsubishi Magna.double quotation markNone of this was roquette science but that didn’t stop me from finding pride in being a tiny, hard-working cog in the restaurant machineWorking at Subway was more demanding than navigating apartment block intercoms and trying not to forget people’s garlic bread. Bins needed to be emptied. Bread was baked daily. Tables were continually sprayed and wiped. Salads and fillings required washing, slicing and cooking. Kind of.
