For one particular sandwich filling, I squeezed biblical amounts of mayo on to shredded seafood extender and massaged the lot by hand.None of this was roquette science but that didn’t stop me from finding pride in being a tiny, hard-working cog in the restaurant machine.I spent almost two years working from midnight till 5am every Saturday and experienced the full spectrum of late-night characters out and about in Perth.There were the pissed clubbers who would prop themselves up against the sneeze-guard and snicker whenever I said “footlong”. There were the beefed-up bouncers and cops whose presence would evoke interest or fear. My boss liked having them around so gave them discounts on their food. There were the guests who wanted a concerning amount of jalapeño.There were also, of course, the troublemakers. While their antics were mostly harmless – think booby-trapped cups that had their bottom cut out so that their contents would spill everywhere when picked up – there were a couple of moments when things could have gotten spicy but, thankfully, didn’t.A job that changed me: As a jeweller, I wanted to avoid sweatshops. Then I realised I’d built one for myselfRead moreSometimes I’d be caught off-guard by small, unexpected moments of humanity. Conversations with customers about media, religion and the realities of being a national-level windsurfing athlete. One customer had chosen Subway Northbridge as his final stop while on day release. I did my best not to sound too curious but he was fairly open in his responses. Then there were those whose stony faces, terse answers and intimidating amount of tattoos – this was the late 90s – that suggested they weren’t in the mood to welcome questions.The sudden appearance of 15 Americans dressed in Fubu and desperate for a taste of home would signal that the sailors were in town – and God help me if I was rostered on solo. They ordered BMT melts (salami, pepperoni, ham, cheese). Americans in general, as I remember, were the only ones who ordered cold-cut sandwiches. Most locals gravitated towards hot fillings including meatball, steak and cheese, and chicken fillets.If you asked most red-blooded Perth blokes at the time, they’d tell you that all these sailors wanted to do was make out with our womenfolk. It became obvious to me that most of these young men didn’t join the navy to serve Uncle Sam. It was simply a job that let them see the world and take care of their families.While I wouldn’t describe my upbringing as sheltered, I did tend to hang with the same kinds of people. Through hospitality, I had the opportunity to see and perhaps even understand the world from different perspectives.Did Subway set me on my current path as a food writer? Not really. I was studying journalism at the time. But in between laying out pucks of sliced tomato and plunging my hand into cold buckets of pickles, I talked and listened to customers – which helped me learn that the secret to telling any food story is understanding the human story behind it.Explore more on these topicsAustralian lifestyleA job that changed meHospitality industryAustralian food and drinkFast foodSandwichesFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Orlando was paralysed and almost died – then became the perfect guide dog | Dogs | The Guardian
description: He had tetanus and I was brokenhearted when it seemed as if he wouldn’t pull through. But he worked hard, made a full recovery and helped to change someone’s life
Author: Jayni Makwana
Headline: He had tetanus and I was brokenhearted when it seemed as if he wouldn’t pull through. But he worked hard, made a full recovery and helped to change someone’s life
Content: Orlando, pictured on his return to puppy training.Photograph: Guide DogsView image in fullscreenOrlando, pictured on his return to puppy training.Photograph: Guide DogsThe pet I'll never forgetDogsThe pet I’ll never forget: Orlando was paralysed and almost died – then became the perfect guide dogHe had tetanus and I was brokenhearted when it seemed as if he wouldn’t pull through. But he worked hard, made a full recovery and helped to change someone’s lifeSarah Judd, as told toJayni MakwanaMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I first met Orlando, he was about eight weeks old. I’m a puppy raiser for the charityGuide Dogs; the puppies come to live with us in Swanley, Kent, until they are 12 to 18 months old. I started training him, but one day, I noticed he was shaking his head, which can mean there is something wrong with a dog’s ears. We took him to the vet and, on the second visit, we were told to rush him straight to the Royal Veterinary hospital because he had tetanus.Dogs aren’t vaccinated against tetanus because it is so rare, and I don’t think I realised how unwell Orlando was. For the first week it was terrifying. He became completely paralysed and I was awake every night expecting a call to say that he had died. He was too sick to carry on training as a guide dog. He had to learn how to eat, walk and do almost everything again.The pet I’ll never forget: Orlando the guide dog recovers from tetanusWhen he came back to live with me, he couldn’t go up the stairs. We had to put mats on the floor, because if he slid it would hurt him, and he could manage only short walks. He was very demanding – he had a unique high-pitched bark and he’d tell you what he wanted. You could be sitting in a cafe and he’d tell you: that’s it, we’ve had enough of sitting, it’s time to go. He was also very cheeky. He’d take my daughter’s smelly socks and then give me a look as if to say, “What? I didn’t do it.”People were always asking after him. He was very resilient and determined – you can’t get much more inspiring than Orlando. He stayed with us until he was 17 months old, and then I gave him to his trainer from Guide Dogs. I felt very emotional, but also proud. It is like your child going off to university.View image in fullscreenSarah Judd with Orlando after he qualified as a guide dog.Photograph: Guide DogsIn just under six months, Orlando qualified as a guide dog. His new owner, who is partially sighted, had been waiting years for one. I was in tears when I read her email saying how happy they were together. Without Orlando, she wouldn’t be getting out and doing as much as she is now.We didn’t know if he’d survive, and to go from a puppy that a lot of people were expecting wouldn’t pull through to a working guide dog that has changed someone’s life is amazing. Knowing him has really changed the way I care for dogs. I am even more conscious of looking out for the little things, because if I hadn’t seen them with Orlando, he wouldn’t be here today.Explore more on these topicsDogsThe pet I'll never forgetPetsBlindness and visual impairmentfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary 1926: How good the damp earth smells  | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: 20 October 1926: After the long dry spell the wood was the place to enjoy it
Author: Janet Case
Headline: 20 October 1926: After the long dry spell the wood was the place to enjoy it
Content: Autumn woodland scene in Bolderwood in the New Forest, Hampshire, UK.Photograph: Gillian Pullinger/AlamyView image in fullscreenAutumn woodland scene in Bolderwood in the New Forest, Hampshire, UK.Photograph: Gillian Pullinger/AlamyCountry diaryTrees and forestsCountry diary 1926: How good the damp earth smells20 October 1926: After the long dry spell the wood was the place to enjoy itJanet CaseMon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 01.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNEW FOREST: After the long dry spell how good the damp earth smells. The wood was the place to enjoy it. It is still very green. The colours are slow in coming this year. Even now there is more colour on the ground than in the trees. The fern has run through gold and copper to rusty red. Here and there a bramble flames, and bilberry patches are shot with crimson. The green tracks were spotted with fungi, white and yellow, brown and purply red. And pale yellowtormentiltrailed across the grass. The white beam has lost its berries, which hung in scarlet bunches a week ago. All that are left hang by ones or twos or are scattered on the ground.The gentle melancholy of autumn: From the archive, 11 November 1840Read moreUnder the Spanish chestnuts the prickly balls lay open, star-shaped, showing their white lining with the shiny nuts up-standing in their places or spilt upon the ground. It was very still in the wood – outside noises were cut off; one’s steps made no sound on the sodden leaves and grass. Once I heard the gurgling of a little watercourse that had long been dry. Twice from the tree-tops came the sudden clatter of a wood pigeon getting under weigh; and that was all.View image in fullscreenThe Guardian Country diary, 20 October 1926.Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsCountry diaryAutumnNew Forest holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re living in darkness’: six years of scaffolding, still no post-Grenfell cladding | Housing | The Guardian
description: Building safety regulator delays leave London tower block beset by security and vandalism problems
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: Building safety regulator delays leave London tower block beset by security and vandalism problems
Content: Natasha Dyett says barely any natural light gets into her home in Archway Heights because of the scaffolding.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNatasha Dyett says barely any natural light gets into her home in Archway Heights because of the scaffolding.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianHousing‘We’re living in darkness’: six years of scaffolding, still no post-Grenfell claddingBuilding safety regulator delays leave London tower block beset by security and vandalism problemsJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 04.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a sunny day with bright blue skies in northLondon, but you wouldn’t know that in Natasha Dyett’s flat. Most of the rooms are consumed in shadow, while her teenage son’s bedroom is almost completely dark, apart from a few slits of light coming through the window.She lives in Archway Heights, a nine-storey block of flats that has been covered in scaffolding for more than six years for cladding works that still haven’t started.The building’s residents say the scaffolding is making life a misery by blocking natural light from entering their homes, especially in places where metal sheets have almost entirely covered whole windows.View image in fullscreenArchway Heights, in north London, has been covered in scaffolding while the landlord waits for approval from the building safety regulator.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianOthers are unable to open windows that have been obstructed by the wooden and metal structure outside. “It’s miserable, it’s like we’re living in darkness,” said Dyett, a 52-year-old market trader living on the third floor.“My son is always in his room and I worry about him getting no natural light. Sometimes, when I go outside, the sun hurts my eyes because I spend so much time here in the dark.”View image in fullscreenNatasha Dyett’s son’s bedroom is left in semi-permanent darkness by the works outside.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianNext to a Covid-era sign about social distancing, a notice outside the building states a scaffolding licence was given from 6 March 2020 to 6 August 2026 – another notice taped above it shows that licence has now been extended by a further 12 months.The block’s residents are among thousands of people across the country bearing the cost of delays by the building safety regulator (BSR) to approve construction works required bypost-Grenfell building safety rules.The regulator has said “complex, older external remediation cases” are taking the longest to sign off and that, in this case, it has been hampered by an “invalid” application.The building is owned and run by Places for People, the UK’s biggest housing association. It contains seven social rent flats and 18 shared ownership properties targeted for London’s key workers.Dyett said she lives in fear about what would happen if the scaffolding caught on fire. In2024, a tower block in Dagenhamthat was covered in scaffolding for ongoing cladding remediation works burned down, with an investigation later finding the scaffolding had caused the fire to spread.“I’m sitting in here afraid because it’s all wrapped in netting and it just takes one idiot to go up there and do something and this block will be alight,” she said. “I try not to think too deeply because I get so scared thinking about it.”The scaffolding has also created serious security problems, with rough sleepers repeatedly climbing up the structure to enter the building through windows.View image in fullscreenTower block residents say rough sleepers have been climbing up on to the scaffolding to enter the building.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianIn July, Dyett woke up at midnight to find a man standing directly outside her third-floor bedroom window. “It was terrifying – he was just standing there watching me and even after I shouted at him to go he still stood there,” she said. She said she reported the incident to the police but was unable to get CCTV footage from Places for People to support her statement.Residents also said someone used the scaffolding to get on the roof, where they removed a skylight, meaning water now enters the building every time it rains.Dwayne Lewis, 50, who has lived in the building for four years, said the scaffolding has caused constant issues and there is frustration that alarms that are supposed to sound if people go on it are not working.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDwayne Lewis moved into Archway Heights four years ago.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianUp on the sixth floor, he’s not as affected by the lack of light as his neighbours on the lower levels, but says the wait for works to start is frustrating. “Service charge has gone up year on year and the rent has gone up year on year. Yet we’re still in a place where there is no line in the sand where that cladding is going to be replaced, just an ongoing cost that is a fire risk, a security risk,” he said.“We all got our hopes up a few months back because some workers came and we thought work was starting – it turned out the netting had just been up there for so long it had become battered and they were replacing it. That was it.”They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new buildingRead moreResidents have begun working with community union Acorn to demand action from Places for People. They want the scaffolding secured to prevent vandalism, the alarms fixed, the metal panels covering bedroom windows removed, and better communication about progress with the works.Earlier this year, the union helped them secure an increase on the £250 bi-annual compensation payments they receive for the scaffolding being there. “It’s just an absolute nightmare for them, they’ve been really neglected for such a long time,” said Acorn organiser Dan Newcombe.A Places for People spokesperson said: “The challenges at Archway Heights are complex, multifaceted and will take time to resolve, causing understandable frustration for customers.“This work cannot begin until we receive approval from the building safety regulator, which has taken far longer than we anticipated.”They added that CCTV was “in place on the scaffold and is triggered by movement. It has been inspected and confirmed as operational, and an alarm system is currently being progressed”.A spokesperson for the BSR said: “This complex case was originally submitted to BSR in April 2024 and was invalidated. A subsequent application was made in January 2025 and has required several requests for further information and ongoing engagement with the applicant for them to be able to demonstrate compliance with building regulations.”Explore more on these topicsHousingCommunitiesLondonGrenfell Tower fireSocial housingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan | US immigration | The Guardian
description: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday
Content: The DHS headquarters in Washington.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe DHS headquarters in Washington.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS immigrationUS grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and SudanDHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on MondaySend us your questions about immigration and the midtermsAssociated PressMon 19 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 100,000 people fromUkraineand Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationUkraineSudanEuropeAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult | Kenya | The Guardian
description: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors
Content: Doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie during a court session of his murder trial judgment at the Mombasa law courts, Kenya on Monday.Photograph: EPAView image in fullscreenDoomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie during a court session of his murder trial judgment at the Mombasa law courts, Kenya on Monday.Photograph: EPAKenyaKenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adultPaul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutorsReutersMon 19 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.View image in fullscreenKenyan high court judge Diana Kavedza Mochache on 19 October.Photograph: EPAMackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.View image in fullscreenA Kenyan national youth service officer talks to a woman while on guard at the entrance to the Mombasa law courts on Monday 19 October.Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty ImagesThe case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.View image in fullscreenPaul Mackenzie and his co-accused during their court appearance on 19 October.Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty ImagesThe plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.Mackenzie facesother charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.Explore more on these topicsKenyaReligionAfricaChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan | Sudan | The Guardian
description: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war
Author: Carlos Mureithi
Headline: Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war
Content: A man stands in a hole filled with drone components in El Obeid, Sudan, in March. There has been an escalation in the use of drones in the war.Photograph: Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man stands in a hole filled with drone components in El Obeid, Sudan, in March. There has been an escalation in the use of drones in the war.Photograph: Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesSudanDrone attack near market kills 80 in SudanWitness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of warCarlos Mureithiand agenciesMon 19 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA drone strike near a market in southernSudanon Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led byMohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.The fighting in Sudan has killedhundreds of thousandsof people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN,warnedthe security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”AFP contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsSudanAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Ebola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key services | Ebola | The Guardian
description: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO
Author: Melody Schreiber
Headline: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO
Content: A nurse works at Nairobi hospital. A Kenyan man fell ill in DR Congo before returning to Nairobi, where he later died.Photograph: Monicah Mwangi/ReutersView image in fullscreenA nurse works at Nairobi hospital. A Kenyan man fell ill in DR Congo before returning to Nairobi, where he later died.Photograph: Monicah Mwangi/ReutersEbolaEbola cases in Kenya highlight US failures amid Trump cuts to key servicesOpposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHOMelody SchreiberMon 19 Oct 2026 10.11 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn eighth person inKenyahas tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region.It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worseningEbolaoutbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia airbase, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.In the meantime, Kenyans were “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with thedemolitionof the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US hasslashed programsacross the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response had also been “weakened”, he said.A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. Since then, seven close contacts have tested positive.Patrick Amoth, the director-general for health, confirmed on Sunday the total number of ‌infections in the country was eight.Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DR Congo and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.A French doctor who returned from DR Congo in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DR Congo to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DR Congo and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.Raphael Warnock, a Democratic senator from Georgia, and Bill Cassidy, a Republican senator from Louisiana, penned aletterin June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts was “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and had “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.Work such as HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests, the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”Explore more on these topicsEbolaTrump administrationUS politicsKenyaAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Trudy menaces Mexico’s Pacific coast and Greece hit by deadly floods | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Trudy weakens to tropical storm after warnings of strong winds and heavy rain, while one person killed in Greece
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Trudy weakens to tropical storm after warnings of strong winds and heavy rain, while one person killed in Greece
Content: Fishing boats on the sand after being pulled from the sea in preparation for the passage of Hurricane Trudy in Acapulco, Mexico.Photograph: Javier Verdin/ReutersView image in fullscreenFishing boats on the sand after being pulled from the sea in preparation for the passage of Hurricane Trudy in Acapulco, Mexico.Photograph: Javier Verdin/ReutersWeatherwatchMexicoHurricane Trudy menaces Mexico’s Pacific coast and Greece hit by deadly floodsTrudy weakens to tropical storm after warnings of strong winds and heavy rain, while one person killed in GreeceAlice Nightingale-Smith and Nick Lee for MetDeskMon 19 Oct 2026 06.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn contrast to the quiet Atlantic hurricane season, there has been ongoing activity in the Pacific, with Trudy being the 22nd and latest named system. Thecategory 2 hurricaneremained roughly 100 miles (160km) south-west of the coast of Mexico, meaning the worst of the conditions stayed offshore. However, the US National Hurricane Center put coastal parts of the states of Jalisco, Michoacán and Colima under hurricane warnings, with sustained winds of up to 60-90mph forecast on Sunday.Rainfall totals of 100-150mm were likely for these areas, prompting warnings of flooding and landslides. Warnings also covered the risk of a dangerous storm surge accompanied by damaging waves in areas of onshore winds across the coast of south-westernMexico. By Monday morning, Trudy had weakened and been downgraded to a tropical storm, with coastal warnings being lifted.InGreece, heavy rain and thunderstorms caused severe flooding and one fatality across Rhodes, Evia and the Sporades islands last week. According to the National Observatory of Athens, a station in Rhodes recorded 202mm between 3.30am and 9.50am (UTC) on 14 October. Regional authorities reported more than 30 rescue and extrication operations in response to flooding, while the Greek coastguard said four passenger vehicles were swept into the sea during the storm. On Skiathos, flood waters swept away two cars.View image in fullscreenCars swept into the sea on the Greek island of Rhodes.Photograph: Kyriakos Finas/ReutersFive deaths were reported due to severe flooding in Istanbul,Turkey, last week. Heavy rain on 14 and 15 October prompted school closures, flight delays, disruptive flooding and landslides across several provinces. According to the Istanbul metropolitan municipality, 242mm of rain was recorded in Beykoz, a district of Istanbul province. Nearly 600 people were rescued after becoming stranded and at least 2,700 people were forced to evacuate their homes.The Turkish state meteorological service issued further alerts for heavy rain and thunderstorms over the weekend across dozens of provinces, with at least an additional 40-60mm forecast for parts of the Marmara and western Black Sea regions.Explore more on these topicsMexicoWeatherwatchGreeceAmericasTurkeynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists | Canada | The Guardian
description: Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding independence vote
Author: Leyland Cecco
Headline: Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding independence vote
Content: ‘Canada Guy’ waves a Canadian flag during an Alberta independence rally at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton.Photograph: Amanda May Erickson/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreen‘Canada Guy’ waves a Canadian flag during an Alberta independence rally at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton.Photograph: Amanda May Erickson/The Canadian Press/APCanada‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatistsVoters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding independence voteLeyland Ceccoin CalgaryMon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 05.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlbertans are going to the polls to decide their place inCanada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself.On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second, binding independence referendum.A minority have long argued that separation is the only way to address their belief that Alberta is short-changed by its financial relationship with Ottawa, and prevented from fully exploiting the province’s vast fossil fuel reserves.Any enthusiasm either side might have held headed into the referendum was muted after a deadly fire broke out at a major military base in the province. On Saturday afternoon, ablaze tore through the CFB Wainwrightand into the nearby town. Canada’s armed forces announced with “profound sadness” that there had been multiple deaths and injuries.The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, argued for years that a referendum was not needed, but called one anyway after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.View image in fullscreenAlberta’s premier, Danielle Smith, called a referendum after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/APNevertheless, Smith did not campaign in favour of independence, saying in June she estimated the cost of separating at about C$400bn (£212bn) for the transition and another $25bn-$50bn in annual costs associated with starting a new country. Smith’s caution prompted some of her supporters to accuse her of betraying the independence movement.Opponents of independence have focused heavily on the costs of separation, with the University of Calgary’s school of public policy saying in June it could be up to $170bn over a five-year period and be highly unpredictable in the long term.The issue has not divided neatly along partisan lines. The former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley – from the rightwing Conservative and leftwing New Democratic party – have appeared on stage together, setting aside a bitter ideological rivalry that more usually defines Albertan politics.Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” the prime minister told a raucous crowd.Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, saw first-hand the effects of the Brexit vote and the economic upheaval that followed.“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said. “Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”View image in fullscreenMark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.Photograph: Megan Albu/AFP/Getty ImagesCarney, whom recent polls identify as the most popular politician in Alberta, joined the former deputy premier of Alberta Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for the latter’s Forever Canadian group. Lukaszuk has driven more than 40,000km (24,855 miles) around Alberta in a 1992 motorhome named the Unity Bus and distributed at least 100,000 lawn signs.Rather than campaigning frequently, Carney has pointed to big projects his government is looking to move ahead with that would benefit the province, including a pipeline to the Pacific coast to increase the flow of Alberta crude oil to Asia.“I won’t sugar-coat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” said Carney.Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa, stemming from the 1980 national energy programme, which sought greater federal control over the energy sector, provoked fierce opposition in Alberta and helped erode Liberal support across western Canada. The sense that the province’s wealth was being siphoned eastward is older still: a 1915 cartoon, “The Milch Cow”, depicted Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as farmers feeding a cow whose milk was funnelled into buckets labelled Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.“Growing up, I remember. I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” Carney told the crowd. “And more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”View image in fullscreenEnergy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa.Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/APThe movement seeking to capitalise on those grievances, however, has been marked by competing interests, personal rivalries and allegations surrounding some of its leading figures. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is alleged to have mismanaged millions of dollars of First Nations trust funds, while David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organiser, was at the centre of avoter-data scandalthat exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of the province’s modern separatist movement, recently publishedthe Alberta transition plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning it into an independent country.Rejecting comparisons to Brexit and the economic fallout, Wilson said: “Every single thing we found that needs to be addressed to do the transition is absolutely doable,” calling most of the tasks “super easy”.Wilson dismissed the idea that negotiations between an independent Alberta and Canada’s federal government would be acrimonious and lengthy.“It would be economic suicide for them to challenge Alberta,” he said. “You want to cut off trade with us? OK. By the way, go buy axes and chainsaws because you’re going to have to cut down all the maple trees to keep warm this winter because you’re not going to get our energy products.”Even within the separatist camp, there are doubts about how quickly independence could be achieved. Bill Jones, a member of the Wildrose Independence party, said its leaders were moving too quickly without the institutions a new country would need, from a police force to a pension system.View image in fullscreenAlberta flags flutter next to a banner calling for separation in rural Alberta.Photograph: Todd Korol/Reuters“We – Alberta – were always meant to be a colony, to get resources that were here to go east,” said Jones. “And that mindset is still there.”“I don’t see the evidence for our independence. If we go out today, we’d be a failed state for generations. The great-great-grandchildren would be still suffering. And that’s the problem.”Monday’s referendum will also include nine other measures unrelated to separation, including proposals affecting social programmes, judicial appointments and the senate.One remain campaign has distributed thousands of “no to the nine” lawn signs around the province. Even some separatists, angry at Smith, have started a “decline the 9” campaign. Smith, for her part, has pushed a “yes to the rest” message in response.In Calgary, the city’s mayor said he was “duty bound” to speak out about the perils of an attempt to fracture the country.“There will be catastrophic impacts that would arise from separation,” said Jeromy Farkas. “And the unfortunate bullshit implication of separation is that it’s invited a conversation about who is a ‘real Canadian’? Who is a ‘real Albertan’? If you are living here in Calgary, you are welcome here. We need to continue to signal that. We need to telegraph that stability.“We stand to lose so much from simply even having this debate.”In October, further details emerged about meetings between unelected Alberta separatists and both Republican operativesand staff at the US state department. Among itemsallegedly discussedwere how oil royalties could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country. They also allegedly offered up Alberta’s fresh water resources.No matter the results on Monday, the referendum could have looked far different if not for the intervention of First Nations, which successfully sued to force the Alberta government to either dismiss the question of separation or change the wording. Key to their argument was the fact that the land of modern-day Alberta is covered by five treaties signed with the crown before the creation of the province.View image in fullscreenProtesters highlight concerns about Indigenous treaty rights and the broader implications of Alberta’s separation.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe president of the Blackfoot Confederacy, Chief Troy “Bossman” Knowlton, said: “These treaties are living documents, but the ignorance of the separatists, and their bigotry, does not allow their mind to accept the fact that they’re not symbolic documents. They have power, and the reality is Alberta does not have the constitutional right to separate.”Knowlton said that if separatists had proactively reached out to First Nations before pushing ahead with independence, it might have led to a different outcome. “But they treated us as a speed bump they could just drive over.”He added that the First Nations’ legal victory was followed by what he viewed as recriminations from the province, including anunexplained haltto talks on land claims and cooperation with Alberta’s government.“At the end of the day, we want Alberta to continue to be a beacon of light,” he said. “Because when the first newcomers came to these lands centuries ago, that’s what our chiefs said: we’ll share these resources we have here. So do we want prosperity for Alberta? You’d better believe it.”Explore more on these topicsCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: China’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exports | Chinese economy | The Guardian
description: Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Third-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demand
Content: China’s economy has grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChina’s economy has grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year.Photograph: Peter Parks/AFP/Getty ImagesChinese economyChina’s economy grows faster than forecast after AI boom boosts exportsThird-quarter GDP up by 4.5% compared with last year as industrial output is buoyed by electronics demandJulia KolleweMon 19 Oct 2026 05.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 15.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.Explore more on these topicsChinese economyChinaEconomicsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Three deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivals | Japan | The Guardian
description: Deputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhere
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Deputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhere
Content: The Saijo festival in Saijo, western Japan. The events are held in thanks to Shinto deities for a plentiful harvest.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Saijo festival in Saijo, western Japan. The events are held in thanks to Shinto deities for a plentiful harvest.Photograph: The Asahi Shimbun/Getty ImagesJapanThree deaths from float crushes raise safety concerns over Japanese festivalsDeputy mayor of Saijo died after becoming trapped under float, days after two similar incidents elsewhereJustin McCurryin TokyoMon 19 Oct 2026 05.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is mounting concern over the safety of Japan’s traditional festivals after the death of a senior local official who was reportedly crushed beneath a float at the weekend, days after two men died in similar incidents in another part of the country.Akihiro Nabae, the deputy mayor of Saijo, in western Japan, was carrying a giant float with other participants in a festival on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure, Agence France-Presse reported. Nabae, 62, was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, local media said, adding that no one else was injured.He died less than two weeks after a 51-year-old man was crushed beneath a wooden float he was riding at one of the annual Danjiri festivals held in southern Osaka prefecture. The same day, a 48-year-old man was killed in a similar accident at a Danjiri event in a nearby town. Police said 16 people were injured in the incidents.View image in fullscreenParticipants push and pull a float during the Danjiri festival celebrations in Anan, Tokushima.Photograph: Keiichi Miyashita/AFLO/ShutterstockThe accidents occurred when the floats, which can weigh up to 4 tonnes, toppled as they were being pulled at speed around tight corners by hundreds of men, police said. The turns, known asyarimawashi, are a highlight of the festivals, originally held to pray for good autumn harvests.It is not clear if Nabae lost his balance or if the contraption toppled on to him, according to police in Saijo, where the festival has been held annually since the Edo period (1603-1868).Media reports said 11 floats, each weighing as much as 3 tonnes, were lined up side by side at the time of the accident.The annual Saijo festivals, featuring more than 100 floats, are held to thank Shinto deities for plentiful grain crops, the Jiji news agency said.View image in fullscreenThe floats weigh up to 4 tonnes each.Photograph: Keiichi Miyashita/AFLO/ShutterstockSaijo’s mayor, Mitsuyoshi Ochi, voiced shock and sadness at Nabae’s death. “Just when we were about to work together to build a new administration for Saijo, this tragedy occurred. I still can’t believe it. I offer my heartfelt condolences,” he said in a statement.In February, two people died in a crush at the “naked man festival” in Okayama, where as many as 10,000 men dressed infundoshiloincloths squeeze into the grounds of a temple and compete to seize a pair of sacred wooden sticks thrown into the crowd by the head priest. The two men who succeed are declared “lucky men” for the year.Explore more on these topicsJapanAsia PacificFestivalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees | Amelia Earhart | The Guardian
description: Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island
Content: Amelia Earhart in the cockpit of a plane in 1931. She and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished on 2 July 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveView image in fullscreenAmelia Earhart in the cockpit of a plane in 1931. She and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished on 2 July 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe.Photograph: Bettmann/Bettmann ArchiveAmelia EarhartAmelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of treesExpedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited islandOliver Holmesin BangkokMon 19 Oct 2026 00.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said anobject they suspected to be her planewas a clump of washed-up trees.“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.Is it a plane or a tree? Amelia Earhart expedition aims to solve mystery of disappearanceRead morePrevious visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.The latest mission stemmed from2020 satellite imagesshowing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.Map showing location of Nikumaroro IslandBy Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashedRead moreIt said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – wascaptured by Japaneseforces or that she survived and lived under an alias.Explore more on these topicsAmelia EarhartPacific islandsAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump borrows from far right to blame unrest in France on immigration | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President ignores school conditions and cost of living and says he warned Macron ‘the whole world was coming in’
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: President ignores school conditions and cost of living and says he warned Macron ‘the whole world was coming in’
Content: Trump speaks to reporters before leaving the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.Photograph: Michael Brochstein/Zuma/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenTrump speaks to reporters before leaving the White House for a campaign rally in Kansas.Photograph: Michael Brochstein/Zuma/ShutterstockDonald TrumpTrump borrows from far right to blame unrest in France on immigrationPresident ignores school conditions and cost of living and says he warned Macron ‘the whole world was coming in’Explainer: why are people protesting across Europe?Joseph Gedeonin WashingtonMon 19 Oct 2026 18.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump and JD Vance deployed a familiar US playbook on Europe, claiming that immigrants were responsible for rioting in France that began as student protests against crumbling schools and thehigh cost of living.The nationwide protests on Saturdaywere called overrising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they escalated into clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday,overnight curfews were issuedfor a number of French cities, including parts ofParis.“France is burning!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, blaming “the immigration of people from an entirely different world” for theviolence and looting.He urged Paris to “Close your Borders and take control”.Vance, a day earlier, argued that the unrest was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” hewroteon X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.The rhetoric echoes France’s far-rightNational Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.The demonstrations inFrancebegan weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.As Trump set off for a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets acrossEurope, in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.Neither have the US president and vice-president commented onprotests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.Earlier in the day, the official White House X account posted: “If you import the third world, you become the third world.” An array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument, seeking to leverage the unrest in France against Congressional Democrats ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which their party faces significant headwinds.House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” he concluded.David Smith contributed reporting from Park City, KansasExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS politicsTrump administrationFranceUS foreign policyEmmanuel MacronProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: French authorities announce partial curfews as PM blames ‘ultra-left’ for exploiting protests – as it happened | France | The Guardian
description: This live blog is now closed.
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: This live blog is now closed.
Content: 16.34 EDTThe day so farPartial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts ofParis, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.An overnight curfew will come into effect from 11pm until 6am local time, for Place ​de la Republique ⁠and the streets around ⁠Les Halles ​in Paris. Authorities earlier issued the country’s first curfew the northern city of Lille and surrounding cities of Douai, Wattignies and Denain. Curfews were also announced in the southern cities of Nice (specifically for minors) and central Lyon, while Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday.It came after France’s PM, Sébastien Lecornu, said after an emergency cabinet meeting that he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed.There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said. Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.France’s interior minister conceded thatpolice had “lost control” in some citiesduring Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.Laurent Nuñez said there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations. Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than half a million and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years. Almost 2,400 arrests have been made.Nuñez said he had offered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”, but the president had refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”. “You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.The original protests, led by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations inseveral other European countriesincluding Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.Share

title: ‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in decline | Cop17 biodiversity summit | The Guardian
description: As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps
Author: Ajit Niranjan
Headline: As Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps
Content: A bee pollinating a cherry tree in Athy, County Kildare. The study confirms that many pollinator species are losing populations.Photograph: Niall Carson/PAView image in fullscreenA bee pollinating a cherry tree in Athy, County Kildare. The study confirms that many pollinator species are losing populations.Photograph: Niall Carson/PACop17 biodiversity summit‘Crucial opportunity to act’ as study finds most of Europe’s wild bee species in declineAs Cop17 kicks off, records since 1921 show more bee species declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the AlpsAjit NiranjanEurope environment correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMost of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, astudyhas found, as a UN biodiversity summit begins in Armenia.Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts ofEuropeexcept the Alpine region. The richness of bee and hover fly species suffered a persistent drop in the Atlantic and Continental regions, the study found, though trends in other regions were mixed or even positive.The data, which covers 88% of bee and hover fly species across the continent, suggests pollinator communities have been reshaped by the “gradual loss of sensitive species and the rise of a resilient few”, according to the scientists. They warned of “deeper functional disruptions” if existing trends were not addressed.Nearly 90% of wild flowering plants, as well as more than three-quarters of major food crop types, depend in part on animal pollination. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization has warned the decline of pollinators sets off a chain reaction that threatens wildlife and weakens the ability of ecosystems to withstand climate change and environmental stress.Carlos Martínez-Núñez, an ecologist at the Spanish National Research Council and lead author of the study, said the findings showed that biodiversity loss could remain hidden behind apparently stable species numbers, “giving us a crucial opportunity to act before further declines occur”.“The fact that some species are increasing today does not mean they will remain winners as climate change and habitat loss intensify,” he added.The findings come as diplomats gather in Yerevan for the 17th UN conference on biodiversity. The summit, known asCop17, will focus on the conservation and sustainable use of the natural world, and the shared benefits of its genetic resources.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCan countries deliver on a deal to save the world’s plants and animals?Read moreThe study found 91% of the species logged over the last century had also been recorded at least once in the modern period, between 2001 and 2020. Although this suggests as many as 9% of species could have been wiped out in Europe, many of the species not spotted recently occur only rarely in the historical record, and the researchers said they “do not expect widespread extinctions to have occurred yet”.However, the species’ occupancy – the probability of being found at a given site – had mostly fallen.Ainhoa ​​Magrach, an environmental researcher at the Basque Centre for Climate Change (BC3), who was not involved in the study, said it “confirms what has long been suspected: many pollinator species are losing populations, and the decline is not affecting all of them equally”.“Until now, most of the evidence came from a few north-western European countries, such as the UK, Belgium and the Netherlands,” she said. “This work shows that the pattern extends across the continent, although some regional differences exist.”Cop17 at a glance: everything you need to know about the UN’s nature summitRead moreWildlife is dying out at an unprecedented rate as humans destroy habitats, spray pesticides, and warp the weather with planet-heating pollution. Despite far-reaching consequences for humanity, including threats to food systems and further breakdown of the climate, governmentshave not meta single UN target on nature since the biodiversity convention was created in Rio in 1992.The Cop17 summit is expected to focus on assessing progress toward this decade’s targets, which include protecting 30% of land and sea, reforming $500bn (£375bn) of environmentally damaging subsidies and restoring 30% of the planet’s degraded ecosystems.Explore more on these topicsCop17 biodiversity summitBeesEuropeArmeniaWildlifeInsectsAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris | France | The Guardian
description: Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public order
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public order
Content: 1:29'It's hell': residents reel after violent weekend riots across France – videoFranceFrance imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of ParisInterior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public orderJon Henleyin ParisMon 19 Oct 2026 14.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePartial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts ofParis, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said.His office later announced partial curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille.Police also imposed a curfew from 11pm on Monday until 6am on Tuesday in two areas in Paris: Place de la République, where rioting took place on Saturday; and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.A statement from police said the orders banned gatherings and demonstrations and prohibited anyone from entering or remaining in the two designated areas.10:46France protests escalate with riots, looting and 2,400 arrests - The LatestFrance’s second city, Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday. French unions, meanwhile, called for a new ⁠round of strikes and rallies on 5 November.Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.Lecornu’s comments came after France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president,Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”.
