Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.View image in fullscreenLaurent Nuñez, the interior minister, offered his resignation to Emmanuel Macron, which was declined.Photograph: Julien de Rosa/Pool AFP/APThe protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said.France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence,” he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.Darmanin said 2,513 people had been arrested and 67 imprisoned since the violence broke out over the weekend, Libération reported.Some 70% of those arrested were adults and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes have been injured.View image in fullscreenAn estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted across France during the rioting.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesMacron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.View image in fullscreenThe Louvre was unable to open as scheduled on Monday because of protesters blocking its entrance.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersOn Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestEmmanuel MacronParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks
Content: Photojournalist Heidi Levine speaks to journalists from a hospital bed in the West Bank’s Ramallah government hospital.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPhotojournalist Heidi Levine speaks to journalists from a hospital bed in the West Bank’s Ramallah government hospital.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockWest BankIsraeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlersMove comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacksEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemMon 19 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalistHeidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.The Israeli prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across theWest Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.Haaretzreportedon Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.It cited the response to anattack on a CNN crewin March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuJournalist safetyMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited | Yemen | The Guardian
description: More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
Content: People line up to refill gas bottles at a refilling station in Taiz on Monday. Fighting is under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the city.Photograph: Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople line up to refill gas bottles at a refilling station in Taiz on Monday. Fighting is under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the city.Photograph: Ahmad Al-Basha/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenHouthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignitedMore than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forcesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 19 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreThere will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.Map of YemenReliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify theHouthisas a foreign terrorist organisation.The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.A person walks past bodies on the groundBodies lie on the ground after the explosion at al-Alam camp in YemenThe killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.TheSaudi Aramco headquarters was strucklast weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after beingattacked this month.Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops toSaudi Arabiadespite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: People scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships | Strait of Hormuz | The Guardian
description: At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
Content: Screengrabs from a social media video show containers and debris floating in the sea after the GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman last week.Composite: ReutersView image in fullscreenScreengrabs from a social media video show containers and debris floating in the sea after the GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman last week.Composite: ReutersStrait of HormuzPeople scour strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container shipsAt least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goodsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 19 Oct 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo afterIranattacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.Therise in Iranian attacksappears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.View image in fullscreenA container from the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride floats alongside small motorboats after the ship sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October.Photograph: Social media/ReutersLast Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in theUnited Arab Emirates, sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast withOman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps(IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.View image in fullscreenA satellite image shows containers and items floating in the water after the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October.Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/ReutersDr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.View image in fullscreenVessels in the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.Photograph: ReutersOn Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.Explore more on these topicsStrait of HormuzIranOmanUnited Arab EmiratesUS-Israel war on IranMiddle East and north AfricaShipping industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in Gaza | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Two-thirds of population face crisis levels of food insecurity and 200,000 people are in danger of famine
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Two-thirds of population face crisis levels of food insecurity and 200,000 people are in danger of famine
Content: A community kitchen serves hot meals at a camp for displaced people.Photograph: Mohamed Hinnawi/WFPView image in fullscreenA community kitchen serves hot meals at a camp for displaced people.Photograph: Mohamed Hinnawi/WFPGazaCuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in GazaTwo-thirds of population face crisis levels of food insecurity and 200,000 people are in danger of famineEmma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andSeham Tanteshin GazaMon 19 Oct 2026 05.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 10.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis winter is likely to deepen hunger for Palestinians in Gaza, after sweeping aid cuts forced the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) to end support for more than half a million people each month, the agency’s director forPalestinesaid.More than a year after a Trump-brokered ceasefire came into force, promised reconstruction has not begun, there are few jobs and the vast majority inGazastill rely on aid to eat.This summer, WFP programmes helped feed three-quarters of Gaza’s population, about 1.6 million people, but funding has fallen by more than half from 2025 levels.View image in fullscreenPeople receiving aid at the Egyptian camp in central Gaza, where thousands of displaced families live in tents.Photograph: Jaber Badwan/WFPAs a result, from October, aid has been scaled back to 1.1 million people each month. Cuts to deliveries of ration boxes, cash stipends to buy food in markets, and hot meals at community kitchens have already been rolled out.The WFP needs more than £300m over the next six months to restore and maintain critical programmes in Palestine.A year of large aid shipments ended a famine declared in summer 2025 and reduced the most severe hunger, but without steps to rebuild Gaza’s economy, most families still rely on food handouts.View image in fullscreenHot meals from community kitchens have only been delivered every other day in October.Photograph: Mohamed Hinnawi/WFP“These are very fragile gains, easily reversed, and the situation is still brutal,” said Shaun Hughes, the WFP’s representative and country director for Palestine.Two-thirds of the population in Gaza face crisis levels of food insecurity, phase three under the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), which is used to assess if a population is approaching famine.Food insecurity is at emergency levels for 200,000 Palestinians, which means immediate humanitarian supplies are needed to prevent deaths from hunger, Hughes said. This is IPC phase four, one step away from famine conditions.Young children and their mothers are particularly vulnerable. After enduring years of food shortages, one in eight children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted, a recentUnicef surveyfound, and may have suffered permanent damage.View image in fullscreenOne in eight children in Gaza are chronically malnourished or stunted, a recent Unicef survey found.Photograph: Mohamed Hinnawi/WFPMost humanitarian organisations are struggling with funding after the Trump administration decimated USAID and other donor nations cut aid spending as they grapple with cost of living crises.The famine and war brought global attention to Gaza last year, ensuring funding. With a nominal ceasefire in place and the most extreme malnutrition curbed, the crisis there has slipped out of headlines and fatigue has set in among many donors.However aid will be needed at scale until Israel and the international community launch the large-scale reconstruction promised last year. There is no way for most people to feed their own families at present, because about 80% of Gaza’s population is unemployed, according to UN data.“We need to invest in recovery. This humanitarian operation isn’t affordable or sustainable in the long term,” Hughes said. “Ultimately that’s also what everyone in Gaza is telling us. They really don’t want to be reliant on these handouts, don’t want to stand in the hot meals queue every day. They want to have some chance of stability and recovery.”Gaza was self-sufficient in fruit and vegetables before the war, but the vast majority of farmland has been occupied by Israel’s military. The sophisticated greenhouse and irrigation systems that supported agricultural production have been destroyed.Fish has historically been a key source of protein in the territory, but the Israeli navy bars fishing boats from waters off the coast.View image in fullscreenAlaa Osama Sarhan, 40, originally from Tal al-Zaatar in Eastern JabaliaPhotograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianAlaa Sarhan, 40, lives with his wife and five children aged between four and 16 in a tent near the “yellow line” the marker of Israeli control. They have already noticed the impact of the WFP cuts.“In recent days, we have had to plan our meals around what is available rather than what we want to eat,” he said. A former paramedic, he was injured by Israeli attacks nearly two decades ago, and his disability benefits buy very little.“Often, I give up my share of food so my children can eat. I got accustomed to doing this because the most important thing is that they have something to eat.”For three years,Israeli restrictionson aid shipments have been the main driver of hunger and malnutrition in Gaza. For months at a time, entry of food was restricted or entirely barred as Palestinians went hungry inside the territory.Now, for the first time since October 2023, lack of funds may also become an obstacle to feeding hungry Palestinians. Israel’s controls on shipments into Gaza exacerbate funding shortfalls, because they make humanitarian work particularly expensive compared with other parts of the world.View image in fullscreenThe cost of delivering aid is pushed up by the limited and expensive warehouse space because of the mass destruction of buildings.Photograph: Mohamed Hinnawi/WFPLimits on fuel, engine oil and spare parts, and complex, opaque shipping restrictions push up transport time and costs. Mass destruction of buildings by airstrikes means warehouse space is limited and costly.Even an influx of cash might not allow the WFP to immediately reverse the cuts. Sourcing and shipping the ingredients for ration boxes can take about three months, and the reduction of cash transfers may already be affecting supply chains.The injection of more than £30m a month has “underpinned purchasing power for the private sector in Gaza”, Hughes said, allowing trucks to come in with relatively expensive shipments of both healthy and unhealthy food.For now, the WFP has tried to reduce the impact of funding cuts by scaling back these programmes rather than cutting them entirely. Families who get ration boxes will receive one, rather than two.View image in fullscreenThe WHP’s ration boxes and flour give families essential supplies to prepare meals and bake bread.Photograph: Jaber Badwan/WFPBut even limited reductions may push families with no other food source or income back into dangerous levels of malnutrition. For the poorest of the poor, reduced rations don’t work, Hughes said. “There’s only so far you can cut [support] until you don’t have the food security impact at the household level.”The WFP is trying to monitor hunger levels so they reach the most vulnerable, monitoring “negative coping strategies”. These include whether people have skipped meals, or are seeking exploitative and dangerous work.Nesreen Muqayed, 50, lives with her husband, four children and two grandchildren. She needs a regular diet to manage kidney problems, and a grandson who is on the autism spectrum cannot tolerate many foods.View image in fullscreenNesreen Muqayed, 50, originally from Tal al-Zaatar in northern Gaza, displaced at Al Amal seaside camp.Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianDespite these urgent medical needs, they often go hungry. “Sometimes we try to save part of a meal for breakfast because we do not know whether we will have anything to eat the following day,” Muqayed said. “The situation has become more difficult over the past two weeks.”View image in fullscreenMuqayed eating with her familyPhotograph: Amjed Tantesh/The GuardianThe hot meals from community kitchens that make up a large part of their diet have only been delivered every other day in October, and their meagre backup supplies are already running out.“I used the last of our flour yesterday,” she said. Beyond grappling with daily hunger, she also finds it painful denying her children healthy food they want and need for their development, because they cannot even afford bananas.“Sometimes I pass a fruit seller and look at what he has on display, but I do not have the money to buy,” she said. “Fruit and vegetables have become luxuries that we cannot afford regularly, even though they are basic necessities that every family should be able to access.”Explore more on these topicsGazaPalestineUnited NationsAidFamineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking fines | Motoring | The Guardian
description: Drivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Drivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session ends
Content: A new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday.Photograph: Ian Lamond/AlamyView image in fullscreenA new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday.Photograph: Ian Lamond/AlamyMotoringAndy Burnham outlines new rules to outlaw ‘rip-off’ private parking finesDrivers to get five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their session endsRupert JonesMon 19 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrivers will get a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park and 10 minutes to leave after their parking session ends before they face a fine under new rules for private car parks thatAndy Burnhamsaid were designed to outlaw “rip-off” charges.In the latest in a series of “everyday fixes” to ease the cost of living and give consumers a “fairer” deal, the prime minister said a new official code of practice for the industry meant motorists in England,Scotlandand Wales would enjoy a range of new rights.The consumer body Which? said the “long overdue” rules appeared to fall well short of what was needed to help drivers fight back against private parking “cowboys”, however.Each year in the UK, private firms dish out millions of parking tickets, and the number has been climbing. In August,the RAC saidthe number issued rose 17% in a year to reach a record 16.9m in 2025-26.Complaints about poor behaviour by some operators are rife, and campaigners say reform is years overdue. Legislation waspassed in early 2019, and an official code of practice was unveiled by the then governmentin early 2022– but lasted less than six months after legal challenges by several parking firms forced it to be withdrawn.In a fresh push, a new private parking code of practice is due to be laid in parliament on Tuesday, though it is unclear when this will take effect. Ministers said they would look to bring the code into force “as soon as possible”.New rights for drivers include “a guaranteed five minutes to decide whether to park, and 10 minutes to leave once their session ends”.The government is sticking with the existing industry maximum parking charge of £100 despite calls to halve it. Which? said: “It is particularly concerning that the government has shied away from a £50 price cap.” The consumer body had called for a maximum £50 fine, and this was also the amount at which some charges were capped under the withdrawn code.View image in fullscreenThe consumer body Which? had called for a maximum £50 fine.Photograph: jax10289/AlamyMeanwhile, fines will be scrapped on appeal for “honest mistakes”, such as stopping briefly to check directions, and for situations such as a medical emergency, vehicle breakdown or broken ticket machine.For “smaller slip-ups”, such as forgetting to display a parking permit or entering the wrong vehicle’s registration, the government said drivers would face a maximum charge of £20 on appeal. This appears to be a less generous system than under the original rules: the code that was withdrawn required the cancellation of a parking charge “in all mitigating circumstances”.Which? said the government had also shied away from an independent appeals body “that could rein in the industry’s worst practices” and had failed to take action on private parking debt recovery fees, which it said were regularly added without motorists’ knowledge and pushed unfair charges even higher.On the latter point, the government has promised to consult on these fees – which are added when a fine becomes overdue – “as soon as possible next year”. These fees are currently capped at £70, and the consultation will look at whether they should be cut or scrapped altogether.Burnham said: “Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn’t end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.“These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I’m putting a stop to them. We are introducing clearer rules, longer grace periods and lower charges for genuine mistakes.”Explore more on these topicsMotoringRoad transportConsumer affairsEnglandScotlandWalesUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control
Content: One option being considered is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines Thames Water owes into a government stake in the company.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOne option being considered is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines Thames Water owes into a government stake in the company.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Sopa Images/ShutterstockAndy BurnhamBurnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames WaterExclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public controlKiran Stacey,Pippa CrerarandJessica ElgotMon 19 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fixThames Waterand present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life”under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.Burnhampreviously saidhe would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies andcould rewritehow the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary,made clear her oppositionto such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for ThamesWaterbefore it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamEnvironment policyThames WaterWaterWater industryUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples | John Crace | The Guardian
description: While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it
Author: John Crace
Headline: While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it
Content: Matt Goodwin wanted Times Radio listeners to believe that Nigel Farage was actually a buffer against racism in Reform.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMatt Goodwin wanted Times Radio listeners to believe that Nigel Farage was actually a buffer against racism in Reform.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianThe politics sketchReform UKITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad applesJohn CraceWhile the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend itMon 19 Oct 2026 13.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTShareIt was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITVexposé of widespread racism and misogynywithin Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing fromNigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’sfailed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelectionwhose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is | Owen JonesRead moreOver in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. You’d have thought that Wes might have wanted to schmooze the chancellor before next week’s budget. To try to get the best funding settlement he could. Not a bit of it. Wes began by slagging off his predecessor as defence secretary for wasting money on unnecessary training exercises and then announced he was confident that Healey would reach the necessary 3% and 3.5% targets at next year’s spending review. So, no, Wes wouldn’t be resigning any time soon. Let’s hope his confidence is well placed.Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trumpswitching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims thatNato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. A nice ice breaker. After that, Pete went out of his way to say Washington was totally behind Ukraine, just so long as Russia won the war.Curiously, the shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, didn’t use his questions to talk up the four drones of the “Britannia shield” that the Tories were sure would protect the UK from nuclear war. So it remains a mystery. Almost as if it was a bullshit party conference announcement that was designed to be forgotten within days. Highlight of the day went to Sharron Davies, the former swimmer turned Tory peer, who demanded to know why Andy Burnham hadn’t invaded France to stop the rioting. Can you explain it to her?On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: North Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warns | Industrial action | The Guardian
description: More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies
Content: North Sea oil companies have cut investment in UK assets, blaming government energy policies and the tax regime.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyView image in fullscreenNorth Sea oil companies have cut investment in UK assets, blaming government energy policies and the tax regime.Photograph: Martin Langer/AlamyIndustrial actionNorth Sea strikes could severely disrupt UK fuel supplies, union warnsMore than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companiesJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorth Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.TheUniteunion said on ⁠Monday that more than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers would take part ⁠in a 24-hour ​strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decisionon the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.Explore more on these topicsIndustrial actionOilUniteTrade unionsEnergy industryOil and gas companiesFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Minister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’ | Miatta Fahnbulleh | The Guardian
description: In now-removed post, Miatta Fahnbulleh criticised home secretary’s proposal to extend qualifying period for settlement in UK
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: In now-removed post, Miatta Fahnbulleh criticised home secretary’s proposal to extend qualifying period for settlement in UK
Content: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, said the debate around immigration had become ‘increasingly depressing and toxic’.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMiatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, said the debate around immigration had become ‘increasingly depressing and toxic’.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesMiatta FahnbullehMinister says Mahmood’s migration policy will ‘prolong integration’In now-removed post, Miatta Fahnbulleh criticised home secretary’s proposal to extend qualifying period for settlement in UKJessica ElgotandKiran StaceyMon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe energy secretary,Miatta Fahnbulleh, appears to have criticised Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy in a post on her constituency website, in which she suggested she had concerns that a longer settlement process could affect integration.Fahnbulleh has since removed the critique, which appeared in a write-up of a community meeting in Peckham, her south London constituency, in September, saying it was not a true representation of her views.In the original write-up of her comments at the town hall meeting, first highlighted by the Telegraph, Fahnbulleh was reported to have said: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.” Her office said the remarks had been paraphrased, and would be rewritten to reflect a more accurate description of what she had told residents.The government has proposed increasing the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain from five years to 10, though it is likely to make concessions for some professions, including care workers.The changes will also mean the pathway to permanent settlement for refugees is extended to up to 20 years, with reviews every 30 months. The government is yet to publish its long-anticipated final response to a consultation on the proposals – though the prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said he is committed to the bulk of the changes.Tensions in the cabinet have already surfaced over the proposals. Last month the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said in an interview that the proposed changes – if left unamended – would unfairly penalise care staff who had “moved their lives here to look after our loved ones”.Fahnbulleh came to the UK as a child after fleeing the civil war in Liberia. Speaking to the Guardian’sPolitics Weekly podcast last month, she admitted her family would have found Mahmood’s changes “tough”.“I represent a constituency which is hugely diverse, where we’ve got first, second, third-generation immigrants, and how we navigate this landscape has been tough,”she added.With Mahmood believed to be considering changing her plans, Fahnbulleh said she wanted the government to recognise migrants’ contributions.“I think we ultimately need to get to an immigration system that has control … but actually then recognises the contribution that people have made. And if you’re in this country and you’re working – I say this as a refugee – and you’re doing your bit, and you’re part of your community, you’re working in our health service, then actually this should be a country that welcomes you,” she said.“I wouldn’t be here if that wasn’t the way that we structured our immigration system. It has always been the case that this country is a welcoming country, and I’m sure it will continue to be that way.”In her address to her Peckham constituents, Fahnbulleh said the debate had become “increasingly depressing and toxic”. She said there needed to be “a more compassionate immigration system. The asylum process is broken and needs reform. Ultimately, I want to see a system based on control and compassion, with a much stronger focus on integration.”She continued: “Peckham is a good example of what can happen when communities are built deliberately, and people are given the opportunity to integrate and participate. If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.“We need to raise the level of the debate, challenge divisive political rhetoric and make the case for communities like the one we have in Peckham. That means talking about immigration with care, control and compassion.”Explore more on these topicsMiatta FahnbullehImmigration and asylumShabana MahmoodnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds | Colorado | The Guardian
description: Elk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completion
Author: Dara Kerr
Headline: Elk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completion
Content: A wildlife overpass for elk, deer, and pronghorn on Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA wildlife overpass for elk, deer, and pronghorn on Interstate 25 between Denver and Colorado Springs.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesColoradoColorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report findsElk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completionDara KerrMon 19 Oct 2026 19.17 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 17.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger system built by the state to assist wildlife crossing the highway, which also includes miles of 8-ft tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses.“One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when [Colorado department of transportation] sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under [Interstate-25],” Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist for Colorado parks and wildlife,told CBS News. “All came to fruition in that one moment. That elk with her calf was just standing there in safety.”The Colorado department of transportation said before the overpass system wasbuilt, there was an average of one wildlife-vehicle crash a day in this corridor.Such wildlife crossings are popping up across the country as a way to protect wildlife habitat and reduce collisions, which can result in injuries and deaths in humans and animals. Research has shown thatoverpass systems are successfulin “nearly eliminating” these accidents and that such infrastructure buildouts often “pay for themselves” by preventing costly crashes.Tents, night-vision goggles and bear tracking kits: America’s first nature library opensRead moreNearly 20 wildlife crossings are under way in the US, with the structure in Colorado currently the biggest. The overpass, which sits between the state’s two biggest cities, Denver and Colorado Springs,spans six lanes of trafficand connects 39,000 acres of habitat on both sides of the interstate. The bridge is covered in grass and measures 200ft wide and 209ft long with gradually sloped entrances to ease crossings for animals.This region of Colorado is known for high movement of large game. State officials say that wildlife underpasses and tunnels often don’t work for big animals, such as bullelk, because they restrict mobility and don’t accommodate their antlers.“Elk and pronghorn like these big open structures where they can see for miles in each direction,” Chuck Attardo, the environmental manager for Colorado department of transportation, told CBS News. “For decades, pronghorn going from Trinidad to Greenland were looking for a place to cross on I-25. And when we open this up, we have pronghorn on video using the overpass, and for the first time in decades they’re coming over here to the west side.”While large game animals have been taking advantage of the crossing, officials have also tracked smaller wildlife using the corridor, including mule deer, coyotes, rabbits, frogs and the threatened Preble’s meadow jumping mouse.The project received $22m in federal funding and $8m from the state, but officials say they were able to complete it for just $15m. Now, the Colorado department of transportation says it is hoping to build other wildlife crossings across the state.Explore more on these topicsColoradoAnimalsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph
Content: The study is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations yet of how AI analysis of a selfie could help to assess a patient’s health and guide their medical care.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe study is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations yet of how AI analysis of a selfie could help to assess a patient’s health and guide their medical care.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggestsSystem can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photographAndrew GregoryHealth editorMon 19 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.Details of the breakthrough werepublished in the Lancet Digital Health journal.The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face,according to the resultsof a study that examined the model.Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”The results of the studysuggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”Researchers foundlifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HealthCancernewsShareReuse this content

title: California to receive $6m settlement after 23andMe data breach | California | The Guardian
description: Millions of customers’ genetic and personal information exposed in 2023, including more than 855,000 Californians
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Millions of customers’ genetic and personal information exposed in 2023, including more than 855,000 Californians
Content: 23andMe headquarters in Silicon Valley, California. The company filed for bankruptcy in March 2025.Photograph: JHVEPhoto/AlamyView image in fullscreen23andMe headquarters in Silicon Valley, California. The company filed for bankruptcy in March 2025.Photograph: JHVEPhoto/AlamyCaliforniaCalifornia to receive $6m settlement after 23andMe data breachMillions of customers’ genetic and personal information exposed in 2023, including more than 855,000 CaliforniansReutersMon 19 Oct 2026 17.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalifornia’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, on Monday announced the state will receive a $6m settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers’ ⁠genetic and other ⁠personal information.California had ​unsuccessfully tried to block the $305m sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a non-profit controlled by the 23andMe ⁠co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state had argued that the bankruptcy sale violated California’s Genetic InformationPrivacyAct, and it had said ⁠consumers did not give express consent to the sale.Once a trailblazer in DNA testing ​kits, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy in ‌March 2025, seeking to ‌sell its business at auction after a decline in demand and legal ‌fallout from the data breach.A US bankruptcy judge ruled against California’s objections to the sale, and later ruled that the state could not sue to recover money from the bankrupt company’s successor. California lost an appeal over the sale in federal district court, and it agreed to drop further appeals as ‌part of the $6m settlement, according to court documents filed on Monday.Customers of 23andMe retained the option to delete their data during ​the bankruptcy sale process, but California had argued that the court should have disallowed the transfer of any data unless 23andMe customers first gave express consent to the sale.“I am proud to fight for the privacy rights of Californians and to ⁠deliver this settlement for consumers who put their trust in 23andMe,” ​Bonta, a Democrat, ​said in a statement on ​Monday. “I want to remind Californians that customers of 23andMe ​can delete their private, ‌genetic data – no ​matter who owns ​it.”The data breach exposed the genetic information of more than 855,000 Californians, according to the attorney general’s office.23andMe agreed to pay $46.75m to victims of the 2023 data breach as part of its bankruptcy.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWest CoastPrivacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Oregon man who killed school shooter reportedly took part in military drills with Iraq veterans | Oregon | The Guardian
description: New details emerge about Kaylub Giamanco, who went on to elementary school campus and shot Bend suspect dead
Author: Auzzy Byrdsell
Headline: New details emerge about Kaylub Giamanco, who went on to elementary school campus and shot Bend suspect dead
Content: A memorial outside Silver Rail elementary school in Bend, Oregon.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenA memorial outside Silver Rail elementary school in Bend, Oregon.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersOregonOregon man who killed school shooter reportedly took part in military drills with Iraq veteransNew details emerge about Kaylub Giamanco, who went on to elementary school campus and shot Bend suspect deadAuzzy ByrdsellMon 19 Oct 2026 17.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew details are emerging about the parent who fatally shot the 16-year-old shooter who killed three children and a teacher inOregonlast week.Ina 2018 Facebookpost, Kaylub Giamanco, the 36-year-old carpenter who shot and killed the shooter, said he had gone through “military shooting drills” with veterans who fought in Iraq.In addition to the four people killed, the shooting in Bend left a seven-year old student in hospital, receiving “lifesaving care”, and 54-year-old teacher Becky Drury with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.The shooter, 16-year-old Griffin J John II, first opened fire outside the school with a shotgun, aiming at a driver who tried to confront him. He then shot through locked doors, forcing entry on to the elementary school campus.Giamanco, who has two daughters at the school, was driving back from his lunch break when he heard gunfire coming from the campus. He parked his car near the building, took a legally registered 40-caliber pistol from his vehicle and raced inside, according to Bend police.Before his arrival, a teacher threw a cellphone at the assailant and tackled him, and tried to wrestle the gun from his hands. Shortly after, Giamanco fired several close range shots at the shooter, killing him.In September 2018, Giamanco expressed that he had gone “shooting with a group of guys who served in combat together in Iraq”. It is not clear if this was part of a training exercise. Neither Bend police nor Giamanco and his family have made a connection between the shooting drills and the incident.After the shooting in Bend, Giamanco called his mother, Kenda Freeman to recount the incident, she told CNN affiliate KOVR in Sacramento, where Freeman lives.“He said, ‘Mom, I just shot and killed somebody.’ And I said, ‘Kaylub, tell me about it,’” Freeman said.He told his mother that he shot the assailant at point-blank range and killed him.“It’s tough because I’m, well, I’m thankful that my babies are OK,” Freeman told KOVR. “There are babies that are not. And that’s … that’s hard to swallow, because my heart goes out to those families. They didn’t get to bring their babies home.”Giamanco’s brother, Kyle Giamanco, told the New York Post he was not comfortable with being described as a hero.Explore more on these topicsOregonUS school shootingsWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: HelloFresh workers claim physical abuse and denied bathroom breaks in class-action suit | Business | The Guardian
description: The meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: The meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’
Content: The contents of a HelloFresh meal delivery kit as seen on 3 January 2018.Photograph: Kristoffer Tripplaar/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe contents of a HelloFresh meal delivery kit as seen on 3 January 2018.Photograph: Kristoffer Tripplaar/AlamyBusinessHelloFresh workers claim physical abuse and denied bathroom breaks in class-action suitThe meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’Michael SainatoMon 19 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorkers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark,New Jersey, have claimed in court documents that they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks, with one former worker telling the Guardian he experienced incontinence issues as a result.The newly proposed amended complaint comes in a class-action lawsuit first filed in August 2024 against the food prep service giant and staffing agencies. ANew Jerseystate court judge is expected to review the amended complaint in a hearing scheduled for 23 October.In the civil lawsuit, workers allege HelloFresh and temp staff managers took ID badges from temp workers that are required to be able to leave the facility, repeatedly threatened to call ICE and immigration authorities on workers, subjected workers to physical and verbal abuse, sexually harassed Hispanic female employees, and discriminated against the temp workforce that consisted primarily of Hispanic workers in violation of New Jersey’s anti-discrimination laws.A spokesperson for HelloFresh denied all allegations in the lawsuit.“Upon learning of these allegations, which date from 2023 and years prior, we conducted a thorough internal investigation and found these claims to be entirely without merit. We vehemently denied these allegations when this lawsuit was filed over two years ago, and we continue to vehemently deny them today,” the spokesperson said in an email.In a reply to the lawsuit filed by HelloFresh in April 2025, the subscription-based meal kit delivery service denied the allegations in the lawsuit.Action Staffing, On Target Staffing and ProStaff Workforce Solutions did not respond to multiple requests for comment but have moved to dismiss the lawsuit.The lawsuit alleges HelloFresh assigned its Hispanic workers “the hardest work”, and that supervisors consistently made racist, abusive remarks to workers and berated them for speaking Spanish rather than English.
