title: ‘Actions speak louder than words’: England’s white-ball captain Harry Brook relishes responsibility | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: Harry Brook is approaching an unwanted Wellington anniversary as England take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI series
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Harry Brook is approaching an unwanted Wellington anniversary as England take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI series
Content: Head coach Brendon McCullum chats to Harry Brook at the Rawalpindi cricket stadium before England play in the tri-nations series.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHead coach Brendon McCullum chats to Harry Brook at the Rawalpindi cricket stadium before England play in the tri-nations series.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesEngland cricket team‘Actions speak louder than words’: England’s white-ball captain Harry Brook relishes responsibilityBatter approaching unwanted Wellington anniversaryEngland take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI seriesPress AssociationMon 19 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Brook is embracing leadership and responsibility as he nears the one-year anniversary of his Wellington altercation, insisting he wants to be “the man England fans and the team rely on”.Brook has in the past admitted he could have been sacked as white-ball captain after being punched by a nightclub bouncer, hours before leading England in an ODI against New Zealand on Halloween last year.Brook and Jacks lead resurgent England into tri-series with World Cup in sightRead moreSince then, though, Brook has stabilised an ailing 50-over side, with England winning their last three series having lost seven of eight before then, while the T20 team sit top of the world rankings.With just under a year to go until the 50-over World Cup, Brook’s ODI average as skipper is 51.3 compared to 25.2 in the rank and file and he is adamant he has grown in the last 12 months.He said: “I’ve learnt a lot as a captain, I’ve learnt a lot as a person. I know it wasn’t an ideal situation to put myself in, but as a captain and a leader I’ve learnt a lot. Responsibilities and leadership aren’t just on the field, they’re more so off the field as well and actions speak louder than words.“I enjoy the extra responsibility. I like the extra little bit of added pressure. I’m not going to go out there and score runs every time I bat but I want to be the man that is in that match-winning situation who can get us over the line.“There have been a few innings where I haven’t managed to do that but hopefully I’ve turned that corner and I can really be the man England fans and the team rely on.”Brook’s Test average of 53.08 is the highest among any England batter to have played at least 20 matches in more than 50 years, but former captain Ben Stokes revealed recently he told the Yorkshireman it should be as high as 65 or 70.View image in fullscreenBen Stokes (left) believes Harry Brook should be averaging 65 or 70 in Test cricket.Photograph: Gareth Copley/Getty ImagesAsked what his initial reaction was, Brook replied with a laugh: “I mean 65 or 70 is a massive average, isn’t it, wow! Personally I’m not that bothered about the stats, I’ve always said I think there should be a match-winning column in your stats – that’s not there.“I write stuff down and I try and judge myself on whether I’ve had a match-winning performance or match-winning impact in that specific game and I try and tally it up at the end of the year and see how well I’ve done.”Brook’s immediate focus is on England’s tri-series against hosts Pakistan, whom they open their campaign against on Tuesday in Rawalpindi, and Sri Lanka, with every team playing each other twice and the top-two finishers contesting the final on Halloween.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRehan Ahmed was overlooked in favour of fellow leg-spinner Mason Crane, more than eight years after his last appearance for England.Brook said: “There’s certainly no line through Rehan’s name at all. Mason’s just performed exceptionally well and we think that he deserves an opportunity to be in and around the squads.”The injured Jos Buttler and rested Jofra Archer are also missing from England’s 16-strong contingent ahead of facing a Pakistan side who beat Sri Lanka on Sunday and are a much more of a force in ODIs than they showed in three abject losses to Joe Root’s Test side recently.Brook added: “It’s a great experience for us and with the potential of getting to a final, it gives us even more experience in those games where it’s do-or-die. It’s going to be one hell of a series.“In the last six to eight months and we’re certainly trending in the right direction as a squad. I think we’re really building towards the make-up of the side that we want.“Me and Baz [head coach Brendon McCullum] feel like we’ve got a squad where if someone does go down five minutes before the toss, we’re in a position where someone else can come in and fill that role perfectly well.”Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamHarry BrookPakistan cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL today: How to watch Commanders v 49ers, TV channels & live stream Monday 19 October | NFL | The Guardian
description: How will the Commanders and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will the Commanders and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: The 49ers are undefeated this season going into Monday’s game.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APView image in fullscreenThe 49ers are undefeated this season going into Monday’s game.Photograph: Lindsey Wasson/APNFL watching and streaming guideNFLNFL today: How to watch Commanders v 49ers, TV channels & live stream Monday 19 OctoberHow will the Commanders and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerMon 19 Oct 2026 16.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Commanders’ first task on Monday night against the 49ers will be to keep track of the clock. A week afterfrittering away a simple game-winning field goal opportunityin overtime against the Giants, Washington’s reward is a trip out west on Monday Night Footballto face one of the best teams in the NFL. The 1-3-1 Commanders entered the week with the second-worst point differential in the NFC at minus-34, and it’ll take a herculean road effort for them to avoid falling out of the mix in the mediocre East.The Niners, meanwhile, are on Easy Street. Their 5-0 start has afforded them a shocking degree of cushion in an NFC West that was expected to be the best division in football but so far looks like San Francisco and everyone else. The defending champion Seahawks and MVP Matthew Stafford’s Rams each dropped three games in the season’s first six weeks. Those included a pair of losses to Kyle Shanahan’s team, meaning the Niners have not just a huge advantage in the loss column but (for now) a head-to-head tiebreaker as well. San Fran could hardly have enjoyed a dreamier start.And yet! TheNFLhas a way of pulling everybody back toward the middle, so perhaps the world should be on alert for something shocking to happen when the Commanders arrive in Santa Clara.Commanders at 49ersDate:Monday 19 October 2026Time:8.15pm ET/1.15am BST (Tuesday 20 October)Stadium:Levi’s Stadium (Santa Clara, California)How to watchUnited States:Watch on ESPN or ABC, or stream on the ESPN appor Fubo(with ESPN or the local ABC affiliate).Canada:Watch on TSN1/3/4 or CTV2 (RDS2 in French), or stream on DAZNor Fubo Sports Pro.United Kingdom:Watch on Sky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream with NOW or NFL Game Pass on DAZN.What to watch forThe Commanders have lots of problems to confront this week, but one of them is new. The bright spot of their tough start has been a robust running game, which ranked fifth in the league in yardage (698) entering the week. The top man in that attack has been second-year tailback Jacory Croskey-Merritt, who carried 11 times for 82 yards in the team’s debacle of a tie against the Giants last week. But Croskey-Merritt is out this week with a groin injury, meaning a heavy running load will shift to QB Jayden Daniels and a veteran running back duo of Austin Ekeler and Rachaad White. Will the Commanders be able to keep up a 4.7-yard rushing average without their lead back?The 49ers don’t have “problems” these days. The absence of star edge rusher Nick Bosa would have been one, but the 49ers just sacked Sam Darnold five times without him, and Bosa is expected to return from his late-September calf strain for this game. Brock Purdy is playing the best football of his career, and somehow his offensive supporting cast of senior citizens – the very old Christian McCaffrey, George Kittle, Mike Evans, and Trent Williams – continues to be timelessly great. The defense has been more average than terrific, but you’d expect it to get better as it gets healthier. One subplot to watch will be how quickly Bosa gets back to looking like Bosa, assuming he makes his third start of the year.Explore more on these topicsNFLNFL watching and streaming guideSan Francisco 49ersWashington CommandersUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Airman who died in rappelling accident at Texas college football game identified | US military | The Guardian
description: US military says Tech Sgt Ian Patterson was killed after he fell from rafters at University of Texas at San Antonio game
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: US military says Tech Sgt Ian Patterson was killed after he fell from rafters at University of Texas at San Antonio game
Content: A Navy quarterback runs with the ball during the football game between the University of Texas at San Antonio Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen at the Alamodome in San Antonio, Texas, on Saturday.Photograph: Joe Nogalski/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA Navy quarterback runs with the ball during the football game between the University of Texas at San Antonio Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen at the Alamodome in San Antonio, Texas, on Saturday.Photograph: Joe Nogalski/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockUS militaryAirman who died in rappelling accident at Texas college football game identifiedUS military says Tech Sgt Ian Patterson was killed after he fell from rafters at University of Texas at San Antonio gameGuardian staff and agenciesMon 19 Oct 2026 08.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS militaryhas identified the air force service member who died after he fell from the rafters of the Alamodome during a rappelling demonstration before the University of Texas at San Antonio (UTSA)’s home game against Navy on Saturday.He was Tech Sgt Ian Patterson, a tactical air control party instructor assigned to the sixth combat training squadron, detachment two, at Joint BaseSan Antonio.Astatementissued on Sunday by the air force said Patterson – of Fort Stewart, Georgia – had served for 15 years. He had been the air force special warfare enlisted instructor of the year at the Headquarters Air Force level in 2022, according to the statement issued by Nevada’s Nellis air force base.Air Force officer killed in rappelling accident before UTSA’s game against NavyRead more“This tragedy is felt deeply,” said a statement attributed to US air force Brig Gen Scott C Mills, commander of the branch’s 57th wing. “Tech Sgt Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing, and to the family, friends, and teammates who had the privilege of knowing and serving alongside him.“Our team is now focused on standing beside Ian’s family, loved ones, and fellow [air force members] as we navigate this profound loss together.”An investigation was under way after Patterson’s death into what led up to his fall during a rappelling demonstration at UTSA’s annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game against Navy.A video of the fall that was posted on social media showed Patterson, in combat fatigues, quickly descending to the ground feet first. The fall occurred with fans in the stands and a band assembled nearby on the field.He was treated on the field for several minutes and taken away on a gurney.In a statement after the game, UTSA offered counseling service contacts for students and said: “We are deeply saddened by the incident that occurred at the start of tonight’s game. Our heartfelt thoughts and prayers are with the soldier who was affected, his family and his military colleagues.”Patterson was among four military service members who were scheduled to participate in the pregame rappelling demonstration.According to the air force, the service members who were participating in the rappelling demonstration were part of a team of specialists who embed with army and marine units and help to direct air and artillery strikes from forward ground locations.Part of their training includes learning to rapidly drop by rope, sometimes from helicopters that are 100ft (about 30 meters) or more above the ground.The game at the Alamodome in San Antonio was delayed for about 10 minutes. After UTSA won 38-34, the American Athletic Conference to which the school’s football team belongssaidit decided to continue with the game “to mitigate speculation about [Patterson’s] medical status” during the time his condition remained unknown.The conference’s statement said it wanted to avoid creating “additional distress” for Patterson’s family and guided itself out of respect for their privacy and adherence to the US military’s process for notifying members’ next of kin of casualties.After the game, the UTSA coach, Jeff Traylor, told reporters that the accident was “heartbreaking” and “tragic”.Traylor said the team could see the effect that it had on the crowd of more than 23,000 people as soon as players arrived on the field for the game, although the coach had only been told there had been an “incident” that would delay the start of the game.“You could tell the energy was just gone,” he said. “It just really puts things in perspective. It really does.”Beside his 2022 instructor of the year recognition, Patterson’s other achievements included earning the air and space commendation medal with three oak leaf clusters. He also earned the army commendation medal, air and space achievement medal and army achievement medal, each with one oak leaf cluster, the military said on Sunday.“Our relationship with local community partners is incredibly important to our airmen, especially during difficult times like these,” Mills said, using a term that the air force uses to refer to its members. “We are grateful to the San Antonio community and our mission partners at Joint Base San Antonio for the care, compassion and support they have shown.”The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsUS militaryUS sportsTexasSan AntonionewsShareReuse this content

title: Ben Simmons’ NBA comeback derailed after tearing achilles tendon in practice | NBA | The Guardian
description: Ben Simmons’ comeback attempt is over before the start of the NBA regular season after he suffered a devastating achilles tendon injury at practice
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ben Simmons’ comeback attempt is over before the start of the NBA regular season after he suffered a devastating achilles tendon injury at practice
Content: Sacramento Kings guard Ben Simmons will miss the start of the NBA season after an achilles injury put his comeback on hold.Photograph: Jed Jacobsohn/APView image in fullscreenSacramento Kings guard Ben Simmons will miss the start of the NBA season after an achilles injury put his comeback on hold.Photograph: Jed Jacobsohn/APNBABen Simmons’ NBA comeback derailed after tearing achilles tendon in practiceSacramento guard to undergo surgery and will miss entire seasonFormer No 1 draft pick has been attempting to revive his careerAustralian Associated PressSun 18 Oct 2026 20.33 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 23.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen Simmons faces a monumental task to revive hisNBAcareer after another devastating injury setback put his comeback attempt with the Sacramento Kings on hold. The Australian will undergo surgery after scans revealed he tore his right achilles tendon during a live drill at practice, just three days out from Sacramento’s season opener against the Los Angeles Clippers.The 30-year-old signed a one-year deal with the Kings in an attempt to revive his career, but will now miss the entire season. It is another massive setback for the three-time All-Star, after five years battling a series of significant injuries and mental health concerns.Michael Jordan Last Dance jersey bought for record $14m in private saleRead more“I’ve faced challenges before that tested me mentally, physically, and emotionally, and I’ve found a way through every single one of them,” Simmons posted in an Instagram story. “This injury is another chapter in my journey, not the end of my story.“It’s never easy being away from the game I love, especially after everything it took to get back here. But if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that adversity doesn’t define you. How you respond to it does. I’ve been knocked down before, and I’ve always found a way to get back up. This time will be no different.”Simmons had shown promising flashes in pre-season, including a productive 26 minutes in Sacramento’s loss to San Antonio. The build-up had led to high praise from a host of NBA greats, including eight-time All-Star Dwight Howard, who predicted a successful return for the Melbourne-born talent. “Ben Simmons going to have the greatest comeback story in NBA history!” Howard posted on X last week.NBA legends Dirk Nowitzki and Blake Griffin also recently backed three-time All-Star Simmons to reproduce some of his best basketball this season. “He is incredibly talented, he’s a big body and he can defend so many positions,” Griffin said at the NBA on Prime launch in New York. “Downhill he gets to the rim and he’s a great passer. I want to see a great year from him because he’s a special talent and I think the league is better off with a guy like him in it.”The latest injury setback continues a rough few years for the former No 1 draft pick, who was named Rookie of the Year and a three-time All-Star before his career went off the rails. Simmons shot to prominence with the Philadelphia 76ers but sat out the 2021-22 season while dealing with mental health concerns and physical injuries. He sought a trade and landed in Brooklyn, where he spent two-and-a-half injury-riddled seasons, and finished the 2024-25 season with the Los Angeles Clippers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSimmons was cut at the end of that campaign and sat out all of last season, leading critics to question whether he had lost his love for basketball. He rubbished those claims after inking his return with Sacramento and was set to play a key role for the rebuilding Kings alongside rookie Darius Acuff and fellow veteran Zach LaVine.Explore more on these topicsNBABasketballAustralia sportUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rays on verge of World Series return after Rasmussen dazzles in win over Guardians | MLB | The Guardian
description: The Tampa Bay Rays moved to within one win of a return to the World Series on Sunday after defeating the Cleveland Guardians 3-1
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Tampa Bay Rays moved to within one win of a return to the World Series on Sunday after defeating the Cleveland Guardians 3-1
Content: Richie Palacios and Chandler Simpson celebrate their team’s win over the Guardians.Photograph: Jason Miller/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRichie Palacios and Chandler Simpson celebrate their team’s win over the Guardians.Photograph: Jason Miller/Getty ImagesMLBRays on verge of World Series return after Rasmussen dazzles in win over GuardiansTampa Bay Rays 3-1 Cleveland GuardiansRays lead best of seven series 3-2Drew Rasmussen shines over seven inningsAssociated PressSun 18 Oct 2026 20.26 EDTLast modified on Sun 18 Oct 2026 23.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTampa Bay’s Jonny DeLuca figured it was going to be a quiet day for the outfielders with Drew Rasmussen on the mound for Game 5 of the AL Championship Series against theCleveland Guardians.With the way Rasmussen quieted the Guardians’ offense on Sunday, that made for a perfect evening.“It gets kind of boring out there because it’s incredible the stuff he has,” DeLuca said. “But you like that because he’s your teammate.”Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win in a 3-1 victory that gave the Rays a 3-2 lead in the best-of-seven series. He gave up four hits, walked one and struck out six.“The way he limited anything was really, really impressive,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “He got in rhythm with the fastball. A lot of power to everything. Then the depth on the changeup throughout the outing was a big pitch for him.”Tampa Bay have won the last two games and will try to capture their third AL pennant and first since 2020 on Monday at Tropicana Field in St Petersburg, Florida.Since the ALCS expanded to a best-of-seven format in 1985, road teams winning Game 5 to take a 3-2 lead have won the series four out of five times.“It’s a great opportunity. All of us are thinking of it. But it all ends tomorrow. We’re going to win tomorrow,” said designated hitter Yandy Díaz, who had three hits.Game 7, if needed, would be Tuesday. The World Series starts Friday at NL champions Milwaukee.Rasmussen had given up two runs over six innings in the opener. After Chase DeLauter’s two-out single in the first, the 31-year-old right-hander retired nine straight batters and allowed only one other baserunner through the sixth.Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA in three postseason starts, striking out 23 and walking three.He used his changeup only 12 times in the opener but threw it 27 times on Sunday, including 21 for strikes.“We were able to attack with the changeup a lot more tonight,” he said. “The ability to drive the cutter to the top I thought was also another strength.”Cleveland finally threatened in the seventh when Steven Kwan and José Ramírez singled to put runners at the corners, and DeLauter grounded an RBI single between first and second.Cam Booser and Tyler Wells worked the eighth, with Wells striking out Ramírez to strand a runner.Bryan Baker came in for the ninth and converted his 35th straight save chance, his fifth of this postseason. Jo Adell was on second base when Travis Bazzana hit a game-ending groundout.View image in fullscreenRays pitcher Bryan Baker celebrates after recording the final out of Sunday’s 3-1 win over the Guardians in Game 5 of the American League Championship Series in Cleveland.Photograph: Jason Miller/Getty ImagesTampa Bay scored single runs in each of the first three innings, the first two off Parker Messick and the third against Tim Herrin.Tampa Bay’s leadoff hitter reached base in the first four innings – scoring in the first three – and six times overall. Rays leadoff batters have reached in 10 of 14 innings dating to Saturday.Díaz scored on a bases-loaded walk by Messick to DeLuca in the first inning. Díaz led off with a line-drive double over center fielder Petey Halpin that bounced on the warning track and off the wall.Jonathan Aranda’s single drove in Ben Williamson for a 2-0 lead in the second, and Liam Hicks looped a curveball from Herrin to center to score Chandler Simpson in the third.“I think we took advantage of getting ourselves in some favorable counts and getting some big hits,” Cash said. “We probably left some opportunities out there, and then they go to the bullpen, and it’s really challenging to piece together big innings when they’re mixing and matching from the third or fourth inning, whatever it was, on.”Kwan had two of Cleveland’s five hits and the four-time Gold Glove winner made two fine defensive plays: he threw out Taylor Walls trying to score from second base on Aranda’s fourth-inning single to left and made a leaping catch at the center-field wall on Victor Mesa Jr’s eighth-inning drive, saving a run.Messick had the shortest outing of his major league career and didn’t make it past the third inning for the second time in four postseason starts. The 25-year-old left-hander went two innings and allowed two runs, five hits and three walks, throwing just 34 of 57 pitches for strikes.Cleveland have not won an ALCS when trailing 3-2, while the Rays are 58-27 at home this year, including the postseason.The Guardians are seeking their first World Series title since 1948.“We know we’ve got our work cut out for us. It’s a really good team and a really good team when they play at home, especially,” manager Stephen Vogt said. “We know this is going to be tough but if there’s a group I’m betting on to get this done, it’s our guys.”Explore more on these topicsMLBTampa Bay RaysCleveland GuardiansBaseballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’ | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listing
Content: Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAnthropicAI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listingLauren AlmeidaMon 19 Oct 2026 08.51 EDTFirst published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 06.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline.What are self-replicating ‘AI worms’, and why is Anthropic worried about them?Read moreThe fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said.The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours.“AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for aslowdownin breakneck development of AI, a warning laterechoed by rivals such as OpenAI.Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.View image in fullscreenElon Musk plans to ‘give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America’.Photograph: Gonzalo Fuentes/ReutersIt said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres.Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away.“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.”He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of mySpaceXshares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June.OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisationto the US government.Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)Technology sectorStock marketsIPOsElon MuskSpaceXnewsShareReuse this content

title: US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report finds | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Using test accounts, Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps with features to generate nonconsensual nude imagery
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Exclusive: Using test accounts, Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps with features to generate nonconsensual nude imagery
Content: Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGovernments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores.Photograph: Spencer Platt/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)US teens can access ‘nudify’ apps despite Apple and Google’s parental controls, report findsExclusive: Using test accounts acting as 13-year-olds, Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps with features to generate nonconsensual nude imageryJohana BhuiyanMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn December 2025, Morgan Dorfman received distressing news: a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school was making AI-generated pornographic material using the daughter’s image.He was using anartificial intelligenceimage-editing app called Movely to create sexual videos from pictures of her daughter and five other girls.What Dorfman’s daughter experienced is not an anomaly:studentsinhighschoolsacrossthe USare reporting similar cases. Their classmates are generating nonconsensual pornographic or nude imagery using so-called “nudify apps”.Governments around the world have moved to ban these AI platforms from app stores, and most US states have implemented laws that criminalize possession of AI-generated child sexual abuse material.However, in spite of regulations prohibiting them,nudification appsare still proliferating and remain accessible to teens,according to a reportfrom the digital advocacy groupTech Transparency Project(TTP) shared exclusively with the Guardian and released on Monday.AI prey: why watchdogs are telling parents to protect children from nudification appsRead moreTTP researchers created four test accounts, two Apple accounts and twoGoogleaccounts, indicating the account holders were 13 years old. They searched for image-editing or face-swapping apps using terms such as “AI video generator” or “adult AI”. Using these accounts for a purported 13-year-old, the researchers were able to download 135 apps with features enabling them to strip people of their clothes or swap their faces on to nude bodies. The researchers disrobed women in AI-generated images in their tests rather than using photographs of real women.At the time of her daughter’s distress, Dorfman didn’t know it was possible to create pornographic material of an everyday person so easily.“All the girls were very scared and confused about what to do next,” Dorfman said. “I knew what a deepfake was, but I thought it was like Taylor Swift and people using celebrities’ [images],” Dorfman said. “I didn’t know it was possible to take any picture or any screenshot of anybody that you have and do this.”Dorfman, a mother of four, spent weeks trying to figure out how the app worked and compiling material to educate other parents. She downloaded Movely and was immediately prompted to create suggestive videos using any image. The free version promoted sexually suggestive templates including “clothes explosion”, “brassiere unfasten” and “underwear drop”, according to a demonstration Dorfman put together for parents that the Guardian reviewed. In the paid version, it became more explicit: she saw templates for the types of pornographic situations in which, according a classmate, her daughter had appeared.BothAppleand Google prohibit these types of apps from being distributed on their platforms. The companies also will often age-gate apps with adult content, restricting or blocking minors’ access. However, TPP researchers found that the companies largely rely on the developers to determine whether their apps are appropriate for certain ages.“Many nudify apps identified in the investigation were inaccurately rated as suitable for minors – meaning the teen users could access them even when parental controls were activated,” the report said.Tool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremismRead moreResearchers found that one face-swapping app, which was advertised to them with an image of a woman performing oral sex, was rated appropriate for ages four and up. The free version of the app prompted users to superimpose real women’s faces on to templates of women in lingerie or, if users paid, in pornographic situations. The researchers were able to buy a subscription to the app from a 13-year-old’s account without an alert to a linked parental account.Google said the company regularly takes “proactive steps to detect and remove apps with harmful content”.“When violations are detected or reported to us, we investigate and take swift action, which in this case included suspending violating apps and restricting related search terms on our store,” a Google spokesperson, Dan Jackson, said in a statement.After TTP contacted Apple seeking comment on the findings of their study, Apple implemented changes that strengthened content moderation guidelines. Thecompany now requires developersto pre-emptively prevent and remove nonconsensual intimate imagery including AI-generated images. Apple also said that the company reviews every app before it is published and that if a developer misrepresents any features, the company removes the app and its developers. The company said in addition to apps they already removed before the TTP report was shared with them, the company has also “taken action” on the remaining apps mentioned in the report.“A number of the apps in this report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities,” said an Apple spokesperson, Adam Dema. “We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process – a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch.”Of the four accounts the researchers created, two were placed under parental controls that only allowed users to download apps marked suitable for 13-year-olds and only then with a parental signoff. However, the researchers found that neither Apple nor Google required or suggested parental signoff to acquire any of the nudification apps.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process’, an Apple spokesperson said.Photograph: Lee Hudson/AlamyOne app, Image to Video Maker-Vidou AI, was rated appropriate for users aged nine and older. Upon opening the app, users were greeted by an image of a topless woman on a bus, according to the TTP study.“The app had a feature that promised to digitally undress any person – and to demonstrate, it showed nude images of female celebrities,” the report read.Age restrictions were also not entirely effective, the study found. In one case, when the researchers tried to download an adult-rated app from the Apple App Store, they came across a pop-up warning that the app contained “age-restricted material”. But all they had to do was confirm they were 17 or older, which Apple allowed the account to do despite its registered age being 13. The Google account without parental controls was blocked three times from downloading an age-restricted app but otherwise allowed the researchers to download nudification apps that were self-reported to be age-appropriate.The Apple account that TTP set up parental controls for was still able to find and download 24 so-called “nudify” apps because they were all rated as appropriate for 13-year-olds. The Google account with parental controls was able to download 51 of these apps.‘I’ve become significantly more cautious’: six parents on limiting their kids’ social media and AI useRead moreRemoving image and video editing platforms from app stores was also not enough to prevent its use. In the course of TTP’s research, Apple took down 25 of the nudify apps, and Google took down six. However, the researchers were able to continue using the app since they had already downloaded it.Dorfman had a similar experience with Movely, she said. While preparing a presentation for parents and law enforcement officials, she returned to the app and App Store to take screenshots when she realized it was no longer available to download. However, the app was already on her phone and it remained entirely functional. She was also still being charged for her paid subscription.Once these nonconsensual images and videos are created, accountability proves evasive, Dorfman has found. “I just wanted someone to make him delete all of these videos,” she said.In her daughter’s case, Dorfman feels her school has downplayed what happened. In a school-wide email the Guardian reviewed, the principal wrote that her daughter’s classmate did use the app to animate images of other students but that there was no evidence he had done anything inappropriate.However, days later, Radnor policecriminally charged himwith harassment.“The whole thing was dismissed as ‘it’s not real,’” Dorfman said. “The haunting trauma as a mom is that I can’t tell [my daughter] those videos are gone or who had them. We can’t search everyone’s phones, and he deleted the app.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingChildrenAppleGoogleAppsChildren's technewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshoots | Social media | The Guardian
description: Backlash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bans
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Backlash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bans
Content: Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc, in Antibes on the Côte d'Azur, no longer allows photoshoots without prior permission.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/PRView image in fullscreenHotel du Cap-Eden-Roc, in Antibes on the Côte d'Azur, no longer allows photoshoots without prior permission.Photograph: imageBROKER.com/PRSocial media‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshootsBacklash against content creators includes restricted hours for filming and even outright bansLauren CochraneMon 19 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStand in any vaguely photogenic spot these days on holiday and the chances are you will come across people posing with raised phones and even ring lights. Some may be influencers with huge audiences on social media, others just overkeenInstagramusers. With hotels and beauty spots now so overrun, however, bans on photography are coming into place.The five-star Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, known for its glamorous clientele, views of the Côte d’Azur and a stunning infinity pool, has brought in rules against photoshoots: no longer allowed without prior permission.According toreports, this has been prompted by people booking lunch reservations and bringing bags of clothing and jewellery. Instead of sitting down to eat, they have used their time at the hotel for photoshoots of themselves in different outfits, creating images to post to their social media accounts.View image in fullscreenThe Hollies farm shop in Cheshire has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.Photograph: chasephoto/AlamyLess glamorous spots are also clamping down. The Hollies, a Cheshire farm shop which has become a popular content stop thanks to the Love Island star Molly-Mae Hague posting images from there, has banned photography and filming between 10am and 4pm.Meanwhile Jeremy King, the London restaurateur behind places such asSimpson’s in the Strandandthe Park, wrotean articlein the Evening Standard earlier this year titled: “I’m fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant – enough is enough.”In the US, a shop on Nantucket, an island off Cape Cod, Massachusetts, went viral earlier this year for a sign reading “no influencers”, while the town of Pomfret in Vermont has banned influencers taking pictures in front of foliage in autumn. In Fujikawaguchiko inJapan, a screen has been put up near a convenience store to stop people taking pictures there in front of Mount Fuji.Part of the argument from venues is that these photoshoots jeopardise privacy and discretion, especially as expected at expensive hotels. Hotel du Cap-Eden-Roc’s manager, Sophie Volant, toldTravel Weekly: “As much as [guests] appreciate having people in the restaurants and in the bars, they also want their summer home to remain private. We had to think about a solution.”View image in fullscreenSimpson’s in the Strand: Jeremy King, whoreopened this London institution earlier this year, said he was ‘fed up with influencers over-running my restaurant’.Photograph: Amy Heycock/The GuardianAnna Fedou, the chief marketing officer at the Beaumier hotel group, says it sometimes works with influencers to capture content to promote its luxury hotels, which include Les Roches Rouges near Marseille, loved for its photogenic pool. The group does not have specific rules around photography, Fedou says, but stays mindful of its primary purpose.“We’re in the business of hospitality, not running photo studios,” she says. “People travel from all over the world to experience the atmosphere, sense of space and feeling that make a hotel unique. It’s our responsibility to protect that.”Rules around photography at hotels and restaurants mirror a trend away from capturing the moment and towards being in it. Alex Goat, the founder of the youth culture agency Livity, compares these rules to clubs asking visitors to put stickers over their phones’ cameras. “They want to signify that they’re here for people who love music. There’s something potentially similar [here],” she says. “It’s ‘I’m here because I want to enjoy the space’ rather than ‘I’m here to document something to other people’.”View image in fullscreenSleepy Hollow Farm in Pomfret, Vermont. The town of Pomfret has banned influencers taking pictures in front of autumn foliage.Photograph: Michael McCormack/AlamyPart of the disapproval towards influencers is a common misconception is that they are paid well for such content. Sometimes, as with Beaumier hotels, influencers will produce posts in exchange for a free room, but the idea is that brands will want to make deals with influencers due to their association with glamorous locations. “The majority are creating most of their content for their audiences for free,” explains Nicole Ocran, an influencer who set upthe Creator Unionto represent those in the industry. “They create content in the hope of courting brands and seeing who will bite.”There has been previous outrage around influencers’ behaviour, asin 2021when Love Island stars travelled to Dubai during lockdown, for example. And if there is an underlying snobbery to a luxury hotel instigating anti-photoshoot policies, there may be sexism, too. “Influencer culture has always been vilified in popular culture,” says Sophie Bishop, the author ofInfluencer Creep. “It’s a very feminised form of media, that’s bound up in promotional culture.”Ocran agrees. “Most people have a particular stereotype in mind,” she says. “That isn’t to say that influencers and content creators can’t overstep or be insufferable when getting their shots and filming in public.”View image in fullscreenA screen was erected to block the view of Mount Fuji from outside the Fujikawaguchiko Lawsons convenience store after tourists crowded the area to take photographs.Photograph: Franck Robichon/EPAFedou believes that the key is to walk a balance that engages with social media content while keeping a restful experience at hotels. “Influencers will generally choose quieter moments for shooting content, to capture the space without disturbing others,” she says. “Les Roches Rouges has a relaxed atmosphere, but guest experience always comes first.”While the backlash might be aimed at influencers with lots of followers,over 5.4 billion people use social media every day.Ocran hopes that rules around photography might promote a more balanced attitude to social media in general. “[It’s] pushing back against the idea that not every space is meant for public consumption, and not every experience should be turned into content,” she says. “And as a creator, that’s quite a healthy message to send to us all.”Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaHospitality industryOvertourismInstagramFranceLondonJapannewsShareReuse this content

title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph
Content: The study is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations yet of how AI analysis of a selfie could help to assess a patient’s health and guide their medical care.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe study is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations yet of how AI analysis of a selfie could help to assess a patient’s health and guide their medical care.Photograph: Addictive Stock Creatives/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggestsSystem can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photographAndrew GregoryHealth editorMon 19 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.Details of the breakthrough werepublished in the Lancet Digital Health journal.The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face,according to the resultsof a study that examined the model.Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”The results of the studysuggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”Researchers foundlifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)HealthCancernewsShareReuse this content

title: Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff | Technology | The Guardian
description: Monitoring tools common in a range of workplaces, including factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being informed
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Monitoring tools common in a range of workplaces, including factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being informed
Content: Employees are increasingly being surveilled through CCTV, tracking instant messaging and monitoring card swipes and keystrokes.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEmployees are increasingly being surveilled through CCTV, tracking instant messaging and monitoring card swipes and keystrokes.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTechnologyCalls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staffMonitoring tools common in a range of workplaces, including factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being informedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterMon 19 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 15.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmployers are increasingly using technology, from CCTV to keystroke monitoring, to track workers’ moves and it is being accelerated by the use of AI, the Human Technology Institute has warned.Examples provided to Guardian Australia by the institute include a fast-food restaurant using surveillance cameras to stop workers using their phones, and AI tracking leading to a cashier warned over making a mistake once every 533 scans.In a report released on Tuesday, the University of Technology Sydney institute said workplace monitoring tools were increasingly common in a range of workplaces, including in factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being aware of the monitoring.Tools include CCTV, monitoring card swipes, keystroke monitoring and tracking workplace instant messaging.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe report highlightedMicrosoftTeams as a common platform for workplace surveillance. The company earlier this year rolled out a tool that updates a worker’s location automatically to reflect they are in the office when they connect to workplace wifi.Researchers at the institute were told during consultations that at one unnamed large fast-food chain, young employees were concerned their employer had put cameras in the change rooms to ensure staff were not on their phones at work. The researchers reported young people did not use the change rooms as a result.This man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacyRead moreThe Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association wrote in its submission to the joint parliamentary inquiry on artificial intelligence that a cashier at one big supermarket received a final written warning because the AI monitoring system had flagged her making too many errors.The error rate was reported to be 0.18%, or roughly one error per 533 items scanned.The Human Technology Institute has called on the federal government to build privacy protections into workplace laws, givenexemptions in the Privacy Actrelated to employee records, as well as small business exemptions, have allowed workplace surveillance to grow.A March 2026 Minderoo-commissioned poll found 43% of Australians were aware some employers use technology including AI to monitor workers, but only 9% were aware monitoring was used in their own workplace.Human Technology Institute co-director Prof Edward Santow said transparency over workplace surveillance was “necessary but far from sufficient”, and said the Fair Work Act should be overhauled to include a test for whether the introduction of workplace monitoring was appropriate.“Make really clear that if you are going to be … monitoring [workers], it has to be fair and reasonable,” he said.The minister should also be given powers to proscribe certain surveillance products that pose an “unacceptable risk” to workers’ rights, the report stated, pointing to recent federal government concern aboutthe rise in the use of smartglasses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Such concern is likely to be particularly strong in a workplace context, as smart glasses could be used to covertly surveil workers,” the report stated.It would require employers to engage with their employees on the workplace surveillance they intend to use and improve the quality of the consent obtained from employees, the report stated.The proposed change to the law would allow employees to make privacy-related complaints to the Fair Work Commission via a dedicated complaints scheme.The Human Technology Institute will present its findings to the joint standing committee on artificial intelligence on Tuesday, as the third week of hearings begins.The committee will focus on AI in the workplace, with several unions to appear this week. The eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, will also appear before the committee this week, as well as representatives from the CSIRO, Australian Securities and Investments Commission, the Australian Medical Association, and tech company Atlassian.Committee member Labor senator Tony Sheldon said that workplace surveillance was becoming increasingly common and was a serious concern for employees.“This report raises critical concerns about the impact of workplace surveillance on the privacy, health and dignity of working Australians, particularly when many employees don’t even know they’re being monitored.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologySurveillanceAI (artificial intelligence)Workers' rightsMicrosoftPrivacynewsShareReuse this content

title: Kylie Minogue songs already used to train AI as tech firms ‘strong-arm’ Australian government, music body warns | Australian music | The Guardian
description: Of the dozens of countries approached to water down their laws, Australia appears to be the only one considering it, publishers’ group says
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Of the dozens of countries approached to water down their laws, Australia appears to be the only one considering it, publishers’ group says
Content: Nick Cave and Kylie Minogue making a video for their duet, Where the Wild Roses Grow, in 1995. They are among Australian artists whose music has been used to train AI.Photograph: Dave Tonge/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNick Cave and Kylie Minogue making a video for their duet, Where the Wild Roses Grow, in 1995. They are among Australian artists whose music has been used to train AI.Photograph: Dave Tonge/Getty ImagesAustralian musicKylie Minogue songs already used to train AI as tech firms ‘strong-arm’ Australian government, music body warnsOf the dozens of countries approached to water down their laws, Australia appears to be the only one considering it, publishers’ group saysGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorTechnology reporterSun 18 Oct 2026 20.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI has already been trained on the works of Australian artists includingKylie Minogueand Nick Cave without compensation, the peak global body for music rights has claimed, as the Australian government has been warned against giving in to “strong-arming” from tech companies seeking to weaken copyright law.The International Confederation of Music Publishers (ICMP) – which represents Sony, Warner and Universal as well as thousands of independent publishers on six continents – has warned that of the dozens of countries approached to water down copyright laws, Australia appears to be the only to consider doing so.John Phelan, the ICMP’s managing director, told Guardian Australia AI companies were asking policymakers to “legitimise larceny”.David Pocock concerned senior Albanese adviser ‘vetted’ bipartisan AI letter that was sent to PMRead more“They’re trying to strong-arm Australian policymakers into ‘if you don’t do this, we won’t invest’.”In July,Anthony Albanese said it would be “theft”if artists did not retain control over whether their work was used to build and train AI, and what they were paid for its use.Music, film, media and news organisations had expressed concerns the government was being lobbied by global tech companies behind closed doors to weaken Australia’s copyright laws to help train AI models, without compensating the creative sectors.But government and opposition members of a parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence appeared to revisit the issue this week, describing the current situation as a stalemate.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThey said AI models were already training on copyrighted works in the United States without compensating creators – but that without changes to local copyright laws, those companies were withholding training frontier AI models in Australia.In a joint letter to the prime minister this week, the inquiry’s Labor chair, Jo Briskey, and its deputy chair, Liberal senator Jonathon Duniam, recommended the government “examine current copyright settings” while ensuring creators retain control and are paid.The independent senator David Pocockhas raised concernsthat the committee was coming to a position on copyright predetermined by the prime minister, after staffer edits were seen in the letter. Briskey has rejected the claim.AI companies’ demandsThe ICMP has been tracking how AI companies are attempting to change copyright law in different jurisdictions to allow training. Phelan highlightedmethods that the companies had usedto train their models on music, such as with spreadsheets containing millions of lines of music available on YouTube.A key claim of the AI industry is that its models are not trained on Australian content due to copyright rules. However, in evidence provided exclusively to Guardian Australia, ICMP showed Google’s Gemini was able to reproduce lyrics from Australian artists including Kylie Minogue, G-Flip andNick Cave.Phelan also pointed to anAI training dataset reported by the Atlantic in June, which contains more than 12m songs pulled from YouTube videos, including tracks from Minogue, Cave and Hilltop Hoods.Google was approached for comment.Phelan said 62 countries had considered making their own legal changes but none of the others had bought into AI companies’ demands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“There isn’t a single country among the other 61 [countries] … which has introduced a new text and data mining exception for commercial purposes, or reduce the idea of exclusive rights and copyright,” Phelan said.“The world is very much watching what Australia does.”“It’s fair to say the global music industry, as well as all creative industries worldwide we work with, are appalled by the idea of a statutory scheme or a government deal which would interfere with how Australian industries work and contract around the world.”Anthropic’s special envoy, Jeffrey Bleich, told the AIcommittee last week the company was not trying to dictate terms, but had shared information with the Australian government about training and what the implications would be “with respect to our capacity to operate here”.“You can’t license the entire internet. Billions and billions of information exists there which is available to be viewed and studied, and that’s essentially what training is,” he said.“Under existingAustralian law, it’s our understanding that that could be determined to be illegal if we weren’t able to find a licence with every single person who had rights within Australia.”OpenAI’s chief of economic policy, Adam Cohen, said the fair use exception in US law “fundamentally protects” the development of new technology. He pointed to agreements made with News Corp and the Guardian as examples of where the company makes deals for the use of work, despite arguing US law did not require such.Phelan said he believed panic had set in among the AI companies over the sheer cost of investment and the need to make a return, coupled with the ongoing litigation over copyright in the US. He said they may be looking to Australia for a legislative solution.“They’re seeing the legislative side as being the way to try to [find] a place to do business without licences, which will secure their future business model.”In a submission to the inquiry, Guardian Australia said that undermining copyright protection would have a “profound impact on civil society” and copyright-protected material should only be available for AI training with the rights holder’s explicit prior authorisation.Explore more on these topicsAustralian musicAI (artificial intelligence)Australian politicsAustralian lawKylie MinogueNick CavenewsShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life | Life and style | The Guardian
description: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning
Content: Life through a lens … Georgina McNamara in her Instagram days in Cambridge, 2023.Photograph: Georgina McNamaraView image in fullscreenLife through a lens … Georgina McNamara in her Instagram days in Cambridge, 2023.Photograph: Georgina McNamaraThe one change that workedLife and styleThe one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private lifeI’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaningGeorgina McNamaraMon 19 Oct 2026 01.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIfirst downloadedInstagramwhen I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed.As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all.View image in fullscreenMcNamara pre-epiphany at Sigiriya, Sri Lanka.Photograph: Georgina McNamaraIt wasn’t until a trip to Sri Lanka last year that I realised how far my obsession had gone. My partner and I spent two weeks travelling through Negombo and Kandy, having dinner in front of the Indian Ocean and visiting ancient heritage sites that I will probably never see again.This would have been memorable even without a third guest: my inner Instagram monologue. It commented on everything I saw in those two weeks, debating the merits of each photo I took and the possible captions (or music, or filters) that could accompany it. On one of our last days, we hiked up Sigiriya, an incredible rock fortress that has been inhabited since prehistoric times and is one of the most remarkable places I have ever seen.My first thought upon reaching the top? Thishasto go on my story. Already, I was imagining how it would look on Instagram. I dutifully made several posts upon my return to London, which were accompanied by hours of anxious scrolling and reloading, wondering why more people weren’t liking or commenting on my feed. Did they think I was annoying? Boring? Ugly? Had I been ungenerous with my own likes and comments, causing my followers (a grand total of 400) to band together to punish me? Should I delete the post? Redo it?Within two days, I couldn’t take my own thoughts any more. I decided to delete Instagram from my phone for a month, reset my habits, and then return with a hopefully healthier mindset.Yet in its absence, certain realisations became unavoidable. I came to see how much of my photo-taking was driven by wanting to appeal to an invisible audience, most of whom I hadn’t spoken to in years. In that first month, I started to take photos for myself and my own memories instead. It made me feel like my experiences could belong to me again.double quotation markWithin two days, I couldn’t take my own thoughts any more. I decided to delete Instagram from my phone for a monthOne month turned into three, then six – next month, it will have been a year since I took that first step. In my Instagram days, I expended a great deal of energy comparing the most normal parts of my life to the seemingly wonderful lives of others. Without the app, I was able to direct this energy into other parts of my life. That’s not to say I became productive every minute of every day. I didn’t. But the background noise decreased substantially. I read more, finished writing my first novel and started another.It has been liberating to live my life privately again. You may laugh, because I’m hardly a public figure, but I discovered how joyful it can be to reconnect with your anonymity and do activities knowing that it’s no one’s business whether you liked them or not.Now, moments matter because I’m enjoying them, or sharing them with someone I care about – not because they have been liked and validated by a hundred other people. I remain fully present for each of them, without disappearing halfway through into an Instagram rabbit hole. My life feels smaller in some ways, but also much more like my own. Whether the Insta-verse has noticed my absence, I couldn’t say. Do I care? Thankfully, not any more.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong
Content: ‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APView image in fullscreen‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’Photograph: José Luis Magaña/APOpinionTrump administrationThe Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain awayEditorialRussia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strongMon 19 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTShareDoes Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history ofchummyphone calls, high-profilemeetingsand attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees tonegotiateUkraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales arefallingfrom European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be abetrayal. European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.View image in fullscreenVladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.Photograph: China Pool/GettyTheWall Street Journallaid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite mostanalystssaying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. MoreRepublicansshould find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from theWhite House. Heated denials from the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, are no substitute for answers.A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “strategically and culturally vital”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments mustprepareto meet that challenge.History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo theThree Emperors’ Leaguethat brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in1881, the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Saudi Arabia is learning the hard way: they can’t count on Trump for protection | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: After Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for help
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: After Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for help
Content: ‘But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APView image in fullscreen‘But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways.’Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APOpinionMohammed bin SalmanSaudi Arabia is learning the hard way: they can’t count on Trump for protectionMohamad BazziAfter Houthis escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the US turned down calls from MBS for helpMon 19 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTShareFor years, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince,Mohammed bin Salman, cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump and his son-in-law and former top adviser, Jared Kushner. The prince understood the president’s transactional approach to power: he signed deals to buy billions of dollars’ worth of US weapons and invested billions more in American companies.Days after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, Prince Mohammed pledged to expand investment and trade with the USby $600bnover four years. He later promised to increase that investment to nearly $1tn, although it wasn’t entirely clear how Saudi Arabia would manage to plough a sum close to the kingdom’sentire annual GDPinto a foreign economy over a few years.On a visit to Washington last November, Prince Mohammed sealed a defense cooperation agreement with the US and signed a deal for the monarchy to buy dozens of F-35 stealth fighter jets, America’s most advanced warplane.Behind this flurry of deal-making, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler expected the US to defend the kingdom if it was attacked, as Washington has done in the past. But Prince Mohammed, like the leaders of other Arab petrostates who have investedbillions of dollarsto appease Trump, is learning a hard lesson: never count on Trump to protect you.Over the summer, Trump’s war against Iran rekindled a years-long conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi militia in Yemen. Last month, as the Houthis intensified their attacks on Saudi territory and the kingdom’s Yemeni allies, the prince called Trumpmultiple timesin September, urging him to launch US airstrikes against the Houthis, who are allied with Iran.For now, Trump has resisted appeals from Prince Mohammed to drag American forces into the Houthi-Saudi battle – one of the best foreign policy decisions of an otherwise disastrous second term.But the conflict is escalating in dangerous ways. On 10 October, the Houthisfired a cruise missileat the international airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, killing at least 13 people and wounding more than 300.After that attack, when reporters in Washington asked Trump whether he would be more willing to order US strikes against Yemeni rebels, he was non-committal. “We may. We’re going to look at it,” he said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision.”The Houthi-Saudi conflagration is the latest illustration of Trump’s decision to attack Iran spiraling into an unpredictable regional conflict, as Middle East experts and someUS intelligence officialswarned would happen. It also reveals that Saudi Arabia and other Arab Gulf countries can’t rely on the Trump administration to protect them, even after they have spent tens of billions of dollars to buy American weapons and build US bases – some of which were decimated byIranian attacksover the past seven months.Trump’s resistance to ordering US attacks on the Houthis has been particularly embarrassing for Prince Mohammed.Billions of dollarsin Saudi investments have been directed into Kushner’s private equity firm and the president’s family business, the Trump Organization.
