If I get loud and pitch up the register, people go: “You did a bit of it then!”After this long, it all blurs into one, but certain moments stick in the mind, like sushi being served off a guy’s naked chest. Or the guy who stuck an entire whisk in his mouth. Or the time someone got their pet snake out and it pooed all over the dinner table. One of the most notorious clips is the “What a sad little life, Jane” rant. There’s not much you can add to that, but I was quite pleased with my “Doggy bag, anyone?” line. In terms of horrific dishes, there’s been quite a lot of roadkill.‘It brings people together’: Global hit Come Dine With Me celebrates 20 yearsRead moreThe longevity of it is bonkers. I assumed it would be one and done. It would’ve been beyond my comprehension that 21 years later, I’d be doing the same job. I think the appeal is about people and their houses. We all have a fascination for where other people live and how they feed themselves. The magic for me is this enormously diverse range of people sitting around the same table.It’s nicely paid but the beauty of it has been a steady income over a long period. We’re closing in on 2,500 episodes. That’s a lot of shouting! Apparently, humans change all their cells every seven years, so I’ve had three entire bodies while doing this and we’re just about to crack into the next.Come Dine With Me is available for streaming onchannel4.comExplore more on these topicsCome Dine With MeHow we madeTelevisionFood TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickening | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: As we witness the endless indignities these grieving families have endured in the six decades since the mining disaster, it is impossible not to turn red with rage
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: As we witness the endless indignities these grieving families have endured in the six decades since the mining disaster, it is impossible not to turn red with rage
Content: The scene at Aberfan, Glamorgan, after a mountain of pit waste slid down on to Pantglas junior school and a row of housing, killing 116 children and 28 adults.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenThe scene at Aberfan, Glamorgan, after a mountain of pit waste slid down on to Pantglas junior school and a row of housing, killing 116 children and 28 adults.Photograph: PATV reviewTelevision & radioReviewAberfan: The Village That Fought Back review – the contempt they have faced to get justice is sickeningAs we witness the endless indignities these grieving families have endured in the six decades since the mining disaster, it is impossible not to turn red with rageLucy ManganMon 19 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’d like to have known her that bit longer, really. Those eight years went very, very quickly. I loved the child. I lost her. And that seemed to me to be the end of everything really, when she’d gone.”Ray Lee, now 90, lost his daughter Anne on 21 October 1966. It was the day her primary school, along with several surrounding houses, in Aberfan was engulfed by an estimated 100,000 tonnes of slurry from one of the colliery spoil tips that overshadowed the Welsh mining village. Anne was one of 116 children killed, alongside 28 adults.View image in fullscreen‘It seemed to be the end of everything’ … Ray Lee, who lost his daughter Anne in the disaster.Photograph: BBC Studios/Mei WilliamsGaynor Madgwick (nee Minett) was in the same school and was the same age as Anne when the disaster struck, but she was catapulted back to the far wall by the initial impact and, although severely injured, survived. Her grandfather dug her out. When she asked her father that evening, in hospital, where her brother and sister were, he told her they had both gone to heaven.Marlene Gerlach remembers screaming and screaming for her three children across the unrecognisable school site. They all survived. The guilt has never left her.Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back devotes the first quarter of its run time to these stories. Even when the focus of a programme is slightly elsewhere – and this hour-long film attends to the underacknowledged aftermath and the sickening behaviour of the National Coal Board and the government of the day – it must be done. It remains unthinkable, inhumane not to. The suffering lives on and so does the duty to bear witness to it.It also throws into even starker relief the astonishing, appalling reactions of the NCB and the ministers, including and especially the secretary of state for Wales, George Thomas, who failed to stand up to the board and its chairman Sir Alf Robens, whose contemptuous attitude towards the village and its unfathomable grief was evident from day one, the Friday, when he went ahead with his installation ceremony as the first chancellor of the new University of Surrey instead of travelling immediately to Wales. He got there on Saturday evening instead. From the foot alone we may infer the anti-Hercules.The waste heap had been built on top of several springs that made it inherently unstable. The coal board denied knowledge of them, saying they had been covered long before they took over responsibility for the tips. The tribunal that was set up to inquire into the causes of the tragedy found evidence that the NCB knew that this and other tips around the village were, in contravention of all guidelines, built over multiple water sources, and in its report detailed many other failings in the “terrifying tale of bungling ineptitude”. It laid the blame firmly with the NCB but no further action against it was taken.View image in fullscreenGaynor Madgwick, who was severely injured but survived, lost her brother and sister in the mining disaster.Photograph: BBC Studios/Mei WilliamsFurther indignities were caused to the stricken villagers, powerfully evoked in this restrained documentary by well-chosen memories from its interviewees. Gaynor remembers her father sitting puce with rage every evening in his chair as the NCB continued to fight liability for the deaths and deny the (expensive) need to remove the tips. “He said it was murder, every day.” Her mother was on Valium and moved through the days “like a zombie”.The Aberfan Disaster Fund had received charitable donations from more than 50,000 members of the public. When the NCB finally agreed to remove the tip, it demanded £250,000 from the fund towards the cost. The fund – left unprotected by the Charity Commission that should have prevented such a payment – handed over £150,000 and work began.When the time came for disbursing funds to the intended recipients, the Commission offered £500 a household – if the parents could prove they had been close to the dead child.The people of Aberfan fought back, and back, and back and back. They formed committees, wrote letters, visited Thomas’s offices in London (and emptied a bag of slurry on to the floor – “He was our minister but he was a coward”) and remained unbowed by the rebuffs and by the condescension and contempt with which they were treated. Release of government material from the time under the “30-year rule” in 1997 shows how deep it ran. The sense of betrayal felt in 1966 – especially from a Labour government and a Labour-nationalised coal board – was confirmed and renewed. The newly elected Blair government returned the money. Ten years later, the new Welsh Assembly adjusted the payment for inflation and added £2m to the pot.Ray went on to have two more children. “It did help a lot that all the love we wanted to give to Anne and we couldn’t, we could give to them.”Nobody was ever held to personal account or punished for the disaster. Sixty years on, with Hillsborough, Grenfell and so many more national disgraces behind us, it is hard to feel that there are not many more catastrophes to come.Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionAberfan disasterreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review – sublime wonders from the Great Wave to that heroic, eternal peak | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduring
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduring
Content: Mount Fuji is the truth … Under the Wave off Kanagawa, 1830-1833, AKA The Great Wave.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection, on deposit at The National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo. Photo by Norihiro UenoView image in fullscreenMount Fuji is the truth … Under the Wave off Kanagawa, 1830-1833, AKA The Great Wave.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection, on deposit at The National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo. Photo by Norihiro UenoArt and designReviewHokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji review – sublime wonders from the Great Wave to that heroic, eternal peakDulwich Picture Gallery, LondonWith its helpless rowers, naked river-crossers and snowbound tea-drinkers, this magnificent series is a warning to put your faith in the essential and enduringJonathan JonesMon 19 Oct 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe giant wave’s foaming white summit spreads high over the heads of the helpless souls huddled in their long thin boats, crackling into what look like many sharp claws. It is a monster, hungry to swallow human flesh. But beyond it, over the wild water, soothing the terror of those in peril on the sea, is Mount Fuji – a solid cone of hope and solace. The mountain, not the wave, is the hero of this masterpiece, as it is the hero of all the prints in Dulwich Picture Gallery’s stunning exhibition – the first in Britain – of the complete Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.When you look closely here at three different, superb impressions of Katsushika Hokusai’s Under the Wave off Kanagawa – widely known today as the Great Wave – your mental picture of this icon is shattered by the violent onrush of water. In reproductions the wave just seems beautiful, an elegant curl of blue and white. But here, to paraphrase Tennyson, it is nature, blue in tooth and claw. The wretched people are the emotional heart of the picture, their imminent risk of drowning its whole point.double quotation markHokusai delights in epic shifts of perspectiveThe wave is out of control, murderous, yet it is also a passing moment, shows Hokusai, a devout Buddhist. He offers this consolation: the wave looks as vast as a mountain but soon it will break and be gone. Meanwhile the sacred peak of Mount Fuji endures eternally. It can’t be hurt by the ephemeral dragon of saltwater. Put your faith in the essential, enduring things beyond the nightmare of mutable appearances and you will find inner peace. The wave is an illusion. Mount Fuji is the truth.View image in fullscreenEjiri in Suruga Province, 1830-1833, Katsushika Hokusai.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection. Photo by Norihiro UenoYet that colossal truth is easy to forget as we move around it, pass it by, catch sight of it in the everyday rush – a distant peak on the horizon. On a city bridge people swarm without looking up from under their round hats at the mountain in the distance. A man working bare-chested, wiry and worn, has no time to study the far-off peak as he concentrates on making a barrel.Hokusai delights in epic shifts of perspective, seeing Mount Fuji as an apparently small insignificant object while filling the foreground with distracting action. You do a double take at Fuji from Kanaya on the Tōkaidō Highway. Dressed people sit on the shoulders of nude men who are almost completely submerged in turbulent blue and white water, while others are sealed inside boxlike palanquins to be carried too over the water by crushed bearers gasping for air. It is no illusion. This crossing point over the Ōi River was a key military point for the city of Edo, so no bridges were allowed to be built there. Travellers had to be borne across.No one in this strange scene looks at Mount Fuji. And yet not to notice the mountain is to miss out on something very big indeed. In another image a ferryman does pay attention to it, set against a golden evening sky under a layer of deep blue, as he rows people across another river: some passengers also look, while others do not. Other people – tourists as well as pilgrims – seek out the views, like Hokusai himself, delighting in nature and its mystery, even in extreme conditions: one group has trekked to a country teahouse in winter to view Mount Fuji in the snow. They’re rewarded with an icy scene of devastating beauty, picked out in golden white and intense deep blue.View image in fullscreenSekiya Village on the Sumida River, 1830-1833, by Katsushika Hokusai.Photograph: Courtesy the Iuchi Collection. Photo by Norihiro UenoHokusai’s miracle colour, Prussian blue, came from Europe, where it was first used in the early 18th century. His knowledge of perspective is also coloured by European art. But the traffic of influence went both ways. It is impossible to overstate the centrality of Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji to the birth of modernism. It is the first global masterpiece. When Hokusai created this series of closely linked prints in the early 1830s he reinvented landscape art as a conceptual and symbolic meditation that would thrill and inspire artists across the world.It’s no secret that Van Gogh, Whistler and other members of the European avant garde collected and emulated Japanese woodblock prints. But I hadn’t realised how deeply Cézanne was in his debt: the French painter’s repeated efforts to paintMont Sainte-Victoirein Provence, fragmenting its rocky mass into shards of perception to see its true nature and discover its secret, echo Hokusai’s journey around Mount Fuji. So do Monet’s obsessive paintings of Rouen Cathedral, a haystack and his (very Zen) waterlily garden. Hokusai taught these Frenchmen to see landscape as metaphysical.That we make icons of separate images from this series – and not just the wave – is understandable. Here is Ejiri Station, Province of Suruga, Hokusai’s depiction of people holding on to their hats as the sky fills with blown paper in an unexpected turn in the weather. Jeff Wall famously restaged it in his photographA Sudden Gust of Wind (After Hokusai).What a timeless artist Hokusai is, influencing Monet and Cézanne and still inspiring remakes today. But it distorts his meaning if we focus on his separate images without seeing them as part of one long meditation on Mount Fuji. By itself, Hokusai’s gust of wind may seem an image of crisis and impermanence. But Mount Fuji is in the background: the godlike summit that shows us there’s a serenity beyond the chaos.Hokusai: Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, is atDulwich Picture Gallery, London, from 20 October to 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designArtHokusaiDulwich Picture GalleryExhibitionsModernismreviewsShareReuse this content

title: With nine new recordings of Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony this year alone, which rises above the rest? | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?
Content: Apocalyptic visions: The London Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Sir Antonio Pappano with Maria Bengtsson soprano and Noa Beinart contralto perform Mahler’s Symphony No 2, ‘Resurrection’ in the Barbican Hall, London on 18 October 2026.Photograph: Mark AllanView image in fullscreenApocalyptic visions: The London Symphony Orchestra and Chorus conducted by Sir Antonio Pappano with Maria Bengtsson soprano and Noa Beinart contralto perform Mahler’s Symphony No 2, ‘Resurrection’ in the Barbican Hall, London on 18 October 2026.Photograph: Mark AllanClassical musicReviewWith nine new recordings of Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony this year alone, which rises above the rest?The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?Clive PagetMon 19 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs it something in the water? Or is it simply that triumph over adversity sells in today’s uncertain world? Whatever the reason, Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony has already received four major UK performances this year: aseason finale for the BBC Philharmonicin Manchester, a season opener for both theCity of Birmingham Symphony Orchestraandthe London Symphony Orchestra, and an 80th season celebratory concert for thePhilharmonia Orchestra in London. Next month the London City Orchestra perform it in Croydon’s Fairfield Halls.On disc, the field of Mahler 2s is even more crowded. Apple Music Classical currently throws up 222 listings;Presto Music’s search engine returns 260 results, many of them complete recordings to download or buy on CD or vinyl (some of these, of course, are reissues of recognised classic accounts).View image in fullscreenSecond opinions … Gustav Mahler in 1892.Photograph: AlamyThree new recordings of the symphony are out this month alone, which will bring the total released into the UK market to an astonishing nine over just 12 months. The lineup of conductors is certainly impressive – including Kahchun Wong,Simon Rattle, Andris Nelsons, Esa-Pekka Salonen, Donald Runnicles and Paavo Järvi – but is it possible the market has reached saturation point? Or is it that we just can’t get enough of Mahler’s apocalyptic vision and the dopamine fix that accompanies the symphony’s choral finale?The statistics clearly speak for themselves: this year there have been nine Mahler 2s released. By way of comparison, the 5th and the 8th symphonies received just four releases each in 2026; Mahler’s other symphonies even fewer.Mahler wasn’t always popular, of course. For all sorts of reasons, not least the Nazis’ aversion to the composer in general, his works were slow to enter the catalogue. The Second was in fact the first Mahler symphony to be recorded in its entirety when Oskar Fried and a pared-back Berlin State Opera Orchestra committed it to wax cylinders during sessions in 1923 and 1924. Perhaps as few as 40 players were huddled around the acoustic horn, but Fried had been coached by the composer himself for a performance of the work in 1905, and, so, tinny as it sounds today, it carries the imprimatur of authenticity.It was over a decade later thatEugene Ormandyand the Minneapolis Symphony Orchestra made the work’s second recording, captured live in 1935, this time using electrical microphones. Acoustically it was a major leap forward, and thanks to the conductor’s urgency – he’s 12 minutes faster than Fried – it still lands blows today.Sixteen years would pass before Otto Klemperer, who as a young man had known and worked with the composer, stepped into a studio with the Vienna Symphony Orchestra in 1951. His visceral, though boxy sounding, account was followed in 1958 by Mahler’s protege Bruno Walter who recorded the work with the New York Philharmonic. At this point we are talking one or two recordings every decade, a far cry from the current rate of almost one per month.Klemperer’s 1962 HMV stereo version with the Philharmonia Orchestra, capturing the conductor at his most monumental, rightly remains a benchmark recording, one of several made in the 60s that would still sit on most recommended listening lists. Bernstein’s first studio recording with the New York Phil, more urgent and certainly more wilful than his 1983 Deutsche Grammophon effort, appeared in 1963 and has now been lovingly remastered. Fine accounts by Solti and the LSO and Haitink with the Concertgebouw were among half a dozen to appear across the decade, while the 70s saw the likes of Mehta, Abbado and Tennstedt enter the lists.The digital revolution of the 80s produced a slew of new Mahler 2s (including Simon Rattle’s first attempt, which won him and the CBSOa Gramophone award), as well as first appearances on disc for some of the great performances of the past (anyone looking for the frisson of a live event should try Tennstedt’s account captured in 1989 with the London Philharmonic at the Royal Festival Hall).The subsequent transition from expensive studio recordings to the easier option of releasing a live performance, often with patching taken from rehearsals, has become prevalent in recent decades and is partly behind this year’s boom. Indeed, none of these nine new recordings was made in a studio.View image in fullscreenGoosebump raiser … Simon Rattle.Photograph: Andrew Fox/The GuardianSo which to listen to? Streamers today of course can take their pick, dipping into each in turn. But for collectors on a budget, the question of where best to spend your hard-earned cash is a thorny one.Among the frontrunners,Paavo Järvi’s accountwith the Tonhalle-Orchester Zürich (released 30 October on Alpha Classics) packs a considerable creative punch. The production values are hugely impressive: just listen to the orchestra’s pristine articulation of the declamatory opening demisemiquavers on cellos and basses. Järvi’s tempi are sound, and Anna Lucia Richter is a glorious mezzo-soprano soloist. It beats Cristian Măcelaru’s muddy, monochrome version with the Orchestre National de France into a cocked hat (released last month on Naïve). Esa-Pekka Salonen’s San Francisco reading is, as would be expected,supple and clean(on SFS Media) but occasionally breathless speeds temper the drama despite a well-thought-through finale.In the end, experience tells. That’s what makesSimon Rattle’s interpretationwith the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra (released on 2 October on BR Klassik) so rewarding. Forty years on from his CBSO recording for EMI, Rattle is now a more spontaneous and organic beast. Changes of tempo and dynamics feel entirely instinctual without any loss of expressive weight and power. The dramatic arc is secure, but the complex journey from a hero’s graveside to the heavens provides ample opportunities for Rattle to raise goosebumps. Like Järvi, he’s blessed with state-of-the-art engineering.The opening and closing movements are emotional rollercoasters daring the listener to come along for the ride. The inner movements are full of telling detail, such as the unselfconscious Viennese portamenti in the elegant Andante moderato and the reedy pungency conductor and orchestra bring to bear on the slippery scherzo. Scottish mezzo-soprano Beth Taylor is an arresting soloist, and the Bavarian Radio Chorus lift the roof as well as our collective spirits in the finale. One hundred and two years on from Oskar Fried’s pioneering account, Rattle delivers another Mahler 2 for the ages.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicSimon Rattlealbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography review – a rhapsodic show to stop you in your tracks | Photography | The Guardian
description: From a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everyday
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: From a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everyday
Content: Vision of love …  Yip Cheong Fun, Father's Care.Photograph: Yip Cheong Fun, Collection of National Gallery Singapore. © Andrew Yip Weng Kee.View image in fullscreenVision of love …  Yip Cheong Fun, Father's Care.Photograph: Yip Cheong Fun, Collection of National Gallery Singapore. © Andrew Yip Weng Kee.PhotographyReviewLight and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography review – a rhapsodic show to stop you in your tracksTate Modern, LondonFrom a Singapore construction worker to a loincloth-wearing Sri Lankan, this awe-inspiring and truly global exhibition finds epic beauty in the everydayCharlotte JansenMon 19 Oct 2026 09.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdon’t remember the last time I saw such a well-researched and truly globally representative exhibition that doesn’t patronise but quietly makes its case unapologetically, fearlessly and through sheer quality. Apart from being the first retelling of the international, pluralistic pictorialism movement, Tate’s new show allows for some refreshing encounters with unknown works for British audiences – around half of the works included here have never been shown in the UK. The effect is to radically deepen and widen our understanding not only of art history but the human impulses that drive us to make images in the first place.We move seamlessly from the sudden shock of colour in three-colour carbon prints of flowers in a London garden in the 1920s to works born of the photographic salons, circles and clubs of Sydney, Hong Kong and Brazil. Historical moments collide; the epic emerges from the everyday. A man rows home across the Norfolk Broads, another works on a construction site in Singapore. None of it feels out of place. It all belongs. It is all extremely, almost ecclesiastically, beautiful.More than a few times, I stopped in my tracks. I could spend hours with Yip Cheong Fun’s 1940 Father’s Care, a cinematic image of a man holding one child with his hand extended to another, helping them down from the rocky crag they are walking over, on a journey across an open rural landscape somewhere. It’s a touching image of parenthood and the passage of time. Like this show overall, it’s about gestures rather than flashy declarations of feeling.View image in fullscreenNoirish … Han Youngsoo, Untitled 1955.Photograph: Collection of Han Youngsoo FoundationFrom this purist vision of love, we find a more ambiguous exploration in Lionel Wendt’s excruciatingly charged study of a young Sri Lankan man’s loincloth-clad body in the private intimacy of his Colombo studio, revealing hidden desires and truths the camera can’t conceal. It’s beauty as a kind of torture: the same medium that can expose the body to anthropological scrutiny transforms looking into something far more complicated.I’m equally intrigued by a 1955 series by Han Youngsoo: small, noirish works of Korean street scenes that beg for narration from the viewer. Two 1925 bromide prints by Kate Smith show a woman in a flowing pre-Raphaelite style, pausing in a field dense with vegetation and foliage. Its title draws me closer: The Listener. What is she listening to, and what does this photograph want us to hear? It leaves me hovering between the visible and the imagined, its silence and stillness charged with the possibility.View image in fullscreenEthereal … Limb Eung-Sik, Feet 2.Photograph: Limb Eung Sik Photo Archive © Estate of Limb Eung Sik.Limb Eung-sik’s Feet 2 has a similarly ethereal atmosphere: flowing, diaphanous material folds around a dancer’s feet so that they dissolve into light and shadows. Nostalgia and sentimentality are dialled up, but it’s irresistible. If you’re attuned to it, these images suggest that anything – shells, shadows, a faucet, a wilting flower, a fishing net – can become magic, and these pictorialists teach us how to see the world that way.This is not by any means a critical look at pictorialism. Mysteries are left intact, politics are largely left at the door. There’s no attempt to unravel the reductionist pitfalls of pursuing the fantasy of beauty. Some of the educational intrusions feel unnecessary – a timeline of photographic techniques is helpful and interesting but risks putting “art photography” back in the realm of craft, as does a full-scale recreation of a darkroom that you cannot enter. The magic of the darkroom is not that it is a dark room with a bunch of dirty aprons hanging outside. It is the transformation that happens within it: the strange alchemy of chemistry and light, which is already accounted for in abundance in the photographs.But I can forgive these things. There’s genuine care and awe here. It’s a reminder that seeking moments of magic and breathtaking beauty is a human instinct, and we have a right to it. This is an exhibition about things that are universally shared and eternally human, that cannot be destroyed by the politics of a time or place, that survive and thrive. Light and Magic is as intelligent as it is beautiful, as whimsical as it is informative, as rhapsodic as it is real.AtTate Modern, London, until 21 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsPhotographyTate ModernArtreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever? | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtime
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtime
Content: Elizabeth Holmes outside court in San Jose, California, in 2022.Photograph: Amy Osborne/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes outside court in San Jose, California, in 2022.Photograph: Amy Osborne/AFP/Getty ImagesPass notesDocumentary filmsThe reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever?Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s headspinning documentary about Elizabeth Holmes is an unprecedented critical success – even with a three-hour runtimeMon 19 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:The best reviewed film in history.Age:Not even out yet, except in the US and Canada.Appearance:Coming soon to a screen near you.How exciting! What is it?It’s calledYou Can See Everything.Who’s in it?DiCaprio?De Niro? Both?It’s not that kind of film.What’s it about, then?The subject of the documentary isElizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of …Did you say documentary? No thanks.But reviews of this particular documentary have been overwhelmingly favourable!I don’t go to the cinema to learn things.Critics have been unstinting in their praise forNathan Fielderand Lance Oppenheim’s unflinching three-hour examination of the Theranos scandal’s architect and …You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThree hours? Are you kidding?I know that seems long, but the Guardian’s critic called it “a stupefying and gloriously destabilising hall of psychological mirrors, a thrilling once-in-a-lifetime collision of director and subject”. And audiences have so far been undaunted by the long run time – it logged a phenomenal$15m at the box officein its opening weekend in the US and Canada.Meh.And the film has earned an unprecedented Metacritic score of 99/100.Unprecedented?Certainly for a documentary – in fact, you’d have to go back to the2016 drama Moonlightto find a best picture Oscar-winner with the same score.You mean it’s higher thanThe Odyssey?The Odyssey got 88/100.Bigger than Digger?Digger got 46.At the end of the day, Metacritic is just one review aggregator.On Rotten Tomatoes, You Can See Everything has a 99% rating from 117 reviews so far, putting it in contention for the site’s best-rated film of 2026. It’s also effectively the highest rated cinema release ever on Letterboxd.Effectively?With a 4.7/5 score, it’s the fourth-highest reviewed overall, but the three above it are a live Radiohead concert and two TV shows (Band of Brothers and Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood).Where are some of the other highest-rated films in history?Metacritic’s top 10 best-rated films include Citizen Kane (1941), The Leopard (1963), The Conformist (1970) and Tokyo Story (1972).Those movies all have one thing in common: I haven’t seen them.It’s early days, obviously, but You Can See Everything is already 24th on Metacritic’s all-time list.What are some of the worst-rated films?Rotten Tomatoes’ bottom 10 (of films that have received 20 reviews or more) includes: Tom & Jerry: The Forbidden Compass (2025); Left Behind (2014), starring Nicolas Cage; Roberto Benigni’s adaptation of Pinocchio (2002); and Superbabies: Baby Geniuses 2 (2004), which Joanne Kaufman of the Wall Street Journal described as “unspeakably ghastly”.Fortunately, I haven’t seen any of those either.I don’t know where you would even find them.Do say:“The hype is deserved.”Don’t say:“The nachos were excellent.”Explore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsPass notesNathan FielderYou Can See EverythingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US counterculture | Music | The Guardian
description: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview
Author: Garth Cartwright
Headline: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview
Content: ‘I’ve always been a peacenik’ … Ed Sanders, right, with his Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg, pictured in 2003.Photograph: Stephen Chernin/APView image in fullscreen‘I’ve always been a peacenik’ … Ed Sanders, right, with his Fugs bandmate Tuli Kupferberg, pictured in 2003.Photograph: Stephen Chernin/APMusicInterview‘We tried to levitate the Pentagon’: the almost unbelievable life of Ed Sanders, trickster god of the US countercultureGarth CartwrightHe gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interviewMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Charles Manson once wrote me a letter saying, ‘If I was as powerful as you claim then you wouldn’t be here,’” Ed Sanders tells me over a video call, savouring the menace in that sentence.Sanders is an American maverick; a musician, poet, activist, journalist and author whose greatest hit remains his bestselling 1971 book The Family, in which he chronicled the lives, crimes and trials of Manson and his followers. Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview.“I’ve always been a peacenik,” says Sanders. “I got locked in a cell in 1961 for protesting against nuclear armed submarines, and today I’m protesting against the Trumpster. I don’t subscribe to apathy and nihilism.”Aged 87, Sanders is speaking with me as Fugs Film!, a feature-length documentary about the Fugs, the offbeat folk-garage-psych band Sanders initially led from 1964-69, and re-formed in the 1980s, gets its UK premiere this week. “I don’t do many interviews,” he notes. “I’m constantly approached by people requesting them. And often they are wanting access only because I knew Jimi Hendrix and Allen Ginsberg and Andy Warhol and Janis Joplin and …” He shakes his head. “Everybody now wants to make a documentary about someone I once knew.”View image in fullscreen‘We thought we could change the world’ … the Fugs in 1968. Ed Sanders top left, with – left to right – Ken Pine, Tuli Kupferberg, Ken Weaver, Bob Mason, Charles Larkey.Photograph: Courtesy of Ed Sanders ArchiveIndeed, Sanders was a Zelig of the Lower East Side, friendly with Ginsberg (“A great man”), William Burroughs (“Unnerving, brilliant”), a then unknown Jimi Hendrix (“He was trading as Jimmy James. We gave him his first wah-wah pedal. Nice, talented guy”), to name just a few of his associates. In concert, the Fugs shared bills with the Velvet Underground, the Stooges and the Grateful Dead, but the biggest impression was made by a then unknown band who opened for the Fugs in Detroit’s Grande Ballroom in March 1968. “I’d never heard of Sly and the Family Stone,” Sanders recalls. “They came on and aroused the audience to ecstasy. When we came on, everyone was limp, worn out by how high Sly had taken them.”Sanders and his bandmates Tuli Kupferberg and Ken Weaver were rudimentary musicians who fused street theatre and dadaist spectacle with poetry and ramshackle songs. Long-haired, anti-war, pro-drugs and articulate, the Fugs attracted plenty of media attention but never troubled the Top 40 and are relatively little known today, so Fugs Film! allows a fresh look at a band at the heart of a nascent counterculture. Blending archive footage with contemporary interviews, director Chuck Smith’s film focuses on New York when it was a cheap city to live in, and many artists shared the absurdist mentality of the west coast’s “merry prankster” dropout hippie-artists.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to meet the best minds of my generation – and I did’ … Sanders on the cover of Life magazine in 1967.Photograph: Life MagazineInspired by Ginsberg’s epic poem Howl, Sanders had hitchhiked from Kansas to New York City as a teenager. “I wanted to meet ‘the best minds of my generation’, as Allen put it – and I did,” he says. “Both Tuli and I came from the beat poetry scene. We formed the Fugs to blend poetry with rock’n’roll after seeing beat poets dancing to a jukebox playing Martha Reeves and the Vandellas and the Beatles. It seemed an obvious thing to do.”Sanders’ literary leanings meant he also ran the city’s Peace Eye Bookstore and published the cheaply mimeographed zine Fuck You/A Magazine of the Arts, which featured writing by Burroughs, Norman Mailer, Ginsberg and other beat poets such as Gregory Corso.“Fuck You’s motto was ‘total assault on the culture,’” recalls Sanders. “We thought we could change the world with words. I sent copies to Picasso, Beckett, Sartre, Castro and Khrushchev inviting contributions, but none of them replied.” He laughs at his youthful audacity, adding that he did get attention from the NYPD, who attempted to prosecute Sanders for obscenity: Fuck You was frequently, cartoonishly sexual. Sanders was “fighting for free speech alongside the beats and Lenny Bruce,” he says.The musicologist Harry Smith produced the Fugs’ eponymous 1965 debut album for the Folkways label. The band shifted to ESP-Disk, home to free jazz pioneers Albert Ayler and Sun Ra, but neither label had any commercial heft, so Sanders was overjoyed when Jerry Wexler of Atlantic Records – who had helped make Ray Charles a star and was about to do the same with Aretha Franklin and Led Zeppelin – signed the band.Yet on hearing the finished masters, Atlantic dropped them. “Wexler told me the Ertegun brothers [co-founders of Atlantic] found a song called Coca Cola Douche offensive,” Sanders says. “I should have said ‘OK, we’ll leave it off’ but I got all pious about it. A mistake, as it meant we didn’t release an album in 1967, so we missed out on all the attention those Summer of Love albums got.”Given Sanders continually faced censorship, I ask him aboutMacklemore: shortly before we speak, the rapper was booted from Ed Sheeran’s US tour due to his onstage calls for a free Palestine. “There are always people wanting to censor you,” Sanders replies, “and when its a very rich guy who owns the stadiums and doesn’t want people to hear your opinion then, yeah, he can order such. For me, being older, it’s inspiring to see young musicians putting their shoulder to the wheel.”The Fugs survived their spat with Atlantic, joining the roster of Frank Sinatra’s Reprise Records in 1968. Label head Mo Ostin had to play Fugs demos to Sinatra before he could sign them. “Apparently Frank said: ‘I guess you know what you’re doing.’” The label released the terrific Fugs album Tenderness Junction, which includes Exorcising the Evil Spirits from the Pentagon Oct 21, 1967, a recording made at the Fugs-led mass protest at which thousands formed a human chain around the Pentagon and chanted “Out, demons, out!”“The Fugs existed to protest against the American war machine, as much as we did to make music,” says Sanders, “and we understood that spectacle draws attention. So to suggest we were going to try and levitate the Pentagon, well, it might sound ridiculous but it gave a focus to our protest and attracted a lot of attention.”Mailer, who attended the protest, wrote about it in his Pulitzer prize-winning book The Armies of the Night, and the Pentagon protests are now regarded as high points in the anti-Vietnam war movement. “We celebrated the 50th anniversary of the protest in 2017 by forming a human chain around the White House and attempting to levitate it,” says Sanders. “Again, we shouted ‘out, demons, out!’ and, again, nothing happened. Just as the Vietnam war continued for another nine years, Trump is back in the White House.”Did that make Sanders feel defeated? “No,” he replies firmly. “I’m an optimist. We must keep pushing, we can’t give in to despair. While things are terrible in the US right now, I do believe the American people will come to their senses and vote out the Republicans.”Alongside public exorcisms and psychedelic hymns, Fugs albums featured a mishmash of satirical skits, choral music, protest folk, mock country, Hare Krishna chants, Yiddish songs from Kupferberg’s heritage and poems by William Blake, Matthew Arnold and Ginsberg read to music. Their eclecticism can be maddening, though the band’s first two albums are very elemental, more akin to US punk bands such as the Dead Kennedys and the Dead Milkmen in their broad humour and anti-establishment fervour than to their 60s contemporaries. Songs such as Kill for Peace remain relevant today, though I’m Gonna Kill Myself Over Your Dead Body (“if you fuck anybody but me”) leaves a nasty taste.View image in fullscreen‘We existed to protest the American war machine as much as we did to make music’ … Sanders (above ‘for’) and bandmate Ken Weaver on an anti-Vietnam war march in 1967.Photograph: Courtesy of Ed Sanders Archive“Some of the songs we wrote then we probably wouldn’t write now,” says Sanders, today more professorial than hippie in appearance and speech. Other songs celebrated marijuana, amphetamine and LSD: “We advocated for mellow drugs, never hard drugs. We had a guitarist who was a junkie and it messed him up. And we avoided cocaine. Today pot is legal in New York, so that’s one of the battles we fought that we actually won.”In 1968, the Fugs visited Britain for the first time, where they were championed by John Peel, played the Roundhouse in London and visited Stonehenge, not returning until 2011 when Ray Davies invited them to play the Meltdown festival he curated. In between those visits, Sanders, tiring of the workload that leading a band involves, disbanded the Fugs in 1969, released two underwhelming mock-country solo albums, then focused on writing.“I couldn’t believe it when I first heard of these hippies driving stolen dune buggies murdering this famous actress,” says Sanders as to why he determined to investigate Manson’s cult. “So I went to LA and attended the trials and looked at how this guy, fresh out of prison, had managed to have these teenage runaways believe he was some kind of messiah.”‘His ache is real’: Bob Dylan and more on the wild genius of honky-tonk hellraiser Gary StewartRead moreHe reformed the band in 1984 with Kupferberg (who died in 2010 aged 86), occasionally performing and recording. Today, Sanders, long resident in leafy Woodstock, keeps the Fugs going with younger musicians. “I still like to jump about on stage,” he says, “and working with young musicians means they all have other bands, so its not like I have to keep them busy”.Sanders hopes Fugs Film! can inspire others to continue the noble tradition of kicking against the pricks. Fighting that American war machine, he says, “is a constant struggle. A holy struggle. A brilliant struggle. To let the human spirit struggle against the warrior caste.”Fugs Film! is showing at the Barbican, London, on 23 October, as part of theDoc’n Roll film festivalExplore more on these topicsMusicExperimental musicPop and rockMusic documentaryPoetryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ellie Goulding admits error over promoting diamonds from controversial Australian mine | Ellie Goulding | The Guardian
description: Singer ‘mortified’ about wearing diamonds from Argyle mine at centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Singer ‘mortified’ about wearing diamonds from Argyle mine at centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land
Content: Ellie Goulding attended the opening of a Boodles store in London and modelled the brand’s diamond jewellery.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for BoodlesView image in fullscreenEllie Goulding attended the opening of a Boodles store in London and modelled the brand’s diamond jewellery.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for BoodlesEllie GouldingEllie Goulding admits error over promoting diamonds from controversial Australian mineSinger ‘mortified’ about wearing diamonds from Argyle mine at centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous landKevin RawlinsonMon 19 Oct 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe singerEllie Gouldinghas admitted her error at having promoted diamonds at the centre of environmental concerns about Indigenous land in Australia, despite having spent years campaigning on environmental issues – including the effects of mining on ancestral lands.She appeared at a event in London earlier this month for the jewellery brand Boodles, modelling some of its newly acquiredpink diamonds, some of which came from a controversial mine in Western Australia.“Protecting the environment is a cause close to my heart. I always strive to uphold those values. Regretfully, in this instance, I fell short,” said Goulding, who was made an MBE for services to biodiversity and the climate last year. “I was not aware of the concerns surrounding the Argyle mine and I am grateful that it has been brought to my attention.“You will certainly not see me wearing diamonds originating from the Argyle mine again. The Indigenous and local communities affected deserve better. While I am mortified to have made this error in judgment, I am letting this moment serve as a reminder and an opportunity to continue to question the status quo, to learn and do better.”View image in fullscreen‘You will certainly not see me wearing diamonds originating from the Argyle mine again,’ Goulding said.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for BoodlesAs well as serving as a global goodwill ambassador for the UN environment programme, Goulding is an ambassador for the environmental organisation WWF, which said it “takes seriously the environmental impact of mining and the effect it can have on Indigenous and local communities”.The charity added: “Ellie is a passionate advocate for nature and human rights and has championed the rights of Indigenous peoples as a WWF ambassador. We have discussed this issue with Ellie and continue to value her support.”A week before the Boodles event in London, it was announced the firm had bought the Argyle Pink Diamonds brand, as well as its inventory, from the mining firmRio Tinto. A source close to Goulding suggested this timing may have led to the singer falling short of her own environmental values.View image in fullscreenThe Argyle diamond mine in the Kimberley region of Western Australia. Mining ended there in 2020.Photograph: Murray Rayner/Nature Publishing Group/AFP/Getty ImagesAccording to the Daily Mirror, which firstreported the news, the Gelganyem Group, which represents the traditional owners of the land that was mined for the diamonds, has expressed concerns about the state it has been left in by the industrial processes now the mining has ceased.The group told the paper: “Gelganyem chair Kia Dowell, a Gija woman, acknowledges Ellie Goulding’s apology and welcomes her recognition that Indigenous and local communities deserve better. She hopes it helps the public and Rio Tinto shareholders understand what is at stake at Argyle and the standard Rio Tinto’s mine closure must meet.”The paper quoted the organisation’s representative as saying traditional owners wanted “unrestricted access without unresolved risks being left for future generations”, adding thatPfas– or forever chemicals – were one of “several technical issues traditional owners, Gelganyem and independent experts have raised”.Rio Tinto said: “Mining at Argyle inWestern Australiaended in 2020 after 37 years, and we are currently undertaking major mine closure works, including rehabilitation, with long-term monitoring and maintenance to follow. We acknowledge traditional owners as custodians of country. We are continuing to talk to them and their representatives, the Gelganyem Group, about closure, including Pfas.”Boodles has not responded to a request for comment. The Mirror quoted a source close to the firm as saying it was not responsible for the mine itself and adding: “Boodles have bought the last batch of pink diamonds and assets from Rio Tinto including their website and Instagram account. Other jewellers have used pink diamonds in their collections.”Explore more on these topicsEllie GouldingMining (Environment)Indigenous AustraliansRio TintoWestern AustraliaMining (Business)Fashion industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A reclamation’: The Simpsons gives Apu a new voice as actor Sunil Malhotra replaces Hank Azaria | The Simpsons | The Guardian
description: It’s been eight years since the character last spoke. ‘It truly IS his homecoming,’ Malhotra says
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: It’s been eight years since the character last spoke. ‘It truly IS his homecoming,’ Malhotra says
Content: Apu from The Simpsons (left) and actor Sunil Malhotra, who will be the new voice of the longstanding character.Composite: Fox via AP/Albert L Ortega via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenApu from The Simpsons (left) and actor Sunil Malhotra, who will be the new voice of the longstanding character.Composite: Fox via AP/Albert L Ortega via Getty ImagesThe Simpsons‘A reclamation’: The Simpsons gives Apu a new voice as actor Sunil Malhotra replaces Hank AzariaIt’s been eight years since the character last spoke. ‘It truly IS his homecoming,’ Malhotra saysEmma JoyceMon 19 Oct 2026 00.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter years of silent appearances,The Simpsonshas given longstanding character Apu Nahasapeemapetilon a new voice.American actor Sunil Malhotra, who moved to the US from India as a child, made his first appearance on the animated TV show as Apu on Sunday night.It’s been eight years since the character spoke during an episode. Apu was originally voiced by actor Hank Azaria, who – along with the producers of the show – was criticised for the stereotypical and racist portrayal of the character, a convenience store owner.In 2020, after a documentary called The Problem With Apu by Indian American comic Hari Kondabolu, Azaria announced he would no longer voice the character. He later appeared on Dax Shepard’s Armchair Expert podcast, saying “I apologise for my part in creating that and participating in that. Part of me feels like I need to go to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise.”Mr Monopoly vs Mr Burns: The Simpsons take over Monopoly GoRead moreMalhotra’s debut as the new voice of Apu was kept under wraps by The Simpsons’ producers. Reviewers weren’t given advance screeners and non-disclosure agreements were in place for the table read of the episode, Treehouse of Horror Presents: The Revengening.Apu’s wife, Manjula, also has a new voice actor:Janina Gavankar (The Morning Show) is taking on the character, who was previously voiced by Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.Gavankar and Malhotra shared a jointInstagram postdeclaring Apu’s homecoming. “Bringing Apu back feels like a reclamation. It truly IS his homecoming,” wrote Malhotra.According toVariety, Malhotra – whose recent credits include Star Wars: Tales of the Jedi and The Legend of Vox Machina – said he was initially hesitant to take on the role.“When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink,” he said. “But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers’ room look different now?“Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologized for past mistakes? Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn’t disappoint fans?”Malhotra met with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos before accepting the role, saying it was “a deeply collaborative experience”. Selman said Apu and the Nahasapeemapetilon family will appear on The Simpsons more frequently now.“We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, ‘Simpsons-y’ way that allowed him to evolve,” Selman told Variety. “We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role, and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future.”Explore more on these topicsThe SimpsonsTelevisionAnimation on TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Linda Cardellini stars in a Friday the 13th prequel from A24 | Television | The Guardian
description: Prepare for blood and guts galore in Crystal Lake. Plus: David Harewood’s great legal drama, Pierre. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Prepare for blood and guts galore in Crystal Lake. Plus: David Harewood’s great legal drama, Pierre. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Jump-scare beats … Crystal Lake.Photograph: PEACOCK/Sky AtlanticView image in fullscreenJump-scare beats … Crystal Lake.Photograph: PEACOCK/Sky AtlanticTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Linda Cardellini stars in a Friday the 13th prequel from A24Prepare for blood and guts galore in Crystal Lake. Plus: David Harewood’s great legal drama, Pierre. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Phil HarrisonandAlexi DugginsMon 19 Oct 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCrystal Lake9pm, Sky AtlanticA Friday the 13th prequel series produced by A24? Halloween has come early for gorefest fans. Linda Cardellini plays small-town single mother Pam Voorhees, who takes her son Jason (Callum Vinson) to summer camp where she works as a cook. But one day Jason drowns in the lake. Fast forward a year, and Pam is grieving but clings to a shred of hope as her son’s body still hasn’t been found. When two cops knock on her door to tell her they have discovered Jason’s remains, things take a huge turn – and it turns out there’s more to her and Jason’s story than meets the eye … It has all the jump-scare beats of a classic 70s slasher movie and Cardellini gets stuck in – blood, guts and all.Hollie RichardsonJamie’s 20 Minute Meals8pm, Channel 4A cheesy quiche with smoky ham and a punch of mustard, and chicken breasts flambéed in a brandy and onion sauce are the two main courses knocked up by chef Jamie Oliver in real time in this week’s episode. And to wash it all down: a prosecco and pomegranate spritz.HRClickbait Clinic With Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneMeet Marcello, a biohacker who is part of the methylene blue movement – he believes the supplement that’s the colour of Sonic the Hedgehog can boost brain function. So much so, he gets it infused into his body in a car park in Surrey. Evidence for its health benefits is scant and you will be passing bright green pee for days. Dooley investigates.Priya ElanAberfan: The Village That Fought Back9pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenA scandal and a tragedy … eyewitness Margaret Griffiths in Aberfan: The Village That Fought Back.Photograph: BBC Studios/Helen GriffithsAs the 60th anniversary of the horrifying Welsh disaster is marked, it’s customary to remember Aberfan as simply a tragedy. This deeply affecting documentary recasts it as a scandal, too: an inevitable result of long-running industrial negligence. The memories of eyewitnesses are interspersed with the story of the tireless campaign for accountability.Phil HarrisonPierre9pm, Channel 4Poor Pierre (David Harewood): his wife and boss are losing patience with the duty solicitor as he attempts to get to the bottom of young client Michael’s death – all while ignoring his recent diabetes diagnosis. But could some footage on Michael’s phone provide a breakthrough? A solid legal drama, lifted by a suave Harewood.HRWalter Presents: Soviet Jeans12.05am, Channel 4The first episode of this Latvian drama gets a terrestrial airing to mark its launch on Channel 4’s streaming service. It’s the classic love story: hidden-market trade guy falls in love with theatre director gal … and so does a KGB agent. Expect plenty of drama from this tale of Riga in the 70s.Alexi DugginsExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger review – does this sequel measure up to The Time Traveler’s Wife? | Fiction | The Guardian
description: More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-up
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-up
Content: Love and loss on loop … Audrey Niffenegger.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLove and loss on loop … Audrey Niffenegger.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianFictionReviewLife Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger review – does this sequel measure up to The Time Traveler’s Wife?More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-upBeejay SilcoxMon 19 Oct 2026 09.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIrun a reading workshop which begins with a little shelf assessment. Participants bring a stack of books that have shaped who they are: childhood treasures; new revelations; comfort reads. Books they once cherished but have now outgrown. The usual suspect in that category is Audrey Niffenegger’s 2003 novelThe Time Traveler’s Wife. Once smitten, readers now find that time-warped romance cruel. What felt like destiny now feels like a cage. As they explain, I’m always struck by the same thought: Wasn’t it always cruel? Wasn’t that the point?Henry DeTamble and Clare Abshire are a couple caught in a causal loop. The irresolvable question is where that loop starts: does a bright young art student fall in love with a junior librarian, or does a time-travelling man groom a child to become his future wife? If the answer is both – and it has to be – what are we to make of their marriage? Can you truly choose someone if you believe the choice is already made?In the last two decades, The Time Traveler’s Wife has been adapted for Hollywood and HBO and sold more than 9m copies in 40 languages. Readers are still arguing about free will and fate. We may have grown queasier about the bind Clare and Henry are in, but Niffenegger’s novel was never hiding its dark heart. Just look at the original cover: a little girl guarding a pair of men’s shoes. She’s in knee-high socks and Mary Janes, her hands by her sides like a tiny soldier. What is she waiting for? A future or a trap? Is there a difference?There’s now a sequel: Life Out of Order. Will Niffenegger conjure the same unease? To cut a 560-page story short, no. There’s plenty of unease here – political, ecological, technological – but none of it gets under the skin (the ick-factor of The Time Traveler’s Wife is treated like an in-joke). We’re in dystopia territory. Again. And it’s hard to get excited about more literary ruin.double quotation markLife Out of Order is at the mercy of every small gust of an idea, and there are decades’ worth blowing about in hereFor all its temporal complexity, the emotional logic of The Time Traveler’s Wife was simple: for better and worse, it was a love story. The book was a kite with a strong string. The sequel cuts that string. Life Out of Order is at the mercy of every small gust of an idea, and there are decades’ worth of them blowing about in here.Just setting out the cast feels like pinning a murder board: Henry is now dead, though he still pops in from the past, and Clare has raised their daughter, Alba, alone. Alba has inherited her father’s time-travel gene, but has more control. Unbound by the conventions of clock time, Alba is married to Zach in the present, Oliver in the past, and both of them in the future. Oliver is a fellow time-traveller seeking refuge in the past (the future is sticky); Zach is mostly harmless and thinks Oliver is his drinking buddy. Clare is now married to Beck, who makes herself scarce when Henry visits from beyond the grave. Beck is the mother of Isadora, a “menace” of a child who spends her days locked in a basement, for spoilery reasons. Isadora is catalytic – everyone can feel it. Will she bring havoc or salvation? Probably both. Whatever happens, it will involve Alba’s violin and a mouldering yellow house in the outer suburbs of Chicago.View image in fullscreenRose Leslie and Theo James in the TV adaptation of The Time Traveler’s WifePhotograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThere are half a dozen ways – at least – to describe Life Out of Order: as ethical non-monogamy meets the space-time continuum; a study of grief and its manifestations; a cautionary tale about teaching machines to dream; a grim vision of a coming America; a hymn to music and all the ways it salves and saves us; and a fatalist eco-dystopia: what it means to fight for a planet that is assuredly doomed.Niffenegger starts some of these stories, and finishes others. Major characters disappear for hundreds of pages; hundreds of years are leapt in a paragraph or two. We seem to be in a counter-historical version of the US, which mightexplain why everyone from the previous book is acting so strangely. Most of the cast have been recruited by Antifa, until that plotline evaporates. What also vanishes is the genetic science of time travel: “Chrono-displacement”. At the end of The Time Traveler’s Wife, that discovery seemed poised to reshape the world (imagine what it would do to financial markets alone). Here, it’s dispatched with a shrug: “I never hear about time travel anymore,” Zach muses. “There was that big announcement, and then it just – died.”In the end, it’s almost impossible to say whose story this is. Alba is the most likely candidate, but also the least interesting. Where her father grappled with the ethics of time travel – those lurking causal cruelties – Alba mostly does what she does because she’s already done it. Why bother to fret or regret when predestination does the moral work for you? She slips in and out of the plot dropping nuggets of portent, juggling husbands, and fiddling (literally) while the world burns. It feels callous rather than cruel: cold-blooded.That’s the big difference here: heat – something a little more carnal than planetary warming. There was ferocity in Henry and Clare’s love, a hunger that twisted their causal loop into a knot. They adored one another, even though their adoration was selfish; each loved the person they helped to make. Because isn’t that what we all do, in our own quiet and needful ways: create the people we love?Life Out of Order is bereft of hunger. What we have in its place is exhaustion. Who has time for the body when the body politic is rotten? When the very notion of embodiment may be obsolete? Alba is not waiting for a pair of shoes to be filled, she’s waiting for the end of the world. “I have loved time travel and have wished to be done with it,” she tells us on the opening page of Life Out of Order. That feels like the prophecy here.Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger is published by Jonathan Cape (£22). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movement | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin
Author: Tom Sperlinger
Headline: A biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan Goldin
Content: Writer and philosopher Hannah Arendt, who foresaw ‘a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security’.Photograph: Fred Stein Archive/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWriter and philosopher Hannah Arendt, who foresaw ‘a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security’.Photograph: Fred Stein Archive/Getty ImagesPolitics booksReviewAnti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movementA biographer’s affecting account of prominent critics of Zionism, from Hannah Arendt to Nan GoldinTom SperlingerMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Everyone in America – at least as far as I knew – was a Zionist,” recalls Benjamin Moser, “especially but not only if you were Jewish.” A Pulitzer-winning biographer of Susan Sontag, he remembers being brought up short in his 20s, when a friend described Israel as “a bunch of foreigners who had no business in the Middle East” and Zionism as a “terrible mistake”. Moser, who recently turned 50, admits: “I was not even aware that Zionism was controversial.” The shift in perspective culminated in a visit to the occupied territories in 2016, during which he found “the reality of the occupation of Palestine … deranging”.His new book includes 12 portraits of Jewish figures who have opposed Zionism, a movement formed in the late 19th century to advocate for the creation of a homeland for Jewish people in Palestine. It is contentious to oppose Zionism today, but Moser wants contemporary Jewish activists to “feel less alone” by showing that debates about Zionism were once mainstream in Jewish communal life. While around90% of American Jewsnow support Israel’s right to exist as a Jewish state (although fewer identify as Zionists),fewer than 1%belonged to the largest American Zionist organisation in 1914. The first character study is of Rabbi Aaron Samuel Tamares, who thought that Judaism offered a vision of a world beyond the devastating nationalism of the first world war. The book closes with a moving account of the photographer Nan Goldin, who spoke out, at considerable cost, as the assault on Gaza began in 2023 following the October 7th attacks.Many of the protagonists, like Moser, were once committed Zionists. When he was 10, Ronnie Kasrils set up a stall in front of his home in South Africa to sell toys and raise funds for Israel. He was later an anti-apartheid leader who became an ardent anti-Zionist during 27 years living abroad in exile: “Ronnie drives them crazy,” a friend of his tells Moser. “And a lot of it is because he’sso Jewish.”Jacob Israël de Haan, an influential Dutch poet, wrote in 1912: “We want our own Land, our own Language, our own Art.” He was horrified after he relocated to Mandatory Palestine: “Zionism is a beautiful ideal,” he lamented, but it had “fallen into the hands of hustlers”. He was murdered in 1924 by Avraham Tehomi, a 21-year-old member of the Haganah paramilitary organisation, after his increasingly outspoken opposition to the Zionist leadership.double quotation markThe sheer scale of the devastation wreaked on the Palestinians disturbs each of Moser’s subjectsHannah Arendt worked for Youth Aliyah in Paris, supporting refugee children to immigrate to Palestine, after fleeing from Germany herself in 1933. Her orientation changed after the Biltmore Conference in 1942, when some 600 delegates from Zionist organisations gathered in New York. Before Biltmore, some in the movement still imagined a single state rooted in the historically strong relations between Jews, Muslims and Christians in Palestine. The Holocaust sharpened the urgency of the argument for a Jewish state instead, but Arendt warned that this would leave the Arabs with “the choice between voluntary emigration or second-class citizenship”. She foresaw, Moser writes, that “a victory [in the fight for a state] would bring the Jews of Palestine neither peace nor security”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: artist Molly Crabapple, actor Debra Winger and photographer Nan Goldin take part in a pro-Palestinian demonstration outside the New York Stock Exchange in October 2024.Photograph: Molly Crabapple via InstagramMoser’s study includes many instances of despair. The scale of the devastation wreaked on the Palestinians disturbs each of Moser’s subjects, many of whom are demonised or accused of antisemitism “so promiscuously that the word would eventually become meaningless”. After the Occupation of Gaza and the West Bank began in 1967, the lawyer Felicia Langer dedicated her life to representing Palestinians. Her first clients, Sheikh Musa al-Bukhari and his wife, knew their son was in prison: “Nobody would tell them why, but when he had picked up his son’s clothes to wash them, he had found a shirt covered with blood.” Langer came to see “the State of Israel as a criminal enterprise” and emigrated in 1990 because she no longer believed it could be reformed.The Arab-Israeli historian Avi Shlaim, who was born in Iraq, was at the forefront of revising the established Israeli histories of 1948 and describes being “radicalised in the [Israeli State] archives … I didn’t have any revisionist ideas. It was the material I was reading which completely, flatly contradicted the official line.” Shlaim describes the situation today as “utterly bleak”. In 2023 he argued: “For all its sins, Israel has not engaged in genocide.” In 2025 he published a book called Genocide in Gaza.Moser’s focus on individual lives is affecting. He makes no claims to be writing a definitive history and is aware of the Palestinian lives that shadow those of his protagonists but fall outside the scope of this study. There are nonetheless gaps. For example, there is no mention of the Satmar Hasidic movement, an ultra-Orthodox Jewish group that believes it is forbidden to establish a Jewish state before the Messiah’s arrival, showing that anti-Zionism can also be theological and conservative.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEarly in Anti-Zionism, Moser reads his grandfather’s copy of Theodor Herzl’s founding Zionist text, Der Judenstaat, and finds it “disquieting”, at best a fairytale and at worst a profoundly disturbing vision. Moser wonders how his own life might have been different “if I had grown up with the Palestinian story” instead. This beautifully written cri de coeur is inspired by an “exilic vision” of equality, an alternative Jewish tradition, resistant to nationalism and rooted in solidarity with others.Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser is published by 4th Estate.
