title: ‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunion | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In the dazzling archival documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a 1972 cocktail party brings together various creative luminaries as they discuss and debate
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: In the dazzling archival documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a 1972 cocktail party brings together various creative luminaries as they discuss and debate
Content: Aaron Douglas, Jean Blackwell Hutson, Richard Bruce Nugent, Eubie Blake, and Irvin C Miller in Once Upon a Time in Harlem.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenAaron Douglas, Jean Blackwell Hutson, Richard Bruce Nugent, Eubie Blake, and Irvin C Miller in Once Upon a Time in Harlem.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonDocumentary films‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunionIn the dazzling archival documentary Once Upon a Time in Harlem, a 1972 cocktail party brings together various creative luminaries as they discuss and debateAndrew LawrenceMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than a flowering of the arts at the dawn of the 20th century, the Harlem Renaissance marked the breakthrough moment when Black Americans asserted their creative control, defining a culture that had been purpose-built to exclude them. The imprints were all over the Jazz Age – on bookshelves and radio, in flapper dresses and cloche hats, in Hubert Julian’s daring flights and the fractious debates between Marcus Garvey and WEB Du Bois.Once Upon a Time in Harlem review – remarkable Harlem Renaissance documentaryRead moreLike theDavid committeeof the Italian Renaissance or the American Revolution’s Continental Congress, the Harlem Renaissance is one of those moments that makes you wonder: what was itreallylike? The Dark Tower salons? Those Cotton Club nights? The rent parties with all those New Negroes – a heady brew of southern émigrés, Caribbean vanguards and New York lifers – holding forth and hootin’ and hollerin’, high on the fact that they had found one another? Could they appreciate the significance of the moment as they were making it? “I remember being in Brooklyn in the 1990s and seeing various artists around,” says film-maker Liani Greaves, reflecting on her early career working with Tupac on Above the Rim and the director Hype Williams on Biggie music videos. “Brooklyn Moon Cafe was the spot. Sometimes we forget that it is The Now. We’re constantly looking to the next thing, looking outside.”Once Upon a Time in Harlem looks back – to the August day in 1972 when Liani’s grandfather, the prolific and pioneering film-maker William Greaves, threw a cocktail party at Duke Ellington House, invited over the surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance and switched on the cameras. (With Ellington himself too ill to attend, it fell to his sister, Ruth, to play host.) For four hours, these extraordinary partygoers – some seeing one another for the first time in 50 years – reminisced, made merry and reckoned with the Harlem Renaissance’s modern-day legacy. The 100-minute film itself is a time capsule, a cinematic Hall of Mirrors at Versailles in which the Harlem Renaissance gazes back at its own legacy, leaving future generations to unearth, interrogate and work from the reflections they find.It’s the kind of artefact today’s Black creatives should have in their library – for inspiration, for accountability, to ground themselves. But until hard copies are available – “That will exist!” says William’s son, director David Greaves, adding that streaming is still a long way off – audiences will have to catch Once Upon a Time in theaters, as the film opens nationwide this month. “We’ve always imagined people coming in groups, going with their family,” says Liani, a producer on the film. “We want people to be in community, visit with the film, and really experience it in that way.”Following in the tradition of A Great Day in Harlem, the documentary about Art Kane’sstunning photograph of jazz greatsgathered on Harlem stoop, Once Upon a Time is a home movie in every sense. William Greaves – an Actors Studio member alongside Marlon Brando before directing the groundbreaking meta-documentary Symbiopsychotaxiplasm – devoted himself to the project until his death in 2014 at age 87. Greaves kept rolling after the party, through the 80s and 90s. Liani remembers William and his wife, Louise Archambault Greaves, turning up with their cameras to a Harlem Aids walk she was working in the 2000s. Among Liani and David’s inheritances was some 60,000 feet of 16mm film held in storage. “I think they were shooting a lot of events, looking for evidence of the Harlem Renaissance,” Liani says. “But it felt to me that they had kind of lost their way. And just like in Symbiopsychotaxiplasm, he had to kind of step away in order for the film to be great.”So Liani and David kept the focus squarely on the party. They enlisted the help of preservation specialist Bill Brand to restore the 1972 footage, an 18-month process, before sending it off to a finishing house. “They did stuff that we could never have done 50 years ago,” David says. “Color correction, cleaning and also – I’ll be honest – taking hair out of the gate.” The results are visible in the richness, warmth and texture of the footage – the kind of craftsmanship movie-making used to be about.View image in fullscreenThomas Harvey, Ernest Crichlow, William Patterson, Romare Bearden, John Henrick Clarke, Ida Mae Cullen and Louise Patterson.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonAnd then the titans of the Harlem Renaissance start filling the frame: the photographer James Van Der Zee, demurring from an invitation to play Duke’s piano before letting his shockingly nimble fingers wander. Ragtime composer Eubie Blake reeling back to the time the papers misquoted him saying he’d never extend his hand to a white man. (He said he’d never extend itfirst, a distinction that mattered under segregation.) Regina Andrews, the essential librarian and curator, considered whether a Black artist could have worked in isolation while the movement was happening around them. “There was no way not to be caught up,” she says. “You were pulled along.”As the 1972 reunion unfolds, the film scrambles to capture every moment, following the connections and conversations across three rooms. David was part of the six-man crew his father assembled for the shoot, each member having to split their attention between the scene unfolding before them and whatever might be bubbling up somewhere else. There’s a lovely moment when one cameraman catches William slating him on from the edge of a scene, the silent soundman confirming with his eyes as another cameraman crosses the shot. (Syncing the picture to the sound was another puzzle that came together in restoration.)As William strains to impose a bit of film-making order on action already beyond his control, it’s clear he wouldn’t have it any other way, that he’s getting exactly what he wants from this crowd – big personalities, lively crosstalk, a tangible sense of those bygone salons. Partygoers in their 70s and 80s, flashing their modern finery, are stirred to youthful passion when the subjects that once animated them resurface – especially in the one-on-one interviews William Greaves shot with some Renaissance contributors after the party. “My father had them wear the same clothes so they would not be clashing,” David remembers fondly.It’s hard not to be awestruck when the Negro Actors Guild president, Leigh Whipper, drops into his Haile Selassie monologue from the Stalinist film Mission to Moscow, or when the civil rights activist Richard B Moore delivers a perfect recitation of the Claude McKay’s poem If We Must Die on cue. “I always say this is what it looks like when your brain is not on electronics,” Liani says. “I have to imagine many of them were writing with one another, to one another – some by hand, which is a different kind of brain skill. They were brilliant people.”View image in fullscreenLiani Greaves and David Greaves speak onstage.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images for FLCThe Harlem romantics also had a knack for expressing their disagreements with one another in erudite style – polite shade, we call it now. In one meaty scene, the multimedia artist Romare Bearden takes exception to the way artists like him were minimized in the seminal book on the Harlem Renaissance by Nathan Huggins; the Harvard professor is standing across the room, holding it. Huggins, though, does offer a credible defense – arguing that art and music are intrinsically more difficult to translate than the written word. “It is kind of poetic, the way they clap back,” Liani says. “It’s all in love and friendship.”Still, there wasn’t genuine affection for everyone in the room. Apparently, the presence of George Schuyler – the commentator who came up during the Renaissance before turning against progressivism and, later, the civil rights movement – was met with twisted faces and cold shoulders. One barb directed at him was cut out entirely. It speaks to the depth of the disagreements among the Renaissance’s vanguards, and the intensity with which they still cared. “It’s like [Garveyite community organizer] Thomas Harvey said at the end of the film: ‘We were on different roads, but all going toward the same goal,’” David says. “It shows that the Renaissance was not a monolith of thinking.”But the issue that really hung over the party was how the Harlem Renaissance would be remembered. Already, William’s guests were lamenting how the younger generation had moved on to zeitgeistier fare: comic books, funk music, blaxploitation films. David Greaves makes a point of tracking the change his father set out to chronicle in the documentary, moving from James Van Der Zee’s gorgeous black-and-white photographs of the neighborhood in full flower to William’s 70s footage of vacant faces and graffiti-strewn walls.Now those kids are the ones clamoring for respect for their artistic contributions. It shows how quickly times change, and how much Black creatives stand to gain by looking to the past as they take the culture forward. “I often think about this film as a recipe for a renaissance,” Liani says. “If you watch, the [Black Renaissance vanguards] tell you what to do. They talk about the importance of being in community, of being audacious. That’s how you create a moment.“Once Upon a Time in Harlem is out in US cinemas now and in the UK and Australia at a later dateExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after all | Movies | The Guardian
description: After Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEU
Author: Ben Child
Headline: After Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEU
Content: Taking flight … Ben Affleck as Batman in Justice League.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarView image in fullscreenTaking flight … Ben Affleck as Batman in Justice League.Photograph: Warner Bros./AllstarWeek in geekMoviesA Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after allBen ChildAfter Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEUMon 19 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTShareNine years after superhero epic Justice League arrived in cinemas, there ought to be very little left to say about how it all went wrong. Zack Snyder shot the film,Joss Whedonsubstantially rewrote and reshot it, and audiences eventually got to see both men’s versions. Any debate over their relative merits long ago disappeared. Whedon is pretty much cancelled; Snyder has reinvented himself as the writer-director of extremely average ersatz Star Wars movies for Netflix, and an entirely new DC universe is under way that has very little to do with either of them.To a greater or lesser extent, the world has moved on. But Ben Affleck’s latest comments raise an uncomfortable question about whether Snyder’s departure was ever presented honestly.Speaking to Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Affleck, who played Batman, described the Justice League reshoots as the lowest point of his career, but reserved his strongest criticism for the circumstances of Snyder’s departure. The directorstepped away in May 2017, two months after his daughter Autumn killed herself, aged 20, with the public explanation that he needed to be with his family. Affleck, however, alleged that studio Warner Bros had used the tragedy to justify replacing him. “The way in which that was, I thought, used as an excuse was one of the shittiest things I’ve ever seen,” Affleck said. “It was so gross.”In July 2020 another Justice League actor, Ray Fisher (who played Cyborg),accused Whedon of abusive and unprofessional behaviour, prompting WarnerMedia to launch an investigation into the film’s production. In December 2020, the company announcedthe probe had concluded and said that unspecified “remedial action” had been taken. In May 2021, Gal Gadot (who played Wonder Woman) saidWhedon had “threatened her career”during production of the film. Whedondenied both allegations in January 2022, but has been largely absent from Hollywood since.Affleck stressed that much of what he knew about his co-stars’ experiences came secondhand. His reaction was blunt: “Wow. This is about as gross as it gets.” On Snyder eventually releasing his own version (a four-hour-plus extended takethat became a draw for Warner’s fledgling HBO Max streaming platform after a fierce social media campaign by Snyder fans), he added: “That was fucking great. I was really happy for him.”View image in fullscreenFurrow-browed … Zack Snyder.Photograph: Chris Pizzello/Invision/APThis is a story that seems to shift and morph the more time passes. Initially, the baton being passed from Snyder to Whedon was framed as a mercy, though there wererumours as early as February 2018 that Snyder might have been forced out for creative reasons. Now, almost a decade on, the film’s biggest star feels comfortable alleging that Warners used a family death to justify bringing in Whedon, who at the time was one of the biggest names in superhero movies (having overseen Marvel’s early Avengers films), but whose breezy, wisecracking writing style couldn’t have been further from Snyder’s furrow-browed, heavy-metal film-making. Warners had spent years allowing Snyder to turn its superheroes into tormented deities, then developed an urgent concern that none of them knew how to do banter.If what actually happened matters, in 2026, it’s because this was the moment that the DC extended universe (DCEU) really began to enter its death spiral. Snyder had probably already lost the confidence of studio executives after 2016’s Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice tanked with critics, but audiences had still flocked to see that movie to the tune of$874m at the global box office. If a Snyder-led Justice League had reached cinemas in 2017 and proved a hit, it’s not impossible to imagine Warners allowing him to continue his vision for the future of the comic book studio. While the director of Watchmen wasn’t exactly the Kevin Feige of DC, he controlled the general direction of travel as the guy who oversaw its highest-profile ensemble efforts. After Justice League, the DCEU’s films crossed $500m at the worldwide box office only once, with 2018’s Aquaman. Somewhere along the way, the promise that everything was connected had become a warning that you might need to slog through another one.The decline, to be fair, cannot all be blamed on one disastrous handover: the pandemic alone was probably responsible for at least some of the dramatic downturn in the DCEU’s fortunes after 2018. Nor does it follow that Snyder would have necessarily delivered a triumphant decade of superbly interconnected superhero cinema if everyone had simply left him to get on with it. His films could be ponderous, self-important and oddly embarrassed by the possibility that being Superman might occasionally be enjoyable. I’m not sure I even want to visit the alternative universe in which this grand plan actually came to fruition but it seems like a lot of DC fans at the time did.Instead, Batman and Superman discovered themselves trapped in a universe whose supreme beings could create entire galaxies but found it impossible to agree on the appropriate number of jokes. Affleck’s comments bring us back to the human cost of all that studio indecision. Nine years on, DC has built a new universe, but still struggles to explain what happened to the old one.Explore more on these topicsFilmWeek in geekZack SnyderDC ComicsSuperhero moviesBatman v Superman: Dawn of JusticeBen AffleckJoss WhedoncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movie | Comedy films | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most easily rewatched comfort films is an appreciation of a smart, funny and tender ode to fan culture
Author: Rachael Sigee
Headline: The latest in our series of writers detailing their most easily rewatched comfort films is an appreciation of a smart, funny and tender ode to fan culture
Content: Tim Allen, Alan Rickman, Sigourney Weaver and Patrick Breen in Galaxy Quest.Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarView image in fullscreenTim Allen, Alan Rickman, Sigourney Weaver and Patrick Breen in Galaxy Quest.Photograph: Dreamworks Skg/AllstarMy feelgood movieComedy films‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers detailing their most easily rewatched comfort films is an appreciation of a smart, funny and tender ode to fan cultureRachael SigeeMon 19 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“By Grabthar’s hammer, by the sons of Worvan … you shall be avenged.”If you have seen Galaxy Quest, those words may bring you close to tears. They mark the moment when Alan Rickman’s character – a Shakespearean luvvie turned sci-fi sidekick – realises that the ludicrous catchphrase he has reluctantly uttered thousands of times does matter after all.‘A rare indulgence’: why Black Swan is my feelgood movieRead more1999’s Galaxy Quest is such a good sci-fi parody that it was once voted the seventh best Star Trek film of all time … by Star Trek fans. Its genre send-up is effective and affectionate, with gags about underwritten female characters and illogical spaceship design. It is also a genuinely fun space caper: there’s a properly scary baddie, a spaceship chase sequence, a high-jeopardy mission on a foreign planet and not one but two romantic subplots. There are Beryllium spheres and a rock monster and an Omega-13 (whatever that is).Rickman’s character, Alexander Dane, is one of a group of washed-up actors from a cancelled cult 1980s sci-fi show, now reduced to appearing at fan conventions. He’s joined by Sigourney Weaver’s continually objectified Gwen DeMarco (“My TV Guide interview was six paragraphs about my boobs and how they fit into my suit”), Tony Shalhoub’s eternally laid-back (read: stoned) Fred Kwan, Daryl Mitchell as former child star Tommy Webber and the show’s insufferable lead, Tim Allen’s Jason Nesmith, AKA “Commander Peter Quincy Taggart”.When some apparent superfans prove to be actual aliens who have intercepted and misinterpreted the TV episodes as “historical documents”, the show’s cast find themselves beamed up to help defeat a lizard-like warlord named Sarris. It is every sci-fi fan’s dream come true: it was all real, all along.What ensues is a beautiful dismantling of cynicism via a comedy in which everyone is totally committed to the bit. Nowhere is that more true than the aliens in question. The Thermians are squid-like creatures who assume a human form albeit one with some of the most unusual mannerisms ever committed to screen. Their utterly bizarre speech patterns were created by Enrico Colantoni, who plays Thermian leader Mathesar in a performance that should have won him a best supporting actor Oscar: hysterically funny but deeply – ironically for an alien – human.When Mathesar confidently puts his people’s future in the hands of their beloved Galaxy Quest crew, the actors must play their parts for real this time. And of course, in pretending to be something they’re not, they discover who they really are.Author and film-maker David Mamet has called Galaxy Quest a “perfect” movie, and I would agree. It is a film in which every decision – every line delivery, every splatter of space goo – feels like the right one. In particular, there is the most satisfying character arc for a scene-stealing Sam Rockwell as Guy Fleegman, an actor who appeared as “Crewman Number Six” in a single episode of the show and was swiftly killed off. As a result, he spends the entire film terrified he’s about to be offed in reality. Another parody might revel in giving him a stupid death but there is an innate kindness to Galaxy Quest. Instead, Guy is gifted many of the film’s best lines – “Look around you. Can you form some sort of rudimentary lathe?” – and sees himself shift from “glorified extra” to “plucky comic relief”.This is indicative of Galaxy Quest’s determination never to punch down. At its heart, there is a deep respect for fandom in a genre where it is often mocked. It understands the inherently funny visual of punters in homemade alien costumes lined up at the urinals, but it never makes jokes at the expense of those people. Indeed, the film’s climax is a salute to the power of nerdery as Justin Long’s teen superfan Brandon – crushingly dismissed by Jason early on in the film – ultimately saves the day (in between his mum making him take the bins out).You don’t need to be even a casual Trekkie to appreciate Galaxy Quest’s brilliance because, really, it is about the value of storytelling. For the Thermians, Galaxy Quest was literal: they genuinely believed that what they were watching was real. But the lesson is that it doesn’t matter how hammy the acting is, how poundshop the sets look or how ridiculous the lore seems if it means something to you. Galaxy Quest gives you permission to immerse yourself in the culture that you love, even – or especially – if it appears silly and slight to everyone around you. In the words of Commander Taggart, “Never give up! Never surrender!”Galaxy Quest is available on Paramount+ in the US, YouTube in the UK and to rent digitally in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsComedy filmsMy feelgood movieScience fiction and fantasy filmsSigourney WeaverComedyAlan RickmanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: After the Snowmelt review – a fatal disaster in a snowstorm leads to devastating act of remembrance | Movies | The Guardian
description: Yi-Shan Lo returns to Nepal to follow the route of her best friend’s ill-fated hike in a harrowing but cathartic documentary
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Yi-Shan Lo returns to Nepal to follow the route of her best friend’s ill-fated hike in a harrowing but cathartic documentary
Content: The weight of grief … After the Snowmelt.Photograph: courtesy of True StoryView image in fullscreenThe weight of grief … After the Snowmelt.Photograph: courtesy of True StoryMoviesReviewAfter the Snowmelt review – a fatal disaster in a snowstorm leads to devastating act of remembranceYi-Shan Lo returns to Nepal to follow the route of her best friend’s ill-fated hike in a harrowing but cathartic documentaryPhuong LeMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAwork of deep personal reckoning, Yi-Shan Lo’s debut documentary feature opens with closeups of the film-maker’s own footsteps as she trudges through a snowbound landscape. Her jagged movement mirrors the rugged trajectory of the film itself, which grapples with a harrowing tragedy. In 2017, Lo was about to join her best friends Chun and Yueh on their hiking trip acrossNepalwhen she came down with a sudden illness; she decided to stay behind while the other two carried on. Disaster struck: the pair went missing during a heavy snowstorm and were not found for more than 40 days. Yueh survived, but Chun died from lack of food coupled with hypothermia.Struggling to make sense of these events, Lo painstakingly retraces the days leading up to and during her friends’ disappearance. She pores over old text messages, Chun’s diaries and footage captured by the Nepali rescue team. These materials shed some light on the ordeal, as well as the pair’s backgrounds. Diving into her personal archive, Lo recalls her burgeoning friendship with Chun at their Catholic girls’ school, where the latter defiantly resisted the institution’s rigid dress codes. Considering Chun’s efforts to express his non-conforming identity and his use of male pronouns, it is even more devastating that he was repeatedly misgendered in death by various news reports.Revelatory as they might be, these artefacts appear insubstantial next to the weight of grief. In the second half of the film, Lo physically returns to the trail of the fateful trek. As digital screens and paper scraps give way to the vistas of babbling brooks and verdant hills, film-making emerges as a cathartic gesture of remembrance. Through Lo’s lens, the cave where Chun and Yueh took shelter ceases only to be a site of trauma, but a shrine to the memories of their love.After the Snowmelt is on True Story from 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsNepalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ghost in the Cell review – Indonesian prison-slasher-satire contains the most unhinged punch-up in decades | Movies | The Guardian
description: Director Joko Anwar uses horror for social commentary as he skewers corruption and hypocrisy with likable silliness and raucous energy
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Director Joko Anwar uses horror for social commentary as he skewers corruption and hypocrisy with likable silliness and raucous energy
Content: Enjoyable blend of camp and politics … Ghost in the Cell.Photograph: Come and See PicturesView image in fullscreenEnjoyable blend of camp and politics … Ghost in the Cell.Photograph: Come and See PicturesMoviesReviewGhost in the Cell review – Indonesian prison-slasher-satire contains the most unhinged punch-up in decadesDirector Joko Anwar uses horror for social commentary as he skewers corruption and hypocrisy with likable silliness and raucous energyPhil HoadMon 19 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGiven the 2020s horror boom, Indonesia’s prolific Joko Anwar – who has worked more often in that genre than any other – should be better known. Using horror for social commentary, as Anwar has done often in the past, this prison-slasher-satire features the kind of scabrous broadsides against injustice you see in Bong Joon-ho’s films, andPark Chan-wook’s recent No Other Choice. But in skewering the corruption and hypocrisy of the director’s native country, it has its own likable silliness and raucous energy. As the inmates keep saying: this is Indonesia, not Norway!Fitted up for the murder of his boss, who is found gutted and spreadeagled on a ceiling fan, timid investigative journalist Dimas (Endy Arfian) winds up in the slammer. But murder, immediately followed by the flamboyant flaying of the victim, dogs him wherever he goes: the prison hitman assigned to dispose of him is in turn found in the washroom rendered into flesh origami. Charismatic prison refusenik Anggoro (Abimana Aryasatya) takes Dimas under his wing; as the victims stack up, an apparently clairvoyant member of his clique called Six (Yoga Pratama) admits that all of them manifested a red aura, signifying anger, prior to dying.You suspect Anwar himself is no stranger to the old red aura from time to time: from the warden-facilitated drug-dealing network to the separate wing of pampered elitist offenders, his film overspills with droll outrage over Indonesian corruption. Dimas’s exposé of an illegal forestry scheme is what appears to have dislodged the demonic entity that is now attached to him, and feeding off the local abundance of negative energy. But Six figures out that partaking in wholesome activities, like praying and dancing, lowers their chances of being picked off.Little more than a string of showpiece slaughters, Ghost in the Cell’s thin plot is really an excuse for Anwar to reel off his hitlist: he takes aim at cronyism, institutional brutality, private militias, secret mistresses, lapsed political idealism and the general degrading influence of money. But his film kidney-punches even harder when fully disguised and dramatised as comedy. This includes scenes where the aura-obsessed lags take a sudden interest in Qur’anic and twerking classes, and the most unhinged punch-up since John Carpenter’s They Live, during which Anggoro must periodically break into dancing to de-escalate his rage. Dynamically shot by Anwar, this is a very enjoyable blend of grand-guignol camp and political manifesto.Ghost in the Cell is on digital platforms in Australia and the UK from 26 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmThrillersHorror filmsCrime filmsIndonesiaWorld cinemareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Vampire Carnival review – it’s Twilight at the fairground as abs run wild in pointy-toothed tug of war | Movies | The Guardian
description: A mortal twentysomething is caught in a love triangle with two hunky vampire carnival workers in a film with good looks but not much to chew on
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: A mortal twentysomething is caught in a love triangle with two hunky vampire carnival workers in a film with good looks but not much to chew on
Content: Fair enough … Paulina Chávez and Corrado Martini in Vampire CarnivalView image in fullscreenFair enough … Paulina Chávez and Corrado Martini in Vampire CarnivalMoviesReviewVampire Carnival review – it’s Twilight at the fairground as abs run wild in pointy-toothed tug of warA mortal twentysomething is caught in a love triangle with two hunky vampire carnival workers in a film with good looks but not much to chew onPhil HoadMon 19 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Does this whole Edward Cullen act actually work?” A distinctTwilightfeeling is in the air in this initially enlivening vampire flick, with willowy twentysomething mortal Gemma (Nell Verlaque) caught in the middle of a pointy-toothed tug of war between tender Italian hunk Sebastian (Alvise Rigo) and her bad boy ex Eric (Kieron Moore). When she strolls with her friends into a hot vampire carnival, the ab count nearly outdoes the haemoglobin one. But this good-looking whirligig winds up disappointingly disjointed.Gemma is still regrouping after her father’s suicide, an unspecified amount of time earlier. So her mum is relieved when she takes a night off from grieving by checking out the local fair with pals Ryan (Corrado Martini) and Olivia (Pauline Chávez). Absent for many years, creepy Eric has apparently joined the circus, featuring as the ostentatiously self-harming Man Who Feels No Pain. But when Sebastian invites Gemma into the carnival’s orgiastic inner sanctum, she learns they are a coven of bloodsuckers who, under leader Toussaint (Jason Isaac), have a strict no-killing code of conduct. Or, in the case of potential initiates like Gemma, obtaining consent. “No means no,” says immortal softboi Sebastian.As befits any self-respecting ringmasters, directors David Charbonier and Justin Douglas Powell operate with much visual panache. They announce the trio’s entrance into the carnival with a splendid one-shot, tracking them, the denizens and local cop Dan (Cedrick Cooper). Later, they mount a crystalline confrontation between Ryan and Eric in a hall of mirrors. But, as with such stage endeavours, some of the effects are a bit cheesy: the supposedly Dionysian bolthole comes over more like a gastropub on deep-house DJ night. And Isaacs, playing the head vamp like a Rada fetish Gandalf, is at odds with the tone of what was previously a pleasingly downbeat slice of American alt.culturedom.The emphasis on general flamboyant ambience is more detrimental story-wise. In particular, the film vacillates between positioning the increasingly insubordinate Eric as kooky undead loose cannon and genuine tragic antihero, though the charismatic Moore does a lot to tie him into a satisfying, lethal whole. The schism in vampire philosophies is underexplored, and not enough ground is laid for the final reveal about Gemma and Eric’s troubled backstories. To turn Sebastian’s come-on to Gemma on its head, Vampire Carnival is too taken with the illusion instead of the truth.Vampire Carnival is on digital platforms from 30 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsJason IsaacsTwilightreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A vigorous apologist for a cruel emperor’: Is Caryl Churchill’s explosive new play about Trump and his press officers? | Caryl Churchill | The Guardian
description: From Thatcherism to global crisis to an ever-online world, Caryl Churchill has chronicled our race to the abyss. Now she’s written a play about a blond-wigged apologist for an un-named, strongman ruler
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: From Thatcherism to global crisis to an ever-online world, Caryl Churchill has chronicled our race to the abyss. Now she’s written a play about a blond-wigged apologist for an un-named, strongman ruler
Content: Reveals the truth on camera … Kate O’Flynn as press officer Iris in Triumph at the Almeida theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenReveals the truth on camera … Kate O’Flynn as press officer Iris in Triumph at the Almeida theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerCaryl Churchill‘A vigorous apologist for a cruel emperor’: Is Caryl Churchill’s explosive new play about Trump and his press officers?From Thatcherism to global crisis to an ever-online world, she has chronicled our race to the abyss. Now she’s written a play about a blond-wigged voicepiece for an un-named, strongman ruler. Who can she mean?Michael BillingtonMon 19 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 02.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTriumph, which has just opened at London’sAlmeida theatre, is Caryl Churchill’s latest piece of explosive minimalism. Running at just 20 minutes, it skewers contemporary barbarism without mentioning the names of Trump, Putin or any of the other supposedly strong national leaders. It works through historical analogy and is a reminder that Churchill – while “always ahead of the game” in the words of the play’s director, James Macdonald – has in recent years developed a form of elliptical drama for which the apt word might be compressionism.At the heart of Churchill’s new play is an edgy romance between a male journalist and a female press officer who dons a blond wig for her screen appearances and who is a vigorous apologist for a cruel, vindictive, narcissistic emperor.double quotation markInstead of retribution, she is showered with praise as ratings rocket. ‘The people like a strong emperor,’ she is toldAt first she merrily trumpets his more acceptable achievements: pearls imported from Britain, gold from the temples of Gaul, statues erected to his own glory. But through her lover she learns of the monstrosities of the regime she represents – such as prisoners trapped in claustrophobic cages and sawn in half – and reveals the truth on camera.Expecting retribution, she is instead showered with praise as the ratings rocket and she is told: “The people like a strong emperor.” Standing at a lectern backed by imperial purple and speaking in an overtly American accent, Kate O’Flynn shows perfectly the way the authentic human being emerges from the glamorised robot who speaks for power: in James Macdonald’s production she even looks uncannily like the most recent and short-lived White House incumbent, Katie Zacharia.View image in fullscreen‘Brilliantly nailed the Thatcherite ethos’ … Top Girls at the Minerva theatre, Chichester, in 2011.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianSo what is Churchill up to? Since all the crimes perpetrated by the emperor are drawn from Suetonius’s The Twelve Caesars, it is clear that a parallel is being drawn between then and now.Two examples prove the point. When Triumph’s emperor reminds his wife that he has the power of life and death over her, it is a direct echo of Caligula’s threat to a spouse, in Suetonius, that “This beautiful throat will be cut whenever I please”. At another point a fisherman, who has terrified the emperor by presenting him with a giant mullet, finds his face rubbed in it. Having foolishly thanked heaven that it wasn’t a crab, he then finds the emperor ensuring that his features are badly scarred by a giant crustacean: a slice of whimsical sadism from the reign of Tiberius.Lest anyone think that Churchill is overstating the case by linking Roman and contemporary decadence, one has only to look at recent events. We live in a world where the idea oflivestreaming a military execution, although now abandoned, was originally endorsed by President Trump and his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth. We have also seen ICE agents shooting nonviolent protesters, whilefishermen in the Caribbean have been killed by American troopson the totally unproved grounds that they were drug smugglers. Churchill’s point in Triumph is that today governments in the western world not only commit acts of extreme brutality: they also attempt to massage them through skilled media presentation.View image in fullscreenVibrant satire … Gary Oldman and Alfred Molina in Serious Money at the Royal Court, London, in 1987.Photograph: Donald Cooper/AlamyAll this is conveyed in a short, sharp shock of a play that is proof of Churchill’s restless experimentalism. But while she never writes the same play twice, I see a clear division between her earlier and later work. In the 1970s and 80s she wrote a series of momentous plays that used a range of expansive devices to expose the defects of our society. Latterly she has created a number of works in which formal brevity is accompanied by a bleak worldview. That may be an oversimplified view of a complex artist but what I see in the later Churchill is a form of cosmic minimalism.In the earlier period she was clearly animated by the absurdities, inequities and injustices she found in British life. That was evident in Cloud 9,about to be revived by the National Theatreand which I signally failed to understand on its first appearance in 1979. The first half is a very funny exposé of Victorian Anglo-Saxon attitudes in which imperialist supremacy is linked to sexual dominance. “There is something dark about women that threatens what is best in us,” one male colonialist tells another. The second half transports us to the more libertarian sexual relationships of the 1970s but, while Churchill palpably applauds progress, she implies that the old class barriers have by no means disappeared.The play that changed my life: ‘Caryl Churchill’s Cloud 9 had us dancing in the aisles’Read moreThat was even more obvious inTop Girls. Appearing in 1982, it brilliantly nailed the Thatcherite ethos by suggesting that the replication by women of the male success ethic was pointless. It began with the famous dinner-party scene in which five notable women from history were seen as both radical pioneers and social victims. It went on to explore the contradictions of the modern working woman. But the visceral showdown came in the final scene where the striving Maggie Thatcher-worshipping Marlene confronted her working-class sister, Joyce.View image in fullscreenThe nature of identity … Daniel Craig and Michael Gambon in A Number, at the Royal Court in 2002.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWhat was great was Churchill’s understanding of both points of view. Joyce’s sense of deprivation led to a rancorous bitterness while the outwardly successful Marlene was conscious of the dubious bargain she had made in sacrificing her child to her career. As Lesley Manville pointed out when introducing a reshowing of the play on BBC Four, this was one of the great plays of the century. I suspect it will last longer than Churchill’s vibrant satire on the greed-is-good philosophy of the City of London inSerious Money. I loved the play in 1987 but seeing it revived recently by a young company called Mad Spirit I felt that it belonged to its moment. Today, I felt, Churchill would be writing about City jitters, cyber-plots and fears of financial collapse.One of Churchill’s qualities, in fact, is her nimbleness of spirit and ability to respond to the times – even to be way ahead of them.Far Away, which premiered in 2000, was a startling evocation of the threat both of localised fascism and of global crisis. The first scene, in which a niece tells her aunt that she has seen her uncle beating people and bundling them into lorries, has acquired an ugly resonance in an age when the far-right sanctions violence towards immigrants. But the final scene offered a terrifying image of a world at war and of nature absorbed into a cycle of unending destruction. I wondered at the time if there was something determinist about Churchill’s vision of catastrophe. A quarter of a century later I find myself admiring her foresight.The same is true ofA Number, first seen at the Royal Court in 2002 with Michael Gambon and Daniel Craig and revived many times since. In the play a father confronts three of his adult sons: from the cells of one taken into care at the age of four a doctor has created a series of clones. But this was less a play about the ethics of cloning than about the nature of identity. If the first son was disturbed, was it the result of a depressive mother or paternal neglect? If the second cloned son was his physical match but psychological opposite, was that because of scientific skill or a stable environment? In a 60-minute play Churchill was posing fundamental questions that have grown ever more urgent in an age when AI poses a threat to human survival.View image in fullscreenDark visions … Linda Bassett, Deborah Findlay, Kika Markham and June Watson in Churchill’s Escaped Alone at the Royal Court, London, in 2016.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianChurchill’s compressionism was equally apparent inEscaped Alone, from 2016, which showed a group of women amiably chatting in a sunlit garden. While talking of times past, they also relished the benefits of living today: “whole worlds in your pocket,” said one of mobile phones. But in their midst was a septuagenarian Cassandra who offered a vision of global catastrophe: a world of flood, fire, thirst and starvation where 80% of food was diverted to TV studios and “commuters watched breakfast on iPlayer on their way to work”.This strikes me as quintessential Churchill. She is a writer with a strong sense of life’s quotidian pleasures and its unexpected delights. But she is also more alert than most to the possibility, whether from geopolitics, climate crisis or technological advance, that we are speeding towards the abyss. To express this, as she does, in works that get briefer and more concentrated with each year makes her the most pungent theatrical prophet alive today.Triumph is at the Almeida, London, until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsCaryl ChurchillTheatreAlmeida theatreClassics and ancient historyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kevin Bridges review – steamroller standup is a joy but what’s with the £10 cloakroom charge? | Comedy | The Guardian
description: In his tour Here If You Need Me, the comic makes laugh-out-loud look easy with jokes about conjugal argy-bargy, smutty downloads – and a bit of politics
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: In his tour Here If You Need Me, the comic makes laugh-out-loud look easy with jokes about conjugal argy-bargy, smutty downloads – and a bit of politics
Content: Brilliantly blunt … Kevin Bridges.Photograph: Andy HollingworthView image in fullscreenBrilliantly blunt … Kevin Bridges.Photograph: Andy HollingworthComedyReviewKevin Bridges review – steamroller standup is a joy but what’s with the £10 cloakroom charge?Hammersmith Apollo, LondonIn his tour Here If You Need Me, the comic makes laugh-out-loud look easy with jokes about conjugal argy-bargy, smutty downloads – and a bit of politicsBrian LoganMon 19 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs there a better no-frills standup at work today thanKevin Bridges? You’d struggle to find a more unfussily funny demonstration of the art form’s traditional virtues than at the Glaswegian’s new touring set. It’s a consistently laugh-out-loud suite of observational material on subjects comics have addressed since time immemorial: nostalgia, marital dispute, the latest cultural trends – alongside, asBen Eltonused to have it, a little bit of politics, too. Bridges really does have the X factor, and – without him ever seeming to stretch himself – Here If You Need Me is a steamroller 75 minutes of standup.For me, it needed to be, after being hit by a £10 – 10 pounds! – cloakroom charge because my innocuous wee bag (a notebook, a novel, a pair of glasses) was apparently too incendiary to be allowed into the venue. Oh that Bridges would turn his satirical eye on that racket. But the show starts with more obvious targets: Donald Trump, whose “negotiating” techniques our host burlesques in a violent dialogue with his electrician; and Benjamin Netanyahu, pausing before another act of destruction to check out Bridges’ Instagram feed.‘A vigorous apologist for a cruel emperor’: Is Caryl Churchill’s explosive new play about Trump and his press officers?Read moreThat latter bit features in a wider routine on celebs “using their platform” to promote political causes – and the counter-argument that it’s just virtue signalling. In the face of all that – on which he has a witheringly amusing last word – Bridges retreats into less contentious territory. One very droll skit from this father to a young son ribs the newfound milestone of the nursery graduation. Another looks back to his own youth at the dawn of the internet, downloading smutty pictures – and rapidly multiplying viruses – on to “Big Dell”, the family home computer.Maybe this material, which develops into a routine about teaching his ageing mum to use technology, paddles in over-familiar comedic shallows. But Bridges fishes there for a new and pertinent catch, as with the sly reversal that turns a joke about online shopping into a paean for real-world connection (while pretending to do the opposite). Likewise, you could see later material on the Bridges household’s conjugal argy-bargy as old-school ’er-indoors shtick. And so it is. But there’s often more going on, too, some strand of social satire or surprising nuance at play, as per the gag about mansplaining while his wife drives him to the pub.Bridges’ trick is to present, in both form and content, as a traditionally male, no-nonsense standup while delivering punchlines that reveal a cheerfully engaged, open-minded and egalitarian fellow. That’s apparent in his gag about school kids identifying as cats – and all the more so in his belter of a closing set piece, proposing a brilliantly basic solution to the problem of the super-rich (the profiteers from his venue’s cloakroom included, I hope). Authoritative, generous with his amusement at all he surveys and as brilliantly blunt as only the Glasgow-accented can be, Bridges shepherds us through this tour d’horizon of his life and world via laugh after irresistible laugh.Touringuntil 31 MarchExplore more on these topicsComedyKevin BridgesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Michael Kiwanuka: Fudge review – rough and instinctive, but also lush and alive with melody | Music | The Guardian
description: Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion album
Content: A change of tempo … Michael Kiwanuka recording Fudge.Photograph: Jodie CanwellView image in fullscreenA change of tempo … Michael Kiwanuka recording Fudge.Photograph: Jodie CanwellMusicReviewMichael Kiwanuka: Fudge review – rough and instinctive, but also lush and alive with melody(Polydor)Its release delayed by ill health, Kiwanuka’s latest was made in tandem with 2024’s Small Changes – but it’s much more than a mere companion albumAlexis PetridisMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 08.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn November 2024, Michael Kiwanuka released his fourth album,Small Changes, an extremely poised and self-assured piece of work. After three gold albums, a Grammy nomination, a Mercury prize win and the ongoing success ofCold Little Heart, a 2017 single hoisted to virality and million-selling status in the US after its use in TV drama Big Little Lies, Kiwanuka – and his long-term production collaborators Danger Mouse and Inflo – evidently felt confident enough to release a beautiful but wilfully understated album. Recorded in LA, some impressive names lurked in the credits: legendary session musicians including bassist Pino Palladino and the drummer James Gadson, who played on Marvin Gaye’s I Want You and Donald Fagen’s The Nightfly; the similarly legendary R&B producer Jimmy Jam served as organist on three tracks. It attracted the kind of critical praise in which adjectives like “unhurried” and “meditative” figured heavily.But it also wasn’t the whole story. It turned out there was a second album, its songs written – or rather, jammed into existence by Kiwanuka and members of his live band – concurrently with Small Changes. It was made not in LA but in a studio that “looks like a medieval hut” in Southampton. August session musicians and legendary R&B producers were not present during its recording, nor were Danger Mouse and Inflo. Indeed, you could read its opening track,Summer Clothes, as a kind of Dear John letter to both of them (“I’m OK, I found another way … we’ll be back here soon, just not today”).Fudge’s release was announced in 2025, hard on the heels of Small Changes: it was reviewed in a handful of heritage rock magazines. Then it just disappeared from the schedules without explanation, until the end of last month, when Kiwanuka made a statement andgave an interview to the Guardian, explaining that he had a stroke. After months in hospital, he is now in residential care in Hampshire. He is belatedly releasing Fudge, he said, “because I don’t know how long it will be until I can release another record”.It opens with a recording of jazz pianist Chick Corea being interviewed: “You have to be certain what you like, not what you think sounds good to someone else,” he avers. It feels like a bullish, abandon-your-preconceptions-now start, but that perhaps tells you more about the pressures brought to bear on artists in the mid-2020s than the actual contents of Fudge.It’s certainly rougher around the edges than Small Changes – there’s a lot of audible tape hiss, the acoustic Across the Sky starts abruptly in the middle of a chord, as if someone frantically hit the “record” button after Kiwanuka started playing – but it’s by no stretch of the imagination a confounding WTF? gesture destined to baffle Kiwanuka’s audience.View image in fullscreenNever self-indulgent … Michael Kiwanuka and collaborators.Photograph: Jodie CanwellThere’s a pleasingly gritty, live-in-the-studio quality to the performances, but there are also beautiful, impressively luscious string arrangements: there’s a particularly lovely example weaving around the vintage drum machine and Why Can’t We Live Together?-style organ stabs of Love in My Heart. You can probably make out the songs’ origins as jams from the extended codas of Just Another Moment or Stars, where Kiwanuka and his band linger on one endlessly repeated chord sequence, but these moments never smack of noodling self-indulgence. Rather, they feel vivid and alive, the sound changing as they proceed. There’s a lambent melancholy to the organ-driven coda of Steve’s Paradise, a spikiness about Kiwanuka’s guitar soloing at the climax of Stars that chafes against the track’s opulent strings. Indeed, whatever their genesis, the songs here might be melodically stronger than those on Small Changes: whether they’re doleful (as on California) or lovestruck (You Sent Me Flying), the tunes are uniformly memorable.‘Everyone can relate to pain and struggle. So I’m sharing mine’: Michael Kiwanuka on life after his devastating strokeRead moreIndeed, you’re left thinking that Fudge could probably have been released as the new Michael Kiwanuka album, with no explanation of its genesis, without spooking any horses. Certainly, it’s as abundant in the kind of qualities you might have come to expect from its author. Warm and unforced, it occasionally takes on a distinctly lysergic cast – the final minutes of Love in Your Heart are dense with psychedelic guitar effects – and the lyrics are plain-spoken and believable, whether putting a concerned arm around the shoulder of a troubled friend on Drowning in Your Heart or expressing uncertainty about his career, a theme that keeps cropping up, onSing, Stars and Across the Sky.Of course, those songs that ponder Michael Kiwanuka’s future in music take on a slightly different resonance, given what’s happened since he recorded them. But on the evidence of Fudge, you do wonder at the crisis of confidence he describes. It may have had experimental beginnings, but it sounds remarkably like the work of a man who knows exactly what he wants to do. You leave it hoping that he’s able to continue doing it at some point in the not-too-distant future.Fudge is released 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsMusicMichael KiwanukaPop and rockSoulPsychedeliaalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Blue for poor, yellow for posh: the London maps exposing centuries of terrible housing | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: From rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persist
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: From rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persist
Content: Poverty and wealth side by side … a section from Charles Booth’s maps showing Clare Market slum (1898-99) in A Place to Call Home at Senate House, London.Photograph: Charles Booth Archive, courtesy of London School of EconomicsView image in fullscreenPoverty and wealth side by side … a section from Charles Booth’s maps showing Clare Market slum (1898-99) in A Place to Call Home at Senate House, London.Photograph: Charles Booth Archive, courtesy of London School of EconomicsExhibitionsBlue for poor, yellow for posh: the London maps exposing centuries of terrible housingFrom rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persistJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 19 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCharles Booth’spioneering poverty mapsof Victorian London show a vivid colour-coded warren of streets, alleyways and slums tightly packed together. Those marked black and dark blue were classed as being “very poor”, defined by “chronic want”. The light blue ones were poor – “18s to 21s a week for a moderate family”. Pink streets housed those who were “fairly comfortable”, and those where the wealthy lived were marked in yellow.The maps by the British social reformer are the 19th-century equivalent of themodern-day indices of deprivation, which rank every geographic area of the UK by its level of social and economic disadvantage. Comparing the two shows how much has changed in the past 150 years – but also what hasn’t. Historical slums have been cleared away and housing conditions have generally improved, but extreme poverty and extreme wealth continue to live side by side in the capital.Booth’s maps form the backbone of a new exhibition at Senate House library titledA Place to Call Home, which charts the history of housing and poverty in London over the past 200 years. “We may not have the same sort of slums that we used to in Victorian times but there are still issues with living conditions for many people living in rented accommodation,” says academic librarian and curator Mura Ghosh. “These issues are on a continuum – continuity and change underline the whole thinking behind this exhibition.”‘There will still be things people find relatable’ … the ‘crawlers’ of St Giles workhouse, from Street Life in London by John Thomson and Adolphe Smith, 1877.Photograph: Courtesy of Senate House Library, University of LondonA collaboration between the University ofLondonand the London School of Economics (LSE), the exhibition looks at the turbulent timeline of housing over the past two centuries, including wartime and postwar redevelopment, the building of estates and changing housing policy, as well as eviction and squatting. People will be able to view Booth’s maps alongside a laptop displaying the current indices of deprivation, so they can see how conditions in their own postcode have changed over time.The curators have also picked out individual stories from Booth’s notebooks detailing interviews he conducted with ordinary working Londoners, such as a chorus girl working at Drury Lane theatre who talked about how much her tights cost. “We wanted tobring out these stories of individual lives in London because that’s what people can empathise with and feel connected to. They’re talking about a city 140 years ago, but there will still be things people find relatable,” says LSE curator Indy Bhullar.View image in fullscreenSome of the earliest examples of collective tenant resistance … a 1936 handmade issue of the Hampstead Tenant.Photograph: Courtesy of Senate House library, University of LondonOne of the exhibition’s rarest objects is a set of pamphlets from the Hampstead Tenants’ Defence League from 1936-39. Some of the earliest examples of collective tenant resistance, they document protests, rent strikes, opposition to slum clearances and challenges to the local council. “It’s quite a unique piece of history, and also utterly unexpected to find in an academic library,” says Ghosh. “They’re beautifully illustrated, and constructed from homemade paper and staples.”The exhibition shows how the burgeoning collective resistance movement solidified over the subsequent decades. There’s a 1974 squatters’ handbook with practical and legal advice on how to squat, including how to change the locks, do your own plumbing and resist bailiffs.“Collective action, rent strikes and protests, and encouraging people not to feel hopeless about the future – that’s an important message because people often feel like they’re alone in their housing situation,” says Emily Chu, a fellow curator and academic librarian at Senate House library. “The exhibition shows that working together sometimes creates a much bigger impact and a louder voice the government can hear.”Moving towards the present day, there will be audio recordings of interviews with people from St Mungo’s who have experienced homelessness, and discussion of how high rents and poor housing conditions persist into the present day. About 27% of Londonerslive in relative poverty after housing costs are factored in, the highest rate in England, with high rent and housing expenses the primary driver of poverty in the region. London has disproportionately high rates of damp and mould in social housing compared with other English regions – eight of the 10 local authorities in England receiving the highest volume of complaints are in the capital.The curators hope visitors will share their own experiences of this on the comment wall. They also call for groups who are campaigning on housing issues today to keep and donate their materials so the history of housing action can be continued.A Place to Call Home: Poverty and Housing in London is atSenate House library, London, 23 October to 5 March 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsMuseumsSocial historySocial housingLondonHousingSquattingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The fascinating tale of a heart that died twice: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: How did two men who shared the same heart and the same wife end up dying the same way? Plus, inside the beef between ‘the Kennedys of Italy’
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: How did two men who shared the same heart and the same wife end up dying the same way? Plus, inside the beef between ‘the Kennedys of Italy’
Content: Gripping … Karen Kilgariff presents Heart.Photograph: PR HandoutView image in fullscreenGripping … Karen Kilgariff presents Heart.Photograph: PR HandoutBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioThe fascinating tale of a heart that died twice: best podcasts of the weekHow did two men who shared the same heart and the same wife end up dying the same way? Plus, inside the beef between ‘the Kennedys of Italy’Alexi Duggins,Hannah J DaviesandHollie RichardsonMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekHeartThis fascinating series opens with the death of a man from a gunshot wound – and the revelation that this isn’t the first time his heart has stopped beating. It previously belonged to another man who died the same way, and who also had the same wife. Hosted by Karen Kilgariff, what follows is an intriguing eight-part tale that veers between a scientific exploration and a gripping true-crime saga.Alexi DugginsApple, from Monday 19 OctoberInheritance: FiatView image in fullscreenGeared up … Gianni Agnelli and his family are under the spotlight in Inheritance: Fiat.Photograph: 2018 Collection/AlamyAnother series of the slick podcast about powerful business dynasties, and the beef behind the scenes of some of the world’s best-known brands. This time, Sofia Bettiza investigates the Agnelli family, sometimes called “the Kennedys of Italy”, who founded the car giant Fiat and were rocked by the death of their powerful patriarch Gianni.Hannah J DaviesBBC Sounds, all episodes out from Monday 19 OctoberDisclosure: Killer on the WardColin Norris was a Leeds nurse who became known as “the angel of death”, convicted for murdering four elderly patients and attempting to kill two more. But new evidence suggests they weren’t murdered. Louise Shorter investigates, starting with the insulin poisoning of Ethel Hall.Hollie RichardsonWidely available, episodes weeklyThe Playground MurderJournalist Audrey Gillan takes an appropriately delicate approach to the story of a 16-year-old girl murdered by a classmate. Diane Watson died in Glasgow in 1991, but the pain for those who knew her continues. title: A perfect weekend in the Lincolnshire Wolds: wide skies and gentle walks | Lincolnshire holidays | The Guardian
description: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to miss
Author: Phoebe Taplin
Headline: The landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to miss
Content: A footpath through the Lincolnshire Wolds near Somersby.Photograph: Keith Skingle/AlamyView image in fullscreenA footpath through the Lincolnshire Wolds near Somersby.Photograph: Keith Skingle/AlamyA perfect weekend in …Lincolnshire holidaysA perfect weekend in the Lincolnshire Wolds: wide skies and gentle walksThe landscape of rolling hills and chalk valleys that inspired Tennyson is the perfect setting for an autumnal short break. Here’s where to eat, where to stay and what not to missPhoebe TaplinMon 19 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWide skies, gentle footpaths through gold and copper wooded hills, thatched cottages, cosy pubs and quirky shops: the Lincolnshire Wolds have all the ingredients for the perfect autumnal mini break. Victorian poet Alfred Tennyson lived in the village of Somersby for most of his first three decades and the local landscapes echo through his verses. In The Lady of Shalott: “Long fields of barley and of rye / That clothe the wold and meet the sky …”TheLincolnshire Wolds National Landscapecovers an area of 216 sq miles. On its southern boundary, halfway between Lincoln and the coast, the friendly market town ofHorncastlebills itself as the “gateway to the Wolds”. With handsome brick houses, great cafes, a market on Thursdays and Saturdays and decent public transport links, it’s a perfect base for exploring the area.View image in fullscreenThe market town of Horncastle is a good base for exploring the area.Photograph: Jasmine Bryan/AlamyHorncastle overflows with antique shops.Laurence Shaw, with half a century’s knowledge of the trade, runs an elegant wholesaler on the corner of East Street. In an old chapel across the road, theTrinity Centrehas all kinds of ancient treasures piled in fantastical heaps under lancets of Victorian glass: porcelain milkmaids, jelly moulds, cotton reels, teetering piles of teacups and thick vines of jewellery. Round the corner inStanhope Antique Centreyou may find anything from a wooden decoy duck to a roulette wheel between chandeliers and grandfather clocks.By the “Ducks Crossing!” sign opposite Tesco, mallards gather on the reedy River Bain. And in the 13th-centurySt Mary’schurch there are gold angels in the rafters and lines from Tennyson’s poemRing out, wild bellsin stained glass. The newRiverscape Walk, launched last year, will take you past the canal basin, watermill and former leather tanning warehouses.Take a hikeThere are plenty of rewarding walks nearby and you don’t always need a car to reach them. The hourly56 busfrom Lincoln to Skegness stops in Horncastle and, 10 minutes later, in Hagworthingham, a peaceful Wold-edge village. From here, asix-mile loopof undulating lanes and footpaths takes in tiny Somersby, Tennyson’s birthplace, andBag Enderby(which sounds straight out of Tolkien), where St Margaret’s church has an intricate 15th-century font, carved with religious symbols and medieval scenes. Bag Enderby’s -by suffix comes from an Old Norse word for village.From Hagworthingham, you can also stroll throughSnipe Dalesnature reserve, where a 3-metre (10ft) wooden snipe, carved by local sculptor Nigel Sardeson,has just been installed on a wooded bank. The valleys here are fragrant with late meadowsweet and water mint and the trees are full of birdsong, from tiny goldcrests in the conifers to huge buzzards over the oaks. If you have time and energy to spare, theViking Waylong-distance walk – waymarked with horned Viking helmets – runs through Horncastle and the Wolds on its 149-mile journey from Rutland Water to the Humber.View image in fullscreenA steel sculpture along the Viking Way near Woodhall Spa.Photograph: Nick Hatton/AlamyDon’t missIn Horncastle, theJoseph Banks Centremultitasks as a tourist info point, local museum and natural history hub.Banks, a botanist and Horncastle’s most famous inhabitant, sailed with Captain Cook and oversaw the creation of Kew Gardens. The museum courtyard is bright with hydrangeas, which Banks helped introduce into Britain.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Bath, Harrogate … Woodhall?’ A short break in one of the UK’s most forgotten spa townsRead moreThe Edwardian village ofWoodhall Spa, six miles from Horncastle, has wide leafy avenues and smart black-and-white buildings; even the public loos next to the Tory club are half timbered. Nineteenth-century entrepreneurs, digging for coal, found instead a source of mineral-rich water, a magnet for the era’s wellness-seekers. I meander past theDambusters memorialand mural, the thrivingKinema in the Woods, opened in 1922, the nearbyTea HouseandCottage Museum, then back to Horncastle along the sculpture-dotted Viking Way.Where to eatHorncastle’s top lunch spots include the cafe atMyers Bakery, fragrant with spice and yeast, where you can buy Lincolnshire plum loaf. Round the corner, the spacious and welcoming bike-themedPedal and Pawsserves pizzas, salads and cakes.No 8 Coffee Shop, which opened in March 2026, is already popular for inventive hot drinks such as cinnamon-bun matcha and pistachio hot chocolate.Montebello, in the former Angel Inn, serves home-cooked Italian food, whileMagpiesoffers refined white linen and candlelight dining, with dishes such as Grimsby crab linguine or loin of Lincolnshire lamb. Magpies also has rooms, in cottages next to a Tardis-likeguitar shop.View image in fullscreenCoffee and cake at Pedal and Paws.Illustration: Phoebe TaplinWhere to stayThe cheerful, timewornAdmiral Rodney Hotelis right in the middle of Horncastle, with affordable rooms and details you might see in pricier places: speedy wifi, retro radio, Twinings teabags. It offers great veggie breakfast options, fresh fruit and pastries, served in a big glass-walled conservatory with peacock fanlights. Dinner dishes such as pan-fried sea bass with pickled fennel, or sticky date pudding with butterscotch sauce, chicly garnished with edible flowers and micro-herbs, make a celebratory end to days spent hiking through the Wolds.Getting there and aroundThe56 busheads to Horncastle from Lincoln bus station hourly and takes 50 minutes. The less frequent30 bustakes 10 minutes longer and winds through warm-stoned villages. Local buses include thenew B617from Horncastle to Woodhall Spa. The coast is 20 miles away, on a bus with top-deck views across the Wolds.Accommodation was provided by theAdmiral Rodney,doubles from around £100, room only.
