title: Gurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol | Indian food and drink | The Guardian
description: These snacks are easy to turn into a more substantial supper
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: These snacks are easy to turn into a more substantial supper
Content: Gurdeep Loyal’s masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.View image in fullscreenGurdeep Loyal’s masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambol.Photograph: Dan Jones/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Thea Hudson.Quick and easyIndian food and drinkGurdeep Loyal’s quick and easy recipe for masala chickpea-parsnip fritters with coconut sambolTasty, spicy fritters to dip into coconut sambol as a snack or treat, or serve with avocado or egg for a more substantial supperGurdeep LoyalMon 19 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThese warmly spiced fritters are inspired by the tikki-chaat carts found all over India, which sizzle fresh chickpea, potato or lentil patties on hot-plates until crisp, then slather them with chutneys. The coconut sambol ushers forth the flavours of south India – coconut, mustard seeds and lime; add a teaspoon of tamarind paste to increase the tartness, if you like. A good dollop of yoghurt is a must, and a fried egg or avocado on the side turns these fritters into a satisfying supper.Masala chickpea and parsnip fritters with coconut sambolPrep10 minCook30 minServes2-360g red chillies(about 4 large ones)5tbsp vegetable oil,plus extra for frying4 garlic cloves, peeled and crushed65g desiccated coconut2tsp black mustard seeds1½tsp fine sea salt2tbsp brown sugar2tbsp tomato pureeJuice and grated zest of 1 largelime, plus 1 lime extra, cut into wedges, to serve400g tinchickpeas, drained2 largeparsnips, peeled and grated2tspgarammasala2tsp coriander seeds, crushed100g ricotta3tbsp plain flour1tbsp baking powder15g fresh coriander, finely chopped, plus extra to serveYoghurt, to serveFried egg or avocado, to serve (optional)In a small blender, blitz the chillies, four tablespoons of vegetable oil and two crushed garlic cloves to make a smooth paste.Toast the coconut and mustard seeds in a small frying pan over a medium heat for one to two minutes, until they take on a little colour. Pour in the chilli paste with 100ml water, then cook for four to five minutes, until much of the water has evaporated and the paste begins to darken. Add a teaspoon of fine salt, the brown sugar, tomato puree, lime juice and zest, then cook for another two minutes, until you have a thick sambol. Empty into a bowl and leave to cool.Blitz the chickpeas and the remaining tablespoon of vegetable oil to a coarse paste in a blender or food processor. Put this in a large bowl with the grated parsnips, the remaining two crushed garlic cloves, the garam masala, crushed coriander seeds, ricotta, plain flour, baking powder, fresh coriander and a half-teaspoon of salt. Mix together using your hands until fully combined, then shape into six large patties, about 4-5cm wide and 1½cm thick.Heat a little vegetable oil in a nonstick frying pan, then cook the fritters in batches over medium heat for seven to eight minutes, flipping occasionally, until golden brown on both sides. Serve warm with a dollop of yoghurt, a generous spoon of coconut sambol and a fried egg or avocado, if you like. Garnish with fresh coriander and a wedge of lime.Explore more on these topicsIndian food and drinkQuick and easyFoodCurryMain courseSnacksVegetablesBeans, pulses and legumesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Spaghetti with lentils, and aubergine veggie-balls: Jacob Kenedy’s autumn pasta recipes | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: They’re vegetarian and full of complex, savoury flavours
Author: Jacob Kenedy
Headline: They’re vegetarian and full of complex, savoury flavours
Content: Jacob Kenedy’s lentils and spaghetti.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.View image in fullscreenJacob Kenedy’s lentils and spaghetti.Photograph: Phoebe Pearson/The Guardian. Food styling: Rosie Reynolds. Prop styling: Florence Blair. Food styling assistant: Stevie Taylor.Italian food and drinkSpaghetti with lentils, and aubergine veggie-balls: Jacob Kenedy’s autumn pasta recipesA deliciously humble lentil and spaghetti dish, and a meat-free riff on meatball pasta made with aubergine veggie-ballsJacob KenedyMon 19 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome plant-based pasta dishes are light, bright and summery –pesto genovese, tomato sauce,aglio e olio– but some have an umami and complexity that is normally associated with more carnal pleasures. Here are two.Pastawith lentils is a firm personal and family favourite – my mum and I make this dish whenever we fancy something really comforting, and the earthiness of the lentils plays against grassy olive oil and parsley, and the texture of the pasta. Truecucina povera– a humble meal, and deliciously so. Veggie-balls are also great things.Polpette(normally translated as meatballs) is just balls (of anything pulped), after all. They can be made of white fish, oily fish or vegetables. I particularly love courgette for its bright, green, fresh flavour, and, above all, rich, velvety, chocolatey aubergine. Of course, you can eat them on their own, but I also love them through pasta, as a vegetarian riff on spaghetti and meatballs.Lentils and spaghetti (pictured top)As I write this, my mum is just as alive and at least as vital as she was when she used to make this dish for me, but, for some reason, this is now a dish I make more often, and for her. I adore it, but every time I have offered it to an Italian they look at me as though I have just insulted their mother. Don’t ask me why; people can be as inexplicable as this dish is delicious. You can add some chilli (dried or fresh) when you fry the garlic, if you like, but I prefer this comfortingly bland and without pep.Prep5 minCook55 minServes4For the lentils (can be made ahead)180g small brown lentils, such as castelluccio or puy2 bay leavesWhen ready to eat400g dried spaghetti– this is also good withbigoli, ditali/ditalini, farfalle, garganelli, linguine, mafaldine, orecchiette, pappardelle or tagliatelleSea salt4 garlic cloves, peeled and chopped5 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil4 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley leaves50g butter, or 3 tbsp more extra-virgin olive oil60gparmesan, suitable for vegetarians, grated (optional)Put the lentils into a small saucepan with the bay leaves and about 500ml water. Bring them to a simmer and cook until completely tender and mushy – about 45 minutes; noal dentehere – adding water so the lentils and water are level at the end of cooking.Cook the pasta according to packet instructions in abundant, well-salted water (10g per litre).Meanwhile, fry the garlic in a saucepan in half the oil over a medium heat until golden, no darker. Add the lentils and a splash of pasta water, then bring to the boil.Drain the pasta a minute or so moreal dentethan you like to eat it, reserving some of the cooking water. Put the drained pasta in the lentil pan, add the parsley, the remaining two and a half tablespoons of oil and the butter (or three more tablespoons of oil), then stir or toss over a high heat until the pasta is asal denteas you like, and the sauce is thickened by pasta starch and mostly emulsified; you may need to add more pasta cooking water as you go. Serve immediately, with or without cheese.Aubergine veggie-balls and pastaView image in fullscreenJacob Kenedy’s aubergine veggie-balls and pasta.The Italian wordpolpette(usually translated as “meatballs”) in fact encompasses any balls of minced or pulped vegetables, fish or meat. They could be made from beef or pork or chicken or veal, or aubergines or courgettes or pulses, or bread or greens, or white fish or salted fish or oily fish or prawns: if you can pulp it, you canpolpetteit.Prep15 minDrain1 hrCook2 hrServes4For the sauce (can be made ahead)2 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil1 small pinch chilli flakes(optional)800g chopped tomatoes(if fresh, keep their skins and seeds and chop finely; if canned, this is 2 cans)Sea salt and black pepperFor the veggie balls (can be made ahead)2 large aubergines(total weight 1kg)1 egg, lightly beaten100g parmesan, suitable for vegetarians, grated, or pecorino romano,100g dried breadcrumbs2 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley leaves1 tbsp chopped mint leaves1 tbsp chopped basil leaves1 garlic clove, peeled and crushedSea salt and black pepperAbout 40g plain flourOlive oil, for fryingWhen ready to eat400g dried spaghetti– this is also good withbucatini, cavatelli, fusilli, linguine, mafaldine, penne or spaghettini1 quantity simple tomato sauce(see below and method)3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil12 basil leaves80g pecorino romano, suitable for vegetarians, gratedFor the sauce, heat a saucepan over a medium heat, not until smoking, but until you think something might sizzle. Add the garlic and oil and fry until the garlic slices just barely start to colour at the edges. Add the chilli flakes if using, then straight after, the tomatoes.Season with salt and pepper and simmer, stirring often, over a low heat, until slightly thickened and with oil rising to the top – 20–30 minutes. Taste carefully for seasoning.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Prick the aubergines and roast them for one hour until completely tender. Cool until safe to handle, then peel them. Drain the peeled flesh in a colander under a weight for an hour or so (or, if you’re in a rush, lay it in a long sausage shape in a clean tea towel, then wring it dry). You should end up with roughly 230g drained aubergine.Chop it finely, put in a bowl and mix in the egg, cheese, crumbs, herbs and garlic, and season to taste. Form into walnut-sized balls and coat in the flour.Fry the veggie balls in the oil until cooked through and nicely golden brown. You can choose either to deep-fry them, in oil not more than one-third of your chosen pan’s depth, for safety reasons, at 180C for four minutes; or shallow-fry them in oil 1cm deep, turning every couple of minutes to cook on all sides. Drain and leave to cool on kitchen paper.Cook the pasta according to the packet instructions in abundant, well-salted water (10g per litre).Meanwhile, reheat the tomato sauce in a wide pan over a medium heat. Add the veggie balls and simmer, stirring occasionally, for five to 10 minutes. Drain the pasta and set it in a large wide bowl.At the last moment, stir the oil and basil into the sauce and pour the sauce and aubergine balls over the pasta. At the table, toss the sauce gently into the pasta and serve on warmed plates with a little pecorino atop.This is an edited extract from Pasta Tricolore: Recipes in Green, White and Red by Jacob Kenedy, published by Bloomsbury at £18.99.
